‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:02:43 UTC
21:02:43 KST

Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported from Sweden.
Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country after Brexit came to an end.
An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has effectively been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated.
“I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow the suddenly homeless can get help.
“All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity.
His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has already deported 458 British people after rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state.
The situation persists despite promises from opposition parties now on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency.
“I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says.
“Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?”
Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened.
Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane.
The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings.
In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks.
There is also a bright yellow envelope handed to him by the captain before disembarking which he opens for the first time.
One is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. The other says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected.
Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case.
They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported.
“It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said.
“They said we think that if we don’t detain you you will abscond from Sweden because you are not co-operating.
“For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.” He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no.
He asked if he could drive back to the UK “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said ‘no, the decision has been made’”.
Before Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism.
After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement.
Campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued to a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas, who had been in the country for 21 years.
A 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was also ordered to leave after 25 years while another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, was deported in January.
The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position had infected decision-making relating to Britons there before Brexit, a cohort with special protection.
Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses.
“When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said.
“Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.”
Jane Golding, chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU.
“This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says.
“This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds.
She also points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement.
“Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding.

- Ukrainian medics from the 1st Separate Medical Battalion traveled to Sweden to share casualty evacuation methods with the Swedish Armed Forces' Life Guards regiment.
- The visit included the first trip abroad for MAUL, a Ukrainian-built ground robot used to evacuate wounded soldiers from areas too dangerous for people or vehicles.
Combat medics from Ukraine’s 1st Separate Medical Battalion traveled to Sweden last week to share their experience evacuating wounded soldiers under drone threat, meeting with medical personnel from the Swedish Armed Forces’ Life Guards regiment, according to a Life Guards post and a LinkedIn account from the Ukrainian company that built the ground robot involved in the exchange.
The Ukrainian unit has developed methods for reaching wounded soldiers inside what both sides call the kill zone, the stretch of ground close to the front line where drones and other weapons from both armies can strike. One method uses unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs, remote-controlled robots that can retrieve casualties from areas where sending a person or a vehicle would be too dangerous.
“I grunden handlar det om att rädda liv. Ju fler människor vi kan evakuera på ett säkert sätt, desto fler överlever,” said Asan Charuhov, commander of the 1st Separate Medical Battalion, according to the Life Guards post. The quote translates roughly to: it comes down to saving lives, and the more people who can be evacuated safely, the more survive.
Charuhov said in the same post that some of the casualties his unit evacuated by UGV would likely not have survived evacuation by any other method, and that each mission is planned around factors including the severity of the injury, the terrain and conditions at the site.
The ground robot involved in the exchange, called MAUL, was built by the Ukrainian company AIDronesUA. Kostyantyn Hushcha, the company’s CEO, said on LinkedIn that the trip marked MAUL’s first trip outside Ukraine, and that Swedish personnel used the visit to learn about the platform’s role in casualty evacuation and the broader experience of using ground robots in combat conditions.
During the visit, the Ukrainian team met General Michael Claesson, commander-in-chief of the Swedish Armed Forces, who thanked the servicemembers for sharing knowledge that Sweden can use to strengthen its own defenses, according to the Life Guards.
The Life Guards, formally Livgardet or IB 1, is one of the oldest military regiments in the world. The exchange took place as Sweden, a NATO member since 2024, continues building ties with Ukrainian units that have accumulated years of frontline experience against drone-heavy Russian tactics.

High testosterone is linked to “loss chasing” behavior after setbacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:00:45 UTC
21:00:45 KST

A recent study suggests that while a person’s baseline testosterone levels do not directly determine how many risks they take, the hormone may influence how their body processes the outcomes of past decisions. By measuring sweat on the skin during a gambling game, scientists found evidence that testosterone alters how men respond to the bodily sensations that follow wins and losses. These findings were published in Psychoneuroendocrinology.
To understand how people navigate uncertainty, scientists often rely on a computer program called the Iowa Gambling Task. In this game, players choose cards from four decks to win virtual money. Two decks offer large payouts but come with massive penalties, making them risky and unprofitable in the long run. The other two decks offer smaller payouts but smaller penalties, making them the safer, winning strategy. Players do not know these rules in advance and must learn them through trial and error.
Past research has shown that our bodies often figure out the rules of the game before our conscious minds do. For example, a 1997 study showed that people generate unconscious bodily warning signals, measured through subtle increases in skin sweat, just before reaching for a risky deck. This phenomenon is known as the Somatic Marker Hypothesis, which proposes that these physical “gut feelings” help guide our decision-making.
Scientists later started exploring what biological factors might alter these gut feelings. A 2011 study indicated that people with higher levels of testosterone made riskier choices on the Iowa Gambling Task, suggesting the hormone might play a role. However, a 2026 meta-analysis covered by PsyPost evaluated dozens of previous experiments and found that testosterone has no reliable direct link to general risk-taking.
Because broad evidence for a direct link between testosterone and risky behavior remained weak, researchers began asking a different question. They wondered if the hormone instead works behind the scenes by altering how the body processes rewards, punishments, and those subtle gut feelings.
“This study is part of a larger research project investigating the relationship between hormones and decision-making,” study author Félix Duplessis-Marcotte, a doctoral candidate in neuropsychology at the Université du Québec à Montréal, told PsyPost. “The main study was recently published in Scientific Reports on the association between stress-induced cortisol (a hormone involved in the stress response) and decision-making.” Duplessis-Marcotte conducted the study alongside Marie-France Marin.
“As for testosterone, recent meta-analyses suggest that testosterone is not simply associated with people being more or less risk-taking overall,” he added. “That raised a different question: rather than asking whether testosterone relates to decision-making, what if it influences how people make decisions?”
To investigate this, the scientists recruited 55 young adults, consisting of 27 women and 28 men. At the start of the laboratory session, the participants provided saliva samples so the research team could measure their baseline testosterone levels. Each participant was then asked to complete 100 rounds of the Iowa Gambling Task on a computer.
As the participants played the game, the researchers continuously measured their electrodermal activity. This involves placing sensors on the hand to detect minute changes in sweat gland activity, which serves as an indicator of physiological arousal. The scientists separated these physical responses into two categories. Anticipatory responses were recorded in the seconds just before a participant selected a card, while feedback responses were recorded in the seconds immediately after the participant saw whether they won or lost money.
When analyzing the results, the scientists found that baseline testosterone levels were not associated with general risk-taking. Participants with high testosterone did not simply pick from the risky decks more often than those with low testosterone. This aligns with recent research suggesting the hormone does not act as a simple volume dial for risky behavior.
The research team also looked at the anticipatory sweat responses. In men, these physical warning signals grew stronger before picking from a risky deck as the game progressed, and these signals were associated with their upcoming choices. Women in the study tended to show fewer differences in physical arousal before safe versus risky choices, and they maintained a steady level of risk-taking throughout the game. However, a person’s testosterone level did not alter these anticipatory gut feelings or change how those feelings related to their choices.
Instead, the researchers found that testosterone was associated with how participants physically reacted to the outcomes of their decisions. When men saw the results of their card draws, their subsequent choices were influenced by a combination of their testosterone levels and their bodily responses to that feedback. For men with lower testosterone levels, a stronger physical reaction to an outcome was followed by a decrease in risk-taking on the next turn.
For men with higher testosterone levels, the opposite pattern emerged. A stronger physical reaction to a win or loss was followed by an increase in risk-taking on the subsequent draw. The hormone appeared to alter the motivational meaning of their physical arousal, turning a bodily signal that usually promotes caution into one that encourages risk. This specific relationship between testosterone, feedback-related sweat responses, and subsequent choices was not observed in the women studied.
“The main takeaway is that testosterone may not make people generally more risk-taking,” Duplessis-Marcotte said. “More broadly, these findings add to growing evidence that testosterone’s role in human behavior is more nuanced than the popular stereotype that it simply increases risk-taking.”
“Rather than directly driving risky behavior, testosterone may be associated with some of the affective and physiological processes through which people learn from previous experiences when making decisions,” he explained.
Beyond those moment-to-moment physical reactions, the scientists also noticed a broader behavioral trend related to testosterone following financial losses. Across both men and women, those with lower testosterone levels tended to switch to a safer deck after losing money. Those with higher testosterone levels showed persistent risk-taking after losses, a pattern that resembles “loss chasing” in gambling. They seemed less sensitive to the negative consequences of their choices.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that testosterone does not drive general risk-taking but instead influences how individuals respond to decision feedback. However, that previous study administered artificial doses of testosterone to men experiencing severe energy deficits, whereas the new research measured natural hormone levels in both men and women.
Additionally, a 2025 study covered by PsyPost similarly found no overall link between testosterone and risk-taking, though it primarily evaluated the effects of an acute hormone dose on financial lottery choices in men rather than natural levels during a card game.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “Our findings should be viewed as evidence of a subtle association rather than a large behavioral effect,” Duplessis-Marcotte noted. “It is important to note that this study is correlational in nature: no variables were experimentally manipulated, and all results can therefore not be interpreted in causal terms.”
“Also, we investigated decision-making with a single gambling task in a controlled lab-based setting,” he continued. “It is possible, and likely, that our results may be different if it was conducted in a social context (e.g., making decisions while being watched by someone), and using a different decision-making task.” Additionally, the measurements of sweat on the skin only indicate the intensity of a person’s physical arousal, not whether the emotion they felt was positive or negative. Future studies might use brain wave recordings to better understand the specific emotions tied to these choices.
Another detail to note is that the sample size was relatively small when the data was divided into groups based on both sex and hormone levels. The researchers also only measured baseline testosterone at the start of the study.
“I think the field should move beyond treating testosterone as a fixed trait measured once in the laboratory and instead examine its dynamic relationship with behavior,” Duplessis-Marcotte said. “Testosterone changes in response to social interactions, competition, and other contextual factors, so its association with decision-making may be strongest when we measure those real-time fluctuations.”
“Future studies combining repeated hormone measurements with physiological signals and more ecologically valid decision-making tasks could help clarify when and how testosterone influences the decision process,” he added.
The study, “Testosterone is associated with affective feedback processing in ambiguous decision-making,” was authored by Félix Duplessis-Marcotte, Valentin Magnon, and Marie-France Marin.

Rabies concerns grow in the US – but it’s unclear if there’s an increase of the fatal disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:00:15 UTC
21:00:15 KST

Recent unusual incidents involving humans and rabid animals and a subsequent Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advisory have prompted concerns about rabies, but it’s not clear if there has actually been an increase in cases of the deadly disease in the United States, experts say.
In recent months, rabid beavers have attacked three people in Maryland, and hundreds of people were exposed to goats with rabies at a petting zoo in North Carolina, according to news reports. The CDC issued a health advisory on 10 September “in response to recent reports of increases in human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals”.
Despite the uncertainty over whether people encountered rabid animals or simply were worried that they did, the increased news coverage and greater awareness of the disease is a good thing, experts suggested.
“Any time that the subject gets good coverage and people can learn a little bit about how they can be safe, I think that is a win for public health,” said Zak Mertz, CEO of the New England Wildlife Center.
Hundreds of people used to die annually in the United States from rabies, but measures like vaccines and animal control programs have led to fewer than 10 people typically dying each year from the diseases, according to the CDC.
Still, from July to August, the federal agency received 17% more rabies-related inquiries, including reports of mass exposure events, as compared with the same period last year. The agency also received reports from state health departments of increased administration of post-exposure prophylaxis treatments after a possible rabies exposure.
In July, a wild skunk entered a baby goats’ pen at a farm in Harmony, North Carolina, CNN reported. Months later, hundreds of people interacted with the goats, at least some of which had rabies. Local health departments then monitored those humans, and hundreds received prophylaxis treatment. There have not been reports of any related deaths.
In Maryland, a 13-year-old was swimming at a state park when a beaver attacked him. The boy survived but had to have three surgeries to his chest and hands to repair nerve damage.
When asked if there was a common cause for such incidents, Meghan Davis, an associate professor of environmental health and engineering at Johns Hopkins University said: “I think what we are seeing is a little bit of bad luck.”
The goats had not been old enough to be vaccinated. Beavers rarely get rabies.
Despite all the scientific advancements, people do still occasionally die from rabies.
In 2011, Tonji Durant’s sister, Ivy, called her local animal control office in South Carolina to inform them of bats in her home. The local officials did not provide her with guidance on what she should do to protect herself, such as getting a medical assessment, Durant, a retired CDC epidemiologist, said.
Months later, she developed flu-like symptoms, Durant said. Only then did providers administer a rabies test, which came back positive, but after symptoms develop, there is little doctors can do.
“The older you get, the more you miss your siblings,” said Durant, who thinks her sister’s death was preventable. “Communication is really critical. Clinicians working with state and local health departments; communities working with state and local health departments.”
If a person is worried that they potentially had contact with a rabid animal, they should contact the state or their healthcare provider, Mertz said.
Those who have been bitten by a potentially rabid animal should wash the wound thoroughly and immediately seek medical attention, Davis said.
“Don’t wait; seek help,” she said.
It’s also important for people to ensure that their pets’ vaccinations are up to date.
“Because [rabies] has largely been under control,” Davis said, “it doesn’t always reach the public eye.”

How to make the perfect apfelschmarrn – recipe | Felicity Cloake's how to cook the perfect …
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:00:15 UTC
21:00:15 KST

Schmarrn, or schmarren, Anja Dunk writes, is “peasant food at its best: filling, simple and comforting”. The usual English translation, pancake, a dish we generally associate with delicate desserts is, I think, somewhat misleading; schmarren, as it’s also spelled, bears very little resemblance to a thin, lacy crepe, and instead sits somewhere between our own plump, rich Shrove Tuesday numbers and a batter pudding. Indeed, you’ll find it on the sweets section of restaurant and cafe menus, but in Germany, Dunk reports in her book Strudel, Noodles and Dumplings, it “passes as a main meal, not dessert, because it is very filling and not particularly sweet in flavour”, and also, I suspect, because “it takes 10 minutes to make from start to finish” and is therefore a brilliantly quick supper. (“Quite frankly,” she adds,” as a mother, I find this recipe a godsend.”)
Austro-Hungarian in origin, it’s eaten in both Germany and Austria, and there are many variations, including kaiserschmarren (studded with rum-soaked raisins), savoury potato schmarren, semolina schmarren and bread schmarren, though fruit, often apples, but also stone fruit or berries, seems to be the most common pairing. Whether you’re serving this as a main course (it goes very well with sausages) or afterwards, it’s a very handy addition to the repertoire, especially when paired with soured cream or ice-cream.
The batter
All the batters I try are made with the same basic ingredients: eggs, flour and milk. Where this differs from a standard pancake, or indeed a batter pudding, though, is that the whites are whisked and then folded into the batter, to give a kind of souffle effect that prevents this undeniably hearty dish tipping over into full-scale heaviness. That said, the ratios of each ingredient are of course important. Alfons Schuhbeck’s recipe in The German Cookbook includes more than twice as much flour as almost every other recipe I try, and more milk, too, yielding a flat, dense result that, while tasty, lacks the lightness of the others. Ernest R Schulz of Larchmont, NY, who sent his recipe to the New York Times in 1980 in outraged response to food editor Craig Claiborne’s description of a kaiserschmarren as a rolled crepe, is the only one to use a similar quantity of milk to flour, which makes for a very liquid batter that’s deliciously smooth to eat, but difficult to turn in the pan.
My testers express a marked preference for the more egg-heavy recipes from Dunk and the Discover SüdTirol website, which prove lighter and fluffier, and have a richer flavour; the latter uses an equal proportion of milk and cream, which is even nicer, though if you don’t have cream in the house, just add more milk. There’s also the question of how hard to beat those egg whites – Dunk goes for stiff, Schuhbeck for soft and Hinnerk von Bargen, author of the Culinary Institute of America’s Street Foods book, for medium peaks. I find the stiffer the meringue, the harder it is to incorporate evenly, and the more air it seems to lose in the pan, so I’ve gone for a soft, creamy foam.
The flavourings
As Dunk makes clear, this is not an especially sweet dish; most recipes use barely a teaspoon of sugar, though Schuhbeck and von Bargen are both a little more generous. Judge your audience and sweeten accordingly, bearing in mind that it will be dusted with icing sugar before serving.
Though you can leave it at that, as Schulz did (one must sadly assume, as he was 70 when he sent in his recipe, that he is probably no longer with us), most people add a little something extra. Vanilla is common – whether in the form of vanilla sugar, fresh seeds or extract – as is lemon zest. Schuhbeck adds cinnamon and rum and von Bargen kirschwasser, all of which are excellent combinations, though I’ve stuck with the zest and saved the cinnamon for the topping.
The fruit
Both Schultz and von Bargen serve the apples in compote form alongside the schmarrn, which works well, but it’s even nicer (and far quicker) to incorporate them into the pancake – any eating variety will do (cooking apples will break down and dilute the batter, so are better stewed and served as an accompaniment). I don’t think there’s any need to remove the peel, whatever shape you’re cutting them into; you can grate the apples, as Dunk does, or cut them into small pieces, as in the SüdTirol recipe, but we all like them best in Schuhbeck’s slightly chunkier wedges, which look prettier and make the fruit feel more like the star of the show. Arranging them on top of the batter, as he suggests, rather than folding them in, gives them the chance to caramelise slightly, too.
Some recipes, including Dunk and Schulz’s, incorporate raisins as well, which, though an apparently controversial addition, are a time-honoured combination with apples. You could substitute another dried fruit, if you like, or leave them out altogether, but those pops of sweetness prove popular in such a plain dish (to make it a kaiserschmarrn, soak them in rum first, as Schulz recommends).
The method
Traditionally, one assumes, this is made on the stovetop, but if you don’t mind turning on the oven, you’ll get a better rise by giving the schmarrn a brief blast of hot air. It will also make life easier; while making the Schultz and von Bargen versions on the stovetop, I realise it’s a very delicate art to achieve a golden, crunchy base on both sides and a fluffy interior all the way through without burning anything. If you’d prefer to use the hob, simply cook the second side in the same manner as the first. Either way, don’t worry if you break the pancake while turning it over; once cooked, it’s then broken into pieces and tossed with sugar to caramelise anyway. (Schuhbeck does this under the grill, but I find it easier to control the browning if I have my eye on the pan).
Almost everyone except for the SüdTirol cooks it in butter, which clearly tastes far superior to their oil. Also – though you might wish to skip this step if you’re making a quick supper – it’s worth browning that butter first, as per Schuhbeck’s recipe; the nutty notes it gives the dish are delicious with the apples.
The topping
A cloud of icing sugar is a must, and we all like Dunk’s idea of turning it into cinnamon sugar instead (as a cinnamon agnostic, I will refrain from suggesting that nutmeg would be even nicer, but it probably would). We also like Dunk’s crunchy flaked almonds, but both are entirely optional. As with the nutmeg, chopped hazelnuts, pecans or walnuts would make a fine substitute for those not concerned with authenticity, and even those who are should know that this can be served with any sort of fruit compote, and is particularly good with plums.
Perfect apfelschmarrn
Prep 10 min
 Cook 15 min
Serves 2-4, depending on appetite
40g butter
  90g flour
  ½ tsp salt
  3 eggs
  75ml milk
  75ml cream (single, whipping or double), or 50ml extra milk
Finely grated zest of ½ unwaxed lemon (optional)
1 tbsp caster sugar
  1 dessert apple
25g raisins, or currants or sultanas (optional)
  1 tbsp icing sugar
  ½ tsp ground cinnamon (optional)
Flaked almonds, to finish (optional)
Melt the butter in a medium ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat, leave to brown to a pale golden colour, then take off the heat – reheating will continue the browning process. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.
Put the flour and salt in a large bowl. Separate the eggs, then put the whites in a large glass or metal bowl and the yolks in a smaller bowl.
Beat the milk and cream, if using, into the egg yolks, then whisk into the flour to make a smooth batter. Stir in the lemon zest.
Beat the egg whites until foamy, then add the caster sugar and whisk to soft, creamy peaks that hold their shape but flop over at the top. Fold a little of the egg-white mix into the batter to loosen it, then fold in the rest.
Cut the apple into thin wedges, and remove and discard the core. Pour two tablespoons of the melted butter into a bowl, put the pan back on a medium heat and, once sizzling, pour in the batter. Arrange the apple slices and raisins, if using, on top, then leave to cook to a rich golden brown underneath. Carefully flip over the pancake (don’t worry if it breaks), then put in the hot oven for five minutes.
Meanwhile, mix the icing sugar with the cinnamon, if using. Use two forks to break the pancake into bite-size pieces. Tip out on to a plate or work surface and put the pan back on a medium-high heat with the reserved melted butter. Add the almonds, if using, and lightly toast, then top with the pieces of pancake and sprinkle with most of the sugar. Toss over the heat to coat, then divide between plates. Sprinkle with the remaining sugar and serve hot.
- 
  Schmarren, schmarrn – however you spell it, please share your wisdom on this homely Germanic mountain favourite. Or do you prefer to enjoy it in the sophisticated coffee houses of Vienna? Sweet or savoury? Fruity or plain? Baked or fried? All tips appreciated!

US environment agency let Bayer pick regulations for destructive weedkiller, documents show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
12:00:14 UTC
21:00:14 KST

The EPA allowed pesticide giant Bayer to pick from a menu of regulation options for the controversial and destructive weedkiller dicamba, newly released internal agency documents show.
The documents provide an unusually clear look into the process of developing pesticide regulations, which is typically done out of public view. It shows in detail how the EPA asked Bayer which regulations it wanted, received a response from Bayer, then put Bayer’s choices into a proposed federal rule.
Dicamba is drift prone and kills vegetation and crops for miles around fields where it is sprayed, and is linked to liver cancer and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Courts have twice ordered it off the market because of its drift problems, but the EPA has re-approved it.
The EPA solicited Bayer’s input on the level of restrictions to limit dicamba volatility and runoff, ranging from more protective to less protective, records released in ongoing litigation over the substance show. The EPA concluded one presentation with a slide entitled “Registrant response needed” which posed the question “Which mitigation option to go forward with?”
Bayer chose the least protective for one regulation, and the middle of three levels of protection for another regulation. It also got one other change it requested into the rule.
Pesticide regulations are typically a negotiation between industry and the EPA, but the exchange that the documents reveal is “crossing a line”, said Nathan Donley, environmental health science director with the Center for Biological Diversity, which is litigating on the issue.
“The EPA is allowing Bayer to choose its preferred measures to limit dicamba’s damage as if it was ordering up a late-night dinner à la carte from Chili’s,” Donley said. “It becomes troublesome when the EPA allows them to regulate themselves by choosing the mitigations.”
The Center for Biological Diversity and the Center for Food Safety brought the lawsuit. The documents come as the EPA has faced criticism for stacking its leadership with industry veterans. The top four toxics office positions at the EPA are held by former chemical industry leaders, including Kyle Kunkler, a former pesticide industry lobbyist who is now a deputy assistant administrator and oversees the pesticides program.
Despite repeated assurances from the EPA that it has put effective protections in place, dicamba drift has damaged millions of acres of farmland and caused damage to orchards, vegetable farms, home gardens, native plants, trees and wildlife refuges across the country since its first approval in 2016. Experts have found dicamba drift damage to be the worst of any herbicide in the history of US agriculture. Still, the current approval provides even fewer protections from dicamba drift and damage than past approvals, the lawsuit alleges.
In a statement to the Guardian, an EPA spokesperson said: “Make no mistake: this is not a compliance failure; it is the regulatory system working exactly as intended.”
“The agency notifies the [pesticide maker] and works with them to identify possible solutions” to risks, the spokesperson wrote. “[Companies] are permitted to submit mitigation ideas that preserve their product’s utility, and EPA also will independently develop its own proposed mitigations. To be explicitly clear: the registrant does not dictate terms.”
During a May 2025 EPA meeting with Bayer, the agency gave Bayer two mitigation choices that would allegedly address dicamba’s high volatility, which is what makes it drift prone. A more restrictive option would have prevented dicamba applications above 85F, and a less restrictive option would allow applications up to 95F, if the acreage treated was reduced.
The EPA also gave Bayer three options for addressing dicamba runoff, documents show. It then concluded the presentation with a solicitation for Bayer to decide.
An EPA manager then wrote in an email that “the next step in the process beyond the [presentation] is getting feedback from the registrants on what mitigation and mitigation implementation option they would like to move forward with”.
Separate documents obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity showed the plan was presented to Nancy Beck, a controversial former lobbyist for the American Chemistry Council who now leads the EPA’s office of chemical safety.
The revelations drew condemnation from “make America healthy again” (Maha) advocate Kelly Ryerson, who said: “It is now undeniable that the EPA remains fully captured by a crooked collection of pesticide company players who so enthusiastically ignore the substantial losses of farmers and the federal courts who mandated a halt to dicamba use.”
Eight days later, a representative from Bayer emailed the EPA: “After discussion with EPA and reviewing these options carefully, Bayer would like to proceed as described below … ”
Bayer chose the less restrictive option for volatility mitigation, which would allow it to be applied at up to 95 degrees as long as the dicamba-treated area would be reduced. Bayer also wanted another option that the EPA had not proposed, emails show. It would allow full-field dicamba treatments at higher temperatures if dicamba was not tank mixed.
The EPA granted both requests, and Bayer’s preferred option for mitigating run off. These were included in the rules proposed a few months later, documents show.
“In return for this egregiousness, I would like the EPA to propose a menu of options to Maha for significantly decreasing our exposure to known carcinogens and endocrine disruptors,” Ryerson added.

Scientists may have solved a 2,000-year-old Dead Sea Scrolls mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:58:13 UTC
20:58:13 KST

Scientists may have solved a 2,000-year-old Dead Sea Scrolls mystery
- Date:
- September 20, 2026
- Source:
- Tel-Aviv University
- Summary:
- Researchers may have solved a long-running mystery surrounding the Dead Sea Scrolls by proposing that the Qumran sect really did use its distinctive 364-day calendar. Its perfectly ordered 52-week system kept holidays on the same weekdays, but it slowly drifted out of sync with the seasons because it was shorter than the true solar year.
- Share:
A longstanding mystery surrounding the Dead Sea Scrolls may have a new explanation. Researchers have debated for decades whether the Qumran sect actually followed its unusual 364-day calendar or whether the system existed mainly as a religious and theoretical ideal.
A study from Tel Aviv University argues that both possibilities may be partly correct. According to the proposed reconstruction, the sect likely used the calendar during its early history, when disagreements over religious dates contributed to its separation from the Jerusalem establishment. Later, however, the system may have been abandoned because of a fundamental astronomical problem and changing political relations with the Hasmonean leadership under Alexander Jannaeus.
The research was conducted by Prof. Eshbal Ratzon of the Department of Jewish Philosophy and the Cohn Institute for the History and Philosophy of Science and Ideas at the Entin Faculty of Humanities. The findings were published in the Tarbiz Quarterly for Jewish Studies.
A Calendar Built Around 52 Perfect Weeks
The Qumran calendar differed sharply from the lunisolar calendar that shaped Jewish religious life during the Second Temple period.
Its year contained exactly 364 days, which can be divided evenly by seven. That produced 52 complete weeks every year and ensured that religious festivals always occurred on the same day of the week.
For members of the Qumran sect, this orderly structure was more than a mathematical convenience. They regarded it as reflecting a perfect divine system.
The calendar also carried political and religious significance. Authorities at the Temple in Jerusalem determined important dates using the prevailing calendar, but the Qumran sect rejected the idea that human leaders should have that power. Its members believed the dates had already been established by God during the Creation of the world and therefore should not be altered by people.
The Hidden Problem With 364 Days
The very feature that made the Qumran calendar so elegant also created a serious practical problem.
A 364-day year is about one day and a quarter shorter than the roughly 365-day astronomical year. That discrepancy seems small at first, but it grows steadily over time.
If the system were followed for twenty years without correction, religious festivals would shift by almost four weeks relative to the seasons. After several decades, a festival associated with spring could eventually fall in winter or even autumn.
That would have been especially troublesome for a community whose religious festivals were closely connected with agriculture, harvests, first fruits, and the seasonal cycle.
The problem can be compared with a clock that loses one minute every day. The error is barely noticeable at first, but after enough time passes, the clock no longer reflects the actual time.
Prof. Ratzon's study suggests that something similar may have happened with the Qumran calendar. Although the system was conceptually elegant and mathematically orderly, it gradually drifted farther away from the natural seasonal cycle it was meant to organize.
Was the Calendar Ever Really Used?
Scholars have offered several explanations for this puzzle over the years.
Some have proposed that the Qumran community periodically inserted additional days or weeks to keep the calendar aligned with the seasons. Others have argued that the 364-day system was never intended for everyday use and functioned only as an idealized religious framework.
Prof. Ratzon argues that the Dead Sea Scrolls do not clearly support either explanation.
Instead, she points to evidence suggesting that the calendar was deeply important to the sect's religious identity and formed a major part of its disagreement with the religious authorities in Jerusalem.
Nearly twenty scrolls discovered at Qumran address calendars and astronomy, an unusually large number that indicates how significant these subjects were to the community.
The Book of Jubilees, one of the important works preserved in the Qumran library, strongly criticizes the prevailing lunar calendar. It presents the 364-day system as the original calendar given to Moses on Mount Sinai.
A Calendar at the Center of a Religious Conflict
Drawing on this evidence, Prof. Ratzon proposes a different historical scenario.
She argues that the Qumran sect actively followed the 364-day calendar during its formative period in the second century BCE. The dispute over how sacred time should be measured may have intensified the sect's conflict with religious leaders in Jerusalem and contributed to its isolation.
But as the decades passed, the growing mismatch between the calendar and the seasons would have become increasingly difficult to ignore.
Political circumstances also changed.
Relations between the Qumran sect and the ruling Hasmonean dynasty improved during the reign of Alexander Jannaeus. He supported a halacha similar to that of the sect and opposed the Pharisaic leadership.
According to the study, this changing political environment may have made it easier for the sect to abandon its previously rigid position and adopt the more practical calendar used at the Temple.
The sect's original calendar did not necessarily disappear from its religious thinking. Instead, it may have survived as an ideal system believed to have been valid during the Creation of the world and potentially destined to return in the End of Days.
A Possible Solution to a Dead Sea Scrolls Mystery
This interpretation could explain why the 364-day calendar occupies such a prominent place in the Qumran writings even though it appears to have vanished from practical historical use.
Prof. Ratzon concludes: "The Qumran calendar has long been regarded as one of the Qumran sect's defining features, but also as one of the most baffling mysteries of the Dead Sea Scrolls. This study proposes an alternative for the seeming contradiction between a functional calendar and a theoretical one. It is quite possible that the calendar was in fact used for a certain period of time, but then, losing its practical role due to both inherent problems and political changes, became a religious ideal and a symbol of identity. This would explain both its centrality in the Qumran scrolls and its gradual disappearance from historical reality."

Israel wipes criminal record of soldier who shot wounded Palestinian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:58:03 UTC
20:58:03 KST

Israel wipes criminal record of soldier who shot wounded Palestinian
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has cleared the criminal record of former IDF soldier Elor Azaria, who was convicted of manslaughter for shooting a wounded and incapacitated Palestinian dead in Hebron in 2016.
The case dates back to 2016, when Azaria, then an IDF sergeant and medic, was filmed shooting alleged knife attacker Abdel Fattah al-Sharif in Hebron’s Tel Rumeida neighborhood.
According to accounts of the incident, al-Sharif and another Palestinian man, Ramzi Aziz al-Tamimi al-Qasrawi, approached an Israeli military post and stabbed an Israeli soldier, lightly injuring him. Qasrawi was subsequently shot and killed by Israeli forces. Al-Sharif was shot, seriously wounded, and left lying on the ground. Several minutes later, Azaria approached him and shot him in the head.
The shooting was filmed by a human rights activist. Azaria was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 18 months in prison, despite prosecutors seeking a three- to five-year term. His sentence was later commuted to 14 months, and he was released in May 2018 after serving nine months.
Footage of Azaria shooting an already incapacitated Palestinian sparked international outrage. The Palestinian Foreign Ministry called it an “extrajudicial execution” and a war crime, saying the video “demolished all the slogans chanted by the occupation leaders about the ethics of the Israeli army.”
Israeli rights group B’Tselem described it as an “extrajudicial street killing.” The UN human rights office called Azaria’s sentence “excessively lenient,” warning that it will reinforce “the culture of impunity.” The case also divided Israeli public opinion and contributed to tensions between political leaders and the military, with then-Defense Minister Moshe Ya’alon later resigning.
Despite the controversy, Herzog’s office announced on Saturday that he shortened the remaining period before Azaria’s record could be erased, effectively clearing it.
“The president believes that the circumstances as a whole, the passage of time, and the regret he expressed justify allowing him to open a new chapter in his life,” the President’s Office said.
It added that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, expressed sorrow in his request. This contrasts with comments Azaria made in his first major interview after leaving prison, when he said he felt “no remorse whatsoever,” arguing that he acted as he did because he believed the attacker was still a threat.
Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, welcomed the decision, saying, “canceling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist” makes him “very happy.” Defense Minister Israel Katz called it a “humane and worthy decision.”
The IDF, however, opposed the move. Azaria’s conviction was a rare case of an Israeli military court ruling against a soldier over a deadly action in the field. Military prosecutors argued that Azaria was seeking revenge rather than responding to an active threat. According to Israeli media, IDF Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir formally opposed clearing Azaria’s record, arguing that he had not fully accepted responsibility or demonstrated genuine remorse.
Scrutiny over military accountability
Extrajudicial and targeted killings by Israeli forces against Palestinians have long been a source of international scrutiny. Palestinian and international rights groups have accused Israeli forces of unlawful and extrajudicial killings. The government argues that its forces act lawfully against individuals involved in planning or conducting attacks.
A UN Human Rights Office report said Israeli forces and settlers killed 1,096 Palestinians in the West Bank since October 7, 2023, one in five of them children, noting that many cases raised concerns over “extrajudicial executions and other unlawful use of force.”
Israeli and international rights groups also said prosecutions of Israeli soldiers for killing Palestinians are rare. Last month, after the military announced internal investigations into the deaths of Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in 2024 and 15 emergency and aid workers in 2025, Israeli rights group Yesh Din pointed to what it called the military justice system’s poor record of securing convictions.
“Nearly zero indictments are served relative to the number of complaints of soldiers and commanders who commit offenses. In rare cases when commanders or soldiers are convicted, they receive ridiculously lenient sentences compared with the severity of the offense,” the organization’s spokesperson said.
According to an August 2025 report by London-based Action on Armed Violence, 88% of 52 publicly reported Israeli military probes into alleged violations in Gaza and the West Bank were either still under review with no public outcome or were closed without finding any wrongdoing. Just one of the 52 cases resulted in a prison sentence.

Israeli settlers storm Al-Aqsa in latest targeting of East Jerusalem sites

Israeli settlers storm Al-Aqsa in latest targeting of East Jerusalem sites
Netanyahu storms Western Wall tunnels amid Yom Kippur settler incursions, drawing fierce condemnation.
Israeli settlers have stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem again and performed Jewish prayers in the courtyard.
The weekend witnessed a series of provocative acts by Israeli politicians and settlers in the build-up to Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, and next month’s Israeli election.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israel arrests 100 Palestinians in a week as West Bank pogroms continue
- list 2 of 4UK charities, protest groups: Israeli ban threat ‘will not intimidate us’
- list 3 of 4Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, stoking tensions with US
- list 4 of 4Palestine weekly: Global outcry fails to break West Bank siege
On Thursday, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and others again stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound for Yom Kippur. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also visited a labyrinth of tunnels below occupied East Jerusalem on Saturday.
Early on Sunday morning, Netanyahu released videos and photographs on his official Instagram account documenting his participation in Jewish “Selichot” prayers at the Western Wall, known as the al-Buraq Wall to Muslims.
The tunnels lie underneath occupied East Jerusalem’s bustling Old City and the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, making the incursions particularly sensitive for the occupied territory’s Palestinian population.
Translation: Happy New Year and a good final signature to all Israelis from the Western Wall.
Under the protection of security forces, Netanyahu, accompanied by several government ministers and thousands of Israeli settlers, made his way onto the plaza of the wall in occupied East Jerusalem on Saturday evening, ahead of Yom Kippur.
Footage shared by the prime minister showed him performing the rituals from behind bulletproof glass. In another video, Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, passed through one of the excavation tunnels running beneath the Western Wall while Jewish prayers took place.
“Well, we are in the tunnels at the al-Buraq Wall. It is moving to touch the rock of our existence. We are here very close to the Holy of Holies. We are here, and we will always remain here,” Netanyahu stated in the video.
Translation: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his wife in prayer for the safety of Israeli soldiers tonight at the Western Wall.
Yom Kippur incursions
The prime minister’s subterranean visit unfolded alongside a wave of settler incursions into the holy site above ground.
On its official Facebook page, the Palestinian Jerusalem governorate reported that about 570 settlers had stormed the courtyards of the Al-Aqsa Mosque by 10am local time on Sunday. According to the governorate, the settlers performed Talmudic rituals and “epic prostrations” to mark Yom Kippur.
The Palestinian group Hamas strongly condemned the incursions in a press statement published on its official Telegram channel.
“The storming by Benjamin Netanyahu, against whom an arrest warrant has been issued by the International Criminal Court, of the tunnels and excavations beneath the blessed Al-Aqsa Mosque and the al-Buraq Wall, and the provocative statements and false claims accompanying it about the so-called Holy of Holies, represents a blatant attack on the identity of the Al-Aqsa Mosque and its status, and a provocation to the feelings of our Palestinian people and the Arab and Islamic nations,” the statement in Arabic said.
The group emphasised Al-Aqsa’s exclusively Islamic heritage and rejected Israel’s ongoing excavations under the holy site.
Religious or political?
Israel has been digging beneath occupied East Jerusalem for years, a move that has been condemned by archaeologists and the United Nations. The works are believed to be intended to find proof of the rampart wall of the Second Temple, but experts say there is no proof of this claim. Others view these measures as an attempt by Israel to cement its rule over occupied Palestinian land.
In 2022, Netanyahu led a cabinet meeting in the labyrinth, describing Israel as the “landlords of Jerusalem”. East Jerusalem has been earmarked as the capital of a future Palestinian state by Palestinians.
The timing of Saturday’s visit not only comes on the eve of Yom Kippur but also at a time of huge political significance for the Israeli leader, who trails in the polls against his rival Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party.
Ahmed al-Hila, a political analyst specialising in Middle East affairs and the Arab-Israeli conflict, told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu is using religious symbolism to try to secure his political survival ahead of October’s general election.
“Benjamin Netanyahu wanted, through this visit … creating this symbolism for himself as a leader spearheading the right wing to consolidate the Israeli political and religious narrative in the Al-Aqsa Mosque, to attempt to gather the largest possible number of votes to serve as an electoral lever for him,” said al-Hila.
“As for the intense security mobilisation and Benjamin Netanyahu’s appearance behind a bulletproof glass shield [during a speech above ground], this is a direct indication that this city has not, up to this moment, submitted to Israeli security control, despite the repeated and frequent talk that Jerusalem is ‘the capital of the State of Israel’.”
The visit could also be a message to the wider world, amid global criticism of the controversial illegal settlement project E1, which the Israeli government has issued tenders for, and which appears designed to sever East Jerusalem from the occupied West Bank.
“What further confirms this conclusion is that initiating the settlement project called E1 does not only isolate the northern West Bank from its south … but this settlement project completes the isolation of the city of Jerusalem from its Palestinian surroundings,” Al-Hila said. “Therefore, this visit with its political symbolism confirms the idea of Israeli sovereignty over the city of Jerusalem.”

Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a Russian Buk-M3 surface-to-air missile system, a Nebo-U long-range surveillance radar, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) manufacturing facility, and frontline command installations across occupied territories on Sept. 19-20.
According to the official military dispatch by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), Ukrainian precision fire engaged high-value Russian air defense and reconnaissance assets deployed across three eastern and southern provinces.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Buk-M3 medium-range surface-to-air missile complex deployed near the settlement of Ukrainka. The Buk-M3 system is among Russia’s modernized mobile air defense assets designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and combat aircraft.
In the Donetsk region, a precision strike targeted and damaged a Russian Nebo-U early-warning radar station operating in the vicinity of Balka. The Nebo-U system operates in the Very High Frequency (VHF) band and is engineered to detect, identify, and track aerodynamic and ballistic targets, including low-radar-cross-section aircraft and missiles, at ranges of several hundred kilometers.
Concurrently in the Luhansk region, Ukrainian units engaged an industrial facility utilized by Russian forces for manufacturing attack drones near the occupied city of Severodonetsk.

Sustained campaign against Russian drone nodes and logistics

In those operations, Ukrainian forces targeted multiple UAV control posts in the Zaporizhzhia region, striking command nodes near Volodymyrivka, Verbove, Dobropillya, and Rivnopillya, alongside two separate drone control installations near Novoprokopivka.
Ukrainian artillery and missile units additionally hit the Russian military’s “Vostochny” training range near the occupied settlement of Novopetrivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
In the Donetsk region, earlier strikes hit Russian UAV command posts near Luhanske and Pokrovsk, while long-range fire struck a material and technical supply warehouse in Rybynske and an ammunition storage depot near Amvrosiivka.

Bulgarian indie band "hug or handshake" puts new spin on Ostava classic

Bulgarian indie band "hug or handshake" puts new spin on Ostava classic
Sunday 20 September 2026 14:10
Sunday, 20 September 2026, 14:10
PHOTO Facebook /hug or handshake
Font size
What happens to a song when, instead of sounding in minor as originally recorded, it is played in major? That is what we hear in Hits with 1% Change, a charity campaign by the organisation One Percent Change.
The first song was Avenue duo’s “Escape”, this time in a new version by Molec. The second title in the series is Ostava’s “Fields of Sunflowers”, given a new interpretation by Bulgarian indie band “hug or handshake”. Both the charity idea and the opportunity to take on the iconic 1994 song immediately appealed to the young musicians, as Anton Georgiev of “hug or handshake” explains:
PHOTO Facebook /hug or handshake
“For us to be making music at all, we already have to believe that it has an inexhaustible ability to help, to heal. And I saw this as yet another way in which we can make music help. Then there was the opportunity to cover not just one of our favourite Bulgarian bands, but our favourite Bulgarian band, so there really was nothing to think about.”
While working on the new version, Anton says he was worried that they had changed its sound by considerably more than 1%. He was told that this was exactly the idea – you start with 1%, but in the process it snowballs into much more.
PHOTO Facebook /hug or handshake
That fits the philosophy of One Percent Change – encouraging people to set aside 1% of their income for causes that need support. And when this becomes a regular gesture for many people, it can lead to major change, as Irina Popova, Community and Communications Manager at One Percent Change, explains:
“The message of the campaign is that the key to doing lasting good is regular giving. And that we should stand together, united by a common cause, helping and changing things for the better.”

====================================================================================================

Israeli-Saudi security coordination remains 'limited and pragmatic,' Saudi analyst cautions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:49:20 UTC
20:49:20 KST

A secret gathering of senior US, Israeli, and Arab military commanders in Germany has offered a rare glimpse of the security coordination taking shape across the Middle East as Saudi Arabia confronts a renewed Houthi offensive and Washington remains heavily focused on its war with Iran.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The meeting, held last week and organized by US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Adm. Brad Cooper, brought together military chiefs from Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, and Egypt, according to Axios, which first reported the gathering. CENTCOM confirmed that it hosted senior military leaders from eight Middle Eastern countries in Germany to discuss opportunities for strengthening regional security cooperation. The conference was not publicly announced in advance.
Its significance lies less in the existence of military contacts - which have developed incrementally for years - than in the circumstances surrounding the gathering.
The commanders met as the conflict with Iran continues to strain American forces and Gulf security, while the Houthis have expanded their position along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Reuters reported that Houthi forces seized Mocha and Perim Island during their latest offensive, increasing their leverage near Bab al-Mandab, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.
The developments have created a difficult security environment for Saudi Arabia. Riyadh must contend with renewed missile and drone threats from Yemen while disruptions around both the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz complicate its energy and maritime calculations.
Germany meeting does not mean Arab-Israel military alliance
Yet the Germany meeting should not automatically be interpreted as the birth of a formal Arab-Israeli military alliance.
Abdulaziz Alshaabani, a Saudi political analyst, cautioned against reading the gathering as evidence that Riyadh is preparing for direct military cooperation with Israel.
“The Germany meeting is significant, but I do not see it as evidence that Saudi Arabia is moving toward direct military cooperation with Israel,” Alshaabani told The Media Line. “Any intelligence coordination would likely remain limited and pragmatic, while Riyadh continues to rely primarily on its own security mechanisms and broader regional frameworks,” he added.
Saudi Arabia and Israel share concerns about Iran and, increasingly, the Houthis, but they do not have diplomatic relations. Operational necessity can produce intelligence exchanges, deconfliction, or parallel military planning without resolving the political constraints that have prevented formal normalization.
The regional security architecture also predates the current crisis. In July, CENTCOM said the United States and regional partners were operating what it described as a large active air- and missile-defense umbrella across the Middle East. The command said a Middle Eastern air-defense coordination cell established in January was intended to improve information sharing, threat warnings and responses to regional contingencies.
That does not mean every country represented in Germany operates within a single integrated command structure. It does show that efforts to coordinate regional defenses were underway before the latest Houthi escalation.
Giuseppe Dentice, an analyst at the Observatory on the Mediterranean (OSMED), sees the current moment through the erosion of confidence in Washington and the resulting search by Gulf states for additional security options.
“What is actually happening is what no one wanted: at this moment, there is total chaos,” Dentice told The Media Line. “The problem is that it is political chaos in which there is no real leadership. The United States is pulling itself out of everything, and the most paradoxical thing is that it is also part of this problem,” he added.
For Dentice, governments are responding pragmatically rather than ideologically.
“Everyone is acting for themselves, and within this ‘everyone for themselves’ approach, the Gulf states are the most prepared to seek some form of action,” he said. “Not so much to resolve the issue, because at this moment neither what is happening in the Red Sea nor what is happening in Hormuz can really be resolved, but rather to try to find some kind of compromise through diplomacy,” he added.
Washington rejecting Saudi requests for direct military assistance
Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct American military action against the Houthis.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman sought US military assistance as Houthi pressure increased, according to Reuters, but Washington limited its involvement to intelligence and targeting support rather than direct strikes. Cooper met the crown prince in Jeddah this week as the crisis intensified.
The United States has also maintained a separate channel with the Houthis. Reuters reported that American officials met Houthi representatives at the US Embassy in Muscat, Oman, over the weekend. Sources familiar with the talks said the Houthi delegation pledged not to target US or Israeli vessels and said it would continue observing its previous arrangement with Washington, while excluding Saudi shipping from those commitments. The State Department declined to confirm the meeting.
For Alexander Portnoy, an independent military and geopolitical analyst, this environment makes behind-the-scenes cooperation more consequential than public declarations of alliance.
“Military contacts and mutually beneficial cooperation between these countries ceased to be sensational news a long time ago,” Portnoy told The Media Line. He argued that disclosure of such contacts can itself serve as strategic messaging.
Portnoy expects any Israeli contribution to a regional response to Yemen to remain discreet.
“Yes, but any Israeli involvement would take place behind the scenes,” he said when asked whether Saudi Arabia and other regional states could coordinate against the Houthis without direct American combat participation.
Israel and Saudi Arabia increasingly face the same types of weapons: ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and long-range drones. Shared threats, though, do not necessarily produce a shared political strategy.
Houthis unlikely to launch ground invasion of Saudi Arabia, analyst says
Alshaabani rejected more dramatic assessments suggesting that the latest Houthi advances make a ground offensive into Saudi Arabia the likely next stage.
“I think the word ‘invasion’ is too strong in this context,” he said. “Saudi Arabia is a vast country, while the Houthis remain a militia with limited capabilities. I do not see a ground invasion as the most likely scenario at this stage,” he added.
Instead, he said, the immediate danger is that the Houthis could exploit their new positions inside Yemen.
“The more immediate concern is the Houthis expanding their control in western Yemen and using that position to intensify missile, drone, and maritime attacks against Saudi Arabia,” he said.
The latest Houthi gains have increased the group’s ability to threaten Saudi territory and maritime traffic, but its territorial advances have so far been concentrated inside Yemen and along the Red Sea coast.
Saudi concerns have nevertheless intensified. Riyadh said this week that it intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca. The Houthis denied targeting the holy city while acknowledging other operations against Saudi targets.
The kingdom is also seeking additional support. Riyadh has approached partners including Egypt, Pakistan, the UK, and France as the conflict strains its missile-defense resources. No broad regional military intervention has materialized.
For Dentice, the central question is less whether a new alliance suddenly emerges than how long individual governments can absorb several interconnected crises.
“There is a strong interest among virtually all the actors in preventing Bab al-Mandab from becoming another Hormuz,” he said. “But we are already very close to that situation. Everyone risks making the same mistakes, because even sending a strong military signal can become counterproductive. Not because the Houthis are militarily superior, but because they retain the ability to strike strategic assets,” he added.
That vulnerability is particularly visible in the energy sector. The Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, while attacks have placed additional pressure on alternative Saudi export infrastructure. On Wednesday, preliminary ship-tracking data showed only three commercial vessels transiting Hormuz, down from 12 the previous day and a 10-day average of 17, according to Reuters. Traffic through Bab al-Mandab also remained depressed. Vessels operating with their tracking systems switched off would not necessarily appear in those figures.
The existence of several active military theaters does not necessarily mean they will merge into a single regional war.
“I do not think the risk of integrating these separate theaters of war into a wider regional conflict is high,” Portnoy said.
He also viewed the Germany meeting as evidence that regional coordination is still being worked out rather than proof that a collective defense mechanism is already operational.
“If these countries were already prepared for a collective response, I do not think the meeting in Germany would have been necessary,” he said.
The Media Line sought additional comment from the US Defense Department and contacted current US military experts and former senior US military officers for their assessments but received no responses by publication time.
The Germany gathering reveals both how far regional security contacts have advanced and where their limits remain. Israel and several Arab governments face overlapping missile, drone, and maritime threats and have reasons to exchange information and coordinate defenses. They also maintain sharply different relationships with Iran, Israel, and the United States.
Dentice similarly described Saudi strategy as one of selective engagement rather than permanent alignment, pointing to the recently signed Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. The pact contains a collective-defense commitment, though its full text has not been made public and questions remain about how its provisions would operate in practice.
“The Saudis are willing to talk to anyone, but not to bind themselves completely to anyone,” he said. “The same applies to the Mecca agreement. It is not a binding agreement; it is based on the availability of the actors involved,” he added.

Five companies lead scoring in $1 billion drone program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
11:46:00 UTC
20:46:00 KST

- Neros, ORQA US LLC, XTEND Reality Inc., Vector and ModalAI Inc. posted the top five scores in the close-quarters battle category of Gauntlet II under the Drone Dominance Program.
- Vector said it received orders for up to 5,000 drone systems and its HV-ESAD arming hardware, while XTEND said it delivered 120 STRIKER systems for testing.
Five companies posted the top scores in the close-quarters battle category of Gauntlet II, the latest round of testing under the U.S. Department of War’s $1 billion Drone Dominance Program, according to results the program released and companies confirmed this week.
Neros topped that category with a score of 88.1, followed by ORQA US LLC at 82.8, XTEND Reality Inc. at 80.2, Vector at 78.2 and ModalAI Inc. at 74.3, per the program’s published scoring. Gauntlet II tested drone systems in operationally realistic scenarios evaluated by warfighters, split across mission categories including close-quarters battle, confined environments and deep strike.
XTEND said September 16 that it delivered and demonstrated 120 of its STRIKER systems for the evaluation, running on the company’s proprietary XOS operating system, which XTEND says is built for tactical missions in confined, complex and GNSS-denied environments, where GPS signals are jammed or unavailable.
“This is a major win for XTEND,” said Aviv Shapira, Co-Founder and CEO of XTEND. “We delivered, we competed, and we proved what STRIKER is capable of in the hands of U.S. warfighters. This achievement demonstrates the strength of our technology.”
Vector said in a LinkedIn post that its selection came with orders for up to 5,000 systems, part of a combined allocation across confined environments and deep strike mission areas that the program has set at 60,000 units total. Vector said it also received orders for its high-voltage electronic safe and arm device, hardware that lets operators safely arm drones with different munitions, and said it is the only American company to win awards for both unmanned systems and that arming hardware in the Gauntlet II flyoff.
The Drone Dominance Program is jointly managed by the Defense Innovation Unit and the Test Resource Management Center, with Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division serving as the contracting authority. The program is meant to build a U.S.-based supply chain for low-cost, one-way attack drones, and Gauntlet II results feed into which companies move forward for prototype contracts.

This will give the enemy the ability to control Shaheds and missiles online via satellites. This will be a huge problem for us. No, it will not even be a problem; it will be a small catastrophe
He emphasized that Ukraine must prepare electronic warfare capabilities before the Russian satellite constellation becomes operational.
We currently have a problem with electronic warfare against MESH. No one worked on this issue for a year. The same thing will happen with "Rassvet". These electronic warfare systems must ALREADY be protecting all key infrastructure facilities. And I will say right away: none of this will be cheap or quick

Germans are heading to the polls on Sunday in two state elections that could prove decisive for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's future.
In Berlin, Merz's ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is facing a close fight against Die Linke, which has strong support among young people and has pledged measures to tackle the housing crisis.
In the coastal state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania in northeastern Germany, the main race is between the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the hard-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD).
The AfD comes into Sunday's vote fresh off the back of its election success in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and will be hoping for further gains.
However, the party faces a sterner test in "MeckPomm," where it will come up against the SPD's Manuela Schwesig, who has served as minister-president of the state since 2017.
The latest polling figures show Die Linke edging ahead of the CDU in the city-state of Berlin, while the AfD leads the SPD in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania - with the CDU flirting with the 5% hurdle required to remain in state parliament.
Gains for the far-right or far-left would heap pressure on Merz, who became chancellor in May 2025 and has seen his popularity continue to decline.
Moritz Lembke-Oezer, 43, summed up that feeling while speaking to the AFP news agency outside a polling station to the south of Berlin, saying that while he feared the vote could benefit the AfD, he hoped it would see the CDU "punished."
"Maybe then Friedrich Merz will be gone," he said, adding that he planned to vote for Die Linke because of the far-left party's vows to address the housing issue.
Speaking to AFP outside a polling station in Schwerin, the state capital of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, pensioner Peter Sommer added: "I'd be in favour of the AfD winning, because then they'll have to prove themselves: either something will happen, or it'll be the last time they get any votes."

Giant pumpkin, 14kg cabbage draw 20,000 to Paunvere fair
A 53-kilogram pumpkin and a cabbage weighing 14 kilograms were among the attractions as the Paunvere exhibition, in Jõgeva County over the weekend.
The fair, held for the 27th time, showcased giant and unusual vegetables, while growers reported a mixed year shaped by weather and cheap imports. and fair drew 20,000 people to Palamuse, population around 550.
The most interesting exhibits were the unusual, strange or giant vegetables. The 53-kilogram giant pumpkin was on display at the Palamuse cuteness contest. According to its owner, growing a winter squash of these proportions requires not only rich soil but also a lot of love.
"You still have to go and pet it, water it. It won't grow weeds, because the pumpkin is so big. But especially cabbage, because cabbage worms are so industrious," said Toomas Puusepp, cultivator of the giant pumpkin.
His giant fruits — a 53-kilogram and a 42-kilogram pumpkin and a 14-kilogram cabbage — arrived at the exhibition on a lawn tractor. The oversized produce found new homes at the fair's auction.
While some real giants could be seen in the "cute tent" (Nunnutelk), this year's vegetable harvest offered mixed feelings for gardeners.
"You can't complain. Compared to last year, we had quite a harvest this year. Everything grew. I could complain about today's sale, there aren't as many people as there have been in previous years," said vegetable grower Tatjana.
However, cool and rainy spring weather almost completely ruined the open-field cucumber and tomato harvest, while the marketing of domestic vegetables is being made more difficult by cheaper imported goods.
"The year was not very productive. There are half as many cucumbers as last year. While we used to pick 300 kilos of cucumbers in the spring, now we only take a total of 300 kilos to Tartu stores. Previously, we took 300 kilos to one store and 300 kilos to another," said vegetable grower Igor.
Meanwhile, a more exotic fruit managed to defy the local cold. Southern Estonian watermelon grower Raimo harvested a whopping four tons of watermelon.
"We grow them in the open field, so that we have them under plastic and in the spring you bury them beautifully with a covering and keep them warm and under a blanket like you would yourself, and that's how they grow," he said.
The Paunvere exhibition was held for the 27th time.
