The strengthening of protection measures came after a series of attacks that disrupted the daily lives of civilians and exposed the vulnerability of infrastructure near the border with Poland, the report says.

Turkish FM says ready to meet Saudi defence needs – what does that mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:23:33 UTC
19:23:33 KST

Turkish FM says ready to meet Saudi defence needs – what does that mean?
Turkiye expresses readiness to assist Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate, testing a recent trilateral defence agreement.
Turkiye says it is ready to help meet Saudi Arabia’s military needs as Riyadh faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis, potentially putting a newly signed Mecca defence pact to its first major test.
Last month, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which treats an armed attack on any of its three member countries as an attack on all three, amid growing regional tensions.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3More than 112,000 displaced by Yemen fighting; thousands flee to Djibouti
- list 2 of 3Pakistan pledges full committment to defence of Saudi Arabia
- list 3 of 3As Houthis grab Bab al-Mandeb, US appears willing to watch from sidelines
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saudi Arabia may require military assistance, particularly on “technical issues”, and that Ankara would have no problem providing it.
“This hints Turkiye’s approach as Fidan possibly implicated Ankara’s strengths in the defence front, including air defence systems, counter-drone and electronic warfare capabilities, radar and surveillance, and maritime security,” Ismail Numan Telci, a professor at Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera.
“There are limitations that prevent Turkiye from having a direct combatant role in the conflict,” said Telci.
His comments come as Houthi missile and drone attacks increasingly target Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, opening another front in a wider regional conflict that began with the US-Israeli war on Iran in February.
The escalation has also raised the stakes for global energy supplies, as the Iran-aligned Houthis tightened their grip on the Red Sea, which has been used as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
So, what does Turkiye’s offer mean in practice, and will the defence pact trigger military involvement by its members?
What did Turkiye say?
Speaking to Turkish media on Saturday, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saudi Arabia could have military requirements because of the continuing Houthi attacks and that Ankara was prepared to provide assistance under its defence agreement with Riyadh and Islamabad.
“We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity, sovereignty,” Fidan told Turkish broadcaster NTV.
He said Saudi Arabia “may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues”, adding that Turkiye would have “no issues in meeting these”.
Fidan did not specify what assistance Turkiye might provide.
Turkiye, which has NATO’s second-largest military, has condemned the Houthi attacks and called for them to stop immediately.
Defence analyst Alex Afirraz Scheer said Turkiye can offer both defensive and offensive support, plus intelligence assistance.
“On defence, Riyadh’s layered air-defence network – built primarily around Patriot batteries and THAAD – has been stretched by the volume and tempo of Houthi missile and drone salvos,” Scheers told Al Jazeera.
“On the offensive side, Riyadh could request combat-proven Turkish drone and missile capabilities … to give it an asymmetric strike option against Houthi launch sites, something it has arguably lacked since Washington rebuffed direct support requests.”
Nawaf Obaid, a senior research fellow at King’s College London, said Saudi Arabia and its allies are putting together a coordinated military response to recent Houthi attacks, arguing that Riyadh is less isolated than it may appear.
“There is a coalition coalescing around the threat on how to properly respond to what the Houthis have been doing,” he told Al Jazeera.
Obaid said the response “is coming”, adding: “It is going to be sequenced. It is going to be massive. It is going to be fused together, and it’s going to be land, sea and air.”
The analyst said countries had already begun moving weapons systems into Saudi Arabia and deploying fighter jets into the Red Sea, identifying Turkiye as a key participant and Egypt as a possible partner in a more limited operational role.
However, Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims made by Obaid.
Meanwhile, Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said that “the Saudis are kind of stuck”.
“They’ve reached out to numerous allies. Allies are producing some measure of support – logistics support, intelligence, weapons – but it doesn’t look like the Pakistanis or the Turks or the Egyptians or the Americans, or anyone else, wants to get directly involved in kinetic military action,” Elmasry told Al Jazeera.
What is the Mecca defence pact?
Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan formally named the arrangement the Mecca Defence Alliance on August 31, after officials meeting in Istanbul agreed to set up a secretariat in Riyadh, to be headed initially by a Pakistani secretary-general.
Its founding principle is that an armed attack against any one of the three states will be treated as an attack against all three – similar to NATO’s collective defence clause.
Fidan said at the time that the alliance was built on “respecting the sovereignty of other states, territorial integrity and not intervening in internal affairs”, and remained open to other countries joining.
The trilateral pact was struck as Gulf states grow increasingly concerned about being pulled into the wider US-Iran war, which has continued for more than six months since Washington and Israel first struck Iran in February.
The military pact also came amid concerns over Israel’s expanding military reach in the Middle East. Israel has bombed several regional countries, including Qatar, since launching its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023.
According to academic Telci, activation is possible in principle, politically and legally, but “complicated in practice”.
“The agreement treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all, and Houthi strikes on Saudi territory fit that description,” he said. “However, the agreement is not yet ratified by the Turkish and Pakistani parliaments.”
Defence analyst Alfirraz Scheers said it would be “premature” to see an activation of the pact.
“The Mecca Pact still lacks the institutional architecture that would make activation a meaningful legal event,” he said. “Still no published strategic concept, no defined triggering threshold, no activation protocol. At this stage, it’s more a political declaration than a functioning alliance.”
What has Pakistan said?
Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director-general of the Pakistan military’s media wing, told the Saudi newspaper Arab News on Thursday that Islamabad stands with Saudi Arabia diplomatically and physically.
“I would like to underscore here the word ‘physically’,” Chaudhry said. “We will go to any extent.”
Last week, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said there had been no discussions about launching a military response under the Mecca agreement following Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.
Islamabad has nevertheless reiterated its commitment to the agreement. Pakistan has said it would act when the “time comes”, without specifying what circumstances would trigger such action.
Pakistan Defence Minister Khawaja Asif earlier this month said any attack on Saudi Arabia could activate the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
“We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact, and … we will honour them in case there is a need,” he said in an interview on September 8.
The latest Saudi-Houthi fighting
Saudi-led coalition forces said on Saturday that the Houthis fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh at dawn before it was intercepted and destroyed.
“The Houthis also attempted to target civilians and civilian infrastructure in Bisha, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu,” coalition forces spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki wrote on X, adding that the attacks were thwarted by the kingdom’s air defences.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Yemen, the armed forces of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government said their fighters thwarted a Houthi infiltration attempt in the al-Fuliahan sector in southern Marib on Saturday, killing 12 Houthi fighters and injuring others.
After capturing the Red Sea port city of Mocha, the Houthis have been advancing on Marib – an oil-rich province still under the control of the Saudi-backed government.
As the Houthis made military gains, Vice President JD Vance said on Monday that Washington was in close contact with Saudi Arabia and has held direct talks with the Houthis.
The current escalation marks the most serious fighting involving the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces since a UN-brokered truce halted large-scale hostilities in Yemen in 2022. The Houthis have made territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including around the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Bab al-Mandeb is a key route connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and its importance has increased while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.
The group has also stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting cities and energy infrastructure.
What is the US position?
US President Donald Trump has so far shied away from direct US military action against the Houthis.
Last week, Reuters news agency, citing sources, reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had sought military assistance from the US president to help fight the Houthis.
Trump did not agree to US strikes on the group, but Washington told Riyadh it would provide intelligence-sharing and targeting assistance, the sources added.
The position contrasts with Washington’s own campaign against the Houthis last year, when US forces bombed the group for two months before the two sides agreed to a ceasefire.
Nevertheless, the Trump administration has continued its broader defence relationship with Riyadh. On Thursday, the US State Department approved the possible sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal valued at $24.3bn, although the sale still requires congressional approval.
William Lawrence, a former US diplomat, said that Washington will likely get involved in the conflict.
“I think they will at some point,” Lawrence, a professor of international relations at American University, told Al Jazeera.
“They’ve shown in the past they’re willing to engage on Yemen when it affects their own interests.”
He pointed to the link between the conflicts in the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb straits and the global economy, as well as US security commitments to Saudi Arabia.
Lawrence said there was a growing view in the US in the last couple of days that it “needs to do something” to help protect Saudi Arabia and prevent the Houthis from consolidating their gains.
“What form that takes is not clear,” he said.
But Lawrence said Washington was already deeply involved, with about 100 US military advisers in Saudi Arabia and extensive intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance support.
“So, it wouldn’t be too much of a ramp-up for the Americans to get further involved,” he said.

The Jewish sin we never confess: Choosing indifference over love - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:18:30 UTC
19:18:30 KST

The law is oddly specific. You go to the person you wronged and ask him to forgive you. He refuses. So you come back – this time with three of his friends, who stand there and watch while you ask again. If he refuses again, you return a third time.
Then the law does something strange: it releases you. You may stop, Maimonides ruled, and the sin moves: the one who refuses forgiveness is now the sinner (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 2:9).
Read that as procedure, not piety. You do not legislate three visits with witnesses for a feeling; you write law like that when someone is not permitted to walk away – and here that includes the person who was wronged.
The season we have now entered is precise about what it cannot do. Yom Kippur atones for what stands between a person and God. For what stands between you and another person, it does nothing at all – not until you have gone to him and he has been appeased. Fasting will not fix it.
The holiest day of the year is powerless in precisely the place where love lives. The vertical relationship can be settled in a day; the horizontal one requires you to knock on a door, or to open one.
And the knocking has a deadline: the obligation to appease falls on the eve of Yom Kippur. The rest of the year you can tell yourself there is time; on that day, there is none: 10 days of love; one day of atonement.
I should say what I mean by love, because the word has been worn smooth. Not benevolence toward humanity – love of everyone is love of no one in particular, and it costs nothing. Not warmth, not compassion. Not identity, not pride, not heritage.
What the tradition means is narrower and harder: an unearned, non-transferable, unbreakable claim that one specific, irreplaceable person has on you.
An apology can be completed and finished with; that is what the release after three refusals is for. The bond underneath it cannot be.
It rests on an axiom the tradition asserts rather than defends: a human being is made in the image of God, and therefore of infinite worth. Not the abstraction, but the man in front of you – which is what makes writing him off expensive.
The season builds this into its grammar. The confession is plural: ashamnu, bagadnu – we have trespassed, we have betrayed. You say it in the plural even if you came alone.
That grammar is a record of what actually held this people together: through centuries of exile, a bond neither calculation nor correctness could dissolve, and no empire could confiscate. Law, land, and belief were the vessels. The bond was the content.
The sin of writing someone off
Which brings us to the sin nobody confesses.
You know who it is. You are not estranged from him by accident. You had reasons, and they were good ones. He said something, or did something, that told you what he is.
What the tradition forbids is not anger. Anger keeps him in the room. The opposite of anger is not peace; it is indifference, which puts him out of the room.
What is forbidden is quieter – the moment he stopped being the address of any obligation, and the relief that came with it. It never gets confessed, because it does not look like a sin. It presents itself as clarity.
The law saw it coming, which is why it refuses to forgive a sin of its own. It is less worried about the man who wronged you than about what you become while being right.
This is not a call for unity. There are arguments in Jewish life that should not be dissolved, and pathologies that should not be accommodated for a family photograph. This love raises the temperature of the argument. It removes one thing only: the exit.
And we too often choose the exit. It is possible to live a full Jewish life today – meaning, ethics, repair of the world – without one actual Jew making a claim on you.
That removal happens in Israel under fire and calls itself principle; abroad, it happens in comfort and calls itself choice. A thin Jewish identity is not a weak commitment; it is a Judaism from which the face of the other has been erased.
The law makes one exception: if the person you wronged was your teacher, Maimonides wrote, you go back a thousand times. There is no release, because there is no version of you without him.
Ask what that exception protects, and you get the shape of the thing: a bond whose claim does not expire, in the place where a person was formed. A people is that, multiplied.
On the Shabbat of these days we read Hosea: “I will heal their waywardness; I will love them freely” (14:5). Freely – not a verdict on their merit. That is what we will ask for on Yom Kippur. It is the exact love we spend the year declining to extend.
You do not have to admit you were wrong, or agree, or find him tolerable.
There are 10 days. God will take you back unearned. He is not the one you have to face.
The writer is the author of the newly released A Jewish Tale of Love: On Defiance, Meaning, and the Fate of a People (Wicked Son, in partnership with the Z3 Institute for Jewish Priorities), which explores the history and present crisis of Jewish love.

The thought that changes everything - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:18:25 UTC
19:18:25 KST

Imagine a courtroom in which the entire verdict comes down to a single decision. No witnesses. No cross-examination. No mountain of evidence. Just one crucial moment in which the judge asks, “Who are you, really?”
We instinctively imagine that our lives are defined by what we have done. Our Sages agree, but only up to a point. Sometimes the decisive moment is not another action at all, but a single thought that reveals which actions truly represent us.
That may be the surprising message hidden in one of the Bible’s most dramatic stories.
David and his men had spent months protecting the flocks of the wealthy landowner Nabal in the Judean wilderness.
When David politely requested provisions for his hungry soldiers, Nabal responded with contempt: “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?”
David, furious about his ingratitude, marched toward Nabal’s estate with 400 armed men, determined to wipe out his household.
Nabal’s wife, Abigail, averted the disaster. Without consulting her husband, she loaded donkeys with bread, wine, sheep, grain, raisins, and figs, intercepted David, and persuaded him not to take revenge.
David immediately recognized that God had sent her to prevent him from shedding innocent blood.
Nabal himself remained oblivious until the next morning. The prophet Shmuel tells us that when Abigail informed him what had happened, “his heart died within him, and he became like a stone.”
Then comes the striking ending: “About 10 days later, the Lord struck Nabal, and he died.”
The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 18a) identifies those 10 days as the Ten Days of Repentance between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. According to this tradition, Nabal died on Yom Kippur.
Why the delay? If Nabal deserved punishment, why not immediately? Why grant him 10 days? Perhaps because God was giving him precisely what Yom Kippur gives every one of us: the opportunity to decide who we really are.
Notice what Nabal did not need to do. He did not need to return stolen property. He did not need to compensate David. Abigail had already sent the provisions. The practical problem had been solved. His entire test had become internal.
Could he acknowledge that his wife had done the right thing? Could he let go of his pride, his resentment, and his anger? Could he simply say in his heart, “She was right, and I was wrong?”
Had Nabal reached that conclusion, nothing more would have been required. No dramatic public gesture. No heroic sacrifice. Just an honest decision that his better self – not his angry, arrogant self – was the real Nabal.
That idea sheds light on one of Yom Kippur’s most mysterious ceremonies in the Holy Temple.
The High Priest stood before two identical goats. One would be offered to God on the Temple altar. The other would be thrown off the Azazel cliff in the wilderness. Their destinies were determined by a simple lottery.
At first glance, this seems arbitrary. But the Torah is teaching us something profound. Two lives can appear almost identical. The difference lies in a single choice, a single moment of truth. A single inner decision about which self we choose to identify with.
The goat’s lot was drawn externally, but the real lottery takes place inside of us.
Decisions of the heart
As Yom Kippur draws to a close, we often imagine that we are desperately trying to squeeze in one last mitzvah before the gates close at Neila. Yet perhaps this final service is guiding us to ask ourselves the most critical question, “Who am I?”
Am I defined by my failures? Or by the moments of kindness, integrity, generosity, and faith that also filled my year?
Teshuva, repentance, is not pretending that my sins never happened. It is deciding that they are not the truest expression of who I am.
It is resolving that the good that I have done defines the person I genuinely aspire to be, and that my mistakes belong to a self that I am leaving behind.
Nabal’s tragedy was not merely that he refused to give David’s soldiers bread. It was that, during those precious 10 days, he apparently never embraced the goodness that Abigail had revealed. He never allowed that better possibility to become his own.
Perhaps that is the deepest message of Neila. In the end, eternity may hinge not on one more deed, but on one final decision of the heart.
Like the drawing of lots between two identical goats, a single sincere thought about who we truly are can make the difference between our Azazel and our olam haba (afterlife). Gmar Hatimah Tova.
The writer is an educator living in Efrat, whose wife, Lucy, and daughters Maia and Rina were murdered by terrorists in April 2023. His latest books – The Seven Facets of Healing and The Business Case for Israel – are both available to order from Amazon and in Israel from Bookpod.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Detroit Tigers rookie Lee Hao-yu (李灝宇) became the first Taiwanese player to hit 10 home runs in a Major League Baseball season on Friday, helping Detroit overcome a six-run deficit to beat the Chicago White Sox 11-8.
Lee went 4-for-5 with a home run, a double, and two singles, driving in three runs and scoring twice as the Tigers rallied from an 8-2 deficit. His performance also gave him 28 extra-base hits this season, surpassing the previous Taiwanese record of 26 set by Yu Chang (張育成) in 2021, per UDN.

The 23-year-old tied Chang’s Taiwanese single-season record of nine home runs earlier in the week, hitting his ninth in Detroit’s 10-1 victory over the Toronto Blue Jays on Tuesday. His next homer moved him into sole possession of the record.
Lee also made history with his first career four-hit game, becoming the first Taiwanese MLB player to collect four hits in a game, per UDN.
The victory improved Detroit’s record to 73-81, although the Tigers remained on the fringes of the American League playoff race with eight regular-season games remaining.

The U.S. has warned that hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis could “escalate rapidly” after a Saturday missile targeted Riyadh for the first time since Yemen’s civil war resumed.
President Donald Trump cut short a weekend at Camp David, a secluded presidential complex in rural Maryland, to return unexpectedly to the White House on Saturday.
The White House gave no explanation for the early return, which came as the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis crossed a new threshold. The Houthis control a large part of Yemen and are fighting government forces backed by a coalition led by Riyadh.
Loud explosions rang out twice Saturday in the Saudi capital, where a fuel tank bearing the logo of oil giant Aramco was on fire near the airport, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).
"This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," the U.S. State Department warned, adding American citizens outside the Middle East should "seriously reconsider travel to and through the region."
The Houthis' lightning offensive seizing large areas of Yemeni territory in recent weeks has left hundreds killed and, according to the U.N., displaced over 110,000 people.
These clashes and the subsequent hostilities with the kingdom have already disrupted Saudi Arabia's exports – the world's leading supplier of crude oil – as well as maritime traffic.
The Riyadh-led coalition confirmed Saturday evening in a post on X that a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward the capital was "successfully intercepted and destroyed."
The coalition added that the pro-Iranian fighters had tried to target "civilians and civilian infrastructure" in several cities in the west of the kingdom, including the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, an important export hub for Saudi oil.
It said these attacks were "thwarted by the kingdom's air defenses."
Saudi Arabia has responded with scores of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas but failed to stop the advance.
The Houthis said they had responded to recent Saudi attacks by carrying out "two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on Telegram.
"The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu."
Saudi authorities had earlier issued an overnight air raid alert.
Hours after the early morning alert, residents told AFP anonymously that they heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.
This is the first time since Yemen's civil war resumed that strikes have threatened the Saudi capital, piling further pressure on a global economy already rocked by seven months of war between the U.S. and Iran.
Riyadh residents received a message just before 3 a.m. urging them to stay indoors and warning, "The area is under a hostile aerial threat."
AFP reported two explosions, before the Saudi civil defense agency lifted the alert 30 minutes later.
"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," a Riyadh resident said. Another resident described the attack as "terrifying."
The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca Wednesday, denouncing it as a "cowardly terrorist attack" on Islam's holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a "worn-out lie."
The group has reported scores of retaliatory strikes carried out daily by Riyadh since their offensive this month to take over the country's entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The United States, according to U.S. news platform Axios, last week refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis.
Washington approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom Thursday to help Riyadh "deter current and future threats," the U.S. State Department said.
Yemen's civil war broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sana and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015.
The fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July, when the Houthis defied Riyadh's control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.
The apparent attack came as the Houthis improve their defenses in newly conquered territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, with members of the group telling AFP they have been installing radar and digging tunnels.

Billionaires abound in California. Why not tax their wealth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:08:50 UTC
19:08:50 KST

Billionaires abound in California. Why not tax their wealth?
Sept 20 - No state may be a more natural fit for a tax on billionaires than California. The state leans left politically, needs funds for healthcare and is home to as many as 250 billionaires collectively worth upwards of $2 trillion.
But the November 3 ballot initiative Proposition 40, which asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5% tax on the state's billionaires, is far from certain to pass, political analysts say, amid a debate that has raised questions about income inequality and the state's future business prospects.
Whether and how to tax the ultrawealthy are questions that extend well beyond the Hollywood Hills and Silicon Valley. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat and democratic socialist, filmed a video in front of billionaire investor Ken Griffin's penthouse as part of an ultimately successful campaign to tax high-end second homes in the city. Even a majority of Republicans see billionaires as creating unfairness and contributing to economic woes, one 2025 poll showed.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found 64% of independent registered voters in the six-day nationwide poll said they support increasing taxes on corporations and billionaires, compared to 15% who oppose the idea.
"Billionaires are no longer very popular," said University of California, Berkeley economics professor Emmanuel Saez, a researcher of wealth inequality who helped write Proposition 40. They have "enormous wealth, enormous power."
Saez describes the proposal as very simply "a tax on billionaires to fund healthcare."
California has more billionaires than any other state, according to a Forbes estimate last year, and is home to some of the country's most valuable companies, including tech giants Google, Apple, Meta and Nvidia.
POLLS SHOW IT AHEAD — FOR NOW
A UC Berkeley IGS Poll in August found 48% of likely voters supported Proposition 40, with 41% opposed, while a September Public Policy Institute of California poll showed it leading 52% to 46%.
California ballot measures typically need robust early support to survive Election Day. Undecided voters are more apt to vote "no" when the time comes, political analysts say, and opponents have yet to crank up their advertising campaign.
"California ballot measures tend to lose support over time, and if it's polling below 50% in August, that's not a good sign for its prospects," said John Pitney, a professor of politics at Claremont McKenna College.
Backers say California's measure would generate $100 billion for healthcare, food assistance and education. But skeptics peg the revenue estimate at closer to $40 billion and say it could also drive some billionaires out of state, depriving California of future tax revenue and investment.
Opposition has been bolstered by billionaires such as Sergey Brin, the Google co-founder who has spent more than $100 million to defeat Proposition 40 and support countermeasures on the same ballot that would effectively void it.
"I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don’t want California to end up in the same place," Brin, 53, whose family left the Soviet Union when he was a child, told the New York Times.
Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat widely believed to be running for president in 2028, also opposes Proposition 40, instead advocating for a nationwide federal wealth tax.
COLORFUL INITIATIVE HISTORY
California ballot initiatives draw unusual attention because the state combines a powerful direct-democracy system with the nation's largest state economy and population. The process allows citizens to propose laws, though most initiatives are drafted by interest groups or lawyers.
Proposition 13 in 1978, which capped and rolled back property taxes, became a national symbol of a tax revolt that shaped US politics.
But California voters have only approved one in three citizen initiatives historically.
In 2022, another California ballot measure aimed at increasing taxes on top earners, Proposition 30, lost 58% to 42%, even though Democrats outnumber Republicans nearly two to one.
"Sixty percent of Californians now reliably vote Democratic for statewide races, but that doesn't mean that they're really liberal on taxing, spending, or even many social issues," said Thad Kousser, a professor of political science at UC San Diego.
European countries including France, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Germany repealed wealth taxes between 1997 and 2018 amid concerns about capital flight, avoidance and economic competitiveness. The California proposition is retroactive to January 1, limiting billionaires' ability to escape the tax by moving.
Saez said the tax was unlikely to prompt many billionaires or the tech startups that are making people wealthy to move, because of the quality of California's universities, research, infrastructure and talent.
"It's just absurd to think that Silicon Valley is going to come to a standstill because of a billionaire wealth tax," he said. REUTERS

Pakistani forces kill 5 militants and free 23 hostages in operation in the southwest

The militants had established an illegal checkpoint near Kalat in Balochistan province overnight into Saturday, stopping vehicles to abduct more people for ransom, extort money and seize vehicles, according to a military statement.
The statement described the killed militants as members of “Fitna al-Hindustan,” a term the Pakistani government uses for the outlawed separatist Baloch Liberation Army and other groups operating in Balochistan demanding independence, which it alleges are supported by India. New Delhi has previously denied accusations that it sponsors militancy in Pakistan.
Security forces recovered six trucks, three buses and two cars, along with weapons, ammunition and explosives. No casualties among security forces or abductees were reported. The military said troops were searching the surrounding area for any remaining militants.
The latest operation came just over a week after Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti ruled out negotiations with insurgents and said security operations would continue until militancy was eliminated from the province.
Insurgents often kidnap people for ransom after establishing illegal checkpoints. Last month, they killed 18 police officers after abducting them. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif praised the security forces for the operation and said counterterrorism operations would continue and vowed to eliminate what he called foreign-sponsored terrorism.
Balochistan has been the scene of a long-running insurgency in southwestern Pakistan with an array of separatist groups, including the BLA, demanding independence from Pakistan’s central government in Islamabad. The groups have staged attacks mainly targeting security forces and people from Punjab who travel to Balochistan for business or employment.
Although Pakistani authorities say they have quelled the insurgency, violence in the province has persisted.

Newsletter: Carney is right on EU associate membership — the name is irrelevant, the politics aren’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:06:05 UTC
19:06:05 KST

Each week, Euronews’ chief Europe editor Maria Tadeo debriefs the ins and outs of continental politics. This week, reporting from Strasbourg, she examines the EU’s pitch for associate membership for Canada.
Welcome back to this newsletter, written en route from Strasbourg to Brussels, after a week of parliamentary coverage. In case you missed it, Mark Carney stole the show and Canada is our new associate BFF, whatever that means.
It's easy to be cynical about the Canadian Prime Minister, but anyone who makes an intellectual effort citing Goethe on a Thursday morning gets my attention amid the sea of poor orators that populate the annual State of the Union (the EU's, to be clear).
Carney chose his references deliberately, reaching for Faust right off the bat. One can only hope the MEPs — including the gentleman who shouted "USA! USA!" as he took the stand — appreciated the reference. Goethe argued that freedom is neither a condition nor a possession: it must be conquered. Nor can it be taken for granted, as freedom is as fragile as it is precious.
Carney evoked that spirit from the get-go of his six-page address, taking the hemicycle on a journey through the forest of Ettersberg. Nur der verdient sich Freiheit wie das Leben, der täglich sie erobern muß (Only those who strive for freedom every day are deserving of it). Canada and the EU share that spirit, he told the European Parliament — and both are being tested on their ability to forge their own paths.
His pitch? A new alliance between two sovereign blocs that looks beyond zero-sum geopolitics and builds on their complementary strengths and dependencies. A single tree, he said, can fall in a storm; a forest will not. For Europe, as for Canada, the storm has three names: Trump, Xi, Putin.
Still, lumping them together would be intellectually lazy. The US doesn't threaten Europe's security architecture the way Russia does — NATO is still largely bankrolled by American taxpayers. Nor is China's economic predation on the European industry the result of Trump's economic agenda.
But together, they have upended the status quo on both sides of the Atlantic and left Europeans feeling defeated, orphaned from a political offer that stands up to bullies. Carney is now their patron saint and newfound maple hero.
You could say this is simply a rerun of speeches we've heard before.
Carney himself said as much in Davos at the start of the year, calling for an alliance of middle powers to stabilise a world increasingly governed by brute force. In 2023, cameras caught China's Xi telling Putin that the world was witnessing changes not seen in a century. He was right. The question is whether nations can still decide their own paths, seal their own alliances, and resist the pull of the tide.
Carney is playing politics — that's true. He owes his political success to Donald Trump: going elbows-up on the US, walking away from lopsided trade talks, and putting sovereignty above all else has resonated with Canadians — a country whose sole raison d'être is not being America.
Carney, a product of the establishment and elite education, would never have been elected had it not been for Trump's provocations, and yet he is now the most popular Canadian PM; every dust-up adds points.
His political calculus is very different to that of the EU, which desperately sought to cool down tensions and had the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, inking a deal on American terms. And that stings. Large swathes of the European electorate are hungry for political courage — courage von der Leyen lacks, and would struggle to project even if she had it, since doing politics has never been her strength. In Carney, Europeans see an alternative.
Von der Leyen has amassed enormous power. She could have been a transformative Commission President; instead, she plays it safe. Let's be honest: Carney saved her State of the Union address — without him, she would have had little new to say. Too afraid to raise the question of joint debt and European financing, her "independence" moment comes without financial muscle.
Mario Draghi put a number on the cost of an independent Europe: €800 billion a year. You cannot implement the Draghi report without addressing the elephant in the room — but she won't touch it. You can argue her institutional neutrality doesn't allow for it, but her peer Christine Lagarde has no problem saying Europe should at least debate joint borrowing.
Plenty can be said about the tribulations and hurdles ahead for a transatlantic partnership meant to deepen trade, cultural, political and educational ties.
CETA is proof enough: the Canada-EU trade deal, still unratified in countries like France, was painful to negotiate and remains unpopular in sectors like agriculture (and farmers are untouchable in Europe).
Most MEPs we spoke to on the floor told us they didn't quite understand what an associate member would look like, but welcomed the move. The head of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola, went a step further, telling Euronews in an exclusive interview that Canada could pave the way for other countries "with so much in common," like New Zealand and Australia. My colleague Vincenzo Genovese overheard a group of Renew MEPs debating the interview over lunch — that's zeitgeist for you.
It’s tempting to write this pairing off as bluff — I mean, they can’t even agree on a name: an alliance for the future, or associate membership? But dismiss it at your peril, because Carney is right: at this point, the nomenclature is irrelevant.
What matters is the political signal, and it's not a futile one — just ask the US president, who has already threatened tariffs if the two turn hostile to American interests. As you know, in MAGA world, you either align or you get punished. And yes, the US already has a deal in place with the EU which cut tariffs on American products.
Before I go, I want to thank our team of reporters, correspondents, producers and cameramen for two marathon days in which Euronews brought you 16 interviews, an exclusive sit-down with the Parliament's President, the Commissioners that mattered on the day, and non-stop coverage. It's long hours and it's not easy. I had cold chicken nuggets for dinner each night, and believe me, you don't want that.
But we take pride in what we do, and Euronews is Europe's newsroom — time to consider an antenna in Ottawa.
Thank you for reading Off The Record make sure to subscribe here. Before you go, Europe Today, Euronews' flagship morning show, is live weekdays at 8am CET.

Ukraine launched a massive long-range drone attack on Moscow and Moscow Oblast overnight on 20 September, striking a major Russian oil refinery and a logistics facility, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Ukraine is increasingly targeting Russian oil refineries, logistics hubs, and other strategic infrastructure that helps generate the fuel, revenue, and supplies Russia needs to sustain its war against Ukraine. Striking them allows Kyiv to put pressure on Russia’s war economy and military logistics far beyond the front line.
The Moscow Oil Refinery was among the facilities hit. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin confirmed that an object at the refinery was damaged, while OSINT analysis by ASTRA of eyewitness footage also identified the refinery as one of the attack’s targets.
Zelenskyy said the strikes were carried out using a range of Ukrainian long-range weapons and targeted infrastructure that generates revenue for Russia’s war effort.
The attack took place on the second day of Russia’s three-day State Duma elections, with voting taking place across the country from 19 to 21 September.
Moscow refinery targeted
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces struck “one of the key enterprises of the Russian oil industry” in the Moscow region, along with a logistics facility.
The Moscow Oil Refinery is operated by Gazprom Neft and is located in Moscow’s Kapotnya district. According to information cited by ASTRA, it can process 11 million tons of oil annually and supplies about 40% of Moscow’s fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region’s gasoline and aviation fuel needs.
Sobyanin said an object on the refinery’s territory was damaged and that there were no casualties there.
Ukraine’s long-range campaign
Zelenskyy said Ukraine used FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sich, and Pelican systems in the operation.
He thanked the Security Service of Ukraine, Unmanned Systems Forces, Special Operations Forces, military intelligence, and Foreign Intelligence Service for their involvement.
“The billions of dollars” generated by such facilities help sustain Russia’s military machine, Zelenskyy said, framing the strikes as part of Ukraine’s effort to reduce Russia’s ability to finance and wage its war.
He also said Moscow should end its war rather than build layered air defenses using systems taken from other Russian regions.
Russian authorities report casualties
Russian officials claimed the overnight attack caused two deaths and six injuries across Moscow Oblast.
Governor Andrei Vorobyov claimed Russian air defenses and electronic warfare systems intercepted or suppressed 249 drones across 17 municipal districts between 3 and 5 a.m.
Vorobyov also claimed that a drone strike in Sofyino damaged six apartments in a three-story building, killing a 44-year-old woman and injuring five people. Another person was reportedly killed in a private house in the Orekhovo-Zuyevsky district.
In Ramenskoye, Russian authorities reported a fire at a 21-story apartment building and said about 400 people were evacuated.
Sobyanin separately claimed that the attack was intended to disrupt Russia’s State Duma elections, which were taking place on 20 September. Ukrainian authorities did not say that this was the purpose of the strikes.

Ukrainian Defense Forces have liberated the settlements of Shandryholove and Derylove in the Lyman municipality of Donetsk region and established full control over the nearby village of Drobysheve, military officials and reported on Sunday, Sept. 20.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrainian analytical mapping project DeepState confirmed the operational gains on Sunday, reporting that Ukrainian forces liberated Shandryholove and Derylove while securing additional tactical positions surrounding Shandryholove.
According to a statement by the press service of the 3rd Army Corps, Ukrainian combat units operating across the first and second phases of the operation have recovered 125 square kilometers of territory, formally de-occupying 50 square kilometers.
Biletsky reported that Russian military casualties during the offensive have exceeded 3,000 personnel across both phases, including roughly 800 Russian soldiers killed in recent engagements.
The commander noted that the offensive actions have systematically degraded the operational capacity of three Russian combined-arms formations deployed along the axis: the 20th Combined Arms Army, the 25th Combined Arms Army, and the 1st Guards Tank Army.
Robotic ground assault tactics
A central operational feature of the offensive involved the integration of automated strike platforms and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) operating ahead of assault infantry formations.
Russia Offering Tours of ‘Sites of Military Glory’ in Donetsk and Kursk
“During assault operations, UAVs and robotic ground complexes always advance ahead of the infantry,” Biletsky said. “The 3rd Army Corps became the first in the world to begin air-dropping unmanned ground complexes. Our heavy bomber drones deliver kamikaze robotic platforms more than 10 kilometers into the enemy’s rear.”
The corps command detailed that tube artillery, rocket artillery, and unmanned aerial strike wings conducted continuous preparatory strikes against Russian tactical command centers, communications nodes, logistic transport routes, river crossings, and mobilization reserves.
Concurrently, integrated air defense units and electronic warfare regiments established an electronic countermeasure shield over the operational theater, masking Ukrainian offensive troop movements and preventing Russian reconnaissance drones from identifying maneuver axes prior to the assault.
The operation involved organic corps brigades alongside attached specialized formations, including the 60th Mechanized Brigade, the 125th Separate Heavy Mechanized Brigade, a battalion tactical group from the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade, the 21st Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment “Kraken,” the 3rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, and the 25th Separate Anti-Tank Battalion.
Attached external units included the 66th Mechanized Brigade, the 85th tactical group of the 8th Special Operations Forces (SSO) Regiment, the “Artan” special operations unit of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR), and the 10th “Dozor” Mobile Border Detachment.
Leadership transitions within Ground Forces command
The battlefield advances along the Lyman operational direction follow high-level structural changes across Ukraine’s military leadership aimed at accelerating combat innovation and tactical decentralization.
On Sept. 2, President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed Major General Hennadiy Shapovalov as commander of the Ground Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, appointing Brigadier General Sviatoslav Zaits to head the service branch under presidential decrees No. 852/2026 and No. 853/2026.
Zaits, an Air Assault Forces veteran, previously served as commander of Ukraine’s 20th Army Corps defending the eastern axis in the Dnipropetrovsk region. Zaits had been promoted to brigadier general in May 2026 following operational reviews with Zelensky regarding frontline equipment modernization, counter-drone requirements, and strike coordination.
Shapovalov had served as Ground Forces commander since June 2025 following senior postings within NATO’s Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine (NSATU) mission in Wiesbaden, Germany, and prior commands of Operational Command South and the Tavria joint grouping of forces.

====================================================================================================

Amit Shah wants UCC in all NDA states by 2029. What will JD(U) do in Bihar?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:01:48 UTC
19:01:48 KST

NEW DELHI: Is the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code emerging as a new point of contention between the Bharatiya Janata Party and one of its oldest allies, Janata Dal (United)?The question has come into focus after Union home minister Amit Shah's assertion that UCC would be implemented in all 21 NDA-ruled states before the next Lok Sabha elections prompted differing reactions within the JD(U).The issue surfaced after Shah, during his visit to Mumbai, put a timeline on BJP's plan to implement one of its longstanding ideological objectives before the 2029 Lok Sabha polls."Triple talaq has been abolished, giving Muslim women equal rights. We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in several states and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029," Shah said.
Shah's message, however, drew a different response from some JD(U) leaders in Bihar.JD(U) general secretary and former minister Shyam Rajak said his party did not favour implementing UCC in the state."Our stand on the issue was made clear by our leader way back. He had said that although our party was supporting the UCC Bill in the Parliament, it was not in favour of implementing the same in Bihar," Rajak said."The chief minister may be of the BJP but the government is being run with the help of allies...
our stand is clear, the question of implementing UCC in Bihar does not arise," he added.
However, Bihar deputy chief minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary, who is considered to be a close ally of former chief minister Nitish Kumar, adopted a more cautious stance and said the party would first study the legislation and would not oppose it "for no reason" if its provisions were found to be unexceptionable."As of now, we are not aware of the details of the legislation on UCC. Let it be placed before us. If we find there is nothing objectionable, why shall we oppose it without any reason? And if there are points of concern, these will be conveyed to the Union home minister," Chaudhary said.JD(U) working president Sanjay Jha has also indicated that party leaders would discuss the issue with Shah.
For now, therefore, JD(U)'s stand is not entirely clear. While some leaders have spoken against implementing UCC in Bihar, remarks by senior leaders such as Chaudhary and Jha have left scope for the party to examine the proposed provisions before taking a final position. The party has historically favoured wider consultations and consensus on the issue.
What is UCC
India already has uniform criminal laws and common civil laws covering matters such as taxation, contracts and negotiable instruments. However, when it comes to personal laws such as marriage, divorce and inheritance of property, different religious communities follow laws based on their respective traditions and practices.Article 44 under the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Constitution says that the State shall endeavour to secure a UCC for citizens throughout India."The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," the Constitution says.A UCC broadly seeks to provide a common legal framework for citizens in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and succession.
BJP's old promise
The Uniform Civil Code has been a longstanding part of the BJP's political agenda and has featured repeatedly in the party's election manifestos over the years.The party has repeatedly included the issue in its election manifestos, arguing that a common civil code would ensure equality before law and strengthen women's rights in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption.Matters such as marriage, divorce, adoption, wills, intestacy and succession fall in the Concurrent List, allowing both the Centre and state governments to make laws on them.
In 2022, then Union law minister Kiren Rijiju also informed the Rajya Sabha that states were empowered to legislate on these subjects."Article 44 of the Constitution provides that the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," Rijiju had said in a written reply."Personal laws such as intestacy and succession; wills; joint family and partition; marriage and divorce, relate to Entry 5 of List-III-Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and hence, the States are also empowered to legislate upon them," he had added.This has allowed BJP-ruled states to take the state route on UCC.Uttarakhand became the first state in independent India to implement a state-specific Uniform Civil Code on January 27, 2025.Since then, UCC Bills have also been passed by the assemblies of BJP-ruled Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh. As of mid-September, the Bills in these three states were awaiting the President's assent.Other NDA-ruled states are at different stages of considering or preparing their own legislation.Shah's latest remarks have now put a 2029 timeline on that process for all NDA-ruled states.
Why UCC needs careful balancing for JD(U)
For JD(U), the issue comes with both political and ideological considerations.Nitish Kumar has long maintained that a reform such as UCC should not be pushed without broad consultation and consensus, particularly given India's social and religious diversity.There is also an electoral dimension.Within the NDA in Bihar, JD(U) has traditionally sought support across a social coalition that includes Extremely Backward Classes, women and sections of minorities. While its support among Muslims has weakened over the years, the party has continued to reach out to the community.Muslims constitute around 17.7% of Bihar's population, according to the state's caste survey. Recent electoral data cited by The Indian Express suggests that only a relatively small section of Muslim voters backed the NDA in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, underlining the challenge for JD(U) in retaining support among the community while remaining part of the BJP-led alliance.In the 2025 assembly election, JD(U) fielded four Muslim candidates, but only Mohammad Zama Khan won from the Chainpur seat.The political setting has also changed since that election.The NDA won 202 of Bihar's 243 assembly seats, with the BJP emerging as the single-largest party with 89 seats and JD(U) winning 85.Nitish Kumar is also no longer chief minister, with BJP's Samrat Choudhary now heading the NDA government. JD(U), however, remains one of its two principal constituents.This makes the UCC question an important one for the alliance: BJP has put a timeline on a longstanding policy commitment, while JD(U) has traditionally stressed consultation before any such move.
When JD(U) differed with BJP
Although an ally of BJP, JD(U) has not always agreed with it on politically sensitive issues.On UCC itself, Nitish Kumar has long cautioned against hurried implementation.In January 2017, as Bihar chief minister, he returned the Law Commission's questionnaire on UCC, arguing that there was insufficient clarity about what the proposed code would contain and calling for wider consultations with affected groups.Nitish argued that diverse customs and practices had existed for centuries and that any effort towards a common code should be based on consensus rather than simply imposed.JD(U) has also differed from the BJP on issues such as the Triple Talaq Bill and the abrogation of Article 370.In 2019, JD(U) opposed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Bill, commonly known as the Triple Talaq Bill. The party objected particularly to the provision making instant triple talaq a criminal offence, arguing that the legislation could create "a lack of trust" in society. Its MPs walked out of the Lok Sabha debate and later abstained during the Rajya Sabha proceedings.In August 2019, the party also opposed the Modi government's decision to abrogate the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and reorganise the former state into two Union Territories. JD(U) MPs staged a walkout when the measures were introduced in Parliament.However, it struck a reconciliatory note later and said that once the law had come into force, it should be abided by all.These differences did not, by themselves, prevent the BJP and JD(U) from working together. The two allies have in the past maintained separate positions on some issues while continuing their political partnership.UCC could similarly depend on what form a proposed law for Bihar eventually takes and whether the allies are able to arrive at a common position.
Mahagathbandhan's offer to Nitish
Amid the debate over UCC, Congress and Rashtriya Janata Dal have taken the opportunity to invite Nitish Kumar to join the opposition alliance.RJD MLA Bhai Virendra asked Nitish to break ties with the BJP and form a new government with its support, saying the parties shared a socialist political tradition.The RJD MLA alleged that Nitish was surrounded by people who were "hellbent on ruining his political career" and said, "We urge Nitish Kumar ji to walk out of the NDA and form a govt with our support."Former Bihar Congress president and Rajya Sabha member Akhilesh Prasad Singh also extended an invitation to Nitish to join the Mahagathbandhan, saying Nitish had long been associated with socialist politics.
"It is the agenda of the BJP and the RSS. Several allies of the NDA may not agree with it, and Nitish certainly should not agree with it. He has always been associated with social concerns and socialism, so I do not think he can ever agree with this," Singh said."Why would Congress have any objection to that? If he leaves, Congress will always welcome him," he added.For now, however, the differing remarks on UCC do not necessarily point to a larger crisis within the Bihar NDA.
JD(U)'s final position remains open. Some of its leaders have opposed implementation in Bihar, while others have said the party should first see the proposed legislation and discuss its concerns with the BJP leadership.Shah, meanwhile, has set a clear target of introducing UCC in all NDA-ruled states before 2029.It remains to be seen whether Bihar eventually follows that roadmap and, if it does, what shape the proposed law takes after consultations between the two allies.

Multi-generational house in Bengaluru designed to be "conducive to reading"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20

Multi-generational house in Bengaluru designed to be "conducive to reading"
Cosy nooks and a study are among the spaces designed for reading at House of Shadows, a multi-generational home in Bengaluru, Karnataka, by Indian studio Cadence Architects.
Located on a quiet, tree-lined road, the house was designed for a family of bookworms who moved back to India after living in the USA for over a decade.
Cadence Architects utilised a predominantly dark, shadowy material palette for the home and fronted it with slatted screens, designed to create a feeling of seclusion and privacy.
"The client, with his young family of two children, was moving back from the USA after having stayed there for 15 years," principal architect Smaran Mallesh told Dezeen.
"As a family of readers, they wanted their home to be a repository for their books and conducive to reading," he continued.
"He wanted to build this home where he could also have his parents come and live with him."
Outside, the home is distinguished by its dark material palette, including a basalt stone base and concrete walls and a roof. A slatted timber facade screens the living spaces while allowing light and air to filter in.
According to the studio, the dark materials were all chosen for their robustness and to help the home blend with "the shadows of the trees and make the home less conspicuous on the street".
Inside, the House of Shadow's spatial organisation is intended to cater for the preferences and needs of the three generations that live there. The ground level of the home has a kitchen, living and dining area for entertaining guests.
Private living spaces for the grandparents are also on this floor.
Above, the first floor is for the parents and their children, complete with a study and reading nooks.
Described by the studio as the "more secluded and introspective" level, it was intended to offer the feeling of a quiet retreat.
"Books and reading spaces form an important part of the interiors, encouraging the family to pause, read, and linger," the studio said.
The third level is given over to an entertainment area for the children to enjoy with their friends. The home is complete with various terraces, decks and balconies that help keep the interiors cool.
Inside, Cadence Architects contrasted the darkness of the exterior with lighter shades through a mix of natural and local materials such as wood and lime plaster.
However, darker shades were still used in more intimate spaces, such as the reading nooks, to add a feeling of cosiness.
"We wanted to make a home that is crafted locally, with local materials," said Mallesh.
"It was important to do that for a client who is moving back and seeking his roots, in a sense. However, we were not interested in the vernacular per se but wanted a modern rendition of these traditional techniques of making."
Other multigenerational Indian houses recently featured on Dezeen include LJ House in Ahmedabad, which Studio Saransh and Iksoi Studio designed with gently curving rooflines and an asymmetrical heart-shaped stairwell, and Splitscape Residence in Coimbatore, which SpaceDNA organised around a triple-height void with an oxide-coated staircase.
The photography is by Syam Sreesylam.

New study links the spread of the internet to a global decline in religious identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:00:38 UTC
19:00:38 KST

The spread of the internet has fundamentally changed how people interact, work, and learn. A recent cross-national study indicates that as internet access grows within a country, religious affiliation and religious self-identification tend to decrease. These findings were published in Sociology of Religion: A Quarterly Review.
Sociologists have long debated the drivers of secularization, which is the historical decline in the social and personal importance of religion. Classical theories often point to modernization. As societies become wealthier, more educated, and more urban, people tend to rely less on religious institutions for basic survival and social support.
More recently, scholars have suggested that digital communication might act as its own secularizing force. The internet exposes individuals to diverse worldviews, lowers the cost of accessing scientific information, and makes it easier to question traditional authority. Online platforms can also replace local, in-person communities with digital networks, potentially weakening the social environments that usually sustain religious participation.
The concept of religiosity itself is complex and multifaceted. To understand religious decline, scientists often look at multiple dimensions of faith. For example, a 2017 study of adolescents proposed that religiosity includes distinct elements, such as personal beliefs, private practices like prayer, and how exclusive a person’s worldview is.
In the context of the internet, different parts of religious life might respond differently to digital connectivity. While earlier studies found links between individual internet use and lower religious commitment, much of this evidence was limited to single countries or snapshots in time. The research, led by Miran Lavrič, a full professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Maribor, sought to test whether internet expansion acts as a broad predictor of secularization across many different countries over several decades.
The idea that digital connectivity might erode faith has circulated for years among scholars and public intellectuals. “Years ago I heard Daniel Dennett say that the internet was the best thing to happen to atheism since Darwin,” Lavrič told PsyPost. “More recently, I was surprised to find that research on whether the internet actually has secularizing effects has remained relatively sparse and methodologically limited.”
“At the same time, a substantial field of research on digital religion has developed, showing that religious communities can be remarkably adaptive and can use the internet to their own benefit,” he added. “So my colleague Tibor Rutar and I decided to examine this question systematically across many societies and over a long period of time.”
To explore this, the researchers assembled a massive dataset covering 81 countries between 1990 and 2022. They combined national internet usage statistics with six waves of data from the World Values Survey. This survey is a long-running international project that tracks human beliefs and values across the globe.
The team constructed a six-item index to measure a country’s average religiosity. This index included rates of religious service attendance, the personal importance of God, the overall importance of religion, self-rated religious identity, confidence in churches, and formal belonging to a religious denomination. They also tracked a wide package of modernization metrics for each country, including economic output per person, average years of schooling, urbanization rates, globalization, demographic aging, and income inequality.
The researchers used statistical models designed to look at changes within each individual country over time, rather than just comparing rich countries to poor ones. They also used a time delay in their calculations. This allowed them to match a country’s internet adoption in one survey period to its religious levels in the following survey period, helping to establish the sequence of trends.
The results showed a consistent pattern. Increases in a country’s internet penetration reliably predicted later decreases in the country’s average religiosity. This negative association held up even after the researchers adjusted for the other modernization factors, suggesting that internet expansion is tied to religious decline independently of general economic or educational improvements.
“The simplest takeaway is that as societies became more connected to the internet, they also tended to become less religious,” Lavrič said. “The associations were meaningful, but not huge. A one-standard-deviation increase in internet diffusion was associated with roughly a 0.20 standard-deviation decline in overall religiosity.”
“What was particularly striking was that internet diffusion was the most robust predictor of religious decline among the standard modernization variables included in our models, while factors such as education, economic development, and globalization were much less consistent,” the researcher explained. “This suggests that, during the period we studied, internet diffusion may have been an important channel through which broader modernization translated into secularization.”
Blake Victor Kent, an associate professor of sociology at Westmont College who was not involved in the study, agreed with this assessment. “The work is robust and finds that internet diffusion correlates with lower levels of religiosity, lending some support to classic secularization arguments which argue that the spread of information and exposure to other views leads to a weakening of plausibility structures,” he told PsyPost.
Kent, who is also a research affiliate at Massachusetts General Hospital’s Center on Genomics, Vulnerable Populations, and Health Disparities and a research affiliate at Harvard University’s Human Flourishing Program, added, “I also appreciated that the researchers noted how internet use emphasizes individualization, which can threaten participation in embodied religious communities, so it’s not just intellectual structures that are affected, but time and place-bound structures as well.”
However, the associations were not uniform across all aspects of faith. The internet’s negative relationship was strongest for institutional belonging and self-identifying as a religious person. In other words, as a population spent more time online, fewer people formally affiliated with a denomination or labeled themselves as religious.
In contrast, the links between internet use and time-intensive practices, like attending religious services or rating God as highly important, were smaller and less stable. This indicates that digital connectivity might erode religious identity and formal membership more rapidly than it changes the daily habits of those who remain observant.
Kent emphasized this distinction. “It’s important to note – to put some larger context on this – that there are dozens, or even hundreds, of ways to measure religion and spirituality, and this study examines just six,” he said. “Of those six, only two show particularly strong associations: denominational belonging and religious self-identification. That these two identity markers change with internet diffusion does not necessarily mean religion is dead, and the authors acknowledge that some evidence shows it’s possible for digital religious activity to complement religious activity in real life, thereby actually reinforcing rather than reducing religiosity.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2018, which found that individual internet use among American adults was tied to a lower likelihood of identifying with a specific religion, but not necessarily a decrease in actual religious activities. The new study suggests a similar pattern plays out on a global scale.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. First, the data cannot completely untangle cause and effect. While past internet use predicted lower future religiosity, the authors also ran the numbers in reverse and found that past levels of religiosity predicted future internet adoption. This hints that religious decline and digital expansion might feed into one another in a reciprocal loop.
Another detail to consider is the nature of the data. The study looked at country-level averages, which cannot speak to the micro-level experiences of specific individuals going online and losing their faith. National averages obscure the varied ways different groups interact with technology.
Finally, the data tracked general internet usage without specifying what people were doing online. The internet hosts vibrant digital religious communities, and some religious groups use online platforms to strengthen their faith and coordinate activities. The current study could not separate secular browsing from online religious engagement, and future studies might explore how specific types of internet use shape modern belief.
“It is important to understand that our findings relate to a particular historical period of rapid internet diffusion,” Lavrič told PsyPost. “There is no reason to assume that the secularizing pattern associated with internet diffusion will persist in the future.”
“Some recent research, including my own work in Slovenia, suggests that online influencer cultures are increasingly intertwined with renewed interest in religion, particularly among young men,” he noted. “This illustrates how unpredictable the future relationship between the internet and religion may be.”
Kent pointed out that human spirituality often adapts rather than vanishes entirely. “Secularization scholars have long been predicting the death of religion, but as early secularization scholar Peter Berger told me once before he died, ‘The world is today as furiously religious as it ever was,'” Kent said.
“The difference is what we are religious about, how we measure religion and spirituality, and if we should expect these patterns to uniformly move continuously in one direction in all times and places,” he explained. “If Elon gets his way and we seed the stars with human consciousness, did religion die? Or do we simply have a new religion and we’re all transhumanists now?”
The study, “Internet Diffusion and Religious Decline: Evidence from 81 Countries, 1990–2022,” was authored by Miran Lavrič and Tibor Rutar.
