TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Pingtung residents can earn gift vouchers worth up to NT$300 (US$9.45) for each invasive green iguana they catch after completing county training.
Registration for 750 places opens at 10 a.m. Tuesday, with six October courses available to registered county residents aged 18 or older, per CNA.
About NT$8.5 million in vouchers had gone to roughly 90 active hunters by July, although 657 people had completed training and obtained permits, per PTS.
Of that total, NT$988,900 went to Liu Tsu-hua (劉祖華) and his wife, whose 5,648 captures put them first in the county.
Vouchers are worth NT$50 for iguanas measuring under 30 centimeters from snout to vent and NT$300 for those at or above that threshold. Trained participants must upload capture records to an app.
This year’s effort could top last year’s record of 130,262 captures, officials said. The county hires professional contractors, but residents accounted for 70% of more than 90,000 removals through July.
Applications will be accessible through the “Latest News” section of the county Agriculture Department website. Courses run Oct. 8, 19, 20, 23, 27, and 30, with three sessions in Pingtung City and one each in Chaozhou, Hengchun, and Xinyuan.

Keelung–Ishigaki ferry service to suspend operations in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:40:28 UTC
17:40:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Ferry service between Keelung and Japan’s Ishigaki Island will be temporarily suspended from Oct. 1, just over four months after the route began operating, per a press release.
Ishigaki City and ShoSen Yaima Co., operator of the ferry Yaima Maru, announced Friday that the scheduled international service would be suspended while the company restructures its operations and works to establish a safe and sustainable business model.
The operator said cargo loading and unloading had not yet fully begun as of September, while operating costs, including sharply higher fuel expenses, had exceeded expectations. Passenger demand was also expected to decline, prompting the company to restructure the business while it works to resolve the cargo-handling issue.
The operator stressed that the suspension is temporary and said it would continue communicating with relevant agencies. A resumption date and future operating arrangements will be announced once they are determined.
The route launched on May 28, providing the first direct scheduled ferry connection between Keelung and Ishigaki. The service offered one-way fares starting at about NT$2,000 (US$63) for basic accommodations during the low season. It initially operated one round trip per week before increasing to two in July.
Keelung Mayor George Hsieh (謝國樑) said Saturday that he contacted the operator after learning of the suspension. The company told him the route could resume during the peak tourist season after operational adjustments are completed, per CNA.
Hsieh said he understood that the suspension was partly related to the autumn and winter off-season and the northeast monsoon, as well as the need to adjust passenger and cargo operations. The operator has not announced a resumption date.

International interest mounts in Estonian scientists' drug-detection meter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:39:00 UTC
17:39:00 KST

International interest mounts in Estonian scientists' drug-detection meter
Researchers in Estonia have developed a portable drug analyzer that can identify both the substance taken and the amount, returning results in as little as 15 minutes.
Developers at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and startup SafePAS say the "Narcometer" device has drawn international interest, and they now aim to make it smaller and drug detection as easy as a breathalyzer test.
When police or ambulance crews need to determine possible drug intoxication at the scene, they currently rely primarily on rapid tests, but whose accuracy often leaves much to be desired. To determine the exact substance present in a sample and its quantity, positive samples need to be sent to the lab for further testing. However, it can sometimes take days to receive those lab results.
If police can find time for additional testing as part of investigative procedures, every minute counts when assessing a person's medical condition. This is particularly important with substances that break down rapidly in the body, for example GHB, commonly known as a date-rape drug.
TalTech researchers and the startup SafePAS have for more than a decade now been developing an analytical device with the English name Drug Hunter, whose aim is to take accurate and rapid drug testing beyond the laboratory. The researchers' analyzer can identify both a narcotic substance and its quantity in just about 15 minutes.
Up to now now, the tech has been tested in close cooperation with the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), but this summer the team also worked with organizers of major events, such as festivals. According to Jekaterina Mazina-Šinkar, an assistant professor at TalTech and the SafePAS founder, the aim was to understand how the device could be used by private individuals themselves. "A saliva test can be carried out on people who, for example, suspect that a narcotic substance has been put into their cocktail. Or someone may have taken something and feel very unwell but not know what it was," the researcher explained.
An ever-changing black market
The device uses capillary electrophoresis technology, which is also used to analyze DNA. "This is a very sensitive method in which we first separate all the substances present in the sample, excite them and detect them with a detector. We then not only identify the substance but also quantify it," Mazina-Šinkar, said, describing how the device works. Positive samples will always undergo additional testing under laboratory conditions too, she noted.
Drug Hunter can at present detect common narcotic substances such as cocaine, amphetamine, methamphetamine and MDMA (ecstasy). The device can also identify tramadol, codeine and morphine, as well as THC.
However, the prevalence of narcotic substances varies considerably by time and place, meaning researchers must constantly keep up with developments on the illicit drugs market. "Research is underway into new narcotic substances, their metabolism and how they can subsequently be detected in the human body. At the same time, so-called classic drugs account for 97 percent of all cases of use, while only three percent involve new narcotic substances," Mazina-Šinkar noted.
The Drug Hunter device tested at festivals and in the course of traffic enforcement is about the size of a computer printer. A year ago, however, the development team received €2.5 million in funding from the Estonian Business and Innovation Agency (EIS) to make the device more compact. The next-generation model, which was tested for the first time in August this year, is already down to about the size of a shoebox.
"The biggest challenge is not simply making the device smaller, but ensuring the reliability of the final result. We tested not only the technology, which we already know works, but also the analyzer's ease of use. We looked for aspects that could be further improved or simplified," Mazina-Šinkar went on.
From lab to international market
The TalTech researchers say their next goal is to render drug detection as simple and reliable as using a conventional alcohol breathalyzer is today. "Technologically, we are already quite close to that, but a distinction has to be made between the technology itself and its official adoption," the researcher said, stressing the role of legislation.
She also noted that greater complexity lies behind even the humble breathalyzer.
"When we think of a breathalyzer, it seems a very simple thing to us today: a person blows into it, the device displays a number and a decision can be made based on that. In reality, this is backed by decades of scientific knowledge and established threshold values. With narcotic substances, it is even more complex because there are different substances with different effects, metabolism and concentrations," she added
All this means that when entering foreign markets, the device's parameters must be adapted precisely to local laws and threshold values in force in the target country. There is, in any case, undoubtedly international demand for fast and reliable analysis. Over the past year, SafePAS has shared its experience with police in England, forensic experts in Germany, and experts in Spain and the Czech Republic. According to Mazina-Šinkar, bringing a research-intensive device out of the lab and into practical use has provided important lessons. "A good scientific result is not yet a finished product," she said, summing up more than a decade of development work. While researchers always seek maximum sensitivity and accuracy, end users are primarily concerned with maintenance, speed of analysis and reliability, she noted.
"Our goal is not simply to bring out yet another rapid test," Mazina-Šinkar stressed. "Our goal is to bring reliable instrumental measurement out of the laboratory and directly to where decisions need to be made."

Echoicide: Who decides which truths survive in Gaza?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:32:45 UTC
17:32:45 KST

Echoicide: Who decides which truths survive in Gaza?
From Gaza to the digital age, visibility has become one of the central political struggles of modern conflicts.
As bombs fell on Gaza in October 2023, Palestinian journalists turned to social media to show the world what was happening to their people. Israel’s siege on Gaza had been intensified, with food and water banned at one point, and the ban on the entry of foreign journalists was likely intended to create a media blackout during the genocidal war on the enclave.
While Palestinian media workers and citizen journalists in Gaza documented the genocide, there were other challenges in sharing evidence of war crimes with the outside world.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4In Gaza, actors perform a war they are still living
- list 2 of 4What’s behind reports that the Israeli army is low on troops, equipment?
- list 3 of 4Lacking equipment, but not ambition: Gaza students try to keep up with tech
- list 4 of 4Ed Sheeran calls Gaza situation ‘unjustifiable’ after Palestine controversy
Human Rights Watch (HRW) documented cases where Instagram removed images and videos showing Palestinian civilians killed or injured in Israeli attacks, claiming they broke Meta’s “violence and incitement” rules.
It highlights a trend of apparent social media subterfuge, which I describe as Echoicide, where a message might not be erased, but the medium through which it travels is weakened to the point that the voice loses its echo.
A social media platform can remove a post or suspend an account, but equally damaging, it can also reduce recommendations, making it harder to find content on Gaza or push users to change their language and posts about the war due to fear of penalties.
Ultimately, a message may remain online, but its audience shrinks, weakening its place in the public record and collective memory.
Palestinian journalist Ahmed Shihab-Eldin, with more than 1.1 million followers on Instagram, has been a key medium for sharing firsthand information and accounts from the people of Gaza with the world.
These included videos of Israeli soldiers committing alleged war crimes, videos of US Senators appearing unmoved by the genocide in Gaza, and videos of Palestinians living under fire.
But soon after these videos or images have been posted, he has found them “disappear” or their reach severely limited for unexplained reasons.
“Some of my posts, particularly the ones in which Israeli soldiers were incriminating themselves, have been used by South Africa in its genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ),” Shihab-Eldin told Al Jazeera.
“People were flocking to my profile in the tens of thousands. And because of that, Meta made my page disappear several times and then started severely shadow-banning accounts like mine that were central to the documentation process.”
Smartphones, livestreams, satellite imagery and social media platforms have made it possible for people across the world to witness wars, including the genocide in Gaza, screened in real time. But it still raises important questions: If information has never been more accessible, why are some wars highly visible while others remain hidden? What happens when a voice loses its “echo”?
Leila Warah, a journalist based in the occupied West Bank, has seen her Instagram account suspended and reactivated several times during the war. But the problem of reach goes beyond algorithms and shadow banning to self-censorship and human impulses, she said.
“The bigger issue goes beyond algorithms and shadow-banning. A viewer can watch footage from Gaza, feel affected by it and then close the app and go back to their life,” Warah said.
“Palestinians living through what appears on those screens do not have that option. Even when the content reaches people, the more important question is: What happens after you press share?”
Digital censorship can be harder to recognise because content does not necessarily disappear, Jillian York, a London-based writer, activist and teacher with the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told Al Jazeera.
Unlike traditional forms of suppression, which can be explicit, algorithmic censorship can leave testimonies online but reduce their reach and discoverability, making it harder to detect and flag.
“Algorithmic censorship doesn’t need to erase testimony. It can leave it online while gradually stripping it of reach, discoverability and an audience,” York told Al Jazeera.
This is an issue that preceded Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and is not limited to this context, but the effects of Echoicide are not new to Palestinians.
In 2021, Meta’s Oversight Board, which monitors and reviews content moderation decisions on Meta platforms, recommended an independent review of whether Facebook had applied its moderation policies fairly to Arabic and Hebrew content.
Meta responded by commissioning the Business for Social Responsibility, or BSR, to conduct a review of the process, including via automated systems.
BSR found no evidence that Meta employees had intentionally tried to benefit or harm one particular community, but it did acknowledge unintended consequences for Palestinian and Arab users, including concerns about their freedom of expression.
But Echoicide does not require a person sitting in an office deciding which voice should be silenced and which should remain. There are many actors and entities shaping what users eventually see.
An engineer can change how a feed ranks posts, while a policy team can change what moderators are told to restrict. A product team can decide what the platform recommends to users. None of these decisions might appear to be a form of direct censorship on its own, but together they can decide which stories travel and which fall short of reaching an audience.
In response to questions from Al Jazeera, Meta referred to a statement it issued in 2023 rejecting Human Rights Watch’s allegation of systemic censorship but said it acknowledged that errors have been made and that changes were implemented to fix these issues.
“But the implication that we deliberately and systemically suppress a particular voice is false,” a Meta spokesperson said. “Claiming that 1,000 examples, out of the enormous amount of content posted about the conflict, are proof of ‘systemic censorship’ may make for a good headline, but that doesn’t make the claim any less misleading.”
Meta also insisted moderation is based on violations of its policies rather than users’ political views and that its policies are designed to give everyone a voice while keeping its platforms safe. Meta did not directly address Al Jazeera’s questions about whether the accounts or content of Warah and Shihab-Eldin had been downranked or otherwise had their reach restricted.
In the wider scope of online censorship, we see elements of Hannah Arendt’s idea of the “banality of evil”, which was used to describe the horrific acts of common people during the Nazi Holocaust against Jews and other minorities in Europe.
The concept refers not just to the unintended consequences produced by large organisations, but also to ordinary actions within systems that produce morally harmful and objectionable outcomes. This can be applied to more familiar and mundane acts we see today than the ruthless and calculated system of the Nazi death camps.
Computer engineers optimising a ranking model, a policy specialist rewriting a moderation rule and a reviewer applying guidelines may not intend to silence anyone, yet their decisions can collectively contribute to systems that determine which stories travel and which do not.
Marwa Fatafta, MENA policy and advocacy director at digital rights organisation Access Now, said the silencing of Palestinian voices cannot be put down to a series of isolated moderation glitches, but appears more “systematic, structural, and widespread” than this.
“Proving systemic harm doesn’t require finding a Meta executive who deliberately pressed a button to remove Palestinian content,” Fatafta told Al Jazeera. “In fact, Meta’s own human rights review after the Sheikh Jarrah protests confirmed arbitrary censorship, attributing it to structural policy flaws rather than explicit intent. But negligence is a choice, and so is how policies are designed, timed, and enforced.”
Edward Said, Michel Foucault and Judith Butler have each examined, in their own ways, how power shapes representation, credibility and whose suffering acquires political meaning. Social platforms now exercise aspects of that power at enormous scales, helping determine what becomes visible, trusted and remembered.
Rebecca L Stein, a cultural anthropologist at Duke University who studies visual politics and digital media in Israel-Palestine, argues that reframing of victimhood can invert perceptions of vulnerability.
This has shifted some global attention away from Palestinian suffering to the perceived injury these images and videos have caused Israel. Claims of anti-Semitism against the Israeli directors of the documentary film NAZA, which documents the systematic killing of Palestinians in Gaza, are one recent example of this.
“The violence of the Israeli state was replaced by the ostensible violence of the Palestinian image. In the process, Israel was refigured as the war’s foremost victim,” she said.
Visibility alone does not explain why suffering in other contexts produces different political reactions. This is where I use a second concept: the Tyranny of Precarity. This explains the process by which powerful actors are able to monopolise the political language of vulnerability, while the chronic insecurity of less powerful communities loses its ability to command the same concern.
Saree Makdisi, coauthor with Ussama Makdisi of the forthcoming book Anti-Palestinianism, told Al Jazeera that the problem is not simply that Palestinian suffering is unseen, but that it is repeatedly subordinated through a “complex of narratives, distortions, carefully cultivated blind spots and forms of denial”.
Powerful actors who possess far greater military or political power than their opponents can ironically invoke fear, insecurity and historical trauma to make their violence against this disenfranchised group appear defensive. Meanwhile, repeated suffering among less powerful communities can become so familiar that it is treated as a background story rather than the crisis itself.
If Echoicide is about whose testimony retains an echo, the Tyranny of Precarity concerns whose vulnerability retains political meaning. Together, they can weaken the ability of a community to be meaningfully heard.
Gaza has brought these questions into sharper focus. Journalists, researchers and human rights groups have documented concerns over how Palestinian content travels online, while restrictions on access to Gaza have made Palestinian journalists and civilians even more central to telling their own stories.
Alana Hadid, a Los Angeles-based activist and creative director, told Al Jazeera that she has seen a drastic decline in views when posting about Palestine.
She says she has witnessed this decline on her Instagram Insights, where her evergreen and fashion content receives substantially higher view counts than her Palestine-related posts.
“We are not fighting simply to be heard. We are fighting for the right to tell our own story,” she told Al Jazeera. “We are not asking for permission to exist. We are insisting that we will not be erased.”

The Moroccan Front for Support of Palestine and Against Normalization (FMSPCN) called for nationwide protests against the government's "decision to deepen and expand official normalization with the Zionist entity [Israel]" from September 25 to 27, the group posted on its official social media on Friday.
Additionally, on Saturday, FMSPCN posted a flyer calling for stopping normalization and "no to the Zionist embassy in Morocco."
FMSPCN's call for protests comes after Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita met in the US, accompanied by US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, on September 16 - the day after the sixth anniversary of the signing of the Abraham Accords.
Israeli media reports that Sa'ar and Bourita are slated to hold further meetings in the US again during the time of the slated protests, as both senior diplomats are likely to travel for the UN General Assembly.
"A representative of the Moroccan Foreign Ministry is meeting with the Zionist and American foreign ministers in New York to issue a tripartite statement stipulating the elevation of Moroccan-Israeli relations to the level of embassies and the exchange of ambassadors, alongside expanding flights and strengthening economic, commercial, military, and security agreements," FMSPCN wrote.
This meeting comes "at a time when the crimes of the Zionist entity against the Palestinian people continue... the occupation continues its policies based on killing, displacement, settlement, and the desecration of the al-Aqsa Mosque," FMSPCN claimed.
"Normal relations cannot be built with an abnormal entity based on occupation, genocide, ethnic cleansing, and displacement," FMSPCN said, "without ambiguity."
'Palestine not a bargaining chip,' Moroccan anti-Zionist group argues
"FMSPCN will remain loyal to its principled position [that] Palestine is not a bargaining chip, and it is not a cause that can be normalized," it said.
"Palestine is a cause of a people, a cause of freedom, and a cause of justice. Normalization will not erase the truth, will not remove the rights of Palestinians, and will not silence the voice of the Moroccan people supporting Palestine," FMSPCN pledged.
FMSPCN considers this "an escalation in the path of normalization... at a historic moment in which all efforts should have been directed toward stopping the aggression and holding accountable those responsible for the crimes committed against Palestinians."
It also "considers this move toward raising the level of relations with the Zionists a stain of shame that contradicts the authentic position of the Moroccan people, which calls for canceling the ill-fated normalization agreements, and directing all efforts toward stopping the aggression and holding accountable and punishing those responsible for the ongoing grave violations against the Palestinian people and their courageous resistance."
"We reject that normalization be presented as an ordinary option or an irreversible path, while Palestinians live under occupation, siege and displacement, and their basic rights violated," FMSPCN claimed.
Moroccan anti-Zionist group rejects using 'embassies, agreements, economic exchange to whitewash occupation'
FMSPCN also "rejected turning embassies, agreements, and economic exchange into tools for whitewashing the reality of occupation and its crimes."
The group restated its "adherence to the right of the Palestinian people to freedom, independence, self-determination, and the establishment of their independent state on all Palestinian territory with Jerusalem as its capital," and "steadfast support for the legitimate Palestinian popular resistance in confronting the occupation."
FMSPCN also "called on all living forces in Morocco, parties, unions, associations, and human rights organizations, to raise their voices loudly in defense of Palestine and confront all attempts to make normalization a familiar matter in Moroccan society."

A 49-year-old Breslov Hassid from Betar Illit, a father of six, was arrested at the Ukraine-Romania border crossing while returning to Israel after spending Rosh Hashanah in Uman, and was drafted into the Ukrainian army.
Jonathan Karlinsky Mashak from Jerusalem, a 49-year-old married ba’al teshuva who studies at a yeshiva, was born in Ukraine and immigrated to Israel about 14 years ago.
He was traveling on a bus operated by the “Derech Tzadikim” company and was carrying an Israeli passport stating that he was born in the Soviet Union. However, according to a friend who was traveling with him on the bus, border officials identified him as also being a Ukrainian citizen after hearing him speak Ukrainian.
They decided to check his details, removed him from the bus, and he has not been seen or heard from since. He managed to send an email reporting what had happened and tried calling his wife twice, but when she called back, she only reached a voicemail message in Ukrainian.
Israeli transferred to Odessa for enlistment
Natan, a friend from Jerusalem, said that contact with Mashak was lost afterward and that he was informed that Mashak had been transferred to Odessa for enlistment in the Ukrainian military.
“He has traveled to Uman for years, even after the war began, and he was never stopped. He probably thought that because he had Israeli citizenship, he would no longer have any problem in Ukraine.”
His wife, Odel, told Walla that she was “very distressed,” mainly because she was unable to answer the two calls he made shortly after his arrest and only later realized that something unusual had happened.
“I never imagined they had caught him. He traveled as he does every year and never thought for a moment that this could happen.”
According to the information she has, her husband Jonathan is being held at a military base near Odessa as part of the enlistment process.
“As long as he is fit, from their perspective he is fit. Until the age of 60 they do not release people from the army. Right now, everything is up in the air. We still do not know exactly what will happen or how we can help him.
“This is not easy for me at all, it is very difficult. But with God’s help, I hope that God’s salvation will come and everything will end,” she said, expressing hope. She and his friends noted that he would not be able to maintain his Jewish religious observance in the army. “As far as kosher food is concerned, there is nothing to even talk about.”
Missing Israeli's wife calls for aid recovering husband
Odel is in contact with the Foreign Ministry but is requesting urgent assistance.
“I believe that the consulate and the embassy will try to do everything to bring him back, but they gently explained to me that anything related to Ukrainian law is in their hands. They told me that what happened was legal, and that is the problem.”
She emphasized the human aspect of the case.
“He has lived in Israel for more than 14 years, he is Jewish, an Israeli citizen, he has a home here and a life here. He is not just a number. Everything must be done to bring him home.”
The Foreign Ministry has not yet responded to the matter.

Following two days of severe flooding, landslides and transport blockages in the eastern Black Sea region, authorities in the northeastern provinces of Rize and Artvin have warned residents to remain vigilant as more heavy showers and thunderstorms approach.
The Turkish State Meteorological Service said locally heavy showers and thunderstorms are expected from Sept 20 in the eastern Rize districts of Pazar, Ardeşen and Fındıklı, as well as Arhavi, Hopa and Kemalpaşa in northern Artvin. It urged residents to take precautions against flash floods, flooding, lightning, landslides and possible disruptions to transportation.
More than 150 kilograms of rain per square meter fell in parts of Rize on Sept. 19, while some areas recorded as much as 186 kilograms, according to Rize Governor İhsan Selim Baydaş. He said rainfall could bring the total to 200-250 kilograms per square meter in some areas.
The downpour caused rivers to overflow in the districts of İyidere and Pazar, leaving numerous vehicles submerged and flooding homes and businesses. Landslides blocked drainage channels with debris, sending muddy water into urban areas. Seven homes were evacuated as a precaution in İyidere, where nine neighborhoods and seven villages were reported to have sustained damage.
Emergency and municipal crews continued clearing debris, draining floodwater and reopening roads. Traffic was heavily disrupted along the Black Sea Coastal Highway, with long queues reported in several locations.
In neighboring Trabzon, 50 kilograms of rain per square meter were recorded. Streets and roads were flooded, some businesses and ground-floor properties were damaged and a retaining wall collapsed in the Yalıncak neighborhood, prompting the evacuation of residents from two apartment blocks.
Trabzon authorities said hundreds of personnel and vehicles were deployed to respond to 144 emergency reports, while damage assessments continued.
The rainfall also caused muddy runoff to change the color of the Black Sea along parts of the coast.
Separately, flooding in Nevşehir’s Ürgüp district trapped people inside a vehicle beneath a bridge. Residents broke the vehicle’s rear window and helped evacuate them.

Rezaei also said Iran’s current nuclear doctrine remained unchanged and that Tehran continued to abide by a religious decree prohibiting nuclear weapons, though he suggested future developments could affect its position.
“Trump’s threats will not achieve any results,” Rezaei told Al Jazeera. “We are prepared for a decisive war.”
Rezaei said Iran was in contact with mediators Qatar and Pakistan and that Doha had relayed Tehran’s conditions to Washington. He said Iran was awaiting Trump’s response.
The publicly disclosed conditions include ending the war on all fronts, releasing frozen Iranian funds and lifting the U.S. naval blockade restricting Iranian oil exports. Tehran has not publicly detailed all seven demands.
The demands resemble conditions Iran previously raised in connection with restrictions on passage through the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway through which a significant share of the world’s oil trade normally passes.
The United States has been conducting operations aimed at protecting shipping and maintaining the flow of oil through the region as the conflict has disrupted energy markets and kept crude prices elevated.
The escalation has increasingly drawn the Houthis into the wider regional confrontation. The group has launched missile and one-way attack drone strikes against Saudi oil and energy infrastructure, while Saudi Arabia has carried out waves of airstrikes against Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen as it supports forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Saree confirmed that the Houthis launched their first attack on Riyadh since the latest escalation overnight Friday into Saturday. He said the group struck “sensitive sites” in the Saudi capital and an Aramco facility in Yanbu.
Yanbu has become increasingly important to Saudi Arabia as an alternative outlet for oil exports amid severe disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi energy infrastructure has also faced attacks elsewhere during the regional conflict, adding to concerns over the reliability of alternative export routes.
The Houthis said their attacks were retaliation for continuing Saudi airstrikes in Yemen. Saree claimed Saudi Arabia had carried out 732 airstrikes since the latest escalation, a figure that could not be independently verified.
The Houthi spokesman also rejected Saudi allegations that the group had launched a drone toward Mecca, Islam’s holiest city, calling the accusation false. Saudi Arabia had accused the Houthis of targeting the city earlier in the week, an allegation the group denied.
Saree said the Houthis would continue what he described as a policy of “blockade for blockade” and “escalation for escalation” until Saudi attacks ended and restrictions imposed on Houthi-controlled Yemen were lifted.
The Houthis have long accused Saudi Arabia of imposing an air and sea blockade on areas under their control. Even before the latest escalation, the group had announced what it called a naval blockade targeting Saudi shipping.
It remains unclear how the renewed Saudi-Houthi fighting will affect the broader confrontation involving Iran and the United States. The Houthis, who are aligned with Tehran but maintain their own leadership and decision-making structure, have made rapid territorial gains in Yemen in recent weeks and expanded their position along the Red Sea coast.
The escalation has heightened concerns over both Saudi oil exports and shipping through the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandab, one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.
Former U.S. diplomat Joey Hood told CNN that Houthi advances in the Red Sea could strengthen Iran’s position in its broader confrontation with Washington and complicate attempts to negotiate with Tehran.
“Iran is now in an existential struggle and is mobilizing all its proxies to fight,” Hood said, according to CNN. He added that while the Houthis are not remotely controlled by Tehran, they rely on Iranian support, meaning their stated reasons for launching the current offensive may not fully explain the timing of the escalation.

Middle powers don’t have to wait for a Trump-Xi-Putin summit

Middle powers don’t have to wait for a Trump-Xi-Putin summit
Rather than waiting for great powers to reshape the world, middle powers can find agency by deepening connections between hubs of cooperation
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Hao Nan is a Susan Strange Associate Fellow with the Helsinki Geoeconomics Society, and a Nuclear Futures Fellow with Ploughshares Fund & Horizon 2045. 
The prospect of United States, Chinese and Russian leaders meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen this November has revived the Yalta analogy. Talk of a Trump-Xi-Putin summit – echoing the 1945 meeting that reshaped the world – surfaced during the first Trump term, and speculation returned last year with the 80th anniversary of the second world war.
No such meeting occurred. However, Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted the two presidents back-to-back in Beijing this May, and Moscow now says a three-way meeting in Shenzhen is possible. The symbolism would be potent: the three leaders around one table as the international order fragments. It would also evoke an enduring instinct – the belief that disorder is ultimately managed by a handful of great powers.
A literal 21st century Yalta remains improbable. Yet its underlying logic is increasingly visible as trade, technology, finance, infrastructure and development are organised through great-power bargains and rivalries.

‘All About Corinne’: When French star Isabelle Huppert plays an extra
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

‘All About Corinne’: When French star Isabelle Huppert plays an extra
At the Locarno Film Festival, Marc Fitoussi presented a comedy in which reality and fiction constantly mirror each other. In an interview on the eve of the world premiere, Isabelle Huppert, Sandrine Kiberlain and the filmmaker discussed acting, self-deprecation and the workings of the star system.
The Locarno Film Festival has long been celebrated for its rich and diverse programme, showcasing filmmakers with radical perspectives, often considered too adventurous for the selections of other prestigious international festivals such as Cannes and Venice.
This focus on making Locarno a showcase for independent art-house cinema does not mean that the festival’s artistic direction takes an exclusive, cinephile approach. One of Locarno’s most iconic sections remains the Piazza Grande. Aimed at a wider audience, with thousands of spectators gathering there every evening in front of one of the world’s largest screens, it features mainly world or international premieres attended by illustrious guests.
On a particularly cheerful and uplifting note, the festival came to a close with the world premiere of Marc Fitoussi’s Ni vue, ni connue (All About Corinne) (2026).
Starring Isabelle Huppert and Sandrine Kiberlain, two stars of French cinema, Fitoussi has made a comedy about the film world, infused with meta-humour, that explores the work of film extras – the invisible yet indispensable force behind every shoot.
From his first feature film, La vie d’artiste (2006), to the miniseries Ça, c’est Paris!, the world of show business and entertainment has been an integral part of the filmmaker’s work. However, it was above all his contributions to the third and fourth seasons of the multi-award-winning series Dix pour cent (2015-2020) that left a lasting mark on his artistic universe.
All About Corinne seems to continue this idiosyncratic exercise in self-deprecation, in which Kiberlain and Huppert had already both hilariously indulged by playing themselves in the episodes of Dix pour cent directed by Fitoussi.
When fiction meets reality
All About Corinne, however, puts a twist on its meta approach: alongside actors such as Sandrine Kiberlain, Diane Kruger and Ana Girardot, who play fictionalised versions of themselves, Isabelle Huppert is cast as Corinne Maclou, a determined extra with an overbearing personality who desperately seeks the role that will finally allow her to prove her talent.
After meeting on a film set, the two women begin spending time together, forging a friendship full of tension and humour arising from the asymmetry in their personalities and their professional, economic and social status.
Seeing Huppert – arguably the most prolific actor in French cinema today, having delivered countless unforgettable performances for Claude Chabrol, Michael Haneke and Paul Verhoeven – struggling as a mere extra from one shoot to the next is, to say the least, surprising and amusing.
The illusion created through fiction does not remain intact for long. When we meet the actor at the Hotel Belvedere on the eve of the premiere, the distant, almost indifferent expression on her face is a testament to the extent of her talent for bringing to life a determined and endearingly awkward Corinne. Accompanied by filmmaker Fitoussi and Kiberlain, no less professional but somewhat warmer than her co-star, Huppert seems, at that moment, to be thinking about anything but answering our questions.
The gap between reality and fiction is certainly one of the film’s key themes. Like most films that reflect on the material conditions of filmmaking – the most famous example arguably being François Truffaut’s Day for Night (1973) – All About Corinne delves deeply into the escapist dimension of the world of cinema.
According to Fitoussi, wanting to make films in itself implies a desire to be in reality: “an improved reality, in any case, as we would like to see it, with the necessary distance that cinema allows.” Isabelle Huppert, meanwhile, stresses that there is a distinction between the reality experienced by actors and that of audiences: “When you are an actor, on the contrary, you are at the heart of reality, in the very making of a film.” Her brief response nevertheless conveys the conviction with which she approaches her profession.
Getting self-deprecation right
As Corinne Maclou, Huppert seems to have greater freedom to shape her character. The task is more complex for the other actors, starting with Kiberlain: despite the film’s obvious self-deprecation, is there not a risk that their roles could be seen as caricatured, implausable versions of themselves?
Yet the filmmaker maintains that “audiences today are used to self-deprecation and actors know how to play with their public image. An actor such as Vincent Dedienne is willing to take on such an unflattering role, while still being credited under his own name”, adding: “It is also a sign of intelligence. I believe that actors ultimately become more like us, almost more approachable.”
Huppert, clearly an admirer of Kiberlain’s approach, says she felt a sense of sisterhood in the way they acted: “It was a good idea to bring us together. I feel that in our acting, we constantly practise self-deprecation, even in the most tragic or melodramatic films. It is something I like to recognise in an actor. You know, people often say that comedy is never far from drama, and drama is never far from comedy. Putting this idea into practice means that we are never completely in one genre or the other, and that also gives the audience a great deal of flexibility.”
As for the film’s humorous tone, Kiberlain praises Fitoussi’s writing and his ability to tailor his humour to each character: “We very quickly realised that not everyone shared our sense of humour. We were very careful because we knew what kind of humour Marc had used in making the film. But there were times when we realised that this or that person could not take the same distance from things as we could. It is a very subtle balance that Marc managed to strike.”
Challenging stereotypes through humour
The film is about more than simply offering a fictional glimpse into the world of cinema. The filmmaker and his two regular collaborators are keen to stress that, above all, it tells the story of a meeting between two people, whose repercussions extend beyond their professional lives.
“The pitfall we wanted to avoid was female rivalry. There is a somewhat persistent cliché in cinema that actors are imagined as tearing each other apart. Yet Corinne is not trying to take Sandrine’s place, and when Sandrine is upset to learn that Diane Kruger has landed a role, she does not seek revenge,” Fitoussi explains of his female protagonists.
The film acknowledges and denounces social determinism and the consequences it can have, regardless of the characters’ intentions. “But to make people smile!” Isabelle Huppert insists. “What I like about Marc’s films, even though he portrays characters living in a certain degree of precarity, somewhat down on their luck, is that he goes beyond the simple opposition between victims and winners. What I find really interesting about my character is that she is never portrayed as a victim. From the very first scene, her constant reactions highlight the inequalities. It is also a purely dramatic device, but one that elicits reactions that are both funny and violent.”

Kars rock art preserves traces of life from thousands of years ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:28:02 UTC
17:28:02 KST

AA Photo
Rock art dating back thousands of years in Kars, an important passage between the Caucasus and Anatolia, sheds light on early cultures in the region and the relationship people had with nature.
Located at a key point on the route from the Caucasus into Anatolia, Kars is among the regions that hosted some of Anatolia’s earliest cultures.
The rock art found in the area of Camuşlu village in Kars’ Kağızman district is an important part of this historical heritage.
More than 100 drawings depicting mountain goats, deer and other animal figures on the rocks in the Camuşlu area preserve traces of the past.
Mustafa Karageçi, an associate professor in the Department of Ancient History at Kafkas University, told Anadolu Agency that numerous rock art sites have been identified through field research conducted in the region over many years.
Karageçi said field studies were carried out under the direction of Professor Alpaslan Ceylan between 1999 and 2012 and Professor Akın Bingöl between 2012 and 2022.
Emphasizing that more than 100 figures have been identified in the Camuşlu rock art, Karageçi said: “Kağızman district of Kars is an important region that contains some of the earliest cultures in Anatolia and is a passageway. As we know, Kars is one of the most important gateways from the Caucasus into Anatolia. As a result of our research, we identified many rock art sites in the region. There are more than 100 figures in these rock paintings, including mountain goats, deer and similar animal figures.”
Karageçi said the rock art provides important information about the lives of people who lived during the period.
“These are paintings in which particularly nomadic groups depicted their relationship with nature, their fears and beliefs on rocks. For thousands of years, especially during periods when there was no writing, people conveyed the message, ‘We were here, and we lived here,’ by carving their own history into rocks through images,” he said.
Karageçi said the rock art has been associated with the Paleolithic Age and subsequent periods.
“Looking at the techniques used to create the rock art, we see that drawing and engraving techniques were particularly prominent in Kars. They took a piece of flint stone, scraped the smooth surfaces of the rocks and patiently carved these images,” he said.

L’Étape Türkiye brings amateur cycling across Istanbul’s continents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:26:32 UTC
17:26:32 KST

DHA Photo
The third edition of L’Étape Türkiye by Tour de France brought nearly 2,000 cyclists together in Istanbul on Sept. 20, offering amateur riders the opportunity to race across the city’s European and Asian sides while showcasing Türkiye as a destination for sports tourism.
The race started and finished at Ümraniye National Garden, with three courses of approximately 100, 50 and 30 kilometers. All three routes included an intercontinental crossing, while the longer courses also passed through the Riva area and along roads connecting the city’s urban and coastal landscapes.
Ömer Kafkas, general director of L’Étape Türkiye by Tour de France, said before the event that the organization had evolved beyond a conventional sporting competition into a broader tourism, promotion and communications initiative.
“We are talking about a multinational race, with nearly half of our athletes coming from abroad,” Kafkas said. He said many international participants arrived in Istanbul several days before the race to explore the city and train on the course, while cyclists from nearly 50 Turkish cities also traveled to Istanbul for the event.
Kafkas said the race had become an opportunity to promote cycling in Türkiye while giving participants access to a course that would normally be impossible to close to traffic. He described it as the only race in the world to offer an intercontinental route, with views encompassing both the Marmara and Black seas.
The 30-kilometer “Intercontinental Experience” course was designed for a wider group of amateur cyclists to take part in the Tour de France experience.
Kafkas also highlighted the extensive preparation required to stage an event under the Tour de France brand. He said the integration process with Amaury Sport Organisation (ASO), which organizes the Tour de France, took around 1.5 years and involved a checklist of roughly 1,000 requirements covering areas including music, podium ceremonies, race convoy management, security, medical services and environmental standards.
Looking ahead, Kafkas said Türkiye could eventually host the Tour de France’s Grand Départ, the opening stage of the prestigious professional race. He noted that such an undertaking would be considerably larger than L’Étape, requiring thousands of personnel, hundreds of vehicles and extensive accommodation and logistical capacity.
Kafkas said ASO officials and Tour de France directors had visited Istanbul during the past three and a half years and responded positively to the city’s setting and organizational capabilities.
“Tour de France is a 123-year-old brand,” Kafkas said, describing it as a major sporting diplomacy platform for France. He added that the growing scale of L’Étape Türkiye reflected increasing interest in cycling in Türkiye and the country’s developing infrastructure for large-scale cycling events.

Delhi pollution crackdown: Hotspots to be mapped, pending road works get Oct 31 deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:22:53 UTC
17:22:53 KST

A thick layer of smog engulfs the India Gate and Kartavya Path as pollution level deteriorates, in New Delhi.
NEW DELHI: The Delhi government has stepped up its crackdown on air pollution, directing district administrations to map pollution hotspots, identify sources within a three-kilometre radius and assign agencies specific corrective measures and deadlines. The government has also set October 31 as the target for completing pending road and civil works, wherever feasible. It ordered tighter action against road dust, construction pollution, waste burning, illegal parking and traffic congestion.The directions were issued during district-level review meetings chaired by Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa for East, North-East, South-East and South Delhi. Officials were told to use AQI monitoring data to identify problem areas, assess the sources driving pollution and take immediate action at the ground level.
Hotspots to get source-specific action plans
District administrations will map pollution hotspots based on data from AQI monitoring stations. Each hotspot will then be assessed for sources such as road dust, traffic congestion, vehicular emissions, construction and demolition activity, unauthorised parking, open or uncovered areas and biomass or waste burning.
Where applicable, pollution-generating activities within a three-kilometre radius of each hotspot will also be examined.Authorities will prepare source-wise action plans setting out the remedial measure, the agency responsible and the timeline for implementation.Locations recording high levels of PM10 and PM2.5 will receive focused attention, particularly areas with heavy traffic, heavy-vehicle parking, significant road dust and congestion. Such locations will be inspected for their pollution sources and immediate remedial action will be taken.
October 31 target for pending road works
The government has directed agencies to complete pending civil works on priority and by October 31, wherever feasible.These include pothole repairs, treatment and development of brown areas and other road and roadside works. Officials have also been told to maintain completed works properly to reduce road-dust generation.Where essential works cannot be completed because other projects are still underway, agencies will have to continue water sprinkling and other dust-suppression measures until the road surface is restored.
Construction, waste burning face tighter action
The government has directed agencies to strictly enforce dust-control norms at construction and demolition sites. Violations will attract stringent action under applicable rules.The ban on biomass burning will also be enforced without exception. Preventive measures will be strengthened against the open burning of garbage, plastic and rubber waste, textile and fibre waste, industrial and organic residues, scrap and other combustible material.
Illegal parking and encroachments targeted
Officials were also directed to remove illegal encroachments from roads and public spaces where they contribute to congestion and obstruct traffic movement.The move is aimed at improving traffic flow and reducing pollution caused by idling vehicles and prolonged traffic movement.At Anand Vihar Bus Terminal, agencies have been directed to step up enforcement against unauthorised parking of buses and heavy vehicles. Cranes will be deployed wherever required to remove or tow such vehicles.
Patparganj gets special focus
Patparganj Industrial Area was identified for area-specific measures targeting road dust, traffic congestion and vehicular emissions.Agencies have been directed to maintain continuous water sprinkling and dust-control measures at vulnerable locations, particularly where road or allied works are underway.
Future roads to minimise exposed soil
For future applicable works, departments have been directed to incorporate end-to-end carpeting or paving of roads and relevant roadside areas wherever technically feasible and in accordance with applicable specifications.The aim is to reduce exposed soil and unpaved surfaces that can contribute to road dust.
The government has stressed closer coordination between departments and agencies, with responsibility for individual pollution-control measures clearly assigned.The meetings involved area MLAs, district magistrates, deputy commissioners of police, MCD deputy commissioners and senior officials from various departments.Officials from the Revenue Department, DPCC, PWD, MCD, Traffic Police, DSIIDC, I&FC, DJB, DMRC, NHAI and other agencies were involved in the coordinated effort.The minister also directed ground teams to maintain regular vigilance at vulnerable locations and take immediate action against violations. DPCC and enforcement agencies were asked to impose stringent penalties, including heavy challans wherever applicable.Officials were further told to ensure prompt resolution of citizen complaints, particularly those received through Helpline 311.

Far from the Holy of Holies: How did ancient Jews observe Yom Kippur 2,000 years ago?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:13:44 UTC
17:13:44 KST

Two thousand years ago, as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur, Jews throughout the Land of Israel and across the Diaspora were fasting. But what else were they doing?
The Yom Kippur rituals and observances practiced in the Temple thousands of years ago are clearly enumerated in the Bible (Leviticus 16), the Mishnah (Yoma), and the Talmud.
During the Yom Kippur Service, the high priest (kohen gadol) offered a bull as a sin offering for himself and his household, and confessed his own sins and those of his household and the other kohanim.
Two identical goats were placed before him, and lots were drawn: one “for the Lord” and one “for azazel.”
The first would be sacrificed; the second became the famous se’ir la’azazel, often translated as the “scapegoat,” which was sent into the wilderness. The Mishnah describes it being taken to a cliff and pushed to its death.
The day’s special status was highlighted by the high priest’s entry into the Holy of Holies, where he offered incense.
While many people undoubtedly came to Jerusalem to see the Temple Service, Yom Kippur is not one of the three pilgrimage festivals, like Sukkot, Passover, and Shavuot, and there was no special mitzvah to go to Jerusalem.
How did Jews living in Beit Shemesh, the Galilee, or Beersheba observe Yom Kippur? What did the Jews in Alexandria, Rome, and Babylonia do on that day?
While the biblical rules of fasting and the prohibition of labor applied to everyone, the major prayers of Yom Kippur that we are so familiar with today – Kol Nidrei, “Avinu Malkenu,” “Unetaneh Tokef” – had not yet been composed.
Did they pray at home? Did they hold prayer assemblies? Did they attend a synagogue? If they prayed, what did they say?
The American writer and humorist James Thurber (1894-1961) once observed, “It is better to know some of the questions than all of the answers.” When it comes to reconstructing Yom Kippur as it was experienced by ordinary Jews 2,000 years ago, Thurber’s observation is particularly apt.
How Jews observed Yom Kippur outside Jerusalem
TO BETTER understand what Jews outside Jerusalem and in the Diaspora did on Yom Kippur during Temple times, I spoke with Prof. Yair Furstenberg of the Talmud department at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Furstenberg suggests that the primary source that sheds light on what Jews outside the Temple did on Yom Kippur comes from the writings of Philo, the Jewish philosopher who lived in Alexandria, 20 BCE-50 CE, while the Second Temple was still standing. Alexandria was one of the most important Jewish communities in the ancient world.
In his work The Special Laws, Philo discusses Yom Kippur and notes that even less religiously observant Jews took the day seriously, a pattern echoed in many parts of the Jewish world today.
In section 186, he writes, “On the 10th day the fast takes place, which they take seriously – not only those who are zealous about piety and holiness, but even those who do nothing religious the rest of the time. For all are astounded, overcome with the sacredness of it; in fact, at that time the wicked compete with the righteous in self-control and virtue.”
Adds Furstenberg dryly, “The commentator here writes, ‘There is nothing new under the sun.’”
Beyond fasting, how did the people observe Yom Kippur?
Furstenberg again cites Philo (ibid. section B193), who writes, “From morning until evening, the people spend their time doing nothing else but offering fervent prayers, seeking to appeal to God and asking forgiveness for their sins, both intentional and unintentional, and hoping for His favor – not because of their own merit, but because of His merciful nature.”
Where and how did they pray?
While Talmudic sources attribute the origins of organized prayer to the time of Ezra, Furstenberg says that the idea of fixed prayer – the formal prayers with which we are familiar – was unknown in Judaism during the Second Temple period.
“We assume that synagogues are made for prayer,” he says, “but Second Temple sources associate synagogues with Torah study.”
Taking the question further, he asks, “Philo says that we’re asking for forgiveness and praying; who knows if there is someone who leads the prayer. Does one pray personally? How do you do it? It’s hard to say.”
If one accepts the Talmudic concept of fixed prayer during the Second Temple period, one could imagine Jews gathering to recite the Shema and the Amida and read the Torah on Yom Kippur.
If, however, Furstenberg’s theory is correct, then the question remains – what did they pray and how did they pray?
While Furstenberg says the standard format of fixed prayer we are familiar with did not exist at that time, the Qumran sect, which existed during the Second Temple period, from the second century BCE until 68 CE, had created its own set of fixed prayers.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, found in caves near Qumran on the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea about 35-40 km. east of Jerusalem, preserve prayers and liturgy from Jews who lived during this period and separated themselves from the religious establishment in Jerusalem.
One of the Yom Kippur prayers found in the Dead Sea Scrolls reads, “Remember, O Lord, the appointed time of Your mercy, and establish it for us – the appointed time of fasting, an everlasting statute.
“You know the hidden things and the revealed things, and You know our nature, our rising and our lying down. We live with sorrow in our hearts by day, and we have no confidence in our lives. Remember our sorrow and our weeping.”
Yom Kippur was not always a day of joy
Interestingly, the sect used the terms “sorrow” and “weeping” (Hebrew: yagon and bechi), which suggests a markedly somber understanding of the day, emphasizing sorrow and weeping with fasting and supplication.
While the Torah states that on Yom Kippur “you shall afflict yourselves” (Leviticus 23:27), Yom Kippur, according to most sources, is not considered a day of mourning.
Furstenberg adds that the Karaites, who appeared many years later, in the ninth century, also adopted the idea of affliction and sadness on Yom Kippur.
In one of their writings, it was stated that on Yom Kippur, one should “stand on one’s feet in prolonged prayer, again and again, to the point of afflicting oneself; deprive one’s eyes of sleep; change one’s clothes and dress in sackcloth and ashes; and weep with a loud voice until one’s strength is exhausted” (Jewish Festivals in the Time of the Mishnah and Talmud, by Joseph Tabory).
This approach sharply contrasts with a Mishnah at the end of Ta’anit (4:8), which states: “Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: There were no days as joyous for the Jewish people as the 15th of Av and as Yom Kippur…”
On those two days – Yom Kippur and the 15th of Av – the Mishnah continues, the daughters of Jerusalem would dress in borrowed white garments, so that poorer women would not be embarrassed, and dance in the vineyards. At the same time, young men sought wives, emphasizing character and family over beauty.
The Talmud connects the joy of Yom Kippur with the giving of the Second Tablets on that day, symbolizing reconciliation between God and Israel after the sin of the Golden Calf.
Furstenberg notes that this passage portrays Yom Kippur as a day of rejoicing. Why did the people of Jerusalem celebrate?
Beyond the Talmudic explanation, Furstenberg suggests that this celebratory spirit was connected to the release of tension surrounding the Temple Service, as the people waited for the high priest to emerge from the Holy of Holies.
Another source of tension surrounded the sending of the goat to Azazel, which symbolized the removal of the people’s sins.
What did Jews pray on Yom Kippur?
WHAT DOES all of this leave us with? How did the people outside the Temple, both in the Land of Israel and the Diaspora, pray on Yom Kippur? Did they have fixed prayers or informal prayers?
Even if they had a set prayer format, there is little reason to assume that they sat in a synagogue all day, listening to prayer leaders chant complicated liturgical poems as many do today.
For many, Yom Kippur may therefore have included far more private prayer and introspection than the synagogue-centered observance familiar to us today.
Furstenberg suggests that for many, the Temple was the focal point of worship that day, and those who were not there had to wait for the results. Something larger than them was happening. “I think that makes sense in an ancient mindset,” he concludes.
We may never know precisely what a Jew in Alexandria, the Galilee, or Babylonia said to God on Yom Kippur 2,000 years ago. Ironically, even today, with hundreds of pages of carefully ordered prayers before us, we can sometimes find ourselves facing the same problem: What do we say?
Prayer throughout the year, and especially on Yom Kippur, can be difficult, and the combination of ritual and introspection can be especially challenging.
Perhaps the challenge of Yom Kippur prayer is not simply finding the right words, but the sincerity behind them.
A story attributed to the Baal Shem Tov (1700-1760) tells of an uneducated man who could not recite the High Holy Day prayers. Knowing only part of the Hebrew alphabet, he repeatedly recited its letters and told God: “Please, Master of the Universe, take my letters and form them into words that will please You.”
His simple prayer embodied the principle of Rahmana liba ba’i – “The Merciful One desires the heart.”

Pahlavi: Iran regime continues to erode from within as defections grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:13:33 UTC
17:13:33 KST

Iran’s exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi said Saturday that members of the Islamic Republic’s military and civilian establishment were already quietly breaking with the regime, describing Iran as having entered an “active defection” phase in the struggle to overthrow the country’s rulers.
Addressing thousands of supporters at the "Cyrus the Great II" gathering in Toronto over the weekend, Pahlavi outlined how in the months since the bloody January uprising, when over 40,000 Iranians were killed on the streets, the opposition had regrouped, adapted its tactics and expanded networks inside Iran, even as the regime sought to convince Iranians that the protest movement had been defeated.
“We are more experienced, more cohesive and more determined today than ever before,” he told the gathering. “Our objective is clear: the overthrow of the Islamic Republic and achieving a free and prosperous Iran.”
Central to his speech was the claim that erosion within the regime itself is continuing. For months, Pahlavi has said that officials from within the Islamic Republic’s apparatus have been quietly reaching out to him to signal their clandestine opposition to the regime.
These members of Iran’s civilian and military structures have used secure channels to distance themselves from the Islamic Republic and side with the opposition. For now, Pahlavi argued, many remain outwardly within the system, retaining their positions while gradually ceasing to perform the functions expected of them.
“They remain within the structure outwardly, but they no longer perform their former functions for the regime,” he said. “Quietly, but decisively, they are eroding the pillars of repression from within.”
Open defections, including soldiers publicly laying down their weapons, would represent a later stage reached once the balance of power had shifted decisively toward the opposition.
Pahlavi placed January's anti-regime protests within cycle of longer period of Iran unrest
During his Toronto address, Pahlavi also placed January’s uprising within a much longer period of unrest in Iran, dating back through several protest cycles.
Rather than portraying December-January’s demonstrations as an isolated explosion of anger, he traced their origins through a decade of growing opposition, from the large Cyrus Day gatherings of 2016, through the protests of 2017-18 and November 2019, to the nationwide uprising that followed Mahsa Amini's death in 2022. Saturday also saw global marches across the Iranian diaspora to mark four years since Amini’s death in the custody of the Iranian regime.
“The great uprising of Dey was not the product of a fleeting burst of emotion,” he said. “Behind it lay a long, difficult and costly road.”
The events of January 8 and 9, when the Islamic Republic launched a massive crackdown as demonstrations spread across the country, had nevertheless changed the circumstances confronting the opposition.
The scale of the killing, Pahlavi said, required changes in how the opposition operated, although not in what it ultimately sought to achieve.
“A change in tactics does not mean a change in objectives. It means adapting our methods to new circumstances.”
Saturday’s gathering was held at Meridian Hall as part of "Cyrus the Great II: From a Great Civilization to a Greater Future," organized by the Cyrus the Great Cultural & Humanity Organization. Organizers had said ahead of the event that more than 3,000 Iranian Canadians and supporters were expected.
The event brought Pahlavi together with Canadian political and civic figures, most prominently Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre, who used his appearance to call for stronger Canadian action against individuals linked to the Islamic Republic.
Canada's Poilievre calls for scrutiny on IRGC-linked actors entering country
Poilievre called for greater scrutiny of those connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps entering Canada, continued targeted sanctions, and measures to prevent regime-linked assets from being moved into the country.
Canada severed diplomatic relations with Tehran in 2012 and designated the IRGC as a terrorist entity in 2024.
Poilievre also spoke of Iran beyond the Islamic Republic, invoking Cyrus the Great and the country’s pre-Islamic history while expressing hope that Iranians would one day be able to return freely to their country and see the Lion and Sun flag raised there again.
For Pahlavi, much of Saturday’s address focused on another battle between the opposition and Tehran: the competing picture each presents of the state of resistance inside Iran. He accused the regime of promoting two central claims – that Iran’s opposition remains hopelessly divided and that no meaningful organization exists inside the country.
On the first, Pahlavi argued that agreement over Iran’s eventual form of government was not a prerequisite for cooperation against the Islamic Republic.
Republicans and monarchists, as well as those on the political left and right, could work together around four principles: Iran’s territorial integrity; separation of religion and government; individual freedoms and equality before the law; and Iranians' right to determine their future system of government through free and fair elections.
“The embrace of Iran’s Lion and Sun Revolution is open to every Iranian who accepts these four principles,” he said.
The second claim – that the opposition lacks organization – brought Pahlavi back to the networks he says now operate beneath the surface inside Iran.
If no organization existed, he asked, how could millions of Iranians inside and outside the country act together at critical moments?
According to Pahlavi, the answer lies in decentralized networks embedded in Iranian society, beyond the regime’s ability to easily dismantle. He claimed Tehran’s intelligence and security apparatus was itself increasingly concerned by their development.
The Iranian opposition leader nevertheless cautioned his supporters against assuming the Islamic Republic’s collapse was inevitable or imminent.
“We must be realistic. The work is not yet finished,” he said. “Overthrowing this criminal sect that has occupied our country is a complex, multi-stage process.”
But the central message of the Toronto speech was that Pahlavi believes that process has moved into a different stage – one increasingly focused on weakening the machinery of the Islamic Republic from within.
“The enemy is decaying from within and is hollow,” he told the crowd. “We are more determined and more organized than ever. Believe that the dawn of freedom is near.”

Russia is Attacking Europe: Let’s Stop Calling it ‘Hybrid’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:13:00 UTC
17:13:00 KST

Let’s stop calling Russian attacks against Europe hybrid attacks. The phrase has become a political sedative. It allows governments to acknowledge Russian aggression while placing it in a category that sits safely below war, Article 5 and any meaningful retaliation.
Let’s call them what they are: acoordinated Russian campaign of covert, warlike attacks, designed to discover how much violence Europe will absorb without imposing a price.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The problem is that each attack is treated as a separate incident against a separate country. The evidence is investigated nationally, the condemnation is issued nationally and any response is left to the country attacked. The campaign against Europe is broken into isolated cases, making a collective response politically much harder.
And it is a collective response that is the best way to respond to these attacks and force Russia into some kind of restraint. Europe should treat every confidently attributed Russian operation as part of an attack on European security, then select a collective and proportionate response from an agreed ladder of measures.
Europe is hardly out of options. It can tighten sanctions, freeze more assets, expel Russian operatives, launch cyber operations and put pressure on the countries helping Moscow, especially China. Further up the ladder come intercepting Russian drones and missiles, protecting western Ukraine from the air and, in the gravest circumstances, direct NATO action.
Largest Drone Strike on Moscow Hits Oil Refinery and Logistics Hub
Most attacks would be answered far below the top rung. A no-fly zone or direct military action would remain emergency options. Keeping them on the table does not mean reaching for them now.
Europe sees incidents but for Russia it’s a campaign
The term “hybrid” once described a useful fact. Russia mixes sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, political interference and deniable kinetic attacks. Sure, the mix is hybrid but the political effect of the label has changed.
It makes acts of violence sound ambiguous, manageable and somehow less real. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys put it plainly: “Russia’s attacks against us are no longer hybrid. They are very kinetic.”
Radosław Sikorski, the Polish foreign minister, spoke in a similar vein, saying on Thursday that “Russia’s hybrid war against Europe has already taken on a ‘kinetic’ dimension” and that these are “on the border between hybrid warfare and outright aggression.”
It’s almost war
The evidence is accumulating. Germany has attributed the explosive-drone attack at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia. European authorities have investigated suspected Russian sabotage against defense companies and infrastructure in Poland, Estonia and Slovakia. Russia has also been linked to cyberattacks, interference with railways and energy systems, threats to undersea infrastructure and repeated violations of NATO airspace.
The Institute for the Study of War, a US based think-tank, says: “The Kremlin is conducting these actions against Europe as part of a series of mutually supporting kinetic and cognitive campaigns.”
Each attack is also as if the Kremlin is checking the cost it has to pay for each provocation. The results have been encouraging for Russia. Poland responded to the Russian-directed railway bombing by closing Moscow’s last consulate in Gdańsk. Germany answered the Leipzig attack by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin. Russia retaliated by closing Germany’s consulate in St Petersburg and its Goethe-Institut centers.
These actions imposed some cost. They were still national and easy for Moscow to absorb. Neither attack automatically brought an EU-wide sanctions package, coordinated expulsions or additional weapons for Ukraine. The extra European cost was effectively zero.
The real target is collective defense
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that Russia could strike NATO territory and then present the incident as “accidental”. The official story, he said, would be that there was no reason to consider a NATO response.
That’s the point. Russia wants Article 5 to appear, in Tusk’s words, “more theoretical than practical”. The immediate target may be a train, factory, airport or undersea cable but the strategic target is the credibility of collective defense. The Kremlin also wants to break European unity and wear down support for Ukraine.
NATO already accepts that a hybrid operation could, in some circumstances, trigger Article 5. The obstacle is political. Allies examine each incident separately, so almost every operation appears too small to justify a collective response.
Europe must reverse that calculation. An attack intended to divide European countries should bring them closer together. An operation designed to weaken Ukraine support should automatically produce more weapons, funding or air defense for Ukraine. Every Russian attempt to frighten one country should trigger a visible response from all.
That would send Moscow a message it could understand. These attacks are failing. They are strengthening European unity, increasing the cost to Russia and delivering more support to the country the Kremlin is trying to destroy.
Russia may be ready before Europe
The danger extends beyond sabotage. “According to all our sources, late autumn and winter will be the most critical moment so far in the Russian-Ukrainian war,” Donald Tusk told parliament. He warned that Russia could extend the pressure to NATO’s eastern flank through supposedly “accidental” drone or missile strikes designed to paralyze the alliance’s response.
Europe is rearming, but many of its new forces, factories and air-defense systems will not be ready until 2029. Meanwhile, Washington wants Europe to take greater responsibility for conventional defense, and the Pentagon is considering a substantial reduction in US forces on the continent, even by as much as 50%, according to the latest reports from NBC.
Russia also retains an effective army despite its slow progress in Ukraine. It has battle-hardened troops, a wartime arms industry and growing experience with drones, missiles and infiltration tactics.
Russia would not need the strength to conquer Europe. A limited incursion, drone strike or missile attack could be enough to test whether NATO could agree on an Article 5 response.
NATO provides the shield. The EU sets the price
NATO remains Europe’s main instrument for military deterrence and defense. The EU controls many of the economic tools most useful after sabotage or a cyberattack, including sanctions, asset freezes, export controls and defense financing.
The problem is that these powers are divided. NATO cannot impose sanctions, the EU cannot command NATO forces, and security powers such as Britain and Norway sit outside the EU.
Ursula von der Leyen has proposed three ways to connect them. A counter-hybrid playbook would list the available responses. An Emergency Security Protocol could be triggered by one EU member and force all 27 to consult. A European Security Council would bring key non-EU partners, including Britain, Norway, Ukraine and Canada, into the political discussion.
The playbook would provide the options, the protocol would trigger the process and the Security Council would build the coalition. The council could still become another talking shop. Its value would depend on governments agreeing the response ladder in advance and arriving ready to act.
