Economic Watch: China's five-year plan to elevate electronic information manufacturing sector
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:54 CST
17:07:54 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly significant role in reshaping the global industrial landscape, China has recently unveiled a plan to advance its electronic information manufacturing sector, a critical foundation for AI development, over the next five years.
The development plan for the electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and the National Development and Reform Commission, aims to further consolidate the pillar role of the industry by 2030.
Industrial firms in the sector with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) are expected to see their combined revenue surpass 30 trillion yuan, and R&D investment intensity of the sector will rise to 3.5 percent, according to the plan.
TO ENHANCE INDUSTRIAL BASE
The electronic information manufacturing industry is a major force in the new industrialization drive. By the end of 2025, China's electronic information manufacturing industry had led the country's 41 major industrial sectors in terms of revenue for 13 consecutive years.
Building on that foundation, the plan presents a systemic framework to strengthen the industrial base, spanning integrated circuits, electronic components and materials, intelligent sensors, specialized electronic equipment and measuring instruments, and the photonics industry.
The framework aims to tackle bottlenecks in key areas and build an independent and controllable industrial base, said Liu Bin, an official with the MIIT.
Liu pointed to photonics as an example, noting that advancing breakthroughs in core technologies and establishing pilot testing platforms for key areas and shared needs will strengthen the sector from the ground up. These efforts, he said, will lay a solid foundation for development and accelerate both technological innovation and industrialization process.
As a representative sector of the electronic information manufacturing industry, China's integrated circuit industry is entering a new phase of rapid growth, driven by the explosive global demand for high-end computing and memory chips brought about by the AI revolution.
Customs data shows that in the first seven months, the country's integrated circuit exports reached 216 billion U.S. dollars, up 99.5 percent year on year, already surpassing the full-year total of 2025.
A semiconductor technology company in southwest China's Sichuan Province has already completed its first half-year production targets, and aims to double its output value from last year, according to its general manager.
TO STRENGTHEN COMPETITIVENESS
While strengthening the industrial base, the plan also sets out strategies to boost the competitiveness of whole devices and systems. This includes enhancing industrial chain resilience in key areas, developing a robust computing ecosystem, and promoting innovation in consumer electronics, among other initiatives.
Terminals form the basic foundation of industrial scale and serve as the gateway through which smart technologies reach hundreds of millions of users, said Liang Linjun, a researcher at China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT).
The plan outlines a dedicated push for innovation in key consumer electronics products, ranging from high-end mobile phones and personal computers to virtual reality devices. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), China's output of core consumer electronics, including mobile phones and computers, maintained a top global ranking.
The accelerating evolution of a new generation of AI is bringing new demand, new product forms, and new ways of development to the electronic information manufacturing industry, while raising higher requirements for basic hardware supply and system coordination, said Liang.
Liang called for efforts to open up typical application scenarios, develop standards for agent collaboration, high-speed computing interconnect, and hardware-software compatibility, increase long-term capital supply that matches innovation cycles, and train more talent with expertise in both AI and electronics manufacturing.
The plan also addresses rising concerns over cutthroat competition in the industry. It calls for timely revisions to industry norms, coordinated planning and early-warning systems for capacity across subsectors, and a comprehensive effort to curb cutthroat competition.
As the "hardware foundation" of the digital world, the electronic information manufacturing industry is undergoing profound changes in its strategic position, competitive logic, and growth model, said Ao Li, vice president of the CAICT.
Turning scale into systemic strength, as well as moving from leading in volume to winning on quality, will be a major task for China's electronic information manufacturing industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Ao said.
Industry insiders say government, industry, academia, research institutions, and users need to work together to translate the plan into results by strengthening the industrial foundation and making the supply chain more resilient.
Such a collective push is expected to put China's electronic information manufacturing sector on firmer footing, with a more complete chain and more active innovation, and to lay a solid base for the country's goals of building itself into a manufacturing powerhouse and a cyber powerhouse, they said. ■

China's August power use tops 1 trillion kWh again, load hits record high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
16:07:16 CST
17:07:16 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's electricity consumption, a key barometer of economic activity, topped 1 trillion kilowatt-hours (kWh) again in August, while the electricity load hit a record high last month, official data showed on Sunday.
Power use totaled 1.03 trillion kWh in August, rising 1.7 percent year on year, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). Electricity load hit a record high of 1.56 billion kilowatts, 49.69 million kilowatts higher than the previous year's peak.
A breakdown of the August data revealed that power consumed by the primary industry rose 2.7 percent year on year to 16.9 billion kWh, while power consumed by the secondary industry increased 2.4 percent to 612.4 billion kWh. Power use by the tertiary industry reached 215.5 billion kWh, up 5.1 percent year on year.
Notably, electricity consumption by the high-tech and equipment manufacturing sector reached 122.2 billion kWh in August, an increase of 7.2 percent. Computer and communications equipment, automobile manufacturing, general equipment manufacturing, special equipment manufacturing and electrical machinery manufacturing saw power use rise 7.5 percent, 7.6 percent, 7.6 percent, 8.2 percent and 12.3 percent, respectively.
The charging and battery swapping service sector and internet data services reported rapid growth in electricity consumption in August, rising 51.2 percent and 37.9 percent, to 17.2 billion and 10.2 billion kWh, respectively.
In the first eight months of the year, China's total power use reached 7.17 trillion kWh, up 4.3 percent year on year, the NEA said. Power use by the primary, secondary and tertiary industries rose 3.3 percent, 4.4 percent and 7.1 percent, to 104.6 billion kWh, 4.53 trillion kWh and 1.43 trillion kWh, respectively.
During this period, high-tech and equipment manufacturing electricity consumption climbed 9.3 percent to 845.1 billion kWh. Electricity use by charging and battery swapping services and internet data services grew 55.1 percent to 114.7 billion kWh and 42.5 percent to 69.5 billion kWh, respectively. Residential power use rose 0.3 percent to 1.11 trillion kWh.
In recent years, China has made major strides in terms of its power infrastructure, helping ensure a stable electricity supply during peak periods and effectively supporting economic and social development as well as meeting people's basic needs, the National Development and Reform Commission said in July. ■

The satellites were carried by a Lijian-1 Y18 carrier rocket and have entered their planned orbits. The launch mission was a complete success. (Photo by Wang Jiangbo/Xinhua)
JIUQUAN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China successfully launched nine satellites into space from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwest China at 12:03 p.m. Sunday (Beijing Time).
The satellites were carried by a Lijian-1 Y18 carrier rocket and have entered their planned orbits.
They will mainly be used for space environment monitoring, disaster prevention and mitigation and scientific experiments.
The launch mission was a complete success.
This was the 17th flight mission conducted by the Lijian carrier rocket series, which were developed by commercial spaceflight company CAS Space. The Lijian series have so far successfully sent one spacecraft and 121 satellites into space, with a total payload mass in orbit exceeding 21 tonnes, according to the company.
The launch schedule for Lijian-1 carrier rocket has been set through the second half of 2027.
CAS Space is China's commercial space company that has launched the largest number of satellites and the heaviest payloads in the country's private space sector, the Science and Technology Daily reported Sunday. ■

US State Department Approves $2.68 Billion Air Defense Sale to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:04:06 UTC
17:04:06 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
US State Department Approves $2.68 Billion Air Defense Sale to Ukraine
The US Department of State has approved a potential Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine for Air Defense Development Upgrades and associated equipment valued at an estimated $2.68 billion, the US Bureau of Political-Military Affairs announced on September 18.
If finalized, Ukraine will fund the purchase through a combination of European financial contributions and US Foreign Military Financing (FMF) appropriated during the prior administration. The FMF funds will be credited as a US capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund via a 1:1 reimbursement framework.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine remains heavily dependent on constant replenishments of air defense interceptors to shield its cities and critical energy infrastructure from sustained Russian long-range missile and drone strikes. With Russian forces launching thousands of aerial weapons every month, securing a multi-layered defensive shield is essential to prevent widespread destruction of key civilian facilities and maintain the country’s operational stability.
The requested procurement package includes non-major defense equipment, specifically S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, and Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, the US Department of State wrote.
Kyiv also requested Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher 1.5 units, mobile launching system modification kits, RPS 202 counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) radars, erectable mast trailers, major modifications, and maintenance support.
Additional elements of the potential sale encompass spare parts, consumables, accessories, repair and return support, software, technical publications, transportation support, and engineering and logistics services provided by the US Government and contractors.
“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic progress in Europe,” the Department of State said in a statement.
The statement also noted that the sale will enhance Ukraine’s ability to conduct self-defense and regional security missions while maintaining that the equipment will not alter the basic military balance in the region or adversely affect US defense readiness.
Principal contractors will be selected through competitive procurements under the Federal Acquisition Regulation.
The European Union had previously approved $7.1 billion for Ukraine under the Ukraine Support Loan framework, clearing the way for Kyiv to purchase American PAC-3 Patriot interceptor missiles via NATO's PURL mechanism . The funding allocation includes specific exceptions to standard conditions to accommodate high-value Ukrainian-made drones as well as critical US-manufactured air defense systems.

Trump Signs Sweeping “Sanctions From Hell” Bill Against Russia Into Law
US President Donald Trump signed sweeping legislation into law targeting Russia’s energy, defense, and maritime sectors, the White House announced on September 18.
Formally designated as the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” often referred to as the “sanctions bill from hell,” the law was named in honor of the South Carolina Republican Senator who died in July after being a long-standing advocate for aggressive economic measures against Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The bill gained final congressional approval after passing the House of Representatives on Wednesday following its passage in the Senate last month.
The landmark legislation specifically targets Russia’s primary revenue streams by imposing secondary economic measures on third-party entities and allowing the president to levy tariffs on foreign nations that continue to purchase Russian energy exports, Reuters wrote.
It also targets Russia’s defense industrial base, major financial institutions, and the illicit “shadow fleet” of tankers used to circumvent international oil price caps.
Critics and foreign policy analysts noted that the legislation grants the executive branch broad discretionary authority, enabling the president to impose secondary tariffs that could remain in place far beyond his administration. Despite these concerns, supporters emphasized that restricting Kremlin revenues is essential to weakening Russia’s war economy as the invasion of Ukraine continues, according to Reuters.
The Russia sanctions bill was previously stalled in the US House of Representatives due to opposition from corporate lobbying groups and concerns regarding expanded tariff powers.
After overwhelmingly clearing the Senate with an 86–11 bipartisan vote, the bill encountered significant resistance from corporate giants—including ExxonMobil, General Electric, Ford, and Pfizer—over potential tariff impacts on American consumers.

Jairam Ramesh attacks Union home minister Amit Shah.
NEW DELHI: Congress on Sunday took a swipe at Union home minister Amit Shah over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging that it was a "Shah Instigated Removal" of voters.Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh said the Election Commission began Phase 1 of the SIR process in Bihar in June 2025, followed by Phase 2 in November 2025 across nine states and three Union Territories.According to Jairam Ramesh, 7.8 crore names were deleted during the first two phases, amounting to 13% of the pre-SIR electoral roll.
Jairam said Phase 3 began in 16 states and three Union Territories in mid-2026. Citing data from 12 states and two UTs, he claimed that 6.18 crore names had been deleted from a total of 36.06 crore voters."The deletion rate works out to over 17% 2. An additional 5.43 crore voters have been issued notices demanding additional documentation to have their names retained on the electoral roll. The risk of deletion rate works to another 15%. This is an unusually high proportion that reflects structural flaws in the entire SIR process," Jairam said.
He questioned how such a large number of voters could still be required to undergo verification after the deletion of millions of names."Thus, a staggering 32% (or about one in three) of voters have had their names deleted or face risk of deletion," Jairam added.
He cited Delhi, Chandigarh, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka, Haryana, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Punjab as states and UTs where he claimed a significant proportion of voters had either been deleted or faced the risk of deletion.The Congress leader also alleged that large-scale deletions were disproportionately affecting voters from economically and socially disadvantaged sections. He further claimed that, in most major states, more women than men had been removed from electoral rolls during the SIR process.Jairam said the exercise had shifted the burden of verification from the state to citizens, who were being asked to produce documents that they may never have been issued. "A test that the overwhelming majority of citizens cannot pass is just a 'machine for exclusion'," he said."SIR is actually a massive Shah Instigated Removal of voters. It is an assault on our Constitution," he added.Tagging his statement on X, he wrote, "SIR is actually a Shah Instigated Removal of voters on a massive scale. Here is a statement on this brazen assault on our Constitution itself."
Jairam also said voter lists facing deletion risks had been made publicly available in Karnataka, Telangana and Jharkhand, allowing voters to check their names. He claimed Delhi made its list public only on September 19, 2026, following public pressure, while other BJP-ruled states and Punjab had not done so.The Election Commission has maintained that the SIR, being conducted after 22 years, is aimed at cleaning electoral rolls by removing ineligible and duplicate entries while ensuring that all eligible citizens are included in the rolls.Opposition parties have alleged that the exercise could target voters who do not support the BJP and its allies. The allegations have been rejected by the Election Commission, which has defended the revision as an exercise to ensure accurate and legally eligible electoral rolls.

Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers.
The independent judge-led inquiry is scrutinising how officers, who spied on tens of thousands of political activists over more than four decades, carried out abuses such as deceiving women into sexual relationships and fathering children.
The inquiry has been running for more than a decade, and is expected to last another two years.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has said she is concerned about the length and cost of the process. It was set up in 2015 and was supposed to have been completed within three years. Latest figures show the inquiry, which has been led by retired judge Sir John Mitting, has so far cost £144m.
Mahmood initiated a public consultation, which closes on Sunday, that she said would help determine whether the inquiry should continue in a different format.
However, those who were spied on say that the Home Office is looking to severely limit or scrap the later stages, leaving the full extent of wrongdoing by the police hidden. They say more than 2,000 people have objected to what they believe would be a cover-up.
The spycops inquiry is one of the longest-running public inquiries. According to the House of Commons, the longest in modern times was an inquiry into a sectarian murder in Northern Ireland which reported last week, 22 years after being commissioned.
It has so far been investigating the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Metropolitan police unit that infiltrated political groups between 1968 and 2008.
The inquiry has heard how the SDS officers formed long-term relationships with women without disclosing to them their true identity, spied on grieving families such as the parents of murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, stole the identities of dead children and lied in court hearings.
It is due to examine a second undercover squad, the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, which infiltrated political groups between 1999 and 2011.
One of the unit’s key undercover officers was Mark Kennedy who infiltrated environmental and left-wing groups for six years. He deceived a large, but unknown, number of women into intimate relationships.
Environmental campaigners had their criminal convictions overturned because crucial evidence gathered by Kennedy was withheld from their trials.
The inquiry is also scheduled to look at the case of an undercover police officer who used his fake identity while infiltrating serious crime to deceive a woman into a 19-year relationship during which they had a child together.
Victims of the surveillance say that the consultation is phoney and rigged as it only offers three alternatives: an inquiry with a narrower remit, one that would not have legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to testify or asking the police to disclose documents to victims without any type of inquiry.
Kate Wilson, who was deceived into a two-year relationship by Kennedy, said: “Whatever the intentions of the Home Office in doing this, the practical effect of them curtailing the inquiry or reducing its powers to compel evidence will be a cover-up, and we may never understand the full extent of the misconduct that has occurred in undercover policing.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The historic failings in undercover policing continue to shock the public. We are determined to get justice and hold those responsible to account.
“However, the undercover policing inquiry was established more than a decade ago, and is yet to deliver justice for those affected, at significant cost to the taxpayer. It’s only right that we ask those affected themselves about the future of the inquiry.”

The UK suspiciously reeks of the late-stage USSR
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:58:00 UTC
16:58:00 KST

The UK suspiciously reeks of the late-stage USSR
“The era of Westminster is coming to an end!” the nationalist leaders of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland declared this week.
John Swinney, Rhun ap Iorwerth, and Michelle O’Neill gathered in Cardiff to sign an agreement asserting their nations’ right to self-determination, as they called on London not to obstruct referendums and outlined their preferred futures beyond the UK, including EU membership for an independent Scotland and Wales, and Irish reunification for Northern Ireland.
In Russia, the meeting has already been dubbed Britain’s version of the Belovezha Accords, and the comparison is tempting because, as in 1991, political leaders from three of a state’s constituent parts gathered around a table to discuss a civilized divorce.
But the resemblance largely ends there, given the driving force behind the Soviet Union’s dissolution was its largest republic, Russia, represented by Boris Yeltsin. He joined his counterparts in dismantling the state that Moscow built, but no representative of England attended the Cardiff gathering, and Westminster has shown little enthusiasm for presiding over its own retreat.
The participants were also considerably more cautious than their Soviet predecessors, so they signed as party leaders, making the declaration a joint political initiative rather than an agreement binding their governments to secession.
This distinction exposes the central weakness of the Cardiff Pact. Its signatories want to leave the UK while remaining within the constitutional framework that holds it together. Their ambitions therefore depend on political and legal processes they don’t control.
Ireland’s experience offers an uncomfortable historical comparison, as the settlement that opened the way to independence followed two years of guerrilla warfare. Today’s nationalist leaders are pursuing an entirely peaceful route, through negotiations, elections, and referendums, but whether London will accommodate them is another matter.
Scotland has already encountered this obstacle. In 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled that the Scottish Parliament couldn’t legislate for an independence referendum without Westminster’s consent, and after the close vote in 2014, London has little appetite for another.
Public opinion presents a further difficulty. Scotland remains divided down the middle, whereas in Northern Ireland, the figure cited for support for Irish unity is around 36% and Welsh independence remains a minority position, however much its advocates have gained politically.
Swinney wants another Scottish referendum by 2031, but his counterparts have offered no comparable timetable and their agreement establishes a direction of travel, but supplies neither a departure date nor a convincing explanation of how they will get there.
Britain’s dissolution is therefore hardly imminent, but nevertheless, London would be foolish to dismiss Cardiff as an exercise in nationalist theater.
Some British coverage attributed the meeting to an ill-judged intervention by Prime Minister Andy Burnham when he suggested that referendums in Scotland and Northern Ireland might be considered if there is broad public consensus, before attempting to narrow the implications of his remarks.
Qualifications rarely travel as far as the original statement and nationalists heard an opening and acted accordingly.
Yet an unfortunate choice of words can’t explain the forces behind this gathering. The more immediate political background was Labour’s local elections defeat in May, which strengthened nationalist parties and created favorable conditions for cooperation and Cardiff gave that cooperation a common platform.
However, the deeper problem is the condition of the British state itself. In 2014, many Scots supported independence because they believed London ignored their interests and governed badly – and since then, Westminster has supplied little reason for them to reconsider, as economic stagnation and trained public services have steadily eroded confidence in the established order.
Conservatives and Labour have each promised renewal, only to leave voters wondering whether either possesses a credible plan, while Reform and nationalist parties have moved into the space created by that failure. Their proposed remedies differ, but their appeal rests on a shared conviction that the old arrangements no longer work.
Brexit sharpened this argument, as Britain’s departure from the EU in 2020 changed the calculation for those considering a future outside the UK. Previously, independence meant leaving a state that already offered access to the EU, but now nationalists can present separation as a route back into it.
The choice, as they frame it, is between joining a larger, more successful economic and political community and remaining attached to a declining imperial center, still occasionally tempted to compensate for its weakening position with displays of former grandeur.
This argument doesn’t remove the economic risks of independence, nor does it guarantee EU membership, but it gives separatists something more persuasive than a historical grievance: A competing account of where prosperity and security might lie.
Cardiff matters principally for this reason. It did not produce a mechanism for dismantling the UK, but it brought together politicians willing to imagine what might follow it and an alternative once discussed separately in Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast has acquired a shared political expression.
It’s far too early to suggest that Burnham will be Britain’s last prime minister, as states can survive years of disillusionment, and nationalist declarations are easier to sign than to implement.
But Westminster’s problem is that preserving the union requires more than obstructing its opponents, and it also requires giving people a convincing reason to stay.

Foreign Minister: Russia's State Duma elections a 'political performance'
Estonia's assessment of Russia's State Duma elections remains unchanged, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said.
Tsahkna said the ongoing elections have been neither free nor fair and had the sole purpose of consolidating Vladimir Putin's grip on power.
"The Kremlin imposed particularly severe restrictions on the opposition and its supporters ahead of these elections," Tsahkna noted. He said candidates deemed unacceptable by the regime, and critics of Russia's war against Ukraine, were excluded from political competition, with distorted registration requirements, administrative measures and criminal prosecutions used to that end.
Tsahkna cited the banning from running of Yabloko, the only registered party running on a peace platform, as "a telling example of the Kremlin's determination to cling to its monopoly on power."
The minister said the absence of independent international observers, alongside growing repression and systematic suppression of the opposition, meant "this political performance orchestrated by Putin bears no resemblance to free elections." He described it as "yet another ritual intended to reaffirm and prolong Putin's rule."
Tsahkna also condemned the holding of elections in Ukrainian territories illegally occupied by Russia: Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. The minister noted this constitutes a clear violation of international law and of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
"Through these so-called elections, Russia seeks to legitimize its illegal occupation policy and create a legal basis for extending its jurisdiction in Ukraine," Tsahkna said. He said Estonia unequivocally condemns this and is working to ensure the organization of elections in occupied Ukrainian territory is met with clear international consequences.
Tsahkna reiterated Estonia's support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Ukraine launched what Moscow's mayor called the biggest ever drone attack on the Russian capital on Sunday, but the Kremlin said the attempt to disrupt the final day of a parliamentary election had failed. The State Duma vote, the first since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine started in 2022, is expected to see Putin's party, United Russia ,retain its dominance in a system critics say does not tolerate dissent, with most anti-war candidates barred from the ballot. Putin has cast the election as a test of public support for the war, and is likely to present the outcome as evidence of national unity.

NATO military chiefs tell industry they are ready to buy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:57:42 BST
16:57:42 KST

Allied chiefs of defence have sent what NATO describes as a direct and united message to the defence industry that allies are ready to buy at scale, and that industry must be able to deliver with speed, scale and predictability, the alliance stated.
The message came from the annual Military Committee Conference, held in Copenhagen on 18 and 19 September, bringing together the 32 allied chiefs of defence with the two strategic commanders, General Alexus Grynkewich as Supreme Allied Commander Europe and Admiral Pierre Vandier as Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.
Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, Chair of the Military Committee, set out the purpose of the meeting as moving from commitments to delivery. He said: “We, the NATO Chiefs of Defence, together with SACEUR and SACT, will do the work that follows from the Ankara Summit, as we shift focus from committing budgets to delivering on capabilities that will enable NATO to deter adversaries and defend the Euro-Atlantic area.”
He added that the conference would address “collective deterrence and defence, innovation and technology, and accelerated adoption of new defence capabilities”.
His language on Russian activity over recent months was considerably blunter than the rest of his remarks. “Over recent weeks and months, we have seen once again the reckless behaviour of Russia, including airspace violations, drone incidents, hybrid activities and attempts to test Allied resolve,” he said. “Let me commend Allied forces for their swift, professional and effective responses to these incidents. NATO remains vigilant. NATO remains ready. And NATO will do what is necessary to defend every inch of Allied territory.”
General Michael Wiggers Hyldgaard, Chief of Defence of Denmark, said: “Today, in Copenhagen, NATO Allies once again show their commitments to strengthening the Alliance, bolstering our innovation and technology and our support for Ukraine. We will do what it takes to defend our common freedom and transatlantic security.”
Alongside the industry message, the conference covered implementation of the summit decisions and capability targets, and the acceleration of allied readiness and the ability to operate across multiple domains.
Allied nations also elected General Carsten Breuer, Chief of Defence of Germany, as the next Chair of the Military Committee. He takes up the post in summer 2027 for a three-year mandate, succeeding Admiral Cavo Dragone.
The line to industry echoes the commitments made at the Ankara Summit in July, where allies pledged to strengthen industrial resilience by expanding manufacturing capacity and removing barriers to defence trade within the alliance, launching the NATO Front Door for Industry and agreeing a Strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation.
The Military Committee meets in Chiefs of Defence Session twice a year at NATO headquarters in Brussels, and once a year holds a conference hosted by a member state, with the next plenary meeting due in Brussels in January 2027.

German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz

German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
- Published
Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future.
These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved.
There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve.
He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau, external.
According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place.
Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election.
How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise.
Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.
But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.
The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig.
Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours.
But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU.
In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away.
"Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down."
He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him.
"He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public."
Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited.
But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him.
The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.
His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave.
Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it.
But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restoring trust in the CDU lay in "listening and taking political action, not in debates over personnel".
But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder.
Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "Fingerspitzengefühl, the feeling for the small persons".
"Maybe he wants the right things," muses Rohloff, but "he cannot communicate well".
Asked if Merz should go, he says it is not an easy question but: "If I have to answer yes or no, I would say yes. There are other people who maybe have better feelings for the public."
Merz has vowed to carry on as his coalition government aims to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms that are finally due before parliament this autumn.
But Sunday's vote brings a danger for the chancellor - that he is already out of time.
The chancellor is reportedly due to meet senior party figures in Berlin on Sunday evening having already cancelled a planned trip next week to New York, in an apparent effort to contain the crisis.
A staunch backer of Ukraine, the fall of Friedrich Merz would trigger further instability in a continent already rocked by warnings of increased Russian aggression.

Japan will provide up to 430 million yen ($2.8 million) in grants to help the Solomon Islands hold fair elections, Kyodo News reported on Sunday.
Tokyo will provide technical advice and assistance to the local election management board to run unified elections scheduled for 2028 in collaboration with the UN Development Programme, the Foreign Ministry said.
"Being strategically located in the Pacific, strengthening relations with the Solomon Islands contributes to the realization of a 'Free and Open Indo-Pacific,' based on the rule of law," the ministry said.
The "contribution marks a significant milestone in bilateral cooperation, reaffirming Japan's commitment to democratic governance and inclusive development in the Solomon Islands," the UNDP said in an earlier statement.
The UN agency added that it is expanding the support already extended to the Pacific country by Australia, Britain and the EU.
Tokyo's latest move is seen as part of its efforts to strengthen ties with Pacific island countries where China has been increasing its clout.
Solomon Islands' Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who took office in May, has signaled a departure from a pro-China stance of his recent predecessors.
After taking office, he announced that his government would review the agreement during his visit to Australia in June.

Earl Spencer has said the relationship between the press and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex “echoes” the way the media treated his sister Diana, Princess of Wales.
In an interview with the BBC to be aired on Sunday evening, Spencer described the press’s coverage of Harry and Meghan as having a “cancerous influence”, adding it would be “beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example”.
He said: “If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant. And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example.
“I’m not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who’s being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life.”
He said Diana was “really brought low” by criticism she received from the media, adding it was a pity to see “echoes of that” in the press coverage of Harry and Meghan.
Spencer’s latest comments come after he accused King Charles of gaslighting him following Buckingham Palace’s response to explosive claims that Charles said “we’ll forget her soon enough” after Diana’s death.
He has made a series of damning claims about the king in a new memoir chronicling Diana’s life that prompted the palace to push back, saying: “The pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason.”
Spencer said: “It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said. I also thought it was a rather poor imitation of the ‘recollections may vary’ quote, which was a much more elegant way of putting things, but in these circumstances entirely out of place.”
He added that “Diana would be cheering from the rafters at this book”.
In response to the claims made in the memoir, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said on Wednesday: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”
In an extract of the BBC interview released on Friday, Spencer said he was telling the truth and described the king’s comments about his sister as “monstrous”.
Asked whether he had evidence of the king’s comments, he told the BBC: “I told friends and family straight away, close friends and family, about what had been said, because it was so monstrous.”
The Sussexes, who returned to the UK from the US on 26 August, have long been critical of their treatment by the media, with Harry in 2021 telling Oprah Winfrey the tabloid press had created a “toxic environment”.

Turkish universities will address the government’s “terror-free Türkiye” goal in opening ceremonies and first lessons of the 2026-2027 academic year, under a directive issued by the Higher Education Board (YÖK).
In a letter signed by YÖK President Erol Özvar and sent to universities across the country, the board said Türkiye is undergoing an important process aimed at strengthening peace and security, national unity and social cohesion.
The directive followed YÖK’s Aug. 27 general assembly and highlighted the significance of the “terror-free Türkiye” goal. The board called on universities to contribute to the process through their scientific knowledge, research capacity and academic expertise.
It asked institutions to examine the initiative from social, economic, legal, political, cultural and security perspectives, drawing on contributions from different academic disciplines. Universities were also encouraged to conduct research and organize panels, conferences and workshops on the issue.
YÖK said incorporating the subject into opening ceremonies and first lessons would help raise students’ awareness of the initiative while contributing to a stronger environment of social peace and security, reinforcing national unity and supporting social integration.
The “terror-free Türkiye” initiative is a government-led process aimed at ending PKK terrorism in the country.
As part of the process, the PKK announced its dissolution and said it had laid down its arms.
YÖK said universities, beyond their roles in education, scientific research and publication, have a broader responsibility to contribute to social solidarity and common values. It urged institutions to show the necessary sensitivity in implementing the directive.

Latvian medical technologies and digital health solutions advance into the German market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:53:23 UTC
16:53:23 KST

During a trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), Latvian life sciences companies, universities and healthcare institutions met with German medical technology, biotechnology and life sciences companies and research organisations in Berlin. The delegation presented Latvia’s capabilities in pharmaceuticals, medical technologies, digital health and the use of health data. The discussions focused primarily on joint product development, clinical research and opportunities for Latvian companies in the German market.
The life sciences programme began on 16 September with a visit by the Latvian delegation to the Campus Berlin-Buch science and biotechnology campus and BiotechPark Berlin-Buch. The site brings together biomedical research institutions, clinics and biotechnology companies. The Latvian delegation learned about the infrastructure available for business development and discussed opportunities for cooperation with German researchers and entrepreneurs.
As Minister of Economics and head of the delegation Viktors Valainis emphasised during the visit: “Germany is not a new market for Latvia’s life sciences sector — in 2025, Latvia’s pharmaceutical exports to Germany reached EUR 44.3 million. This provides a strong foundation for the next step. Our objective is not merely to sell more finished products, but to establish cooperation throughout the entire development cycle — from research and clinical trials to manufacturing, certification and distribution. Germany’s scientific and clinical capacity, industrial scale and market access, combined with the ability of Latvian companies to develop and implement new solutions rapidly, can create competitive products for the entire European market.”
On 17 September, the delegation also visited BIOTRONIK, a Berlin-founded medical technology company that develops cardiovascular care and neuromodulation solutions and operates in more than 100 countries.
From a biotechnology park to a hospital
The delegation also visited the German Heart Center at Charité, one of Europe’s leading cardiovascular medicine centres. It comprises seven clinics and two institutes and provides inpatient treatment to approximately 20,000 patients annually.
The programme continued with a round-table discussion involving representatives of the Latvian and German life sciences sectors. Companies, researchers, healthcare institutions and industry organisations discussed cooperation in digital health, medical technologies, artificial intelligence, health data and innovative healthcare services. The event was organised in cooperation with the German Eastern Business Association, the German Health Alliance and Berlin Partner, the city’s business and technology development agency.
“The strength of this delegation lies in its composition — Latvian companies travelled to Berlin together with hospitals, universities and research organisations. This enabled us to demonstrate to German partners not only individual products, but Latvia’s capabilities throughout the entire life sciences value chain — from research and the use of health data to clinical environments and manufacturing. The sectoral programme included visits to research centres, hospitals and medical technology companies, while individual business meetings allowed companies to approach the partners most relevant to them. LIAA will continue working with the contacts established in Berlin to help the most promising discussions develop into concrete agreements,” said Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of LIAA’s Export and Innovation Services Department.
The Berlin-Brandenburg region is one of Germany’s most important centres for life sciences and healthcare. Approximately 22,000 companies operate in the region’s healthcare sector, employing around 410,000 people. Berlin alone is home to more than 300 biotechnology companies and over 380 medical technology and digital health companies.
Latvia represented by companies, hospitals and research organisations
The life sciences business delegation included ARMGATE, Continental Structures, Double Helix Technologies, GASTRO CENTRS, MentatCore, Olpha, PrintyMed and The Force Latvia.
The delegation also included representatives of the Latvia University of Life Sciences and Technologies, the Latvian Academy of Sciences, the National Research and Innovation Institute, Pauls Stradiņš Clinical University Hospital, Riga East Clinical University Hospital, Rīga Stradiņš University, the Association of Latvian Chemical and Pharmaceutical Industry and Turība University.
Latvia’s offering covered pharmaceuticals, medical devices, biotechnology, health data infrastructure, artificial intelligence solutions for healthcare institutions and laboratory data integration. In Germany, the companies sought research and clinical partners, medical device manufacturers and distributors, technology integrators, investors and opportunities for cooperation in product certification.
For example, ARMGATE presented INCORI HeatGuard, a neonatal thermal care system developed in Latvia. It is designed to maintain a stable temperature for newborns both in a cot and during skin-to-skin contact with their parents. In Germany, the company sought partners for the product’s further development, certification, clinical testing, manufacturing and distribution.
“Latvia has particularly strong expertise in pharmaceuticals, biomaterials, precision medicine, biomarker research and diagnostic solutions, as well as medical technologies and digital health. These are precisely the areas in which we see the greatest export potential. We already have a solid foundation for cooperation with Germany — the Rīga Stradiņš University branch in Stade. Rīga Stradiņš University can help German partners develop solutions for earlier and more accurate diagnoses, as well as provide testing and validation of new health technologies in simulated environments and in cooperation with clinical partners. We are open to cooperation with German companies, universities and hospitals on joint product development, research, technology commercialisation and the implementation of international research and innovation projects,” said Agnese Oļševska, Director of the Innovation Centre at Rīga Stradiņš University.
Trade mission covers several technology sectors
The Latvian business trade mission to Germany, organised by LIAA, took place from 14 to 17 September. It brought together 53 Latvian companies and organisations representing information and communication technologies, financial technologies, life sciences, and defence and dual-use technologies. The programme was organised by sector, combining company visits and joint events with individual business meetings.
Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states. Since 2020, Latvian exports of goods and services to Germany have increased by more than 40%, rising from EUR 1.47 billion to approximately EUR 2.1 billion in 2025. Last year, Latvia exported more to Germany alone than to the United States, France and China combined.
Growth has continued this year: during the first half of 2026, exports to Germany increased by 11%, while Latvia’s total exports grew by 6%. Germany is also Latvia’s largest export market for services, with service exports reaching EUR 779 million in 2025. More than 1,000 companies with German capital operate in Latvia, with their combined investment in share capital exceeding EUR 800 million.
LIAA organises participation in foreign trade missions under the European Union co-financed Innovative Business Development Programme for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises. The programme is supported by funding from the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget. Companies may participate in trade missions either for a fee or by receiving support to cover eligible costs.

China may be building mothership for giant submarine drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:52:13 UTC
16:52:13 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Satellite imagery suggests China may be building a mothership to carry extra-extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles (XXLUUVs).
Images provided by US geospatial intelligence company Vantor show a vessel under construction at the Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard in Shanghai, The Telegraph reported.
Defense analyst H I Sutton wrote in Naval News that two types of XXLUUV have been observed undergoing tests in Hainan. He said China is the first known country to have developed full-size uncrewed submarines.
The vessel has a well deck and a large internal hangar that could house the submersibles, Sutton said. He estimated that it could carry four XXLUUVs in the hangar or a larger number of smaller vessels.
One of the observed submersibles measures 35 meters long, while the other measures 45 meters. They are approximately six to eight times the overall size of the US Navy’s Boeing Orca XLUUV, according to Sutton.
Sutton said the vessel would probably serve as a mobile tender, maintaining the XXLUUVs and keeping them out of the water when not in use. It could also launch and recover the vessels during combat missions.
The XXLUUVs appear intended for long-range combat operations, Sutton said, “potentially including deployment off the west coast of the US during periods of heightened tension or conflict.”

Taiwan to hold 5 TV debates for nuclear power referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:52:03 UTC
16:52:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Central Election Commission (CEC) will hold five nationally televised presentations or debates ahead of a Nov. 28 referendum on using nuclear power to stimulate the economy and abolish the government’s “nuclear-free homeland” energy policy.
The referendum, designated National Referendum No. 22, asks voters, “Do you support the government using nuclear power to boost the economy and thereby abolish the ‘nuclear-free homeland’ energy policy?”
The five televised events are scheduled for Nov. 12 at 3 p.m., Nov. 14 at 7 p.m., Nov. 16 at 3 p.m., Nov. 18 at 10 a.m., and Nov. 20 at 7 p.m. The Legislative Yuan will nominate representatives supporting the referendum, while the Cabinet and authorized opposition campaign offices may nominate representatives opposing it, per a CEC press release.
People seeking to serve as opposition representatives must first apply to establish a campaign office under Article 20 of the Referendum Act and complete the registration procedures by Oct. 15. Those seeking to represent the supporting side must register through the designated representative with the legislature, which will submit its list to the CEC.
Representatives nominated by either side must sign a pledge confirming that they will present the position they have been selected to represent. Failure to sign will be considered a waiver of participation in that session.
Applications to establish campaign offices and recruit staff must include an office registration form, a staff roster and electronic copies, as well as copies of staff members’ national identification cards or household registration transcripts issued within the preceding three months.
The commission said each city or county may have no more than one such office, while the number of staff members, excluding volunteers, is capped at 100. Offices may not be established in government agencies, schools, legally established organizations, regular polling or vote-counting locations, or other public places.
The Nov. 28 vote will be Taiwan’s fourth national referendum concerning nuclear power since 2018, when voters approved a proposal to remove the statutory deadline for ending nuclear power generation. In 2021, voters rejected a proposal to restart the Fourth Nuclear Power Plant. A 2025 proposal to resume operations at the Third Nuclear Power Plant if regulators deemed it safe failed to pass.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s 7A Drones and the North American Taiwan Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Association signed an agreement Friday to market Taiwan-made drones in the US.
The company and association signed the memorandum of understanding at the Asia UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center in Chiayi, with County Magistrate Weng Chang-liang (翁章梁) witnessing the ceremony, per CNA.
Association members then received a briefing on Taiwan’s drone industry and practiced operating drones at the center.
Association President Arthur Chen (陳世修) said Taiwan’s drone industry is at a turning point amid geopolitical changes and growing demand for supply chains that exclude China. He said the association aims to use networks of Taiwanese businesses across the US to promote Taiwan-made drones.
Chen said US government agencies are seeking non-China supply chains and gradually replacing drone systems and components supplied by Chinese companies. The shift presents an opportunity for Taiwan’s drone industry to enter the US market, he added.
Weng said Taiwan has strong capabilities in small and medium-sized drones, while the US specializes in large drones. He said drones could become a key Taiwanese industry as countries work to establish supply chains that exclude China.
7A Drones CEO Dwayne Hsu (許新勝) said drones are aerial platforms integrating AI computing, encrypted communications, sensors, and precision controls. He added that Taiwanese companies are highly flexible and able to customize products for US clients.
The association said the US is seeking to reindustrialize and rebuild domestic production capacity for defense and commercial drones. The partnership will connect Taiwanese technology with US industry to address gaps in local supply chains and improve systems integration, it added.

Turkish Tulpar medium tank fires with Leonardo turret
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
08:50:30 BST
16:50:30 KST

Otokar and Leonardo have completed integration work and live firing trials of the Tulpar medium tank fitted with Leonardo’s HITFACT MkII 120 mm turret, a configuration intended to combine main battle tank-level firepower with the mobility, protection and modular tracked architecture of the Turkish platform, the companies stated.
Before any rounds were fired, engineering teams from both firms carried out an integration programme covering the mechanical, electrical, electronic and software interfaces between the hull and the turret. Functional checks, safety inspections and system validation activities followed, and the companies said these confirmed the performance, reliability and interoperability of the integrated system.
The vehicle then moved on to a series of live firing trials conducted under both static and dynamic conditions, in which the integrated weapon system was assessed across a range of representative operational scenarios. According to the two manufacturers, the weapon system, fire control system, stabilisation performance and overall system functionality met all planned test objectives. They added that the campaign validated Tulpar’s growth potential and its flexibility for future mission requirements.
Sedef Vehbi, Military Cluster Head at Otokar, said in the joint press release:
“The successful completion of this programme demonstrates TULPAR’s capability to integrate advanced large-calibre turret systems while delivering the mobility, survivability and firepower required by modern armed forces. It also reflects Otokar’s engineering excellence and our commitment to developing modular architecture, enabling rapid integration of mission-specific weapon systems to meet diverse operational requirements of our customers. This achievement reinforces the strong engineering collaboration between Otokar and Leonardo and highlights the capability of both companies to deliver integrated, high-performance land combat solutions for international users.”
Luca Perazzo, Deputy Managing Director of Leonardo’s Defence Systems Business Area, was also quoted in the release:
“We are pleased with the outcome and proud to showcase the technological excellence of our systems. The integration of our HITFACT MkII turret onto the Tulpar further demonstrates turret’s modularity. The HITFACT turret is currently the only system in the world equipped with a 120 mm smoothbore gun offering the same firepower as an MBT system, while being capable of being integrated onto a light or medium platform and of employing the new guided Vulcano 120 ammunition for precision-guided engagements. This turret is just one of the weapon systems that Leonardo is able to offer today, alongside the HITFIST family of medium-calibre turrets, which can be equipped with Leonardo’s proprietary 30 mm X-GUN technology.”
Tulpar is Otokar’s modular tracked armoured combat vehicle family, and its scalable design covers a gross vehicle weight range of 28 to 45 tonnes. Otokar says the common architecture allows a high degree of hull and subsystem commonality across variants, and that the vehicle can be configured for roles including medium tank, infantry fighting vehicle, fire support, air defence, mortar carrier, recovery and medical evacuation. The company also states that the platform has been tested in demanding climatic and terrain conditions and offers high levels of ballistic and mine protection.
The HITFACT MkII itself is described by Leonardo as a lightweight, modular and fully digitalised turret, fitted with panoramic electro-optical sights for both the commander and the gunner. It can accommodate either a 105/52 mm rifled gun or a 120/45 mm low-recoil smoothbore gun, and Leonardo states that the design is qualified, in production and in operational service. The firm describes it as the first large-calibre turret carrying a high-pressure main battle tank gun that can be integrated on both wheeled and light tracked vehicles. For protection against uncrewed aerial threats, the turret can also be fitted with the HItrole counter-UAS remote weapon station mounting Leonardo’s new Blaze 30×113 gun.
Otokar, part of Turkey’s Koç Group, produces 4×4, 6×6 and 8×8 tactical wheeled armoured vehicles, tracked armoured vehicles, uncrewed vehicles and turret systems from a 552,000 square metre production site in Sakarya that employs more than 3,500 people. The company has supplied military vehicles to NATO and the United Nations since the 1980s and says it has more than 33,000 military vehicles in service with over 80 users in around 50 countries. Leonardo, for its part, employs more than 62,000 people and reported new orders of €23.8 billion and consolidated revenues of €19.5 billion in 2025. Both companies said they intend to explore further cooperation opportunities.

Dragone stated that NATO continues to expand its operational capabilities across the eastern periphery, reinforcing both troop levels and materiel readiness.
While allied commanders did not dedicate the Copenhagen summit to reviewing specific recent warnings issued by individual member states, Dragone underscored that the alliance possesses comprehensive operational blueprints to defend every inch of allied territory.
The operational documentation, comprising roughly 4,000 pages of classified regional defense plans, outlines response protocols ranging from localized border crises to large-scale military incursions.
The comprehensive blueprints build upon the three regional defense plans formally approved by NATO heads of state at the 2023 Vilnius summit, establishing assigned forces, pre-allocated defensive sectors, and rapid reinforcement routes across the continent.
“Allies are ready in case of escalation. In case of an attack, we know what to do,” Dragone said. “Russia’s irresponsible behavior over recent weeks and months continues to test allied resolve, aiming to undermine confidence and weaken our unity.”
Ukraine, Russia, Hard to Reconcile on Black Sea, Turkish Minister Says
The admiral emphasized that the Kremlin’s coercive tactics have produced the opposite effect, consolidating allied resolve rather than fracturing collective defense.
“These attempts do not divide us. They hone our tools, make us more united and determined,” Dragone added.
4,000-page defense plans
The defense frameworks discussed in Copenhagen represent NATO’s most comprehensive overhaul of collective defense planning since the Cold War.
Under the 4,000-page blueprint, NATO has transitioned from rotational reassurance deployments to pre-assigned combat formations capable of executing high-intensity defense from the first hours of a conflict.
The plans divide the European theater into three geographic zones – the High North and Atlantic, the central European and Baltic corridor, and the Mediterranean and Black Sea regions – linking national defense forces under supreme allied command.
Allied defense planners have focused heavily on logistical mobility, air and missile defense integration, and rapid troop positioning along NATO’s eastern frontier, aiming to deter conventional aggression through pre-positioned equipment caches and standardized command architectures.
NATO officials noted that the plans provide automated response options for commanders to scale readiness postures immediately if Russian forces mass near allied boundaries.
Eastern flank alerts
Dragone’s public assurances arrive amid contrasting assessments delivered by frontline European leaders regarding specific vulnerabilities in collective air defense.
Speaking in Washington, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs cautioned that most NATO member states would struggle to intercept a mass Russian missile assault if the conflict spreads beyond Ukraine.
Rinkēvičs warned that aerial warfare and unmanned systems are advancing at “lightning speed,” warning that Western procurement cycles and defensive preparations risk becoming obsolete by mid-2027.
The Latvian head of state highlighted severe bottlenecks in securing Patriot batteries and surface-to-air interceptors, a shortfall exacerbated by the depletion of American stockpiles during military operations in the war against Iran.
Frontline states have also voiced alarm over deniable Russian incursions designed to probe allied resolve without triggering an overt military retaliation.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned parliament that intelligence dispatches indicate Russian plans include staging hybrid drone and missile incidents across eastern Europe, aiming to portray NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense guarantee as “more theoretical than practical.”
Concurrently, US President Donald Trump stated that Russia has already attacked Ukraine’s allies for “about five years,” treating Russian hybrid warfare, physical sabotage, and cross-border airspace breaches as an established reality facing European partners.

IGArchitects builds tokyo house from field of structural timber walls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:45:22 UTC
16:45:22 KST

forest of timber walls replaces a conventional room sequence
House of Wall Forest in Tokyo, Japan, by IGArchitects explores how the spatial clarity and structural presence commonly associated with reinforced-concrete architecture can be translated into timber construction. Rather than using timber to create a conventional sequence of rooms, the house is organized around a series of structural walls. These walls simultaneously define space, carry the building, guide movement, and frame views. The spaces emerge between and around them, creating a continuous sequence rather than a collection of enclosed rooms.
all images by Ooki Jingu
a strong timber framework opens the house to changing uses
The project deliberately gives timber a sense of mass and permanence. Its structure is expressed clearly, creating a spatial character closer to that of a reinforced-concrete building while retaining the material qualities of wood. Openings and gaps between the walls allow light, movement, and views to pass through the house. Although the architectural framework is strong and clearly defined, the resulting spaces remain open to different uses and interpretations. For the design team of IGArchitects, House of Wall Forest is part of an ongoing investigation into architecture as a durable framework for living. Rather than prescribing how a house should be used, the architecture establishes a strong spatial order that can accommodate changing lifestyles over time.

Pizza dough and TV prison dramas: how Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe survived jail in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:44:09 UTC
16:44:09 KST

It is a TV show about women confined to prison in the US, but Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe found watching Orange is the New Black with her fellow inmates a strange comfort after smuggling episodes into her Iranian jail cell, downloaded on to an illegal USB stick.
The British-Iranian former charity worker was detained in 2016 for more than five years and kept in the notorious Evin prison in Tehran.
She told an audience at the Big Brue festival in Bruton, Somerset, that she thought she would never be released, so did not mind risking her freedom by sneaking in contraband.
This included USB sticks preloaded with Netflix shows. She said: “We watched Breaking Bad, Prison Break and Orange is the New Black. It was very unusual, but it kind of connected us to the life we had before. Orange is the New Black is a whole different kind of genre of somebody who’s in prison.”
Zaghari-Ratcliffe also danced with her fellow prisoners to contraband Zumba videos and cooked pizza for them in an oven she managed to cobble together money for and have sent to the prison. “I was the queen of the pizza dough in prison,” she said.
She also discussed how she got permission to use the prison sewing machine, which helped her pass the time as she sewed clothes for her young daughter and her friends, the other prisoners.
This newfound artistic hobby spawned a collaboration with London’s Imperial War Museum and the fabric department of Liberty, creating three new prints that explored her experience as a prisoner.
The riskiest item of contraband she snuck into prison was a Swiss Army knife. She said: “I realised, they don’t care what I do. I’m just a political hostage. So I can basically do anything in prison. I can be naughty. I can smuggle things, and once I smuggled this massive whopping Swiss knife.”
She placed it in her shoe, but said: “It was so chunky, I just couldn’t walk. Having a knife in prison is a real crime. But I felt if they had found it, they would have given me what sentence? I was already in prison, and they couldn’t have done anything else to me.”
Zaghari-Ratcliffe was released in March 2022 after the then Conservative government paid back a multimillion debt the UK owed to Iran. The Iranian regime had accused her of spying – a charge she denied and for which no evidence was ever produced.
It became increasingly clear she was being held as a state hostage to try to force the UK to pay back its debt arising from a military deal struck with the deposed Shah of Iran.
Though she is still traumatised by her time in prison and is visiting a therapist, Zaghari-Ratcliffe said she had continued to find solace in sewing.
“When the military attack on Iran happened at the end of February, for five days, I didn’t do anything. I just couldn’t do anything. The only thing that I could do was sit at my sewing machine and sew,” she said.
“I thought, I don’t even know where my parents are. There was an internet blackout for a good two months, and I just couldn’t control the world around me, but I could control my own world. Sewing was the only thing that could calm me down. So yes, still, that’s still my refuge.”

'Voices From The Last Days Of Freedom': Showcasing the pre-communist Cuba we lost - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:33 UTC
16:37:33 KST

Cuban American Genie Milgrom is a researcher, historian, and author who has published extensively about her family’s connections to Medieval Spain. In The Cuba We Lost: Voices From The Last Days Of Freedom, she revisits the period from January 1, 1959, when president Fulgencio Batista fled the island, to the 1962 Bay of Pigs invasion.
Below are some excerpts from her book, which showcases the personal accounts of those who were young children when they fled with – or without – their parents and families as Communism took over. And while, as Milgrom notes, the Cuban exiles went on to thrive and contribute vastly to the United States, I am reminded of a 1967 Spanish-language song by singer-songwriter Luis Aguilé that expresses the feelings this book lovingly revisits: “When I left Cuba, I lost my life, I lost my love... I left my heart buried.”
From the introduction
This is not an easy book to write, as I find myself reading and recalling events and emotions that had been kept hidden deep inside me for more than six decades. As I recount my own history and read and listen to the stories of the contributors to this book, I do so with tears in my eyes...
I read the accounts of dolls’ heads being yanked off, of a soldier taking the doll away from a toddler, or of witnessing a bombing in a department store in Cuba, and the pain is palpable.
January 1, 1959, at 3 a.m., Fulgencio Batista fled Cuba after having been in power for seven years.
At the exact moment that the wheels lifted off the ground toward the Dominican Republic, the Communist regime of Fidel Castro claimed victory over the island nation. Rebel forces quickly entered major cities, including Havana. Fidel Castro began a triumphal journey across Cuba and entered Havana on January 8. A provisional government headed by president Manuel Urrutia was established, while revolutionary leaders began to gain control of the military, police, and government institutions. The first trials and investigations of former Batista officials also began during this same period.
The dominant mood across much of Cuba was one of celebration, hope, and expectation. Large crowds welcomed the rebel leaders, believing that democratic elections, along with a constitutional government, as well as political freedoms, would soon be restored.
At the same time, families connected to the previous government, the military, and especially the business sector experienced major anxiety about the future. While optimism remained widespread, the first signs of political division and uncertainty were beginning to emerge underneath the revolutionary enthusiasm.
Perla Abrams, nee Ziegenhirt, recalls
My uncle was ministro de gobernación, a member of Batista’s cabinet; we have translated it as “secretary of state” in the past. His name was Santiago Rey Perna. My dad was a captain of police but served as my uncle’s assistant.
We left Cuba and went to Santiago de Chile, where we stayed for a few months; then we traveled to Mexico City before settling in Miami. I was five years old in 1959 when my family had to flee Havana.
The revolution was successful, and the barbudos [“bearded ones”] wanted to apprehend my uncle. My uncle was part of Batista’s regime and, with my aunt and father, took refuge in the Chilean embassy. The ambassador was extremely brave and risked a great deal by not giving them access to my relatives seeking asylum. They did manage to escape and reach Chile, where the rest of the family soon followed.
There were beautiful memories... My pretty cousin turning 15 and having the party of the season. It was very glamorous, with all the debutantes of that time attending. A platform was constructed over the swimming pool which connected all our family homes in Santa Fe to serve as the dance floor. The beauty of this remains with me still.
... my father surprising me with a “chemis” dress in my size, which was all the rage in Havana, and high-heeled shoes also in my size to go with it. That was a good memory that I cherish.
I remember my aunt’s breakfast room, which had a tree with a little real monkey that I found fascinating, and I also recall my uncle’s collection of cat statues... beautiful cats made of all kinds of materials. We subsequently heard that the collection had been sent to Russia after the revolution.
Little did I know that this beautiful life would soon end.
My mother, brothers, and I flew to Nassau... until we were able to reunite in Chile with the rest of the family. Our lives would never be the same.
I recall my mother telling me that our house staff were the people ransacking our home after the revolution, and how they removed all my beautiful dresses. I have a mental image of this happening, but it materialized from my mother’s story and not from witnessing it.
The rest of the memories of that glorious golden age arise from family stories: My father saying how no fruit was ever sweeter than our Cuban fruit and how our sugar was so superior to others that you only needed a fraction of what you use now to sweeten your coffee. How there were no better mangos or avocados; and so much more.
My father would tell me how lucky we were and proudly describe the high modern standard of living enjoyed by Cubans in Havana in the 1950s... He would explain how generous the US was in its negotiations with us for the purchase of our sugar, for example.
My parents so loved their country, and they could never fully accept that they would not be returning. My father and two cousins all fought in the Bay of Pigs invasion and spent two years in prison until the Kennedy administration traded farm equipment for their freedom. That was an especially dark period in my childhood. My mom was left alone with three small children, with only the support of my dad’s family.
It must have been extremely hard for him to do, but he felt it was his duty to fight for Cuba’s freedom. The day the men returned, we picked my dad up at Dinner Key Auditorium [in Miami, where 10,000 Cuban exiles gathered on December 23-24, 1962, to welcome home the freed prisoners of Brigade 2506 following the Bay of Pigs invasion], and this was the day of the greatest joy in our family history. ■
By Genie Milgrom
Milgrom Publishing
300 pages; $20
