Most Israeli Jews fast on Yom Kippur, while over half take part in prayer services, survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:23 UTC
16:37:23 KST

Three-quarters (74%) of all Israeli Jews fast on Yom Kippur while over half (57%) participate in the day’s prayers, a new survey from the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) found.
About 63% of Israeli Jews fast fully and 11% fast partially (part of the day or in some years), but the figure varies across secular, religious, and non-religious traditional Jews.
Among secular Jews, less than half (47%) fast on Yom Kippur, with 28% fasting fully and 19% partially, while the number among non-religious traditional Jews and religous Jews is significantly higher.
Some 90% non-religious traditional Jews fast on Yom Kippur (77% fully and 13% partially), and 97%–98% of Haredi (ultra-Orthodox), religious, and religious-traditional Jews fast fully.
According to the survey, more Mizrahi Jews fast on Yom Kippur than Ashkenazi Jews and those of mixed background, with 81% Mizrahi Jews fasting fully and just about half (50.5%) of Ashkenazi Jews doing the same.
Only a small number of those who reported fasting partially or not at all are older, according to the survey data, suggesting the reasons are more linked to health or principle.
There is little variance between the genders of those who fast, the survey found, as 65% of men fast fully, compared to 61% of women. By contrast, 13% of women fast partially, compared with 10% of men.
A breakdown by age shows that the gender difference exists only among the aged 18–44; among those over 44, the proportion who fast fully is the same for men and women.
How many Israeli Jews participate in Yom Kippur prayers?
Of those who participate in Yom Kippur prayer services, 51% attend Orthodox services while a minority (6%) attend Reform or Conservative services.
Most religious-traditional Jews (90%) participate in Yom Kippur prayers.
Among non-religious traditional Jews, 67% participate (9% in non-Orthodox services), and among secular Jews, the number drops further, with only 20% participating (7% in non-Orthodox services).
In total, between a fifth and a quarter of Haredi, religious, religious-traditional, and non-religious traditional Jews participate in Yom Kippur prayer services, alongside 11% of secular Jews.
Of those who participate in Reform or Conservative services, half are secular and 48% are traditional.
Men participate in Yom Kippur prayers at a slightly higher rate than women, with the difference reflected clearly in Orthodox prayer services, where 54% of men participate in Orthodox prayer on Yom Kippur, compared with 48% of women.
Another 6% of both men and women participate in Reform or Conservative prayer services.
Differences across gender
Differences between participants genders are also pronounced among traditional groups, with 76% of men and 56% of women participating.
Mizrahi Jews also participate in Yom Kippur prayers at a higher rate (68%) than Ashkenazi Jews and those of mixed background, with the numbers at about half (50% and 51%, respectively).
However, non-religious traditional Mizrahi Jews have a lower rate of prayer participation which sits at 63% while that Ashkenazi Jews (74%) and people of mixed background (76%) is slightly higher.
Among secular Jews, the rate of Yom Kippur prayer participation among Mizrahi (22%), mixed (22%), and Ashkenazi Jews (18%) is similar.
For 18% of Israeli Jews, attending synagogue on Yom Kippur is their only synagogue visit of the entire year, including 37% of non-religious traditional Jews, 21% of religious-traditional Jews, and 16% of secular Jews.
Among those who attend synagogue services on Yom Kippur, 32% say it is their only synagogue visit during the year.
The survey was conducted by the Israel Democracy Institute in July–August 2026 for the "Religion and State in Israel Biannual,” with a sample of 1,002 Jewish respondents aged 18 and over, and was representative of Israel's Jewish population. The fieldwork was conducted by IPanel. The maximum sampling error is 3.1%.

Thousands of IRGC, Basij volunteers march through Tehran in show of defiance against US, Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:17 UTC
16:37:17 KST

Hundreds of thousands of Iranians participated on Friday in a rally organized by the regime in Tehran, in the largest display of defiance of its kind since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Participants said they were prepared to take up arms and defend the country after months of war and a worsening economic situation in Iran, the Associated Press reported.
The rally was held as part of an initiative called “Janfada Iran,” meaning “those who sacrifice their lives for Iran.” Participants marched through central Tehran in combat uniforms and carried flags, while crowds along the streets cheered them on. Some protesters stepped on US and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.”
In the days before the rally, state media called on the public to join the initiative and announced that limited training in the use of assault rifles would soon begin.
The volunteers are intended to serve as an additional layer of defense alongside the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij militia, which has played a central role over the years in suppressing protests against the regime.
Tehran IRGC commander General Hassan Hassanzadeh told state television that more than 600,000 people had already registered for the program and that the regime expects more than 1 million people to participate in training. Iranian television estimated that more than 300,000 people took to the streets of the capital on Friday, although the figures could not be independently verified.
Basij head says recruits will be 'nightmare' for Iran's enemies
The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, announced at the opening of the rally that the volunteers would be ready for “comprehensive defense” and that similar events would soon be held in additional cities. He said the new recruits would become a “nightmare” for Iran’s enemies.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders, and other senior regime officials watched the parade.
“I came to tell Trump that we Iranians are not afraid of his threats against our homeland,” said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her husband and young child. “No one throughout history has managed to invade Iran and remain there.”
The rally also served as an opportunity for the regime to display military equipment. Air defense systems were deployed on the streets, and female IRGC fighters wearing black head coverings were seen alongside machine guns mounted on vehicles.
The IRGC also displayed drones of the type used in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran claims responsibility for tanker attack in Strait of Hormuz
At the same time as the events in Tehran, Iran claimed responsibility for an attack on the oil tanker Trend, sailing under the flag of Togo.
According to state television, the tanker was targeted because of what it described as an “illegal attempt” to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a vessel was struck by a projectile and that a fire broke out onboard, which was later extinguished.
According to UKMTO, the number of vessels passing with US military assistance off the coast of Oman averaged 24 per day over the past week. However, overall maritime traffic in the area remains about 90% lower than in the period before the war.
Iranian attacks and threats in the strait have severely disrupted oil and natural gas shipments from Gulf countries to markets around the world.
Expanded Basij enables greater suppression of future protests
According to AP, the recruitment initiative also has domestic significance: expanding forces aligned with the Basij could strengthen the regime’s ability to suppress future protests.
In January, shortly before the outbreak of the war, Iran saw some of the largest nationwide demonstrations in the country’s history. The protests began over the economic crisis and expanded into calls against the government.
Human rights activists claimed that more than 7,000 people were killed in the crackdown on the protests and that tens of thousands were arrested.
In May, government officials claimed that more than 30 million of Iran’s roughly 90 million residents had volunteered through an online form or at public events to sacrifice their lives for the regime.

Expansive exhibition in Jaffa gives Gaza border artists a chance to air their trauma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:16 UTC
16:37:16 KST

As emotive art showings go, Voices from the Gaza Envelope has most of them beat. The voluminous group exhibition opened at the Amiad Center in Jaffa on September 14 and features more than 200 works from some 75 artists. The vast majority of them come from our southern communities near the border with Gaza and, hence, experienced the horrors of Oct. 7, 2023, firsthand.
Shosh Segev certainly did. On that fateful day, the septuagenarian multidisciplinary artist was at home, on Kibbutz Kfar Aza, with her husband, Benzi. “Our house is right next to the young people’s quarter,” she explains. “There were terrorists inside the residential secure spaces (mamad) in those homes,” she adds.
The Tree of Life
When the IDF eventually made it to Kfar Aza, just 5 km. east of Gaza, one of the soldiers tried to pry the Hamas gunmen out by using a bulldozer to smash the windows of their hideouts. Unfortunately, when he reversed towards Segev’s house, he knocked down a Prosopis cineraria tree. However, that mishap turned out to be a cloud with a life-saving silver lining.
“The tree, which was massive, probably 6 meters or more tall, crashed into our balcony,” Segev recalls. “It blocked the sliding glass doors at the rear of our house. When the terrorists ran out of our neighbors’ mamads, they couldn’t get into our house from the back, because of the tree. Since then, I call it the Tree of Life.”
For the past three years, Segev, who has several works on show in Jaffa, and her husband have been living at Kibbutz Shefayim along with some 100 other families from Kfar Aza. That’s a long time to be in temporary accommodation. She says she and Benzi have been given another year to stay at Shefayim before they return to their – by then – rebuilt domicile down south.
“Benzi doesn’t want to go back at all, and I am ambivalent about it.” She says they have a persistent feeling their home has been violated. “I used to live by the maxim that my home is my castle, a place where I can feel safe and secure. But that isn’t the case anymore, not since Oct. 7. Now I’m afraid to go back home.”
That sounds like a challenging state of affairs but, like all the exhibitors in Jaffa, at least Segev has an outlet for her trauma, her fears, and her pain. But you won’t see that too clearly in her work. She primarily engages in painting, but there are also merry papier-mâché figures in her extensive portfolio. The latter seem to burst with bright, rich colors, exuding a sense of optimism and hope. Neither of those sentiments is in generous supply these days for many of us, particularly among the likes of Segev, who still bear the deep-set scars of that terrible day.
But, unlike the majority of the other exhibitors, you couldn’t tell that from her post-Oct. 7 work. “If I feel down, I wait until my mood lifts before I get back to work,” she notes. “I can’t create out of depression. For me that just doesn’t work.” Segev’s acrylic paintings are mostly awash with color, and convey a sense of joie de vivre. Her slot in the Jaffa collection, which was curated by Iris Elhanani and initiated by the Gershoni Foundation to support artists from the Sha’ar Hanegev region, in collaboration with the Sha’ar Hanegev Regional Council and the Sha’ar Hanegev Community Center, takes in a couple of paintings and a fetching polychromic mischievous-looking papier-mâché character.
Stubborn as goats
Daniel Ohana’s brace in the exhibition grabs the eye and also tugs on the heartstrings with gusto. He clearly has a thing about goats. His mosaic-looking paintings present the sturdy milk-giving farm animal in an alluring manner that imparts something of a sense of the creature’s subconscious. “The goat is an animal of contradictions,” he explains. “It can fall prey but it is also more readily associated with survival in extreme living conditions.”
Ohana takes the metaphor a step further, into national climes. “For me, it symbolizes the character of our nation: stubborn, fearless, always pushing itself to climb higher towards the summit, against all odds.” Stirring words indeed, and his artwork is no less moving and impressive.
He has the existential Oct. 7-related credentials for his place in the exhibition. “I am a born and bred resident of Sderot and have always lived in the shadow of war. And having experienced Oct. 7 close up, for me my attraction to this figure [of a goat] is essential escapism.”
That comes through in spades in his delectably crafted paintings. “Through these two works I chose to take the experience of survival – collective and my own – and transpose it to an animal that refuses to succumb to the conditions that nature puts before it,” he declares. “This is an attempt to find strength, beauty and optimism in a place where it is all too easy to fall, and to remind us that we too, just like the goat, are always climbing.”
Bringing in the crowds
There are, indeed, positive messages to be gleaned right across the spread that fills the cavernous venue, which, Elhanani informs me, was made available gratis by the Municipality of Tel Aviv. “They and Mayor [Ron] Huldai have been very supportive,” she says.
The curator also pulled out several stops to help Gaza border artists get their lives back on creative track. She was instrumental in organizing an auction of works by Israeli artists in London, with the proceeds going to funding the establishment of studio facilities for evacuated artists.
She is well-versed in the work and lives of many of the artists, and is delighted to have the opportunity to push their art out there, to culture consumers of all ilks. The Amiad Center, she says, fits the bill on various levels. “It is a very large space. It is a wonderful venue. And we get thousands of people coming to see exhibitions here. I’ve curated shows that have drawn 25,000 visitors.”
That’s pretty good going, and a traffic volume which Establishment art repositories such as the Tel Aviv Museum would be more than happy to bring in. Not disparaging the Jaffa location one iota, I still wondered whether Elhanani might have been happier to have Voices from the Gaza Envelope run over at the more prestigious downtown venue on Shaul Hamelech Street. “Yes, of course, I’d like the Tel Aviv Museum to take the exhibition on. The question is whether they would want to.” Her intonation and facial expression clearly conveyed her skeptical take on that.
From the collective to the personal
Oct. 7, And all its corporeal and emotional fallout, comes through time and again across the display, and in all sorts of guises. Limor Klein Tivoli went for a definitive military apparel hook and embroidered a broad range of faux military unit insignia that tell the story of that cataclysmic event down south going on three years ago now, in her own unique way.
Her set goes by the highly suggestive moniker Where Did You Serve? It comprises a complement to a series she called Trauma Treatment, which she contributed to the Women Relate War: Voices from the Front exhibition, which took place earlier this year. That show, in turn, fed off stories related by female soldiers who took part in running battles with the Hamas terrorists on and immediately after Oct. 7, 2023. “This body of work was inspired by my encounter with the testimonies of female combat soldiers following the events of Oct. 7,” Klein Tivoli says.
The line she took was to try to portray some of that battlefield emotional detritus in physical aesthetic form. “I focused on the way in which trauma continues to be absorbed into the body, in memory and daily life, even after the actual event is over,” she explains.
Where Did You Serve? was sparked by the testimony of a particular soldier. “She is dealing with PTSD. Her story served as conceptual raw material for looking at the possibility of translating an ongoing psychological experience into visual language, and examining the tension that exists between the female experience and the military system which is associated with codes of strength, hierarchy and belonging.”
That led directly to Klein Tivoli’s choice of epaulet insignia, and the way she flexed military aesthetics into a very different philosophical domain. “The insignia – a definitive symbol of identity, belonging and role – are diverted away from the original meaning. They stop representing a military unit and become repositories of personal memory, vulnerability and resilience,” she expounds. “They enable us to consider the relationship between the collective and the individual, force and fragility, and between an institutional symbol and personal testimony.”
Klein Tivoli manages that artfully by delicately crafting designs that, at first glance, appear to be bona fide army shoulder tags. But as you spend a 
moment or two getting into the colorful compositions, the finer details begin to filter through with their patently non-military components, and extramural line of thought and execution. That is partly a result of the time Klein Tivoli spent in Japan, where she learned to note and leverage the minutiae of everyday life around her.
Blood flowers across the earth
There are so many images that flash before our eyes when we recall the carnage at the Nova Festival and the kibbutzim and moshavim near the border with Gaza. The color red has dual, and ambivalent, significance for that area of the country. Nature lovers may be familiar with the Darom Adom – Red South – festival, which takes place there towards the end of winter when the whole region is swamped by anemones as the normally arid plains sprout thousands of the beloved red flower.
Yaffa Solomon took that ubiquitous seasonal highlight and ran with it every which way. “The anemone is primarily a memory of the earth on which anemones bloom after the rain,” she says. Her contribution to the exhibition in Jaffa takes the form of a large sculptural affair with dozens of ceramic red flowers with elongated metal stems. Her sweeping artistic rendition of the Oct. 7 tragedy features thousands of crafted anemones she installed across the Nova site, and at other relevant locations such as the Oct. 7 victim section of the cemetery on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem.
She recently also finished work on a book on the floral memorial venture called Anemones Before the Rain. The tome is due out for distribution in the near future. I asked about her choice of temporal preposition. Her response brought tears to my eyes.
“When the dry and arid ground of the Western Negev was soaked with the blood of the murder victims [on Oct. 7], it was dyed red with the blood of the fallen. That is the same soil that, after the rain, drowns in the red of the anemones. The war broke out on the same ground where the anemones bloom after the rain.” Hence also her choice of material for her grand sculptural tribute. “It is a metaphor. The ground is the clay [of the ceramic flower heads], and the blood is the anemone which also plants hope in us, and reappears anew every year.”
There is no missing the angst in Nadine Bar-Noy’s portraits. The monochromic paintings drip with melancholy and a sense of inner searching for tranquility or, at the very least, acceptance. “She lives in Sderot,” Elhanani tells me. “She is still in shock after Oct. 7. She is suffering, badly.” That spills out of her works in a – hopefully – cathartic outpouring of her sorrow.
Furrows of life
Brit Einstein from Kibbutz Magen, less than 5 km. east of Gaza, was one of those who chose an active response to the trauma. “She was evacuated to Jaffa and then went back down south to work on a tractor. They were short-handed down there,” Elhanani explains.
Einstein’s stint plowing the fields on the kibbutz left her with an enduring image of the furrows. She subsequently photographed them and then transposed them into a set of nuanced monochromic paintings that convey the texture of the parched pre-autumnal rains soil, and the stillness of the air as the violence of the barbaric Hamas attack hovers over the future crops.
Orly Landber Tokolevsky’s ceramic set feeds off a pragmatic view of emergency situations and is a delight to the eyes. Her ceramic work is called Residential Secure Space Kit and comprises deftly fashioned items that may serve one well in such dire circumstances. A hefty-looking colorful glazed bowl contains an apple, a pencil, paintbrushes, and even a wad of dollar bills.
“There are some wonderful works here, with some big-name artists too, like Eyal Asulin,” says Elhanani. “There are works that express the sorrow, and there are others that impart optimism and hope for the future.”
Bridging the mortal artistic divide
The exhibitor roster also includes creations by artists murdered on Oct. 7, such as Aviv Atzili, Haim Perry, Roy Idan, Eliko Reichenstein, and Yuval Reviya. “Their work is shown alongside that of artists who continue to create today, creating a dialogue between voices that endure and voices that were silenced. The exhibition is not only an act of remembrance, but also a testament to artistic resilience, hope and continuity,” the curator notes.
There is quality art to be found among the ashes of the ravaged southern communities. “Our goal is to reveal the extraordinary artistic richness of the Western Negev and to present outstanding contemporary art that continues to flourish despite loss and devastation,” Elhanani states. “This exhibition speaks about the strength of artistic creation and the resilience of the human spirit.”
There are a number of events lined up for the exhibition, through to the closing date of October 3. There will be a conversation with South African-born former hostage in Gaza Aviva Siegel, from Kfar Aza, about her book The Main Thing Is to Wake Up to a New Morning. Siegel wrote the book together with journalist and author Amir Tibon, about her experiences on Oct. 7 and in captivity in Gaza. There will also be live dance and music, and film screenings.■
For more information, in Hebrew: 
www.tel-aviv.gov.il

Nearly 150,000 people participate in final slihot prayers ahead of Yom Kippur at Kotel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:37:15 UTC
16:37:15 KST

Approximately 150,000 people participated in the final slihot prayer service at the Western Wall ahead of Yom Kippur on Saturday night, marking the conclusion of 2026's traditional gatherings.
The gathering began in the early evening hours and reached its peak during the central ceremony at the Kotel, with participants standing in the Western Wall Plaza and spread across nearby balconies and throughout the Old City's alleyways.
Due to the large number of participants, the gathering was also broadcast on giant screens at the outskirts of the plaza, on the walls of the Jaffa Gate at the entrance to the Old City, and at IDF Square (Kikar Tzahal).
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, Sephardi Chief Rabbi of Israel David Yosef, Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi Kalman Meir Bar, Rabbi of the Western Wall and the Holy Sites Shmuel Rabinowitz, and Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion took part in the ceremony.
During the event, Netanyahu offered a prayer for peace and another for the safety of the IDF and Israel's security forces. Israel's chief rabbis similarly prayed for the peace and unity of the Jewish people.
Western Wall: Jewish people's beating heart
“This month has once again proven that the Western Wall is the beating heart of the Jewish people," Rabinowitz said in his address during the ceremony. "From every corner of the country and from all parts of the people, multitudes came here: members of every community, opinion, and outlook, those who wear a kippah and those who do not, and stood together as one person with one heart."
"Together we offered prayers for the success of IDF soldiers, for the recovery of the wounded, for the consolation of the families, and for the peace and unity of the people of Israel."
"From the holiness and spiritual elevation of the Selichot gatherings, we enter the new year with great hope: a year of healing and consolation, of victory and blessing, and above all a year in which we remember that we are all one people, sharing one destiny and one prayer," he concluded.
Former hostages attend slihot ceremony
Also in attendance were former hostage Eliya Cohen and his wife, Nova survivor Ziv Abud, as well as former hostages Rom Braslavski, Elkana Bohbot, and Ohad Ben Ami.
"Father in Heaven, I have come all the way to the Western Wall in our beautiful homeland to tell You I’m sorry," Braslavski wrote in a late Saturday post to X/Twitter. "I’m sorry that I didn’t do more at Nova. I’m sorry for all the times in captivity when I broke down, when I doubted, when I lost faith."
"I always knew in captivity that You would save me. I always knew that You would not let me remain in Gaza. I felt You with me in Gaza every single day, every single hour."
Braslavski went on, noting that every time Hamas attempted to convert him to Islam, he "did not give in to their pressure. Even in captivity, I always knew that a father would never abandon his children."
"A year ago, on the most recent Yom Kippur, I was a prisoner of Zion in Deir al-Balah. And today I am free at the Western Wall," he said. "On my way to the Wall, I passed by and saw the Al-Aqsa Mosque. With God’s help, Father in Heaven, You will return that to us as well."
In its own statement, the Western Wall Heritage Foundation added that nearly two million people visited the Kotel throughout the month, including former hostages, bereaved families, IDF soldiers, and members of Israel's security forces.
The foundation also completed its preperations for the Yom Kippur prayers, which will take place at the Western Wall Plaza throughout the fast and end with the Ne’ilah prayer and the blowing of the shofar on Monday night.

Ukrainian Council of Churches asks Pope to help save occupied Oleshky from starvation
The Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organisations (UCCRO) has reported a critical humanitarian situation in the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, where more than 6,000 people, including around 200 children, may still remain, according to various estimates.
Source: an appeal by the UCCRO
Details: The UCCRO said the last food supplies reached Oleshky in late May 2026. Residents of the city remain without sufficient food, drinking water, medicines and other essential aid.
The organisation said Russian troops are preventing people from leaving the city.
Oleshky is located near the front line, and civilians who remain there are constantly at risk of attacks and drone strikes. The city's critical infrastructure has been virtually destroyed, and there is no electricity or gas supply.
The UCCRO recalled that Oleshky also experienced large-scale flooding in 2023 after Russian forces destroyed the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant dam.
Quote: "The city of Oleshky, located in the territory of Ukraine temporarily occupied by Russian forces, is under a humanitarian blockade and is on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe."
Details: The UCCRO appealed to Pope Leo XIV, the World Council of Churches, the World Evangelical Alliance, other religious leaders and human rights organisations, asking them to use all available means to prevent people from starving to death.
It also called on UN member states and the International Committee of the Red Cross to facilitate a humanitarian mission and the evacuation of Oleshky residents to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
The UCCRO stressed that Ukraine has repeatedly drawn international organisations' attention to the critical situation in the city and has attempted to negotiate the evacuation of civilians.
Background:
- On 16 September, Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said that Russia has for a long time refused to confirm whether it is ready to organise a humanitarian mission to evacuate civilians from Oleshky.
- The 34th Separate Marine Brigade posted footage of Oleshky, describing it as a city "the Russians have turned into a ghost".

2 Dead in Moscow Region, Drones Hit Oil Refinery in Russian Capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:35:56 UTC
16:35:56 KST

Two people died in one of the biggest Ukrainian drone attacks on the Moscow region and an oil refinery in Russia's capital was hit, authorities said on Sunday, as Russia enters the final day of parliamentary elections.
Ukraine and Russia have continued attacks on each other's energy infrastructure despite an announcement by U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday that they had agreed to stop.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on his Telegram channel that the biggest Ukrainian drone attacks had been thwarted, with Russia downing more than 1,600 drones since Saturday, including 450 headed for Moscow.
Several drones reached the premises of the oil refinery and one hit an apartment, Sobyanin said, adding there were no casualties in the city.
"The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections," he said. "The adversary failed to achieve this."
Reuters witnesses heard blasts in Moscow and saw plumes of smoke billowing from the site of the Moscow refinery. The scale of any damage to the facility was not immediately known.
Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia's oil refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country's 11 time zones.
The Moscow plant, which has been targeted multiple times, processed 11.6 million metric tons of oil in 2024, producing 2.9 million tons of gasoline and 3.2 million tons of diesel, the latest available data shows.
Ukraine has not commented on the attacks. Both sides say they do not target civilians.
In the wider Moscow region, in addition to the two deaths, 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-storey apartment block in the Ramenskoye district and a number of homes were damaged, said Governor Andrei Vorobyov.

Aamir Latif

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launch of the first missile about 3 p.m. (0600GMT) from the Wonsan area, according to Yonhap news.

CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO journalists denied access to the White House after Trump said he'd bar them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:30:53 UTC
16:30:53 KST

The White House Correspondents’ Association, led by Fox News’ Jacqui Heinrich called on the Trump administration to immediately restore access to the representatives of the media organisations it barred, arguing that the move sets a dangerous precedent for free speech.
Reporters from three major news organisations were denied access to the White House on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump said he was barring them because of reporting he found to be “fake news.”
The media outlets, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, have previously been targeted by the Republican president, particularly CNN, who Trump kicks his antics up a notch, regularly mocking their reporters and lambasting their authenticity.
The actions were a clear escalation of Trump’s long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States.
Trump said on Friday that he would ban all three outlets because of coverage he disliked.
White House reporters from the two cable networks — Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW — both went live to report they’d been turned away, their press badges deactivated, when arriving for their jobs at the White House.
Soon after, Politico said its White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry and had her badge confiscated. All three news outlets hinted at legal action.
“We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in a statement to the Politico newsroom. A CNN statement said the network “will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account."
And MS NOW said it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”
In his second term, Trump and his administration have routinely punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action.
Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — insulting them in briefings, or in his recent speech at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner, where he called CNN’s Kailtan Collins “very dumb and unhappy”.
The White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich called on the administration to immediately restore the three outlets' access.
“The implications extend beyond these organisations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future,” she said.
“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favourably.”
The move follows the president’s decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet’s decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico.
The AP said that it would note, when appropriate, that Trump had ordered the water body, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, renamed the “Gulf of America.”
The US news agency filed a lawsuit against their barring, and the case remains ongoing.
Since returning to office, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.
His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation involving ABC over renewal of its broadcast licenses.
The AP said on Saturday it supported the news organizations banned this week. In a statement, the news cooperative said: “No news organisation — or person — should be retaliated against by the government over the words they use.”

Details
According to him, Turkey has already sent its proposals to Kyiv and Moscow, but has not disclosed their content.

We sent a proposal to both sides and are waiting for a response. We see that if the grain harvested from the fields does not reach world markets, many countries will face food security problems
He also recalled the Black Sea Grain Initiative, concluded in 2022 through the mediation of Turkey and the United Nations. Under the agreements, a mechanism was established to ensure the safe export of Ukrainian grain through Black Sea ports.
According to Fidan, the situation has changed significantly now - Russia and Ukraine are carrying out attacks in the Black Sea, particularly against ports and maritime infrastructure.
In fact, several years ago we concluded an agreement that was subsequently violated, but despite this, there was a de facto system that functioned — the sides did not interfere. However, they are now actively interfering in each other’s affairs. In particular, they are attacking ports and all types of maritime activity
He added that Ankara is trying to use the experience of previous agreements to find a new mechanism that would reduce tensions in the Black Sea.
Frankly speaking, we are trying to bring this matter to a logical conclusion. In this case, it is difficult to reconcile the positions of the sides, drawing on the lessons learned during the implementation of the previous agreement

Alex de Minaur fires as Aussie pair clicks in Davis Cup triumph

Australia defeated Poland to secure progression to the penultimate round of the Davis Cup.
Alex de Minaur beat Kamil Majchrzak 6-3 6-3 to clinch a 3-1 result for the Aussies.
Earlier, Australia's doubles pair of Rinky Hijikata and Max Purcell triumphed in a thrilling match against Jan Zielinski and Karol Drzewiecki.
Alex de Minaur has returned to form to seal Australia's Davis Cup progression, with the hosts beating Poland 3-1 in Brisbane also thanks to some earlier doubles brilliance.
The world No.9 found top gear on Sunday at Pat Rafter Arena, beating Kamil Majchrzak 6-3 6-3 to clinch a 3-1 result that sends Australia into the Cup's penultimate round next year.
With his backhand and serve firing, de Minaur followed up his 57-minute annihilation of Maks Kasnikowski on Saturday with another therapeutic response to a disappointing second-round US Open exit earlier this month.
Loading Twitter content
Earlier, Max Purcell's scintillating tiebreak tennis alongside rock-solid Rinky Hijikata swung their doubles match, and the tie, in Australia's favour.
The pair's 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 defeat of Jan Zielinski and Karol Drzewiecki followed the win and the loss posted in singles by de Minaur and James Duckworth respectively on Saturday.
Purcell, on the comeback from a controversial 18-month anti-doping ban, turned the match on its head after a tight first set progressed to an inevitable tie break.
He drilled a backhand return to win the opening point on the Polish serve, then produced a pair of aces to shoot the hosts clear 3-0.
An unforced error from Poland was followed by two more Purcell winners, and he then held his nerve on a series of low volleys to eventually clinch the set.
Hijikata then held impressively and, after missing two break-point chances, nailed a forehand return to nab the match's only service break.
That was all Australia needed, with the composed pair energising the sold-out Pat Rafter Arena to secure a pressure-relieving victory in 77 minutes.
Australia's win followed a shock loss on the road to Ecuador earlier this year that plunged it into the must-win encounter against Poland.
The Aussies still need to win next year's qualifying round, against an opponent still to be decided, to progress to the finals in Italy in November, 2027.

Failing to supply Ukraine with sufficient air defense systems and interceptor ammunition directly increases the military threat to Poland, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned.
Speaking before lawmakers, Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that Polish fighter jets were scrambled again overnight to secure national airspace amid Russian missile and drone barrages targeting western Ukraine. The defense minister emphasized that recurring incidents along NATO’s eastern frontier can no longer be interpreted as accidental deviations.

“These are no longer isolated incidents; this is planned aggression against NATO member states. It is not an accident, it is the strategy of the Russian Federation,” Kosiniak-Kamysz told parliament, as reported by broadcaster TVN24.
Kosiniak-Kamysz criticized opposition parliamentarians over statements questioning defense aid to Kyiv, arguing that rhetoric seeking to curb military assistance aligns with Moscow’s strategic objectives rather than Poland’s national security interests.
“Missiles fall and drones fall one kilometer from the Polish border,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said. “If Ukraine does not have air defense assets, if it does not have ammunition to shoot down these drones, most of these drones will fly through Ukraine and reach Poland. Is that what you want?”

Border drone threats
The defense minister’s remarks followed an address by Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of the right-wing Confederation (Konfederacja) party. Mentzen had criticized the condition of Poland’s armed forces, pointing to shortages in domestic artillery ammunition reserves, deficiencies in reserve personnel training, and inadequate civil defense and bomb shelter infrastructure.
Responding to the criticism, Kosiniak-Kamysz insisted that sustaining Ukraine’s frontline interception capability remains the most effective operational barrier preventing Russian aerial munitions from penetrating deeper into allied territory.
The debate in Warsaw coincides with a series of cross-border security alerts along Poland’s eastern frontier.
On Sept. 13, Russian munitions struck within two kilometers of the Polish border in the Volyn region, damaging a commercial filling station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk checkpoint and hitting the locomotive of a passenger train operating on the Kyiv-Warsaw rail corridor.
Polish air defenses and allied aircraft stationed along NATO’s eastern flank have repeatedly entered elevated readiness postures to monitor incoming Russian strike waves, with military planners cautioning that the deployment of high-speed jet-powered drones increases the margin of error near international boundaries.
Regional missile defense integration
The parliamentary debate follows Poland’s formal accession to a European defense coalition dedicated to countering ballistic missile threats alongside Ukraine and nine other European nations.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Poland’s participation during a joint press conference in Ukraine on Friday, Sept. 18.
Tusk characterized Poland’s initial omission from the initiative’s July launch in Paris as an administrative misunderstanding that has been resolved, noting that Polish defense enterprises are reviewing options to contribute industrially to joint interceptor programs.
The coalition encompasses Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, the UK and Ukraine, aiming to establish collaborative production lines and integrate regional radar architectures.
During their bilateral talks, Tusk and Zelensky also discussed the formation of the “Carpathian Eight,” a proposed regional security and economic format designed to reinforce infrastructure resilience and institutional alignment between Central European states and the EU.

In Belgium, an 800-year-old medieval structure was discovered with the help of moles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
10:16:57 EEST
16:16:57 KST

In Belgium, an 800-year-old medieval structure was discovered with the help of moles
Kyiv • UNN
Near Damme, 2,810 archaeological fragments were found in 814 molehills. Among them was a brick gate dating from the 13th–14th centuries.
In Belgium, moles helped archaeologists uncover the remains of a medieval estate. In 814 molehills near Damme, researchers found 2,810 archaeological fragments, including remains of a brick gate dating from the 13th–14th centuries. The Arkeonews publication reported this, UNN writes.
Details
The finds pointed to the existence of a brick entrance gate dating from the 13th–14th centuries and provided new information about a medieval rural estate that had long disappeared from written sources.
In total, the researchers recovered 2,810 fragments weighing slightly more than two kilograms. They included construction debris, ceramics, metal objects, and fragments of natural stone.
The ceramics helped refine the dating of the site. Among the 294 fragments, locally produced gray pottery predominated, followed in quantity by red pottery. Decorated ceramics, proto-stoneware, and imported German stoneware were also found. Overall, the finds span a period from approximately the 12th to the 15th century, although most date from the 13th–14th centuries. This makes it possible to confidently attribute the gate to the medieval period.

Estonia's Niina Petrõkina wins Bergamo figure skating round
Two-time European figure skating champion Niina Petrõkina took first place at the ISU Challenger event in Bergamo, Italy.
Petrõkina improved her personal best by nearly seven points in the short program to take the lead, then finished second in Saturday's free skate with 133.21 points. South Korea's Shin Ji-a won the free skate, scoring 1.12 points more than Petrõkina, while Lara Naki Gutmann finished third on 132.14 in front of her home crowd.
Petrõkina won the competition with a combined 210.41 points, just under six short of her personal best. Ji-a took second with 209.26 and Gutmann third with 202.74.
Of other Estonian competitors, Maria Eliise Kaljuvere was fourth after the short program and scored 94.32 in the free skate, placing tenth in that segment and ninth overall with 157.84 points.
In the men's singles, Mihhail Selevko leads after the short program with 91.09 points, with the free skate to follow on Sunday afternoon.

Estonian experts say social media should be improved for children instead of banned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

Estonian experts say social media should be improved for children instead of banned
The European Union is discussing a safe‑internet regulation that includes several restrictions planned for minors' use of social media. While EU plans propose setting a minimum age of 13, Estonian social scientists argue that blunt bans will not solve all problems and may even create new ones.
Tallinn University media professor Indrek Ibrus is critical of the EU initiative, saying the planned restrictions conflict with children's fundamental rights.
"In my opinion, it's generally a pretty bad idea," Ibrus said, explaining that it ignores the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. "Children must have opportunities for self‑expression and free access to information to support their development and identity. Any age‑based restriction on access to information essentially disregards children's rights," Ibrus said.
According to Ibrus, the European Commission is effectively giving up by proposing restrictions.
"Instead of working on these environments, these platforms, these spaces in a way that would make them safe and suitable for children, the European Commission throws up its hands and gives up. They don't have the strength to deal with regulation, even though the regulatory framework — the Digital Services Act — already exists and simply needs to be enforced. In a sense, children are being sacrificed because of the Commission's own inability," he said.
University of Tartu media studies professor Andra Siibak agreed that relying solely on bans and restrictions is not the best solution, highlighting the need to change platform business models. Siibak said it is positive that the EU demands concrete measures from service providers to make platforms more protective of children's rights, well‑being and privacy.
Like Ibrus, Siibak pointed out that all these recommended changes are already written into earlier EU regulations — whether the Digital Services Act or the AI Act. "The European Union itself must start thinking carefully about how to demand these changes from platforms and monitor that they actually implement them," Siibak said.
Tallinn University participation‑culture professor Katrin Tiidenberg warned against overly rigid bans, citing Australia's experience.
"Based on what we know from Australia and how their ban doesn't actually work, children under 16 are still online, which mainly means we don't know what they're doing on social media or where they're logged in," Tiidenberg said.
One of the biggest questions surrounding the EU Kids Act is how to verify users' ages without massively violating people's privacy.
Ibrus sees major risks in age verification. "It may be a direct privacy intrusion, and it may also be harmful in the sense that platforms could use identification for more precise profiling of users, which can be dangerous in several ways," he explained.
Ibrus added that although the EU is developing a digital wallet solution that could provide secure infrastructure in the future, any restrictions must be approached with extreme caution.
Siibak also noted that finding a reliable and transparent age‑verification method is currently difficult. Attempts with facial‑recognition software have not worked, and young people easily bypass restrictions using, for example, their parents' documents.
"We know from Australia's experience how skillfully young people bypass such age‑assessment apps and solutions. To access a platform, they show their parents' documents or take a photo with a famous footballer's poster in the background instead of showing their own face. Young people certainly have many ways to get around such systems. Finding a method acceptable to all member states will be a very difficult discussion," Siibak said.
Tiidenberg also stressed that mechanical age‑verification methods bring risks. "It's a very important issue, because if it means a child must log in with an ID card, then it means everyone must log in with an ID card. We want to avoid mass surveillance and monitoring of which sites we visit and who does what. In my view, maintaining freedom is important," Tiidenberg said.
"That doesn't mean age verification cannot be done in a reasonably safe way, but the method must be developed very carefully and not by quickly trusting the first private company that says: 'Look, I built you a solution,'" Tiidenberg said.
Experts say protecting children and young people on social media should focus on improving the platforms themselves.
Tiidenberg highlighted the need to pressure platforms to create well‑being‑oriented and responsible design. This means placing strong emphasis on curbing addictive algorithms — for example, giving users the option to choose between a chronological feed and recommendation algorithms. She also supports separate child‑ and youth‑friendly accounts (for example, ages 13–15) where harmful content is automatically limited.
Ibrus reminded that in addition to tightening rules, it is important to support young people's digital skills and critical thinking instead of creating artificial barriers that do not actually protect them online.
"Instead of bluntly banning communication environments because they may involve certain risks, those risks must be addressed. Platforms must be adapted, regulated, existing regulations enforced, and at the same time media literacy must be developed for different age and social groups," Ibrus said.
Tiidenberg added that digital skills are important, but a person can be both competent and helpless at the same time — including children.
"Critical awareness is very important, but obviously children have different self‑regulation abilities at different ages. Even many adults do not have very good self‑regulation. You may know something is harmful to you, but you still may not be able to avoid certain social media content," she said.
"Skills are important — they are part of the toolkit — but they are not enough if we allow user interfaces to be designed manipulatively, because they still measure the user's slowing finger while scrolling. If we do not regulate how quickly systems must respond when I say that I or my child does not want to see certain content, then digital skills alone are of little use," Tiidenberg added.
On Thursday, the European Commission adopted the safe‑internet regulation (EU Kids Act), which increases children's online safety in the EU. The package includes proposals to ban social media use for children under 13 and to require companies providing online services to create safe accounts for children.
Under the proposal — which EU member states and the European Parliament will negotiate — accounts for children aged 13–15 would be under parental control.
Social media and video services, online games and AI‑based companions and chatbots intended for users under 18 would be subject to a list of permitted and prohibited activities.

China's consumption shifts toward smart, health-related products: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
15:14:08 CST
16:14:08 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market showed a stronger move toward smart, health-related and higher-quality products in the first eight months of 2026, with sales of smart glasses on major platforms surging 120 percent year on year, the Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday.
Sales of electrocardiogram monitors jumped 75 percent during this period, while those of action cameras and organic food rose 26.9 percent and 7.4 percent, respectively, according to an official with the ministry.
The latest breakdown offers a closer look at changes within China's consumer market after official data revealed that the combined retail sales of goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year in the January-August period.
Demand also remained robust for a range of consumption-upgrade products. Sales of communication equipment increased 16.3 percent, while cosmetics items registered growth of 6.1 percent, and sales of cultural products and office supplies were up by 6 percent.
In contrast, sales of petroleum products fell 6.1 percent year on year in this period, which the official partly attributed to substitution by new-energy products.
Services continued to outpace goods consumption. Retail sales of services expanded 4.9 percent in the first eight months of 2026, 3.9 percentage points faster than retail sales of goods.
Demand for tourism consulting and rental services, as well as cultural, sports and leisure services, maintained relatively rapid growth during the summer holiday season, as Chinese consumers increasingly spent on services alongside physical goods, according to the official.
Consumption growth also continued to spread beyond major cities. Rural retail sales of consumer goods reached 4.4 trillion yuan (about 651.65 billion U.S. dollars), up 2.3 percent year on year, and 1.3 percentage points faster than the growth recorded in urban areas.
Boosting consumption remains a policy priority for China this year. In July, China unveiled a five-year plan for expanding consumption, outlining measures to upgrade both goods and services consumption and expand quality services in areas including catering, tourism, elderly care and healthcare.
China has also expanded policy support for smart and energy-efficient consumption. Under its 2026 consumer goods trade-in program, backed by ultra-long special treasury bonds, subsidies cover automobiles, six categories of home appliances and four types of digital and smart products.
Smart glasses were included among the nationally subsidized digital and smart products for 2026, with eligible purchases receiving subsidies of 15 percent of the sales price, capped at 500 yuan per item. ■

Public memorial held for former HKSAR Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa
China
Unknown Publisher

Shi Taifeng, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and vice chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) National Committee, delivers a speech at a public memorial for Tung Chee-hwa, former vice chairman of the National Committee of the CPPCC and former chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR), in Hong Kong, south China, Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Duo)
HONG KONG, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- A public memorial was held in Hong Kong on Sunday for Tung Chee-hwa, former vice chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and former chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR).
Tung died of illness at the age of 89 in Hong Kong on Sept. 8. He is regarded as an outstanding contributor to "one country, two systems," a renowned patriot, an outstanding social activist and a close friend of the Communist Party of China (CPC).
Tung served as vice chairman of the 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th National Committees of the CPPCC. He was the first- and second-term chief executive of the HKSAR.
While Tung was critically ill, the central authorities expressed deep concern over his condition. President Xi Jinping and other central leaders instructed the Liaison Office of the Central People's Government in the HKSAR to convey best wishes and demanded all-out efforts to treat Tung.
Following Tung's passing, Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi, Han Zheng, Hu Jintao and others expressed their deep grief in various forms and extended sincere condolences to his family.
Shi Taifeng, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Leung Chun-ying, vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Wang Dongfeng, vice chairman and secretary-general of the CPPCC National Committee, Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macao Work Office of the CPC Central Committee and of the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office of the State Council, and John Lee, chief executive of the HKSAR, attended Sunday's memorial service.
The memorial service started at 9 a.m., with all those present observing a moment of silence. Leung, vice chairman of Tung's funeral committee, presided over the event.
Shi, chairman of Tung's funeral committee, delivered a speech at the event, reviewing Tung's life and highlighting his important contributions to the country, to Hong Kong, and to the society.
Following the speech, all participants bowed three times to Tung's portrait, came up in turn before his remains to pay their final respects, and expressed condolences to his family members.
Leaders from the central government institutions in Hong Kong, senior officials from the HKSAR government, HKSAR deputies to the National People's Congress, HKSAR members of the CPPCC National Committee, and representatives from various sectors of Hong Kong also attended the memorial to pay their respects. ■

The US military said its forces struck a suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean on Saturday, killing four people.

As part of this push, the US launched operation "Southern Spear," which aims to "disrupt the flow of narcotics in the Western Hemisphere" through a campaign of air strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific.
Trump has also spearheaded a new security coalition including nations from across Central and South America - dubbed the "Shield of the Americas" - in a bid to combat cartels.

Russian Election, Cast as Test of Support for Ukraine War, Enters Final Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:10:45 UTC
16:10:45 KST

A parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for Russia's war in Ukraine entered its third and final day on Sunday, with the ruling United Russia party expected to retain its dominance in a political system critics say does not tolerate dissent.
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is likely to be presented by the Kremlin as evidence of public backing for Putin's policies and for the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.
Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict deemed illegal by authorities.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news are punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine. It casts the conflict as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West and says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.
Putin on Friday accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he said was a Ukrainian strike on the home of an election official in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region that killed Yelena Astanina, the official. Reuters could not independently verify details of the attack and there was no immediate comment from Kyiv.
Russian electoral officials also said on Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a "pseudo election."
Despite what most experts see as the election's predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated "a foreign agent", said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
"The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot," it said in a note.
It said the Communist party and the New People party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia. Both parties have consistently voted in line with United Russia on major issues.
Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.
"Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us," said Putin.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 18:00 GMT on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

South Korea plans to dispatch more than 1,400 medical items, including automated external defibrillators, to North Korea as part of a humanitarian medical support program.
The Unification Ministry has drawn up a list of 1,431 medical items covering 166 categories to a hospital in the North Korean capital Pyongyang, necessary for diagnosis, surgery and treatment, Yonhap news agency reported, citing a government document.
The items, with an estimated cost of $6.75 million, include diagnostic equipment, such as X-ray machines, stethoscopes and blood pressure monitors, along with operating tables and other surgical and treatment equipment.
The ministry said the plan still hinges on discussions with the North Korean side and could change.
Pyongyang's willingness to accept aid also remains unclear as inter-Korean exchanges and dialogue channels are virtually non-existent amid strained ties between the two arch-rivals.
Seoul secured a sanctions exemption in May from the UN Security Council's North Korea sanctions committee to provide the equipment.
Some South Korean lawmakers in the National Assembly voiced concern over the plan, saying medical equipment could be diverted toward biochemical weapons production or repurposed to inspect flaws in weapons systems.
Unification Minister Chung Dong-young, however, pushed back on the concern, saying humanitarian medical aid should not be tied to North Korea's military policy and that the North's medical conditions are dire enough to warrant urgent support.

====================================================================================================

Don’t discount Reform because it's had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:00:09 UTC
16:00:09 KST

Despite the energised start Andy Burnham has made as prime minister, plenty of his party’s MPs and hardcore activists are still haunted by a familiar sense of insecurity. Underpinned by a political version of impostor syndrome, it runs deep – and, bar the odd spell of Labour optimism, it always has. So it is with the battle between Labour and Reform UK that will define an election that could arrive much sooner than some people think, and a widely held ambivalence on the left about the possibility of Nigel Farage’s party taking power. Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?
Investigations into the party and its leadership’s finances by both the Metropolitan police and parliament’s standards commissioner may worsen Reform’s woes. Those investigations predate the two recently announced £36m donations from the crypto tycoons Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, which themselves risk being backdatedly ruled illegal and are reportedly already being spent on 400 “field agents”. The two mega-donations symbolise two connected stories. One is about the possible buyout of our fragile democracy. The other centres on how, from much of the public’s perspective, all the allegations about Farage and his party might have already turned into an indecipherable blizzard. So, although Reform is down, it is still far from out.
But the reasons for that extend much further than money. Reform still has a serious chance of either leading or forming the next government because of the same basic fact that Burnham says he has come to avenge: that since the crash of 2008, millions of British lives have pinballed from one crisis to the next, leaving many people resentful, insecure and plain scared.
If anyone hadn’t already noticed, ours is an age of fear: of economic insecurity, wildfires and unprecedented weather, seemingly unending wars, and massed and chaotic human movement. Reform – and the Tories – lean into all that anxiety, offering the kind of crass solutions (witness Farage’s recent promise of a state of “national emergency” as soon as he takes office) that only heighten people’s sense of crisis. Labour, meanwhile, can only offer another variation of its age-old answer: modest hope and constructive change. Such will be the choice sooner or later presented to voters. And in that sense, the next election will be more emotional than political.
Make no mistake: the campaign has effectively already begun. If, for instance, John Healey’s first budget is not peppered with vivid symbols of a different approach to the economy, it will threaten to be a very serious dud, with lasting consequences. Moreover, at some point during the autumn – presumably beginning at the Labour conference – we will start to get a sense of Burnham’s 10-year plan. He will have to talk about AI, and its dire threats and huge opportunities, and the climate emergency – a subject he has so far been strangely reluctant to address. But he will also need convincing answers to less apocalyptic problems. Right now, I can think of no better example than the million or so young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) who have mums, dads and grandparents terrified – fear, once again – on their behalf.
He is also going to have to walk some very precarious tightropes. We all know what sits behind much of the public’s feelings about immigration: as well as misapprehensions about the relevant numbers – which are actually going down – and straight-up racism, too many working lives sit on the borderline between the official and illicit economy, and are defined by “employers being able to import cheap agency labour to undercut existing pay and conditions in the name of free-market orthodoxy”. Those last words were once uttered by that sainted socialist Jeremy Corbyn: they were intended as a rational explanation for yet another example of people’s deep sense of worry.
From that vantage point, footage of so-called small boats is bound often to spark a callous and fearful response. To many people, such sights look – look – like proof of even more people who have come to disappear into the cracks that run through our labour market, and then surface offering to work longer hours than you, for a lot less money. That makes you feel even more scared than you already were. And as any student of the 20th century knows, nothing warps politics – and helps demagogues – like that kind of anxiety.
A visceral dread is now the basis of the picture of modern Britain – and England in particular – offered to the public by Reform, the Tories and their allies in the press and online. We are, in fact, living through the comprehensive reinvention of English rightwing politics as a byword for angst, fury and paranoia. Anything that could reasonably be termed conservatism is nowhere to be seen: their England is now a country where summers are spent willing on unrest, and where quasi-paramilitaries menace our ports. Last week saw that Passport to Pimlico-esque village of Piddington in Oxfordshire hold a referendum on leaving the UK – with 92% of votes in favour – because of what the Telegraph calls a “migrant camp”. From Reform in particular, one often gets the sense that any degree of contentment is seen as being tantamount to complacent wokeness; as they see it, England is – or should be – a righteously stroppy little country, prone to the raging, nihilistic impulses that Farage et al seem to see as the essence of our national character.
As much as Labour needs a solid, credible approach to immigration, it is going to have to remind people of the truth. We are a country with problems, for sure, but one whose people have not abandoned hope and largely get along with one other – and where, to quote July’s bulletin from the Office for National Statistics, “The cost of living (88%), the NHS (78%) and the economy (70%) were the most commonly reported issues facing the UK today.” Whatever our fears, earlier this month, YouGov reported that 57% of us are “fairly satisfied” with life. Labour should attack Farage, Badenoch et al for their lack of faith in the essential moderation and calm of most Britons; Burnham is the first senior Labour figure in a long time who may have the authenticity, energy and principle to make such talk actually ring true.
And then there are more solid, tangible matters. A fortnight ago, the new prime minister announced £1bn of investment in a new fleet of trains that are going to be built in Derby, “supporting over 350 jobs … and almost 6,000 across [the] UK supply chain”. Self-evidently, we need a lot more of that kind of stuff. Highly visible sites should be quickly set aside for new council housing, so Labour can point at the plots and promise people transformed and secure lives. In our further education colleges, money must soon be spent on teaching the absent skills that will help revive the economy, not least in construction, and provide good, dependable jobs.
The list inevitably goes on, but it may soon mark the difference between the meaningful survival of our democracy and the arrival of a munificently funded barbarism. Labour high-ups ought to remind themselves that that great Labour godhead Aneurin Bevan titled his only book In Place of Fear: in those four words lie this new government’s basic mission, the high stakes involved, and the almost impossibly hard work it will take to even begin to achieve it.
- 
  John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Lithuania seeks full CERN membership as Vilnius hosts particle physics community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Scientists from the European Organization for Nuclear Research, CERN, are meeting in Lithuania for the first time as the country seeks full membership in the organization at an annual cost of more than 4 million euros.
The weeklong gathering in Vilnius comes as CERN’s Large Hadron Collider in Geneva undergoes an upgrade. The world’s largest particle accelerator was shut down in late June to allow work to begin, with scientists expecting the upgrades to expand their ability to study the fundamental properties of the universe.
The 27-kilometre underground collider accelerates particles to nearly the speed of light and brings them into collisions. Scientists use the resulting data to investigate how the universe developed after the Big Bang.
The CERN community meeting in Vilnius includes scientists working on the LHCb experiment, which studies differences between matter and antimatter.
“At the beginning of the universe we had equal amounts of matter and antimatter. Today the universe is made only of matter, not antimatter. So the fundamental question is: How did that happen? And we still don’t understand it,” said Timothy Gershon, spokesperson for the CERN LHCb experiment.
The LHCb collaboration has published more than 900 scientific papers, said Mindaugas Šarpis, head of the LHCbVilnius group at Vilnius University.
“These are our ideas, our reports on how the universe works,” Šarpis said, noting that the research has also led to discoveries including pentaquarks, particles that scientists had not previously known about.
Vilnius University is one of the institutions participating in the experiment, alongside leading universities including the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Oxford and Cambridge.
“Vilnius University is an equal partner,” Šarpis said. “We can give our students memberships and study the data collected by the LHCb detector. We have billions upon billions of particle collisions that we want to analyse.”
Lithuania became an associate member of CERN about eight years ago, with membership currently costing the government about 1 million euros a year. The country has now begun the process of seeking full membership, which would raise its annual contribution to about 4 million euros.
“The membership procedure has already started,” said Gautier Hamel de Monchenault, CERN’s head of research and computing.
Lithuanian scientists can already work with CERN, but full membership would give Lithuania a vote on the organisation’s council and a role in its governance, Hamel de Monchenault said.
Lithuanian industry would also have opportunities to participate in developing future particle accelerators, he said.
Vilnius University Rector Rimvydas Petrauskas said the financial contribution would be only one part of the process.
“It costs money. The membership fee is quite substantial, but that is not enough,” Petrauskas said. Other member states must also approve Lithuania’s membership and determine whether it meets the required standards, he said.
Lithuanian officials and researchers also point to potential economic benefits from deeper involvement with CERN.
Saulė Mačiukaitė-Žvinienė, a professor at Vilnius University’s Business School, said businesses that have become involved with CERN while Lithuania has been an associate member have seen revenue growth of up to 3% over the past five years.
She said full membership could provide a larger boost, citing research that found businesses in full-member countries can increase revenue and employment by about 14% to 15% annually.
Startups based on CERN technologies have attracted about $4 billion in investment, she said.
CERN’s scientific work has also had broader technological and medical applications. The organisation’s researchers developed the World Wide Web while seeking a way to share large amounts of scientific data, and technologies developed from particle physics research have been applied in medicine, including cancer treatment.
