The comments before a nearly full stadium came after a tumultuous week that began with rapper Macklemore, Sheeran's original US opener, being dropped in response to saying “Free Palestine” during a 5 September tour stop in New Jersey.
Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday. Within hours of Sheeran’s statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.
Sheeran has performed many songs solo during his Loop Tour concerts, but was joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga before they dropped out in support of Macklemore.
Macklemore was replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out, and Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out this week.
Before Saturday's show, a small group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators convened outside the stadium.
Hillary Steinberg, 34, said she got concert tickets a year ago but wound up getting a refund and attended the demonstration instead, after she was disappointed that Sheeran refused to take a stand to defend Macklemore or empathise with the plight of the Palestinian people.
“I was, until this week, a big Ed Sheeran fan,” Steinberg said. “I think all art is political, and all music is political, and so this choice — even though he was saying that he wasn’t complicit — is a political choice.”
Diane Savitz, a 53-year-old from Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, got tickets months ago and attended. She said she is a big Sheeran fan, doesn't think he did anything wrong and a concert is not the place for politics.
“A concert should be for people enjoying the music. Music should bring people together,” Savitz said. “Everyone has their right to freedom of speech, but not every platform is the place for it.”
The Grammy winning artist was adamant earlier this week that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues. But, as the controversy grew, and ticket prices and sales declined, he decided to address the issue head on.
Sheeran told the crowd in Philadelphia that everyone is welcome at his concerts, and they can have opposing points of view while still singing his songs, which are about “love, hope and unity.”
He also told fans he worries about venues pre-approving performances.
“This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” Sheeran said.

Denmark Expedites $275M Military Aid Package for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:26:00 UTC
15:26:00 KST

Denmark will expedite its 31st military aid package to Ukraine, valued at approximately $275 million, with a primary focus on reinforcing Ukrainian air defense capabilities ahead of the autumn and winter period, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine announced on Sept. 19
The Ukrainian defense ministry stated that specific details regarding the contents of the package are being withheld for operational security reasons. However, the assistance is designated to expand the capability of the Armed Forces of Ukraine to counter Russian missile and drone barrages against infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ministry noted that Denmark has remained one of Ukraine’s primary defense partners since the launch of Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, consistently contributing military hardware and pioneering multilateral procurement frameworks.
The Danish government decided to accelerate the delivery of the assistance package, having announced on Sept. 18 its intention to fast-track air defense support for Kyiv. The decision followed a Baltic Sea confrontation on Sept. 14 in which a Russian warship fired signal flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
Baltic Sea naval confrontation
The expedited military aid arrives amid heightened friction between Copenhagen and Moscow following the naval encounter near the Danish island of Gedser.
According to the Danish Armed Forces Command, the Baltic Fleet corvette Soobrazitelny launched two signal flares toward a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter that was conducting routine photographic surveillance over international waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea.
Donbas Is More Than a Line on a Map: Lessons From Gettysburg, Normandy, Iwo Jima
Danish defense officials reported that one of the flares passed within close range of the aircraft. No damage or crew injuries were recorded.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the incident as part of an intensified Russian hybrid campaign aimed at probing allied resolve along NATO’s maritime periphery, calling for increased European defense cohesion.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen characterized the naval firing as “completely unacceptable” and formally summoned Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus criticized the Russian crew for “very unprofessional seamanship,” asserting that Moscow’s threshold for operational risk had shifted.
Moscow rejected Copenhagen’s characterization of the event, asserting that the Danish helicopter had approached the corvette and failed to respond to radio communications on international channels. Barbin delivered a formal counter-note to Danish authorities demanding that Copenhagen prevent hazardous aerial maneuvers near Russian naval vessels.
Two days after the incident, Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov awarded the commander of the Soobrazitelny the medal “For Combat Distinction,” commending what the Russian Defense Ministry described as “skillful and decisive actions” in launching the flares to repel the surveillance flight.

China's space station gets kitchen upgrade for long-term stays
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:30 CST
15:24:30 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's orbiting space station has improved its kitchen with advanced appliances and more food choices to keep its residents well-fed during long stays in orbit.
The Astronaut Center of China, working with several private companies, has upgraded the "space kitchen" with a suite of intelligent appliances for drinking water, food reheating and baking, enabling astronauts in orbit to eat hot meals within 20 minutes instead of waiting longer or eating cold food.
At an aerospace medical engineering conference in Tianjin Municipality in north China on Saturday, Liu Weibo, a center expert, gave examples such as a space water dispenser that ensures reclaimed water is safe to drink, and a space microwave heating device that allows rapid reheating at low power with no microwave leakage.
Liu also noted that the hot-air baking oven, the world's first designed for space use, achieves efficient, low-energy removal of cooking fumes and has allowed astronauts in orbit to enjoy baked chicken wings, steak and cake.
The menu on the Chinese space station has also expanded. Astronaut food now includes nearly 200 varieties, while the flight menu cycle has been extended to 10 days. Fresh vegetables, nuts, cakes and meats can be baked and processed in orbit, and yogurt can be fermented in space.
"We are continuing to raise the level of life support for astronauts in orbit," Liu said. "The variety, quality, flavor, appearance and nutrition of space food are getting better."
China's space station, Tiangong, which means Heavenly Palace, has now entered an era of long-term human habitation. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay, while the country's 2030 crewed moon landing mission is advancing steadily. ■

Interview: China-ASEAN Expo delivers shared development dividends: expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:23 CST
15:24:23 KST

MANILA, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- The China-ASEAN Expo (CAEXPO) serves as a bridge for ASEAN and China to boost trade flows and strengthen supply chain cooperation, helping both sides reap shared development dividends, a Filipino expert said.
"ASEAN and China boast complementary economic structures, and the CAEXPO provides a matchmaking venue to connect supply and demand between both sides," said Lucio Pitlo, member of the board of directors and former president of the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies, in an exclusive interview with Xinhua.
Scheduled to run from Sept. 17 to 21 in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, the 23rd CAEXPO draws more than 3,400 exhibitors from over 70 countries and regions.
Pitlo said China supplies high value-added products such as electric vehicles, solar panels and wind turbines, making it an "indispensable trade and development partner" for ASEAN.
He said ASEAN produces high-quality fruits including avocados, coconuts and durians, and is also rich in rubber, oil and gas, and mineral resources, which can meet China's demand for consumer goods and industrial raw materials.
Referring to trade corridors, Pitlo highlighted the Pinglu Canal, which officially opened to traffic Wednesday. He said the waterway will help improve economic activity and deepen connectivity between China and ASEAN.
He elaborated that goods from inland parts of central and southwest China previously had to be shipped via ports in Guangdong for overseas destinations.
"Now with this direct waterway access to the sea, transportation distances will be shortened. ASEAN countries like Vietnam can also deliver fresh fruits faster and more easily to reach Chinese consumers' tables," he added.
Pitlo said mobile payments and e-commerce are playing a growing role in ASEAN countries, areas where China has made much progress, with advanced and mature cashless payment schemes. "Robust and superb technology, supply chains, logistics networks and industry standards" can help ASEAN countries update their online commerce ecosystem.
"ASEAN countries can learn from China's experience in digital transformation. This will help us make more efficient supply chains, find ways to reduce costs, and improve service delivery," he said.
Established in the 1980s, the Philippine Association for Chinese Studies promotes cultural, educational, economic and academic exchanges between the Philippines and China. ■

Public memorial held for former HKSAR Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:16 CST
15:24:16 KST

HONG KONG, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- A public memorial was held in Hong Kong on Sunday for Tung Chee-hwa, former vice chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and former chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR).
Tung died of illness at the age of 89 in Hong Kong on Sept. 8. He is regarded as an outstanding contributor to "one country, two systems," a renowned patriot, an outstanding social activist and a close friend of the Communist Party of China (CPC).
Tung served as vice chairman of the 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th National Committees of the CPPCC. He was the first- and second-term chief executive of the HKSAR.
While Tung was critically ill, the central authorities expressed deep concern over his condition. President Xi Jinping and other central leaders instructed the Liaison Office of the Central People's Government in the HKSAR to convey best wishes and demanded all-out efforts to treat Tung.
Following Tung's passing, Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi, Han Zheng, Hu Jintao and others expressed their deep grief in various forms and extended sincere condolences to his family.
Shi Taifeng, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Leung Chun-ying, vice chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, Wang Dongfeng, vice chairman and secretary-general of the CPPCC National Committee, Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macao Work Office of the CPC Central Committee and of the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office of the State Council, and John Lee, chief executive of the HKSAR, attended Sunday's memorial service. ■

China's loan prime rates remain unchanged
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:24:00 CST
15:24:00 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's one-year loan prime rate (LPR), a market-based benchmark lending rate, stood at 3 percent on Sunday, unchanged from the previous month.
The over-five-year LPR, on which many lenders base their mortgage rates, also remained unchanged from the previous reading of 3.5 percent, according to the National Interbank Funding Center.
LPRs, published each month, reflect financing costs for households and businesses and serve as a pricing reference for bank lending. Lower rates can ease borrowers' financing burdens and encourage investment and consumption.
China's one-year and over-five-year LPRs have remained unchanged for 16 consecutive months since June 2025.
Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, attributed the unchanged LPRs partly to the resilience of the economy. He cited continued strength in exports, a pickup in year-on-year growth in both the consumer price index and producer price index, and a marked acceleration in industrial output growth in August.
Wen also noted that lending rates remained relatively low in August, which provided strong support for the real economy and reduced the need for a policy rate cut.
Data showed that the weighted average interest rate on newly issued corporate loans was below 3 percent in August 2026, about 0.2 percentage point lower than a year earlier, while the rate on newly issued personal housing loans remained unchanged at about 3.1 percent.
China will continue to implement a more proactive fiscal policy and adopt an appropriately accommodative monetary policy in 2026, this year's government work report noted. ■

France's Macron meets Carney to bolster Canada-EU ties amid US trade rift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:23:58 UTC
15:23:58 KST

President Emmanuel Macron is scheduled to visit the French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon on Sunday, where he is due to meet Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, weeks after US President Donald Trump posted an image on social media showing the archipelago covered by the American flag.
Macron's visit, the first by a French president since Francois Hollande travelled there in 2014, comes as Canada seeks to deepen ties with the European Union amid trade tensions with the United States.
Located off Canada's Atlantic coast, Saint Pierre and Miquelon is France's only remaining territory in North America.
French officials said the trip would underscore France's sovereignty over the archipelago and highlight its close relationship with Canada.
"For a territory of 5,800 inhabitants, it is rare to find so many issues that are important for France as a whole concentrated in a place of this size: France's geostrategic presence in the North Atlantic, at the doorstep of the United States and the Arctic, maritime sovereignty, adaptation to climate change; and cooperation with Canada," a French presidency official told reporters.
Diplomats said the visit, which Macron was undertaking on his way to the annual United Nations General Assembly gathering of world leaders, would also carry symbolic weight after Trump posted a map depicting the United States, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean draped in the US flag and labelled "United States of America".
The image included Saint Pierre and Miquelon and several French Caribbean territories.
France chose not to publicly respond to the post at the time.
Macron and Carney are expected to discuss the energy crisis and Canada's increasingly close relationship with the European Union after the bloc opened the door to Ottawa becoming its first associate member.
More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.

China thrashes Bangladesh in Asian Games women's hockey opener
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
14:23:50 CST
15:23:50 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 20 (Xinhua) -- China opened its title defense in women's hockey with a resounding 13-0 victory over Bangladesh at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Sunday.
China quickly took control of the match, with Zhong Jiaqi breaking the deadlock with a smart deflection in front of the goal.
Chen Yang, Li Hong and Zhong each added a goal to give China a 4-0 lead at the end of the first quarter.
Chen, Zhang Ying and Zhong scored in the second quarter as China extended its advantage to 7-0 at halftime.
Just one minute into the third quarter, China's Ma Ning received the ball, adjusted and fired home. Zou Meirong and Chen Yi then scored twice each, while Yang Liu added another goal as China completed the 13-0 victory.
"We made thorough preparations and targeted training before the match, especially for the pace of an early-morning game, the pitch and the time difference, so everyone was able to get into the game relatively quickly today," Ma said.
"As the match progressed, we gradually took control of the game. This opening win has laid a good foundation for our Asian Games campaign. We will remain focused, carefully review the details of this match and give our all in every remaining group-stage game," she added.
China head coach Alyson Annan expressed satisfaction with her team's overall performance, but said that the side could further increase its tempo, particularly in transitions between attack and defense and in the intensity of its pressing.
"The significance of the opening match is to establish a good start, identify problems and build up our form," Annan said. "We will carefully review this match, build on our strengths, address our shortcomings, refine our tactical details and get the team into the best possible competitive condition, so that we can play at a faster tempo, maintain more consistent form and perform better in the matches ahead."
China will face Chinese Taipei on Monday. ■

War update: 234 clashes on front line over past day, Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk sectors see heaviest fighting
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in a Facebook post on the battlefield situation as of 8:00 on Sunday, September 20.
The enemy launched 98 airstrikes, dropping 313 guided aerial bombs. In addition, Russian forces used 10,856 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,689 shelling attacks on settlements and Ukrainian military positions, including 58 using multiple-launch rocket systems.
In the Sumy region, the settlements of Bezsalivka, Pustohorod, Bachivsk, Korenok, Ulanove, Rivne, Kruzhok, Potapivka, Obody, Mala Korchakivka, Pysarivka, Sadky, Mohrytsia, Korchakivka, Sumy, Sopych, Hirky, Romashkove, Fotovyzh, and Volfyne came under fire. In the Chernihiv region, the settlements of Khrinivka, Krasnyi Khutir, and Mykhalchyna-Sloboda were shelled. Vilcha Sloboda and Korenok also came under airstrikes.
Ukraine’s aviation and artillery struck four clusters of Russian personnel and equipment, four command UAV posts, four artillery systems and artillery positions, a command post, and an anti-aircraft missile system.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, four Russian assault actions were recorded. The enemy carried out 122 attacks on Ukrainian positions and settlements.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukrainian units repelled 10 enemy attacks. Russian forces attempted to advance toward Lyman, Artilne, Ternova, Mala Vovcha, Vilkhuvatka, Shevyaikivka, and Dovzhanka.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces made two attempts to improve their positions and conducted assault operations near Kurylivka and Kivsharivka.
In the Lyman sector, Russian forces attacked 15 times near Novoiehorivka, Cherneshchyna, Novoselivka, Zarichne, Stavky, Lyman, and Dibrova. Their attempts to penetrate Ukrainian defenses were repelled.
In the Sloviansk sector, the enemy launched four assault actions near Yampil and Mykolaivka as well as toward Pyskunivka and Orikhuvatka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian forces conducted one offensive action toward Yurkivka.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, 25 attacks were recorded near Kostiantynivka and toward Osykove, Dovha Balka, Illinivka, Rusyn Yar, Mykolaipillia, Stepove, and Vilne.
In the Pokrovsk sector, Russian forces launched 21 attacks. In particular, they attempted to advance toward Dobropillia, Vodianske, Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Serhiivka and Molodetske.
In the Huliaipole sector, the enemy launched one attack toward Kopani.
No Russian attacks were recorded in the Oleksandrivka, Orikhiv and Dnipro River sectors.
No signs of Russian offensive force buildup were detected in the Volyn and Polissia sectors.
As reported by Ukrinform, total Russian combat losses since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, through September 20, 2026, are estimated at approximately 1,517,990 personnel.

NATO has 4,000-page plans for escalation on eastern flank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:20:00 UTC
15:20:00 KST

NATO has 4,000-page plans for escalation on eastern flank
NATO has 4,000-page plans in place in case the situation on its eastern flank escalates, NATO Military Committee chair Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said Saturday.
Responding to a journalist's question about a possible low-intensity provocation and the deployment of additional personnel and capabilities to NATO's eastern flank, Dragone said this was one of NATO's many plans.
"We have plans for the eastern flank — three plans, to be precise — to be ready for any kind of escalation," he said, noting that the plans cover actions, movements and countermeasures.
He said the decision-making process has been standardized to ensure it works as quickly as possible, and that this work has already begun. NATO has plans covering everything from a minor crisis or intervention on alliance territory to the invocation of Article 5 and beyond.
"The plans are ready, the structure is ready, and the troops, systems and weapons are on standby," Dragone said. "In the event of an attack, we know what to do," he added, saying that in the event of an attack, the risks of losses would far outweigh any potential gains.
Responding to a journalist's question about a possible Russian attack on border crossings between Poland and Ukraine, Dragone said NATO is already quite accustomed to hybrid attacks and, in his assessment, is dealing with them successfully. He noted that NATO is a defensive alliance and that the possibility of escalation is part of its thinking and approach. At the same time, Dragone said a direct attack on the Polish-Ukrainian border area has not been discussed as a realistic scenario.
"We have to demonstrate strength and send the message that no part of our territory, not a single centimeter of it, can come under attack," he said. Dragone explained that hybrid operations do not automatically trigger Article 5 of the NATO treaty because they generally remain below that threshold. "A direct attack is not on our agenda in the sense that we are planning for it, but in the event of a direct attack, the immediate invocation of Article 5 would be requested," he said.
Speaking about ammunition stocks in the event of a possible prolonged conflict with Russia, Dragone acknowledged that NATO is fully aware of the issue, particularly given the war in Ukraine and the enormous amount of ammunition both sides use every day. He said this is precisely why NATO is investing in and encouraging the defense industry to change — moving away from the peacetime mentality that prevailed just four years ago and increasing production capacity so that the industry is prepared for a prolonged war and can meet the necessary demand.
According to Dragone, the financial resources are available, as allies have decided to invest significantly more in defense. "The funding will be provided, and we need to accelerate their delivery capacity," he said. He said the defense industry is working on this and moving in the right direction, but efforts must be intensified further because the daily expenditure of weapons and ammunition is very high.
At the same time, other activities are taking place on the eastern flank involving both the use of drones and defenses against them. These activities are part of measures aimed at strengthening security on the eastern flank in all respects, from air defense and drone use to counter-drone capabilities.
Responding to a question about physical attacks on European defense industry factories and warehouses, Dragone said such incidents could be regarded as criminal offenses, but they could also be elements of hybrid warfare. He said intelligence services are dealing with the issue, but NATO does not know how many incidents have been prevented or thwarted before they occurred, partly because they are not reported. According to him, there have been many cases in which threats have been prevented or stopped in time, but the exact number of such cases is unknown.
"In defense, the results are not immediately visible or tangible. That is what security is," Dragone said, urging people to trust the work of the security services.
Dragone's remarks came at a meeting of NATO chiefs of defense in Copenhagen, Delfi reported, and followed warnings from several European leaders that Russia could stage a drone or missile attack against a NATO country supporting Ukraine. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday that Moscow could send drones or missiles into the territory of an eastern flank country as part of a staged provocation, an assessment echoed by French President Emmanuel Macron and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten. NATO's official threat assessment has not changed, and a NATO representative told Politico there is currently no imminent threat of attack.

US embassies issue security alerts over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:17:19 UTC
15:17:19 KST

The alerts advised Americans to "be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions" and said the conflict could "escalate rapidly."
US embassies across the Middle East have issued security alerts warning Americans to maintain "heightened vigilance" following attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Embassies in Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE said the "military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly" and that the security environment remained "complex."
The alerts also advised people to "be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."
It comes after the Houthi rebels on Saturday said they had carried out two operations using ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones to target Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi attacks.
"The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu," the group claimed.
A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces - which were formed in 2015 to back Yemen's internationally recognised government - later confirmed that the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces had intercepted a ballistic missile fired towards Riyadh. The spokesperson added that the group had also targeted the cities of Baish, Taif, Farasan, and Yanbu.
On Saturday, residents of Riyadh reported seeing flames and smoke at the capital's King Khalid International Airport.
Video footage circulating on social media appeared to show a towering column of smoke rising from the airport, which flight tracking site Flightradar24 had said was experiencing "major problems."
Yemen's Houthi rebels, who declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, have been launching increasing attacks on Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia has hit back with its own strikes on the group - which has seized vast stretches of territory in Yemen this month in a lightning offensive - but has failed to stop its advance.
In a press briefing on Friday, Stéphane Dujarric, a spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General, addressed the situation in Yemen.
"Since hostilities escalated in August, the Human Rights office has documented 110 civilian casualties in 31 incidents, including 28 killed and 82 injured, across Taizz, Al Hudaydah and Marib. Insecurity and access constraints continue to hamper our ability to verify the actual number as you can imagine is very likely higher," Dujarric said, according to a transcript shared by the UN.
"We urge all parties, and those with influence over them, to act immediately to de-escalate, protect civilians and facilitate humanitarian access. Every effort must be made to prevent further loss of life," he added.

Kelly Sildaru second in New Zealand as winds cancel final
Estonian freestyle skier Kelly Sildaru kicked off her competition season with a second-place finish at the Snow League event in Cardrona, New Zealand.
The season-opening event saw Sildaru overcome Australian Indra Brown in her first halfpipe duel, scoring 77 points on her opening run and 74 on her second, while her opponent's best was 72.
Sildaru, 24, is competing in the Snow League's World Challenge format, where teams of four comprise a male and female snowboarder alongside a male and female freestyle skier. She is part of Team Europe together with Finnish freestyle skier Jon Sallinen and snowboarders Queralt Castellet (Spain) and Jonas Häsler of (Switzerland).
The win sent her into the final, but strong winds forced the cancellation of her duel with Challengers team representative Mischa Thomas. The winner was decided on semifinal results, where Thomas had scored 83 and 91.
Sildaru earned seven points for Team Europe with her second-place finish, and her team finished second overall on 27 points. The Challengers team won with 37, Team Asia-Pacific were third with 22 and the North Americans fourth with 14. Finley Melville Ives and Ryusei Yamada also took victories alongside Thomas.
The next Snow League event takes place in Aspen, Colorado, in early January, with the World Cup season starting ahead of that in Innsbruck, Austria, in late November.
Estonian freestyle skier Henry Sildaru, Kelly's brother, was drafted to XC Golden State for the X Games' new team league and will team up with Eileen Gu.

Hundreds of drones target Moscow on last day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:04:48 UTC
15:04:48 KST

Ukraine has targeted Moscow and elsewhere in Russia in a large-scale attack that involved hundreds of drones and the first acknowledged use of ballistic missiles by Kyiv in the war.
The attack killed at least two people and damaged what Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said was one of Russia’s “key oil industry facilities” on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday.
Zelenskyy said that among the weapons used in the attack was the Pelican, a short-range ballistic missile, which has an estimated range of about 350km (220 miles), not enough to reach Moscow directly.
Though the president did not offer any further details, the missile was likely to have been used as part of the overall complex of attacks; he listed 10 different weapons types, all largely developed in Ukraine.
Ballistic missiles fly at several times the speed of sound in their terminal phase, making them very difficult to intercept, unlike slower-moving cruise missiles and drones. Until recently, Ukraine had lacked its own missile technology.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had used its domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Moscow. The long-range weapon has previously been used against targets deep inside Russia and has the range to reach the country’s capital.
Ukrainian and Russian Telegram channels posted images of what they said was debris from a Flamingo missile found in the Moscow region, though the claims could not be independently verified. Ruslan Leviev, the head of the open-source investigation group Conflict Intelligence Team, said the debris probably came from a Flamingo missile.
Moscow’s mayor, Sergey Sobyanin, said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow, though these figures are often exaggerated, and Ukraine’s daily drone fire rate estimated a number in the low hundreds.
Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election in Russia that is expected to tighten Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.
Moscow’s regional governor said at least two people were killed – a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man – in two separate locations.
A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drone’s origin.
Kyiv has stepped up its campaign of long-range drone strikes against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure, a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort.
Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil-refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones.
A facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties were reported and emergency services were on the scene. The refinery has already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.
The Pelican missile is understood to be the FP-7 made by Fire Point, Ukraine’s most successful long-range drone and missile maker. The company is also developing the longer-range FP-9, which has a range of more than 500 miles, meaning it could be used to target Moscow in the future. A test flight is expected later this autumn.
The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s first parliamentary elections since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

Thousands of pregnant women in England are reporting domestic abuse. Midwives are struggling to cope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:09 UTC
15:00:09 KST

About 20,000 disclosures of domestic abuse are estimated to be made to maternity services in England every year, analysis has found.
The figures are likely to be an underestimate of the true scale of disclosures, according to experts, highlighting the role maternity professionals play in identifying abuse.
About 3.3% of maternity bookings made within NHS trusts across England involved a disclosure of current or non-recent domestic abuse.
Applying this proportion to national NHS maternity bookings activity suggests there are approximately 20,000 disclosures of domestic abuse made within maternity services in England every year.
Of the 118 trusts contacted by the charity the For Baby’s Sake Trust, 74 provided usable data, and the figures are based on a three-year average of the most recent data available.
Gill Walton, the chief executive of the Royal College of Midwives, said the findings “lay bare” something that midwives already know from their day-to-day practice.
“Midwives are often the only professional a pregnant woman sees regularly and alone, which makes them uniquely placed to spot the signs of domestic abuse and respond with care,” Walton said.
“But recognising a disclosure is only the first step – staff need proper, specialist training to know how to respond and services need the time and resources to follow through with support, so that no disclosure is ever a missed opportunity to protect a parent and their baby.
Experts have also called for midwives to receive adequate support and training on handling such domestic abuse disclosures, while also working long hours on busy maternity wards that can also face staff shortages.
“Midwives and other maternity staff play such a crucial role when it comes to reporting disclosures of domestic violence which are made to them. However, maternity staff also need better support so they know what the next steps are regarding what to do with these disclosures,” Veronica Oakeshott, the interim head of external affairs at Women’s Aid, said.
She added: “They’re already facing immense pressure working on busy maternity wards, so it’s essential that they receive adequate support and training on how to handle these disclosures moving forward.”
Judith Rees, the chief operating officer and designated safeguarding lead at For Baby’s Sake Trust, said: “Having worked as a midwife, health visitor and nurse across 33 years within the NHS, I know how important the relationship between a maternity professional and a parent can be. Creating the right opportunity to ask about domestic abuse, and knowing how to respond when someone says ‘yes’, can be life-changing.”
She added: “Midwives need to understand the impact domestic abuse can have on a parent and their baby, be able to recognise risk and respond safely, and know where to go for specialist support. Pregnancy and the early postnatal period give us a critical window to intervene, and when we get that response right, we have an opportunity to improve outcomes for parents and babies.”
Kate Brintworth, the chief midwifery officer for NHS England, said: “All staff working in NHS maternity and neonatal services are committed to ensuring that any disclosure of domestic abuse will be met with compassion, sensitivity and clear options for support. Midwives receive mandatory safeguarding training, alongside specialist training on how to ask sensitive questions about abuse, and can refer women to specialist domestic abuse services for support with issues such as housing and legal advice where needed.”

Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:09 UTC
15:00:09 KST

About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.
But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.
This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.
Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.
Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.
“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a representative for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”

Nigel Farage has said he wants to “hijack” Donald Trump’s hardline ICE adviser and bring him to the UK “to secure our borders”.
Speaking at an event in the US, the Reform UK leader also called for Europe to take a “more sensible view” of the US president’s administration rather than seeing it as “villainous”.
Farage complimented Tom Homan, Trump’s adviser on the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Speaking at the event where Homan was a guest, he said: “I’ve got terrible news for you. We’re hijacking Tom Homan and taking him back with us to secure our borders.”

Salgado Araujo and Durán Guerrero were the 29th and 30th people that immigration officers have opened fire on since Trump took office last year, according to The Trace, an outlet that tracks shootings in its gun violence data hub.
Homan has taken a more hands-on approach to immigration policy since Trump brought him in to “de‑escalate” tensions in Minneapolis, which was the scene of a brutal immigration crackdown in January.
In Trump’s first term, he helped to design some of the administration’s most draconian measures – most notably family separation, a strategy reportedly deemed too severe by officials in the Obama White House, but which later became central to Trump’s “zero tolerance” policy.
Reform UK has committed to a more hardline immigration policy than proposed by other mainstream parties, promising mass deportations of people who have entered the country illegally and deployment of the Royal Navy to intercept small boats in the Channel.
The party did not respond to a request for comment on whether it would seek to emulate Trump’s style of immigration enforcement under ICE which has been criticised for its brutality.
Farage interviewed Homan for his GB News show last year, describing him as uncompromising and saying he had achieved remarkable results on deportations, while acknowledging there had been “some backlash”.
On Trump in general, Farage said at the event that it was “important that our country, and Europe too, get a better, more sensible view of America than it gets of the Trump administration through traditional mainstream media who frankly paint the whole project out to be villainous”.
Farage’s positive remarks towards Trump and his administration come after the Reform UK leader appeared to distance himself from the president, saying in April they had not spoken for many months and questioning his judgment on the Iran war.
His latest trip to the US comes at a time when relations between the White House and Downing Street are under strain over Iran and policy towards Israel since Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer.
Burnham will have his first meeting with Trump in New York next week, with the US president having previously described him as “extremely liberal” but also having praised him for potentially opening up the North Sea to further drilling.
Farage did, however, depart from Trump’s views again earlier this week after the US president said he would love to see a united Ireland.
“Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom,” Farage said. “The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum nor unification.”

Chiltern Railways enters public ownership in Labour nationalisation push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:08 UTC
15:00:08 KST

Chiltern Railways has become the latest train operator to enter public ownership as the government closes in on its ambition to renationalise all major passenger rail services.
The operator, which runs commuter rail services on the Chiltern mainline between London Marylebone and Birmingham, on Sunday became the sixth to be nationalised under Labour, with the remaining four to follow by the end of 2027.
The Department for Transport (DfT) said the move would bring more reliable services, with plans to end what it termed the “daily frustration” of overcrowding.
It has promised a package of improvements for Chiltern passengers, including more services and seats, new trains, upgraded stations and better onboard facilities including upgraded wifi.
The government legislated in 2024 to renationalise private train operations as contracts allowed, joining the four operators already in public ownership and Network Rail to eventually establish an integrated body, Great British Railways (GBR).
The rail minister, Peter Hendy, said: “Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time.
“As we set up Great British Railways, we’re putting passengers first. It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes.”
Another 25 daily services will be introduced on the Chiltern network from December, with 10,000 extra seats each weekday, as more new trains are rolled out.
Tony Baxter, the interim managing director of Chiltern Railways, said customers would see “improvements made possible thanks to years of planning, dedication and hard work by Chiltern colleagues. Public ownership will further strengthen that progress through closer collaboration across the industry.”
The DfT said the move “also provides a fresh opportunity to deliver East West Rail”, the long-awaited services that should have started under Chiltern last year on a completed stretch of the future Oxford-Cambridge line.
However, it is unclear if a start date for East-West services between Oxford and Milton Keynes has come any closer after the transfer to the state operator, DfTO. Although a variety of reasons have been given for the delay, unions oppose plans to run the trains without a guard.
The RMT union is due to demonstrate outside London Marylebone station on Monday, and members are being balloted for strike action over plans backed by the DfT for driver-only operation.
The row threatens to further cloud the horizon for GBR, as the government seeks to demonstrate the benefits of the publicly owned railway.
The next operator to transfer into public ownership is due to be Great Western Railway in December.

10 of the best mountain huts in Europe: bunkrooms, bothies and bonhomie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:08 UTC
15:00:08 KST

Cabaña Verónica, Spain
A good mountain hut, I reckon, should be small and only accessible on foot after considerable effort. Throw in a bit of historical interest and I’m bound to be happy. In which case, Cabaña Verónica in the Picos de Europa is a fine start to this list. It sleeps six, and at 2,325 metres requires a two-hour trek from the nearest cable car station, never mind road. It has incredible views and a friendly custodian who keeps things in good order. Yet the real attraction is that this place was formerly a gun turret of a US navy battleship that was scrapped in Bilbao in 1960. An enterprising engineer, Conrado Senties, had it carried up on horseback and reassembled on a plug of rock in the middle of nowhere. Don’t ask why, just enjoy the eccentricity.
€15, reservarefugios.com
Låktatjåkko, Sweden
An absolute gem just over 100 miles north of the Arctic Circle and 1,228 metres up a mountain, Låktatjåkko is well placed to deliver that other essential experience of a decent hut: cosy conviviality while surrounded by frequently hostile conditions. When I visited, it was hard to find the hut because it was coated in thick ice and half-buried in snow. The snug timber-clad lounge is the perfect spot to sit in front of the fire and read old accounts of Arctic explorers such as Fridtjof Nansen (there is no phone coverage). The kitchen bangs out endless plates of waffles with cloudberry jam and cream as well as more substantial fare. Be warned, however: in winter the chances of being marooned are quite high and the skiing can be a serious challenge due to extreme cold and fast-changing mountain weather.
From 515 Swedish kronor (£40), laktatjakko.se
Gaustatoppen, Norway
Like many other huts belonging to the wonderful Norwegian Trekking Association, this place is small, well-run and traditional. It’s the route up to it that is astounding. You enter a mountainside, take a thundering old-school funicular railway one kilometre inside the granite, then wander through tunnels of military-grade concrete, before exiting through a blast-proof steel door and climbing down a short way to the hut. All that startling infrastructure is the cold war relic of a Nato communications station now doubling up as a museum and underground route to the hut, which dates back to 1893. This unique means of access gives the hut an advantage: you can stay in winter (weekends only) on the summit of the highest peak in Telemark province, Gaustatoppen, a popular ski resort, and then ski down. When I was there, the view was about 10 metres into thick mist. On a clear day, however, they say you can see one-sixth of Norway.
From 1,550 Norwegian kroner (£122), dnt.no
Chata pod Rysmi, Slovakia
The Tatra mountains have some excellent huts, but this is my pick. Close enough to the summit of Rysy (2,501 metres) for an early start to catch dawn on the top, it is traditional, well-run and basic. The weather here can take a brutal turn at any time of year and, like all the best huts, this is in precisely the right position to be a genuine bolthole. If it looks younger than its 1933 start date, that is because it has been destroyed several times by avalanches and rock falls, which is also why it only opens 1 June to 31 October.
€65, chatapodrysmi.kst.sk
Kredarica on Triglav, Slovenia
This is, in many ways, a standard, old-fashioned mountain refuge, but Kredarica has the great advantage of being the last potential stop en route to the summit of Slovenia’s highest peak, Triglav (2,864 metres). Given that every Slovene feels compelled to visit the summit at least once in their lifetime, this can be a busy place in summer, especially as the views are magnificent. The hardcore, however, savour its spartan winter comforts, when the dormitories are unheated bunkholes for those about to tackle the final, rather tricky ascent to the top (ice axe and crampons essential).
€30 half-board, triglavskidom.si
Le Refuge de Ciottulu di Mori, Corsica
One of the attractions of Corsica’s epic GR20 long-distance footpath is its unapologetically old-fashioned mountain huts. No emergency helicopters swooping in when the G&Ts run out: this is gruff, mule-supplied, mountain hospitality. Ciottulu is a good example of the genre: bare bones dining room and a dormitory with communal sleeping benches for 26. Its ambience is more like a bothy set at 2,000 metres in a vast stony panorama with a slightly unpredictable caretaker. 
€15, le-gr20.fr
Breiðuvik, Iceland
The east of Iceland is home to a scattering of superb huts like this one. Breiðvik is actually on the coast and has the usual bunk rooms and well-appointed kitchen. The location is the big attraction: a wild, desolate coastline of volcanic sand beaches and abandoned villages. Together with 39 other locations, Brieðvik is part of a useful network run by the Icelandic Touring Association.
11,500 Icelandic kronur (£70), ferdaf.is
Scotland’s mountain bothies
The UK has always remained aloof from the continental urge to build something cosy on a mountain top. We are much happier sitting inside our leaky waterproofs eating soggy sandwiches. The Mountain Bothy Association is doing a little to encourage us away from such Spartanism, but not too much. Most are former cottages for miners or shepherds; many now have a fireplace or even a wood burner. In some, there are a few supplies left on a shelf by previous guests. I have a soft spot for the hard charms of the least comfortable, where you may find only a stone bench and an open doorway. A few have become over-used and afflicted by visitors who don’t understand the ethos of mucking in, sharing out and cleaning up. For that reason, I’m not sure it’s worthwhile picking out any particular bothy (pictured is the Elphin Bothy in the Assynt region of Sutherland), suffice to say that the roster contains some absolute classics. Go and find them.
mountainbothies.org.uk
Rifugio Nuvolau, Italy
The Dolomites are so blessed with exceptional huts and Nuvolau is one of the best. Only accessible on foot, it was originally built in 1883 as a bequest from the Baron Richard von Meerheimb, the man who coined the term “psychodrama”, something he may have dreamed up while watching a Nuvolau sunset. The impeccable location is famous for its stunning shifts in light and colour. Inside is a dining room that serves excellent food, including a three-course dinner; upstairs is a small dormitory.
€51 B&B, rifugionuvolau.it
Rifugio Lagazuoi, Italy
Many huts in the Dolomites have learned that economic survival is via tourists rather than hikers and climbers. Lagazuoi is one of them. Built as a climbers’ refuge, it has expanded over the years and been connected to the road by cable car, which enables coach parties to stay. And yet, it remains magnificent. The south-facing terrace is lovely and there are fantastic walks all around, not least through the tunnels and terraces of the first world war frontline that lie on the cliff face below. Mount Lagazuoi (2,835 metres) was one location where the Austro-Hungarian empire faced off against Italians. Many years later, in 1965, Ugo Pompanin, a local Alpine guide and rock-climbing pioneer, recognised the potential and built the first hut, which, several additions later, is still run in great style by his son Guido.
From €85 with breakfast, rifugiolagazuoi.com

‘Flip the table and rise up’: Lib Dems’ president in combative mood as party gathers in Brighton
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:07 UTC
15:00:07 KST

Standing outside Toynbee Hall in the East End of London, Josh Babarinde doesn’t exactly look like a rabble-rouser. But despite the well-cut suit and disarmingly large smile, the president of the Liberal Democrats is, apparently, up for a fight.
“There are big modern giants that are getting in the way of people’s ability to thrive, and it is the job of Liberal Democrats to address that,” says the 33-year-old. “How are we going to do that? Well, first of all, we’ve got to flip the table over and rise up.”
Flipping over tables is not behaviour normally associated with Liberal Democrat members, about 5,000 of whom are in Brighton for its annual conference this weekend.
But Babarinde, frequently described as a rising star in the party’s ranks, wants his comrades to channel the spirit of the great Liberal thinker William Beveridge, who finessed his radical ideas on social reform in the 141-year-old Whitechapel building.
Beveridge decried the five evils of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. However, Babarinde, the Eastbourne MP, is taking aim at targets from big tech to crypto billionaires. “People are looking for a force to help break some of those giants and give power and cash back to people who this country is meant to be working for,” he says.
That people are seeking alternatives to the status quo is undeniable, but whether they are looking at the Liberal Democrats is a matter of debate.
The historic 2024 election result gave the party 71 MPs, yet it has been stuck at about 11% in polls for months.
The Lib Dems gained 153 councillors in England in May and six seats in the Scottish parliament, although the party’s advances were more modest than those of the Greens and Reform UK. The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, also struggles to command attention. Lib Dem MPs grumble that Nigel Farage only has to sneeze to attract media covverage, while Davey has to resort to bungee jumping.
“You’ve got a very crowded multiparty system. You’ve got Reform saying any old shit in the media and getting coverage for it with no plan for delivering,” says Babarinde. “As Liberal Democrats, we’re not going to fall into that trap. But what we have got to be clear about is the diagnosis of the problem, who it is standing in the way and what needs to be done.”
He dismisses the idea that the party is yet to produce eye-catching retail policies – “There’s oodles and oodles of it!” – but says it needs to reach beyond its middle England strongholds with digital campaigning that is as strong as its much-envied ground game.
Babarinde, who has spoken about his mother being subjected to domestic abuse and how it shaped his politics, has experience engaging with hard-to-reach communities. He set up a social enterprise smartphone repair service staffed by former offenders and at-risk youth more than a decade ago, which earned him an OBE.
After a stroll through the East End, he points to the stand in Spitalfields market where they had pinned up sheets of A4 paper with “Cracked It” written across them in felt-tip, and laughs. “I would never have got my phone repaired there,” he says. “But when people were giving their money over … I was seeing these guys think: ‘Oh my God, wow! Someone wants my skills. They want what I can offer.’”
Do the Lib Dems want what the ambitious Babarinde has to offer? Despite being elected in 2024, he was elevated to the role of president in November, giving him a vital say in strategy and organisation. He bats away the inevitable question about whether he would like the top job – but when asked if he is a natural leader, he smiles.
“I roll up my sleeves and get stuck in,” he says. “When I saw those young people in the East End prolifically involved in crime amid a lack of opportunities. I wasn’t waiting for someone to swoop in to come to address that issue. I decided to come up with a solution.”
So if the problem is that the Liberal Democrats – despite a seemingly advantageous political backdrop – are stuck on 11% in the polls, what does he see as the answer? “The solution is exactly what is in the strategy we’re talking about this week,” Babarinde says.
“I stood to be party president because I thought I had something to offer: to help develop a new strategy for the party so we can reach new heights.”

Reαd carefully: how to spot – and avoid – a homoglyph attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:07 UTC
15:00:07 KST

You’ve read the email carefully and it looks legitimate. The link it asks you to click on has none of the usual red flags: there are no weird numbers or extra parts to the URL. You feel safe to proceed.
But if you had looked slightly closer you may have noticed something slightly wrong with one of the characters. Just as in the headline of this piece where instead of “a” we used the Cyrillic “α”.
Fraudsters can use letters from different alphabets to create URLs and email addresses that look almost identical to the real thing, but in reality send anyone who clicks on them to a spoof website or inbox. From there they can harvest personal details to use in their scams.
There are other letters and symbols that are easily switched. Last year tech experts spotted fraudsters using the Japanese hiragana character ん to look like a / in an address designed to look as though it was on Booking.com’s website.
Jake Moore, global security adviser at cybersecurity company ESET, says the fraudsters “love Microsoft” as a company identity to spoof. “A fake site might use the Cyrillic “с” instead of the Latin “c” (miсrosoft v microsoft),” he says.
Moore says this type of fraud – known as a homoglyph attack – is becoming increasingly popular. A homoglyph is a character that looks very similar, or even identical, to another one.
“Most phishing attacks are designed to point people to links these days instead of downloading attachments. Attachments can easily be scanned and caught by security software if malicious,” he says.
“Therefore, criminals need to design their websites where the links look genuine and casually request people to click on them without thinking.”
Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, says homoglyph attacks “are really more of a psychological trick than a technical one”, because the fraudsters are typically trying to panic you into responding quickly, rather than taking time to check things out.
“The goal is to create a sense of panic so you don’t look too closely at the URL. They’re betting that when we’re in a rush, our brains see what we expect to see,” Briedis says.
 It just goes to show that the split-second decision you make when clicking a link is often the most vulnerable part of the whole security chain.”
What it looks like
The real thing. Until you look closely.
You will receive an email or text message suggesting you need to click on a URL or email to sort something out.
Some fonts make substitutions almost impossible to detect. In an email address given in comic sans , for example, the Cyrillic a does not look at all out of place.
“We’ve spent years telling people to check the website before trusting it but the problem with this technique is that you can do exactly that and still be fooled as it can look as it should,” says Moore.
If it’s a URL, Moore says typically it will lead to a site that encourages you to enter your credentials for the real site, including your username, password and even a one-time passcode.
What to do
If you are sent a link, take a moment to think rather than reacting immediately.
“If any text, WhatsApp or email is asking you to log in anywhere, it is vital that you independently visit the genuine website rather than trusting the link in front of you to save a few seconds,” says Moore.
And apply the same thinking to email addresses. Type in the address you know to be correct, rather than clicking on a link.
Keep your browser updated. It will flag up suspicious websites, and by keeping it updated it will catch the criminals’ latest workarounds.
Put in place two-factor authentication, or multifactor authentication (2FA or MFA), which means you have two steps to log into a site.
If you find that your details have been compromised, change your passwords immediately. Contact your bank and report the phishing attack to Report Fraud.

Germany: Polls open in two key state elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Germany: Voting underway in two key state elections
Published September 20, 2026last updated September 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Regional elections are taking place in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state Berlin
- Voters are also electing members of district assemblies in Berlin
- The outcome of the elections could determine the political future of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose approval rating is at a record low
- The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to gain ground in both states but is unlikely to be part of government
- For the first time, 16- and 17-year-olds are eligible to vote in both states
We're expecting exit polls at around 6 p.m. local time (1600 GMT/UTC). Follow along here for all the highs and lows today:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Berlin election turnout up sharply by midday
Voter turnout in Berlin's state election was running significantly ahead of the 2023 election by midday on Sunday, according to the city's election authorities.
By noon, 27.9% of eligible voters had participated, including postal voters. That was 4.5 percentage points higher than the 23.4% recorded at the same point in the 2023 election.
About a third of the voting certificates issued were for postal ballots, state election officer Stephan Bröchler told Germany's DPA news agency.
Election officials said voting at Berlin's 2,542 polling stations had so far proceeded without major problems. Polling stations opened at 8 a.m. and are set to close at 6 p.m.
Around 2.5 million people are eligible to elect Berlin's state parliament. Seventeen parties are contesting the election with their own lists, about half as many as the last vote, in 2023.
For the first time, 16- and 17-year-olds are also eligible to vote in a Berlin state election.
Berlin has been governed by a coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) since a court-ordered rerun of the troubled 2021 state election was held in 2023.
German voters cast ballots on a bus after polling station glitch
Some voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania had an unusual start to election day on Sunday, casting their ballots on a public bus after officials were unable to open their polling station.
Election authorities in the northern city of Rostock temporarily turned the vehicle belonging to the local public transport company into a polling station in the Kassebohm district.
The makeshift arrangement lasted for about half an hour before voters were able to use the intended polling station, located inside a privately run school building.
Rostock has 134 polling stations for the state election.
Berlin reports minor vandalism at polling stations
Berlin police said they had received reports of property damage at several polling stations as voting got underway on Sunday.
In one case, the lock of a polling station had been glued shut. Police said the station was nevertheless able to open on time and voting was not disrupted.
Authorities also received reports that campaign posters had been placed too close to polling stations.
Police advised people who notice such posters to contact the officials responsible for the respective polling station, saying emergency services were coordinating closely with election officials.
Candidates cast votes in key state elections
Voters have been lining up at polling stations to cast their ballots, as have the candidates (presumably to vote for themselves) in Berlin and in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
In the German capital, Werner Graf (Green Party) and Steffen Krach (center-left Social Democrats) cast their votes in the Tempelhof-Schöneberg constituency.
Further north, Leif-Erik Holm (far-right AfD) cast his vote in Schwerin, the capital of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Holm told local public broadcaster NDR outside the polling station that he was "optimistic" about his party's chances.
"The clouds have parted and the sky is turning blue," he said, referring to the color of his party.
His rival, the incumbent state premier Manuela Schwesig of the Social Democrats (SPD), cast her vote a short time later.
IN DEPTH: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.
Find out more about how foreigners are not included in Berlin's elections in this report.
WATCH: Elif Eralp: From daughter of refugees to Berlin mayor?
In the run-up to Berlin's election, Elif Eralp's socialist Left Party is narrowly ahead in major polls — setting up a close race with the conservative CDU. But her party faces controversy over antisemitic rhetoric.
IN DEPTH: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: Will economy shape the vote?
Voters in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania head to the polls on Sunday, with the Social Democrats and far-right AfD neck and neck.
Here's a look at key economic issues that could influence the election.
WATCH: German local election races taking place after AfD's historic victory in Saxony Anhalt
The elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are taking place two weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged to first place in Saxony-Anhalt, securing nearly 44% of the vote in the state.
Here's what you need to know:
WATCH: Is Berlin heading for its Mamdani moment?
The Left Party is hoping to secure its candidate Elif Eralp as mayor of the capital city if the party finishes in the first place in state elections. Here's what you need to know about her:
Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election guide: What you need to know
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the fight is between the Social Democrats (SPD) led by the popular Manuela Schwesig and the far-right Altnerative for Germany (AfD).
The 52-year-old Schwesig has made it her mission to beat back the advance of the AfD, which is polling at around 37%, ahead of the SPD at 33%.
"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW recently. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."
What to watch out for in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania
Besides keeping tabs on whether the AfD comes out on top, all eyes are also on how the CDU performs in the state.
CDU is the conservative Christian Democratic Union party that is chaired by the chancellor of the country, Friedrich Merz.
His party is polling at around 7% in the state, which is slightly above the 5% threshold required by a party to enter state parliament.
In the 2021 elections, the CDU had just 13.3% of the vote.
If the CDU fails to achieve the 5% threshold, there's going to be immense pressure on Merz to fight for his job.
Who are the main candidates?
- SPD: Manuela Schwesig, also the incumbent state premier.
- AfD: Leif-Erik Holm is the AfD's candidate for state premier, whom the party would put forward to head the state government if it can form one, while Enrico Schult is the AfD's candidate leading the party's election campaign in the state. Holm is the better-known candidate out of the two.
- CDU: Daniel Peters, who has been the chair of the CDU parliamentary group in the state parliament.
- The Left (Die Linke): Simon Oldenburg, who is the current minister for education in the state.
What's the likeliest scenario?
Even if the AfD comes out on top in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, that's not a guarantee that it will govern the state.
In Germany's parliamentary system, a party needs a majority in the state parliament or coalition partners to elect a state premier.
That means that the AfD could be pushed to the sidelines if other parties reject cooperation with it under the so-called "firewall" policy.
Berlin election guide: What you need to know
The campaign so far has been dominated by a battle between the far-left Left Party and Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)
Both parties are neck and neck, according to polling in recent weeks.
If Merz's party wins the elections, that'll be good news for the chancellor, whose popularity has taken a big hit, especially following state elections in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) trounced the CDU.
Seventeen parties are contesting the election in Berlin, including the Left Party and the CDU. The four other major parties are the AfD (which has consistently polled in third place), the environmentalist Green Party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the left-wing, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).
What is the top issue for Berlin voters?
With the German capital struggling with a severe housing shortage in a city where 85% rent their homes, housing and rental costs are voters' top concerns.
Advertised rents have doubled since 2014, and the city needs 211,000 more homes by 2040.
So far, the Left Party has been the only major party that has promised to act on a 2021 referendum when 59% of Berliners voted to have the government take control of apartments from the biggest landlords to protect rents.
For the AfD, Berlin's housing crisis has fed into its argument for restricting immigration that has driven support for the party.
Who are the main candidates?
- CDU: Stefan Evers is the CDU's lead candidate after the outgoing mayor, Kai Wegner, withdrew from the race.
- The Left Party (Die Linke): Elif Eralp will be leading her party into an election as its lead candidate for the first time. She was born in Munich to Turkish parents. She has been compared to Zohran Mamdani, the democratic socialist who won the New York City mayor race following his campaign around an affordability agenda for residents of his city.
- The Greens (Die Grünen): The Greens are fielding a two-person team consisting of Bettina Jarasch and Werner Graf.
- AfD (Alternative for Germany): Kristin Brinker has campaigned on issues of crime and immigration.
- SPD: Steffen Krach, who has experience working in the Berlin city government and was until recently a top politician in Hanover, the capital of Lower Saxony.
Germany's state elections and the fate of Chancellor Merz: What to know
Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a rare campaign appearance for his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at an event in Berlin on Thursday but has largely stayed away from the campaign trail.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU might even fail to make the 5% threshold required to enter parliament.
At the national level, Merz's own approval ratings fell to as low as 14% earlier in the week , while the far-right AfD has surged to first place with 27-29%, according to opinion polls released earlier this week.
Merz's CDU was polling nationally at 18-20%.
The chancellor has been under mounting pressure over whether he's the right person for the job, amid frustration over the slow pace of his promised reforms and the rise of the AfD.
Merz insisted this week that he's still committed to leading the nation and his governing coalition with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).
"I was elected for four years and I want to use this time to solve problems," he said on Tuesday, insisting: "We have to prove that this can be achieved with this coalition."
However, a YouGov survey released on Friday showed that around half of Germans don't expect Merz to still be chancellor by the end of the year.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen and welcome to our coverage of elections in Berlin and the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Polling stations are open for voters to elect members of the state parliaments. There's also a third vote open to EU citizens for electing members of one of Berlin's 12 district or borough assemblies.
While the elections are regional, they are set to have a national impact, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose popularity has severely dipped in recent weeks, struggling to keep his job.
That's due to a host of reasons, including the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) that secured a historic result with nearly 44% of the vote in elections two weeks ago in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
In Berlin, the race is tied between the Christian Democratic Party (CDU) and the Left Party (Die Linke). The AfD has consistently been polling third in Berlin, which is both the capital city and one of the country's 16 states.
In the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the race is tied between the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the AfD.
Stay tuned for the latest developments in these two crucial elections throughout the day.
