Are global stock markets heading for a crash?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

At the height of the summer, the mood was optimistic in the world’s financial capitals. Powered by the AI revolution, the US stock market had rallied to a fresh all-time high, as investors bet the multitrillion-dollar investment spree would overshadow the hit from the Iran war.
Now the warning lights are flashing red. As the fighting in the Middle East intensifies without clear sign of a resolution, financial markets have been thrown into renewed turmoil. A slowdown looms in the AI arms race, and tinderbox conditions in the market for government debt are fuelling alarm.
In the past week the US government’s borrowing costs climbed to the highest level since 2007, with knock-on consequences for the finances of households, businesses, and other governments worldwide. The fear is that Donald Trump’s war is igniting higher levels of inflation. The president’s tax and spending plans – driving Washington’s debt levels above $40tn (£29.9tn) – also has investors worried.
But as the soaring global oil price to above $100 a barrel stokes heavy selling pressure in the bond market, could shares be the next in line for a crash?
With the S&P 500 index of leading US companies 3% below an all-time high, and a combined value of more than $20tn for the “magnificent seven” tech stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Tesla – the concern is that markets are overextended just as the storm clouds gather for the world economy.
“These are febrile times,” Albert Edwards, a senior analyst at the French investment bank Société Générale, wrote in a note to clients. “The key worry for investors and policymakers alike is the extent to which the current oil price ‘shock’ will ripple through the global economy and whether it will necessitate sharply higher, recession-inducing, interest rates.”
Famed for his gloomy predictions, Edwards thinks the ingredients for a financial crisis could be coming together.
Such is the worry over the Iran war stoking inflation that the US Federal Reserve defied Trump this week with its first interest rate rise since 2023. As households and businesses come under pressure from rising energy bills and surging fuel prices, central banks elsewhere are also taking action.
Financial markets suggest the Bank of England will raise interest rates four times before the end of next year, even after it kept borrowing costs on hold this week. The European Central Bank raised rates last week, highlighting the hit to the eurozone from the escalating conflict, and the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to a 31-year high on Friday.
The rationale is that adding to the cost of borrowing will weigh on the economy – limiting the potential for short-term higher rates of inflation from becoming entrenched. However, it will hit households and businesses already struggling with a cost of living crisis. Job losses will probably rise, in-turn compounding the challenges facing governments swimming in debt.
A US recession has historically followed about three to 3.5 years after the first rate rise, on average, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid has calculated. Markets have a habit of falling, or even crashing, before a recession begins, and often start to recover before the economy does.
However, the big concern among investors is that the main hope of economic redemption – AI – could also turn out to be a dud, amid fears it has fuelled an almighty bubble in the US stock market.
One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – has risen to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.
The CAPE ratio for the S&P 500 share index is almost 41 points, more than double its long-term average of about 17 points, and approaching the record high of 44.19 points in December 1999, just before the dotcom crash.
Highlighting the challenge, research by Fathom Consulting shows that for the multitrillion-dollar AI boom to turn a profit, it would need the AI-related sales of the tech companies involved to rise by between $600 and $800bn within two years.
Against a febrile backdrop as investor patience is increasingly tested, the consultancy gives a 30% chance that the AI bubble pops next year.
Brian Davidson, an economist at the consultancy, said: “For all the impressive advances in AI technologies in recent years, the economics behind the current capex boom do not work.
“Yes, recent AI advances could yet unlock huge productivity gains; but sales of AI models need to increase by hundreds of billions of dollars per year over the next two years to justify the current spend. Such growth appears unlikely.”
Investors are clearly worried. More than 1,000 investors registered for an analyst call conducted by Jefferies this week into “AI Extinction Warnings”, after the bosses of the world’s top tech companies called for a slowdown in “reckless” development.
The situation has parallels with the dotcom crash of the year 2000, when many internet companies that had been billed as the next big thing dramatically tumbled in value. That was a reminder that even if a technology is going to be revolutionary, investors can still lose their money if they finance too much infrastructure too early.
“It took a decade or more for demand to catch up with the infrastructure laid down in the British canal and railway and US telecoms and fibre booms – and many investors never recovered their capital,” points out Adrian Cox of the Deutsche Bank research team.
There are also sobering comparisons with the buildup to the great crash of 1929. A hundred years ago, many small US investors were buying stocks “on margin” – acquiring them with borrowed money. They blew up in the market turmoil that preceded the Great Depression.
This year, South Korea’s army of traders have been buying shares in AI-linked chip makers on margin – doubling the value of the blue-chip Kospi index. But once the market started to fall, they were hit by a massive wave of margin calls – when investors are told to stump up more cash to keep borrowing. Many were forced to sell their shares. According to Goldman Sachs, 1.2 million South Korean retail investors were hit by margin calls – which is the equivalent of one in 30 adults getting a nasty call from their broker asking them to hand over more money.
The huge spending plans announced by AI companies are causing concerns that they may simply borrow too much.
One firm with ambitious AI plans is Oracle, the database software vendor. Oracle’s shares surged a year ago after it announced a cloud computing deal with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.
However, they have halved since, as investors have fretted that Oracle could be borrowing too much to fund datacentres.
There are other signs of rising stress in the credit markets. The Bank of England reported this summer that the spread between the riskiest and safest high-yielding debt has widened since the Iran war began, showing that investors are warier of holding risky debt.
Government bonds have been sold off in recent weeks, and that fall in prices pushes up the yield (or rate of the return) on sovereign debt. Those higher bond yields make owning shares less attractive – an investor has less incentive to buy equities (which are riskier) than bonds, which are seen as safer.
For the US this week the rise in borrowing costs involved the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year bonds, known as Treasuries, climbing above the psychologically key threshold of 5%.
That level is “seen by some as a threshold above which financial markets might go into meltdown,” said John Higgins, the chief economic adviser at Capital Economics.
“While we aren’t convinced that 5% is that ‘magic’ number, higher Treasury yields would certainly pose a risk to the sustainability of the US public finances as well as threaten equities,” Higgins told clients.
Bloomberg macro strategist Simon White argues that trouble would really start if the US 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.25%. He has calculated that this is the “inflection point” where, historically, stocks and bonds have reinforced losses in one another.
Despite the turbulence there are still hopes that a crash can be avoided, including optimism that markets are overestimating the inflation risk from the Iran war.
“A major downturn would need a trigger. Further geopolitical instability could be the catalyst, but we’ve long argued that the impact of geopolitical shocks on economic activity is overstated,” analysts at Oxford Economics wrote in a note to clients.
“Resurgent inflation and policy rate hikes by the Fed and other central banks are another candidate. However, our view on inflation is less alarmist – we think market expectations overstate the risk of further policy tightening.”
For many investors a slowdown in feverish AI investment will guard against the danger of a bubble.
There are signs that AI is beginning to power economic growth. The US economy has recorded a rise in productivity growth, while AI is also among reasons the UK economy has beaten expectations to grow at the fastest rate in the G7 in the first half of this year.
Such a turnaround in productivity could help the companies with sky-high share prices to begin justifying their valuations. However, it is a high-stakes play at a time of intense global volatility.
“Do I think there’s a significant dose of reality though in that productivity miracle in AI? Yes,” Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, told LBC this week. Still, he warned the situation is fragile.
“I don’t think outright collapse in a dotcom bubble type fashion. But could I see a slow release of air that doesn’t collapse the world economy, but slows it down? Yes, I could.”

Kid, London W1: ‘Fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

Earlier this month, a kind-of Turkish ocakbaşı opened on a corner in London’s Soho. The brains behind Kid are chef Sertaç Dirik and restaurateur David Carter, and I say “kind-of” because, yes, while it has a Turkish-influenced menu – sucuk with grilled peach, pide, börek, hummus, içli köfte with aged beef – and the whiff of live fire, nothing either of them does is ever remotely straightforward, hence the buzz around their new place.
Carter founded Smokestak a decade ago in Shoreditch, a wild, Americana-tinged barbecue joint where, somehow, he made brisket in buns and peach cobbler old fashioneds London’s hottest ticket. Five years later, he opened Manteca, also in Shoreditch, a reimagining of the Italian trattoria for the 2020s, followed by Oma, his Greek-influenced Michelin-starred venture in Borough, and its little sister Agora, and all of them remain dependable places where you get serious bang for your buck. All of those influences – American smoke, Italian flair and Greek boldness – are present and correct at Kid. Dirik’s story, meanwhile, has about it elements of TV’s The Bear: a Copenhagen-trained chef cajoled home to bolster the family business and going on to create the hugely loved Mangal 2 in Dalston. What Dirik and Carter have in common, aside from reputation, is a love of setting fire to stuff, in a culinary sense rather than in a Prodigy’s Twisted Firestarter sense. Kid’s Galata mackerel is testament to this: it’s almost completely blackened and has an incredible hit of smoke in its flesh.
Kid’s website says it’s on Frith Street, but the entrance is actually on Bateman Street, thanks to an aggressively discreet front door that will have you wandering around the glass-fronted corner like some confused visitor at Sea Life, pressing their nose against the tank looking for jellyfish and turtles. Here, however, there are diners beyond that glass, and you may cry when you see them inside sipping their gemlik martinis (black olive, black pepper, white vermouth, frozen gin). Warning: do not accidentally wander into Regulation, a boutique emporium of a very different persuasion just 10 metres away and where a very different type of lubrication is on offer. And of stuffing, for that matter. I shall leave the parallels there.
 Kid, as its name suggests, favours the use of kid goat, which will either delight or unsettle the British diner, because as a nation we still quibble about goat meat but for some reason raise no such objection to lamb. They have much in common taste-wise, and Kid’s signature dish – a £65 kid with fig leaf and freekeh for two – comes in an earthenware pot looking very much like a plump lamb shank just waiting for all that flesh to be pulled through the cooked grains beneath. The dish arrived heavy and somewhat intimidating, and left picked completely clean, as did the pickles alongside: fat, richness, sharpness, all in perfect balance.
The room is a rhapsody of browns, with an industrial feel and wilfully uncosy, a design movement that I’m calling “sumptuous sackcloth and ashes”, and there’s a long counter that focuses on a central grill. We visited on day four, and the place was already packed with Smokestak cultists, Mangal 2 zealots and assorted food writers, all of them gazing at the fire and tearing at blistered, kaymak-slicked grilled pide, as well as seeded ramazan pide as fluffy as a Turkish morning after too many rakis.
 We began with courgette flowers, which at £7 each will make some people reach for the smelling salts. But these are not those flaccid petals draped over unseasoned ricotta with which Brits habitually offend the French. Here, the batter is intensely crisp, the goat’s cheese insides rich, with atom honey to cut through: it’s a crunchy, sticky, oozing delight. A round of bluefin tuna ezme, a fine, fresh tartare in the Turkish style, comes on what can only be described as a poppadom-like cracker – fried, decadent and completely naughty.
The mackerel, however, is when you understand the point of all this live-fire hoopla. A huge butterflied fish with blackened skin comes crisp from the grill, its flesh all soft and meaty, and stuffed with a carrot-based slaw cooked in what tastes like rich, deep shellfish liquor. It’s the undoubted star of this show.
 We end with mountain tea rice pudding infused with sideritis, a wild Anatolian herb that’s warm and vaguely honeyed, and finished with a crunchy, brulee top; it’s also one of the finest desserts I’ve eaten all year. Don’t skimp on the mint oil-topped mastic ice-cream, either: it tastes exactly like toothpaste, and I mean that as a compliment.
 A very long lunch closed with shots of Turkish coffee that even Carter admitted tastes “slightly muddy”. That coffee sent me blinking into the daylight and I was still wired six hours later. Much as Kid did itself: distinctive, delicious and thoroughly making its mark.
- 
  Kid 53-55 Frith Street, London W1 (no phone). Open Mon-Sat, lunch noon-3pm, dinner 5.30-10pm. From about £45 a head à la carte, plus drinks and service

Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces
Danish design brand Fritz Hansen has teamed up with audio specialist Technics to transform its Farringdon showroom into a series of domestic listening scenes for London Design Festival.
As part of the Fritz Hansen Sound Club, the showroom has been organised into four domestic scenes where guests are invited to listen to a curated selection of vinyl records.
The installation combines Fritz Hansen's furniture and lighting products with turntables, headphones and speakers from Japanese firm Technics.
A 90th anniversary limited edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp and Technics' SL 40CBT turntable form the centrepiece of the various settings, both reimagined in a matching burgundy hue.
In reference to the table lamp's modernist origins, the interior styling evokes the Bauhaus movement and combines 1930s furniture with pieces from Fritz Hansen's catalogue.
Fritz Hansen Sound Club originally debuted during 3 Days of Design in Copenhagen, with the aim to explore how sound informs the way users experience interior settings.
,"Sound plays a direct role in how we experience space," said Fritz Hansen creative director, Els Van Hoorebeeck. "It shapes how we move, where we pause, and how we relate to furniture, light and materials."
"With Fritz Hansen Sound Club, we explore how these elements work together to define the character of a space, and how this way of thinking continues to shape our design today."
The Study area pairs steel-framed desks with Arne Jacobsen's Ant Chair in a cherry veneer finish, while the designer's iconic Egg Chair provides a cosy spot for relaxing in the nearby Reading Corner.
Downstairs, the Living Room provides a setting for socialising, with a turntable and speakers oriented towards the guests.
Furniture including Poul Kjærholm's PK31 sofa and PK80 daybed creates a relaxed, lounge-like feel, while a 1930s drinks trolley and PK61 coffee tables encourage conversation and interaction.
Fritz Hansen was founded in 1872 and is known for working with famous architects and designers, including Jacobsen and Kjærholm, as well as Hans J Wegner, Børge Mogensen and Verner Panton.
More recently, the brand has collaborated with contemporary talents such as Piero Lissoni, Jamie Hayon and Cecilie Manz, who created a compact and comfortable plywood chair that can be used in a variety of contexts.
A new version of Manz's Monolit chair forms part of the presentation, alongside a more compact, wall-mounted take on the Kaiser Idell lamp and an upholstered version of Japanese studio Nendo's N02 Recycle chair.
Other highlights from this year's London Design Festival include the debut show of design platform Collate Lobby and a bamboo pavilion covered in traditional Indian police shields.
Fritz Hansen Sound Club is open daily to the public until 20 September at 78 Cowcross Street as part of London Design Festival. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

NRL finals: Newcastle Knights defeat New Zealand Warriors 12-10, projectiles thrown at refs
Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.
Newcastle, last season's wooden spooners, silenced the huge 48,511-strong crowd at Auckland's Eden Park to secure a nail-biting 12-10 win, advancing to the NRL preliminary finals for the first time in 13 years.
Some in that large Eden Park crowd hurled projectiles at referee Ashley Klein and his team, while Warriors coach Andrew Webster described three late decisions that went against his side as "frustrating".
Warriors centre Leka Halasima was knocked to the ground before he could contest a high kick in the 79th minute, with Klein clearing the contact made by Knights prop Tyson Frizell and not giving the home side a chance to send the match into extra time with a penalty goal.
Frizell had his eyes on the ball, but did appear to cut across Halasima's line, allowing Fletcher Sharpe to leap high and catch the ball for Newcastle.
Minutes earlier, the Warriors were left fuming when Bunker official Chris Butler overturned a Knights knock-on but did not overturn a strip penalty against them, with the home side believing the ball was dropped because of a loose carry.
"It was frustrating. I feel like they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Webster said in reference to the two Bunker reviews.
"The last one, and two points would have drawn the game, he's [Tyson Frizell] going across Leka [Halasima], pretending to try and catch the ball, which they [NRL] have told us you can't do."
Webster made it clear those decisions were not the reason his side will not be facing Penrith next Sunday in Sydney, while Knights coach Justin Holbrook said he thought the officials made the right calls late.

Knights stun Warriors, set up prelim date with Panthers
— reporting by AAP
Newcastle's fairytale finals run has claimed another scalp as the Knights toppled the Warriors 12-10 to set up a preliminary final showdown with Penrith.
In front of a heavily pro-Warriors crowd at Auckland's Eden Park on Sunday, the undermanned Knights celebrated one of their most famous victories with tries from Fletcher Sharpe and Dominic Young.
The Knights will play the Panthers at Stadium Australia on Sunday in their first preliminary final since 2013, which further underlines the club's incredible revival under coach Justin Holbrook after they finished with the 2025 wooden spoon.
Holbrook, who guided the Knights to seventh at the end of the regular season, is the strongest candidate to be crowned Dally M coach of the year after his troops battled to finals wins over South Sydney and the Warriors without their first-choice front row and prized playmaker Dylan Brown.
From the kick-off, the Knights — led by captain Kalyn Ponga and the electrifying Sharpe — chanced their arm and were unlucky to have not scored twice in the opening 10 minutes of the semifinal.
Dane Gagai threw a forward pass to Young after a blistering break from five-eighth Sharpe, before the number six had his only try chalked off because of a Francis Manuleleua knock-on in the lead-up.
The Warriors could also count themselves lucky that Ali Leiataua was only placed on report after collecting Ponga high with no intent to wrap his arms.
Centre Leka Halasima crossed soon after Sharpe's try was ruled out to give the Warriors a 12th-minute lead.
The home side enjoyed a bounty of possession and territory for the next 15 minutes, but a combination of poor last-tackle options and courageous Newcastle defending meant the Warriors came up empty-handed.
The Knights have made a habit of striking from distance this season and a break down the left through Bradman Best levelled the game.
Best burst through the Warriors' right edge in the 29th minute and found Sharpe on his inside, the five-eighth juggling the infield pass to race 30 metres to score.
Sandon Smith had no issue with the conversion to make it 6-6 at half-time and Newcastle didn't take long to hit the front.
Manuleleua jolted the ball loose from Dallin Watene-Zelezniak and on the first tackle the Knights spread the ball to the right where Gagai unleashed Young with a flick pass and the towering Englishman touched down.
Smith again made the conversion to open up a six-point buffer with 35 minutes to go and it felt as if the Warriors were running out of chances as winger Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad failed a head injury assessment and Leiataua had a try ruled out for obstruction.
Halasima scored with an incredible 70th-minute finish to give the Warriors hope but Taine Tuaupiki missed the sideline conversion.
Both Tuaupiki and Ponga went off for head injury assessments in a nail-biting final 10 minutes, but the Knights held firm to win.

BEIJING, September 20. /TASS/. China has increased its imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) by 28.2%, to 5.15 million metric tons year-on-year in January-August, the General Administration of Customs of China reported.
According to the statistics, Russian LNG supplies to China grew by 13.2% in value terms in the reported period, reaching $2.66 billion. Russia is in the top three of China’s LNG suppliers, after Australia and Malaysia.
Also, China increased its purchases of Russian oil by 18.1% in January-August 2026, to 77.65 million metric tons.
According to figures released, Russian oil deliveries to the country grew by 33.3% in value terms in the reporting period, to $44.84 billion. This makes Russia the largest supplier of oil to China.

Two civilians killed as Ukrainian drones strike homes near Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
04:31:56 UTC
13:31:56 KST

Two civilians killed in Moscow suburbs as Ukraine launches ‘unprecedented’ attack during elections – officials
Two civilians were killed and several others, including two children, were injured in Moscow Region during a powerful Ukrainian drone raid that was aimed at derailing Russia’s parliamentary elections, local officials said.
In a statement on Sunday, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said more than 1,600 UAVs were repelled since the previous day, adding that 450 UAVs were intercepted on approaches to the capital.
“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned to disrupt the elections. The enemy failed,” he said.
Several drones reached the premises of the Moscow Oil Refinery, where one unidentified facility was damaged, and one struck a residential building, according to Sobyanin, who said there were no fatalities in the capital.
The consequences of the raid, however, were much more destructive in the suburbs. Earlier in the day, Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported damage in the Ramenskoye District, southeast of Moscow, where a 44-year-old woman was killed and five others, including two children, were injured when a drone hit an apartment building in the village of Sofyino.
In the nearby city of Ramenskoye, around 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-story apartment block after falling drone debris sparked a fire on the roof, with 20 vehicles also damaged.
Another person was killed in the Orekhovo-Zuyevo District, where a private home was destroyed and caught fire during the attack. The victim was an elderly man who was inside the building, according to the governor.
Elsewhere in Moscow Region, a warehouse complex caught fire in Sofyino, and a drone struck an apartment building in Kotelniki, setting apartments on three floors ablaze. The authorities are still determining whether anyone was injured.
Private homes were also damaged in Kolomna and Yegoryevsk, while fires broke out at apartment buildings in the Leninsky District, Lyubertsy, and Lytkarino. A residential building and an industrial facility were damaged in Istra, with no casualties reported.
The massive raid struck Moscow and the surrounding region just hours before polling stations were due to open for the final day of Russia’s three-day parliamentary elections. Despite the attack, all 1,443 polling stations in Moscow opened on time, Moscow Election Commission Deputy Chairman Dmitry Reut told TASS.
Moscow has accused Kiev of undermining diplomatic efforts while publicly calling for renewed negotiations. On Friday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the Ukrainian leadership is “talking about peace” while doing everything to prevent peace and negotiations.

Hurricane Hunters reveal 4 warning signs that a storm is about to strengthen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
04:29:23 UTC
13:29:23 KST

Hurricane Hunters reveal 4 warning signs that a storm is about to strengthen
Scientists have identified four clues that could reveal when a tilted tropical cyclone is about to straighten up and become capable of rapidly strengthening.
- Date:
- September 20, 2026
- Source:
- University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science
- Summary:
- Nearly three decades of Hurricane Hunter data reveal four features that can help a tilted tropical cyclone straighten its circulation and become capable of intensifying. The findings could give forecasters an earlier warning that a seemingly disorganized storm is becoming primed to strengthen.
- Share:
Tropical cyclones generally need to become vertically organized before they can grow much stronger. That means the storm's rotating centers at different levels of the atmosphere must line up rather than remain tilted away from one another.
Using nearly three decades of observations from NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft, researchers have now identified four features that appear to help tilted tropical cyclones become vertically aligned and more capable of intensifying.
The research was led by scientists at the University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science, working with colleagues at NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory. Their findings suggest that successful alignment depends on several factors working together, including the storm's internal structure, the direction of surrounding winds, and environmental conditions around the cyclone.
Understanding this transition is important because rapidly intensifying storms can give coastal communities and emergency managers very little time to respond. If forecasters can recognize earlier when a poorly organized tropical cyclone is becoming more favorable for strengthening, they may be able to provide communities with additional time for evacuation decisions and other preparations.
"A tropical cyclone has to stand up straight before it can intensify," said Michael S. Fischer, the lead author and an assistant professor in the Department of Atmospheric Sciences at the Rosenstiel School. "Strong winds higher in the atmosphere can push the top of a storm's circulation away from the center near the ocean surface. Until those centers come back together, the storm usually cannot intensify substantially."
Four Signs That Favor Storm Alignment
The researchers identified four characteristics that can help determine whether a tilted tropical cyclone is likely to straighten vertically.
The first is a compact, tightly organized circulation close to the ocean surface. The second is a storm tilt positioned favorably relative to vertical wind shear. The third is stronger rising air and heavier rainfall near the storm's lower-level center. The fourth is an environment that includes warm ocean water, plenty of atmospheric moisture, and relatively weak winds in the middle levels of the atmosphere.
Meteorologists use the term "tilt" to describe the separation between a tropical cyclone's circulation centers at lower and middle altitudes.
Vertical wind shear refers to changes in wind speed or direction with height. Strong shear can interfere with a cyclone's organization by pushing the upper portions of its circulation away from the center closer to the ocean surface.
Nearly Three Decades of Hurricane Hunter Data
To investigate which storms successfully became aligned, the researchers examined data from the Tropical Cyclone Radar Archive of Doppler Analyses with Recentering, known as TC-RADAR.
Developed by Fischer and colleagues, the database includes 1,510 radar analyses gathered by NOAA Hurricane Hunter aircraft across 28 hurricane seasons from 1997 through 2024.
That extensive record allowed the team to compare storms that eventually became vertically aligned with those that remained tilted.
"The storms that aligned already looked different about a day beforehand," said Fischer, who also is a core faculty member of the Frost Institute for Data Science and Computing. "They had stronger, more tightly wound circulations near the surface and more widespread, vigorous thunderstorms lifting air near that center. Our findings suggest those thunderstorms are not simply a sign of organization. They may also help pull the storm's leaning circulation upright."
The findings suggest that thunderstorms developing near the lower level circulation may play a more active role in storm organization than simply serving as a visible sign that strengthening is underway.
Earlier Clues That a Storm Is Becoming Organized
NOAA reconnaissance aircraft already collect many of the measurements highlighted by the study during operational flights, including low-level wind strength, storm size, thunderstorm coverage, and the direction of a cyclone's tilt.
That means the newly identified features could potentially help scientists evaluate whether high-resolution hurricane forecasting models are accurately reproducing the physical process that allows tilted storms to become vertically aligned.
The research may also provide forecasters with additional clues about which disorganized tropical cyclones are beginning to transition into a structure that is more favorable for intensification.
"Even a modest increase in forecast confidence a day earlier can provide more usable preparation time for communities in a storm's path," Fischer said. "This study gives us real-world evidence about what separates a storm that is becoming organized from one that remains tilted and less capable of strengthening."
The study, "To Align or Not to Align? That Is the Question," was published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres.
In addition to Fischer, the authors are George R. Alvey III of the Cooperative Institute for Marine and Atmospheric Studies and NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory; Deelan Jariwala, who earned bachelor's degrees in meteorology and mathematics from the University of Miami in spring 2026; and Paul D. Reasor of NOAA's Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory Hurricane Research Division.
The research was supported by the National Science Foundation under award No. 2241605.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Michael S. Fischer, George R. Alvey, Deelan Jariwala, Paul D. Reasor. To Align or Not to Align? That Is the Question. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 2026; 131 (14) DOI: 10.1029/2025JD045986

MOSCOW, September 20. /TASS/. The vote to elect the ninth convocation of the Russian parliament’s lower chamber, the State Duma, enters its final day on Sunday, with slightly less than 45% of citizens already casting their ballot.
The turnout stands at 44.75% as of 6:00 a.m. Moscow time on Sunday (3:00 a.m. GMT).
All polling stations will close by 8:00 p.m. local time. First results will be known after 9:00 p.m. Moscow time (6:00 p.m. GMT), when the polling stations close in Russia’s Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad.
The schedule of the vote varies from region to region. For example, in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR), polling stations will close at 2:00 p.m. Moscow time (11:00 a.m. GMT). The decision was made amid the intensified drone attacks and the need to safely deliver ballots after the vote is over.
On the second day, a number of high-ranking officials cast their ballot, including Federation Council (upper chamber) Speaker Valentina Matviyenko and her First Deputy Vladimir Yakushev, Defense Minister Andrey Belousov, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov and Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev. Russian Presidential Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov told TASS he had voted online on Friday evening.
Electronic vote
Even before day two of the elections was nearing its end, over 5.8 million voters already cast their ballots online. This exceeds all previous figures.
Over 3.2 million people used the Remote Electronic Vote (REV) platform, while another 2.6 million votes were received by the Moscow electronic vote system.
At the same time, electronic vote systems have been targeted by attacks. In the early hours of Saturday, the Moscow election system came under a powerful outside attack, Central Election Commission (CEC) Chair Ella Pamfilova said. She added that all attacks have been repelled, and remote electronic voting in Moscow was in the standard operational mode.
Election monitoring
In all, the Central Election Commission described the second day of the vote as calm, although sporadic incidents were reported. The Russian Interior Ministry received 367 reports related to the electoral process. Also, 24 false terrorism alerts were received in 15 Russian regions.
At the same time, public observers said the majority of reports about irregularities have not been confirmed.

4 killed in U.S. strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat in Caribbean, Pentagon says
The U.S. military attacked a boat suspected of being used to smuggle drugs in the Caribbean Sea on Saturday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its monthslong campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.
The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 231 in 69 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls "narcoterrorists" about one year ago.
As with most of the military's statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes.
The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed an image of what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash.
The Trump administration is pursuing deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama last month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal.
Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March. Last month, the U.S. military worked with Ecuador to board and sink a vessel that was allegedly being used as a refueling station for drug-trafficking boats in the eastern Pacific, according to U.S. Southern Command.
President Trump has said the U.S. is in "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the U.S. and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing smugglers.
In the very first attack, conducted on Sept. 2, 2025, the same boat was struck twice, or what has been described as a "double tap" or follow-on strike.
Sources previously told CBS News that the follow-on strike killed two people who had survived the first strike and were waving overhead. A total of 11 people were killed by both, according to the U.S. military. Some lawmakers and legal experts have questioned the legality of the strikes and have said the so-called "double-tap" may have constituted a war crime.

US overreliance on AI contributed to deadly Iran school strike – Bloomberg

Unknown Publisher

US overreliance on AI contributed to deadly Iran school strike – Bloomberg
Heavy reliance on AI, staff cuts, and rushed targeting procedures contributed to a US missile strike on an Iranian girls’ school in Minab, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing officials involved in a Pentagon investigation.
On February 28, two Tomahawk missiles hit the Shajarah Tayyebeh Elementary School in southern Iran, killing at least 157 people, including 123 children. The strike took place during the opening wave of US and Israeli attacks across the country. The school stood across from a naval base, which was likely the intended target.
Some US Central Command (CENTCOM) personnel reportedly expected Palantir’s Maven Smart System to flag stale or inconsistent intelligence when selecting potential targets. Previous reports suggested that the military relied on outdated satellite imagery that depicted the school as part of the base.
According to Bloomberg, Maven allowed the process of assembling target lists to be condensed to just several minutes.
A Palantir spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company was “not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies” and that there was no evidence its software was at fault in the Minab strike.
The AI giant has since upgraded Maven to “re-review underlying intelligence to identify factors that would disqualify a target and flag inconsistencies and inaccuracies that human review may have missed,” Bloomberg said, citing a person familiar with the matter.
Investigators also reportedly noted that, under orders from Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon dismantled most of its civilian harm mitigation (CHM) units and cut their staff by around 90%, to fewer than 20 people. A CHM team at CENTCOM was reportedly reduced from ten people to one, and no CHM official reviewed the Minab site before the strike.
UN Human Rights Chief Volker Turk said at the time that the bombing of the school “evoked a visceral horror.” On Thursday, a UN fact-finding mission said there were “reasonable grounds” to believe that the strike constituted a war crime. The US State Department rejected the finding, accusing the UN of pushing “anti-American rhetoric and anti-Semitism” and appeasing “repressive regimes.”
The US has not publicly acknowledged responsibility for the strike, with President Donald Trump suggesting that the missile could have been Iranian. However, investigations by US media outlets suggest that the missiles were American.

Coalition vows to cut $15 off tank of petrol when global prices spike

Coalition vows to halve fuel excise when global prices spike under new policy
In short:
The opposition is proposing to cut the fuel tax in half when global prices hit $US100 over two weeks.
The Coalition says it will fund the measure through $8 billion generated from its planned cuts to the tobacco excise.
What's next?
Treasurer Jim Chalmers dismissed the policy and said the government was not considering any future cuts to the fuel excise.
The opposition is promising to cut fuel costs when global prices spike, saying the measure would slash about $15 off the average tank of petrol.
Under the policy announced today, the Coalition said it would halve the fuel excise when the global price of Brent crude oil averages $US100 a barrel over two weeks.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the initiative, called Fuel Price Shield, would be "fully funded" through the Coalition's policy of cutting back the tobacco excise.
"Fuel Price Shield is all about providing relief at the bowser when it really counts," Mr Taylor said in Canberra.
"When we see two weeks where the price has averaged over $[US]100 a barrel, which means we're getting up towards $3 a litre at the bowser, there will be relief for Australians under a Coalition government."
He said Australian motorists were feeling pain at the pump, amid a re-escalation of war in the Middle East pushing up the price of petrol.
"We want to see $15 off a tank of petrol, 27 cents a litre, and that's fully funded through our cut to the tobacco excise,"
The fuel price shield would end three months after being triggered, or once the eight-week average price fell back below $US100 — whichever came first.
Some motorists told the ABC they would welcome lower petrol prices.
Mitch Stanton, from Brisbane, is travelling across Australia and has noticed a jump in the price of fuel.
"It definitely puts a dent in our pockets that we didn't expect," he said.
"We were paying not too long ago $1.80 in Cairns and all of a sudden we're paying now $2.60, $2.70 … it takes a big chunk out of the budget.
"I trust that our government's trying to make the best decisions for Australians but I think every single Australian would be happy with an excise coming back and having a bit more money in our pockets at the end of each week."
Chloe Anderson, from Karratha, said she would "definitely" welcome a cut to the fuel excise from the government.
She said the higher prices affected how she spent her money.
"I've just been on … a road trip holiday, and the fuel prices for that certainly changed how long we could go for and what else we spent," she said.
Mr Taylor said the Coalition would also eliminate the 32-cent road user charge for heavy vehicles to take pressure off the cost of transporting goods.
Economists divided on inflation impact
Treasurer Jim Chalmers dismissed the opposition's fuel policy, saying it was "uncapped and unfunded".
He told News24's Sunday Agenda the policy had more to do with "polling numbers than petrol prices", suggesting the Coalition was under pressure from One Nation.
Economist Chris Richardson said most economists had consistently said cutting the fuel tax was a "bad band-aid" that worsened inflation.
"That's the thing about a fuel tax cut, it simply adds to the amount of money sloshing around Australia," he said.
"It may reduce your bowser bill, but that comes at the cost of higher prices for everything else.
"It's a dumb policy at the best of times, and particularly dumb right now."
He said both sides had either enacted or proposed fuel tax cuts in recent years, and both "have slagged off the other side for doing it".
But Luci Ellis, Westpac's economic spokesperson, told ABC's 7.30 last week the experience of the last fuel excise cut suggested that such a measure could help curb inflation.
"[In June and July] petrol prices came down, and that actually stopped all those fuel levies and extra price increases coming on in other prices, so if we can nip that in the bud, that would be a good outcome," she said.
She said because Australia was also an energy exporter, increasing gas prices would result in extra tax revenue for the government.
"[A fuel excise tax] is one way to redistribute what would otherwise be more tax revenue from the government," she said last week.
Saul Kavonic from MST Financial told the ABC that cutting the fuel excise in periods of high prices was "not good economic policy".
"What it does is it actually removes the incentives to conserve fuel at a time of scarcity," he said.
"It also tends to be inequitable where it's just transferring money from taxpayers to road users.
"That said, it is popular and we've seen political parties of all stripes do this over the last five years."
He added that what the Coalition was proposing would make the fuel cut triggered by a predetermined threshold, rather than leaving it open to political discretion.
Government not considering future fuel excise cuts
The government implemented a cut to the fuel excise, the amount of tax the government collects on petrol, from April 1 until the end of July this year.
That saw the fuel excise cut from 52.6 cents a litre to 20.6 cents a litre, a discount of 32 cents.
The measure was extended until midnight on August 2, but a rate rise in the excise rate meant the discount was 16 cents a litre.
Mr Chalmers was asked if the government would ever consider another fuel excise cut.
"It's not something that we've been discussing or considering, but we've shown a willingness over time to respond to the economic conditions," he said.
Mr Taylor said it was "incredibly disappointing" to see the treasurer rule out the measure.
The opposition leader said Australians were facing potential further interest rate rises and cost-of-living pressures.
The Coalition's policy to cut the tobacco excise by 80 per cent would raise $8 billion, according to modelling from the Parliamentary Budget Office.
Illegal sales of cigarettes have cost the budget billions in lost revenue, and the Coalition's policy assumes consumers would purchase legal cigarettes instead if the prices were lowered.
The government has previously criticised the Coalition's planned cuts to the tobacco tax, which would see a 20-pack of cigarettes drop from between $40–$50 to about $16–$26.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said that policy was "a guarantee we will see smoking and vaping rates in this country increase" and "will lead to deaths".

Australia wants a seat at the UN's most powerful table. What power would it yield?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
03:00:49 UTC
12:00:49 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia is campaigning for a seat on the UN body responsible for international peace and security.
- A seat would give Australia a vote and role in key negotiations, but not the veto held by five permanent members.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is heading to New York with a diplomatic pitch that has been more than a decade in the making: Putting Australia back on the United Nations Security Council.
Australia is campaigning for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2029-30, which would mark its first stint on the powerful UN body since 2014.
The government says a seat would give Australia a stronger voice on decisions affecting the country and the region.
Australia's campaign is expected to focus on issues including artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety, as well as climate action, international law and support for Pacific nations.
But what exactly does the UN Security Council do, and what would Australia gain by being on it?
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
What is the UN Security Council?
The Security Council is one of the six main bodies of the United Nations and has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.
It is made up of 15 countries, each with one vote.
Five of them — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — are permanent members, while another 10 countries are elected by the UN General Assembly to serve two-year terms.
Unlike most other UN bodies, the Security Council can make decisions that member states are obligated to implement.
It can impose sanctions, establish peacekeeping operations and, in some circumstances, authorise the use of force. It can also investigate disputes, call for peaceful settlements and make recommendations aimed at maintaining or restoring international peace and security.
For a substantive resolution to pass, it needs at least nine votes.
And there is an important catch — each of the five permanent members has veto power, meaning a negative vote from any one of them can block a substantive resolution even if it otherwise has enough support.
Australia would not gain that veto power if elected, as it belongs exclusively to the five permanent members of the Security Council.
Non-permanent members such as Australia have the same single vote on council decisions, but cannot unilaterally block a substantive resolution.
So what would Australia actually gain?
While a non-permanent seat does not come with a veto, it gives countries a direct role in decisions they would otherwise largely have to influence from outside the council.
Australia would have a vote on Security Council decisions and be involved in negotiating resolutions and other outcomes on conflicts and security crises around the world.
It would also take part in closed meetings and consultations between council members and could chair subsidiary bodies, including sanctions committees.
Every member also takes a turn holding the presidency of the Security Council for one calendar month, allowing them to preside over meetings and help shape the council's program of work.
Australia's previous term shows the practical difference membership can make.
During 2013-14, Australia participated in hundreds of council meetings, including closed meetings available only to members, and was closely involved in negotiating dozens of resolutions and presidential statements.
Its seat became particularly significant following the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014, which killed 298 people, including 38 Australian citizens and residents.
Australia authored and led negotiations on Security Council Resolution 2166, which was unanimously adopted four days after the crash.
The resolution condemned the downing of the plane, called for a full and independent investigation and demanded access to the crash site.
Australia also used its term to work on humanitarian access in Syria, counter-terrorism, small arms and the protection of civilians.
Why does Australia want a seat again?
The government argues that Australia's security and prosperity depend on an international system in which countries follow agreed rules and work collectively on global problems.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said a seat would give Australia "a stronger voice in the decisions that affect us and our region", describing the country as an active middle power with a role to play in international peace and security.
The bid is also increasingly focused on what Australia argues will be emerging security challenges by the time it takes up the seat.
Technology is expected to be central to the campaign, with the government arguing that artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety will increasingly intersect with international peace and security.
Speaking at a Security Council debate last year, Wong said AI had the potential to transform conflict and diplomacy and argued the council should play a role in developing international rules and norms around its use.
She said Australia's experience in digital infrastructure and technology partnerships would form part of what it could bring to the council.
Australia's broader foreign policy priorities, including the Pacific, climate change, protecting civilians and supporting international law, are also expected to feature in the campaign.
How does Australia get elected?
Australia cannot simply nominate itself and take a seat.
The 10 non-permanent positions are distributed between regional groupings, with five seats coming up for election each year.
Australia belongs to the Western European and Others Group, or WEOG, and is seeking one of the group's two seats available for the 2029-30 term.
So far, Australia and Finland are the only candidates for those two positions, meaning the positions are currently uncontested.
But Australia must still win the support of two-thirds of UN General Assembly members present and voting when the election is held in June 2028.
If all 193 UN member states were present and voted, that would mean securing around 129 votes.
It helps explain why the government is campaigning years before Australia would actually take its seat.
The bid itself is not new. It was first announced in 2015 under the former Coalition government, following Australia's previous stint on the council.
Australia has served five terms on the Security Council since the UN was established, most recently in 2013-14.
A sixth term would not give Australia the power enjoyed by the council's five permanent members.
But for two years, it would give Australia something it otherwise does not have: a seat, a vote and a direct role in negotiations at the UN body responsible for some of the world's most consequential decisions on peace and security.

Cuba plunges into darkness amid nationwide blackout
Unknown

Cuba plunges into darkness amid nationwide blackout
Cuba has suffered another nationwide blackout, leaving millions without electricity amid severe fuel shortages and US restrictions on oil supplies. It is at least the sixth major outage the island has experienced since the start of the year.
Under a US embargo for decades, Cuba has faced worsening fuel shortages since Venezuela, previously Havana’s main oil supplier, stopped shipments following the US capture of President Nicolas Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump subsequently declared a national emergency over Cuba, moving to block oil shipments to the island and threatening tariffs against countries that continued supplying it. Trump has repeatedly said he intends to take Cuba “one way or another,” and described regime change there as a “question of time.”
Cuba’s Ministry of Energy and Mines said the latest grid collapse was triggered on Friday by a transmission-line failure in the western part of the country and compounded by unstable weather.
Officials immediately activated restoration protocols, gradually bringing generating facilities back online. Power had returned to parts of the island by Saturday.
Cuba’s electricity system relies heavily on aging oil-fired power plants, many of which have operated for decades and require frequent maintenance. Fuel shortages and difficulties obtaining spare parts have forced generating units offline, leaving the grid with little spare capacity when other facilities fail.
Washington has meanwhile stepped up economic pressure on Havana. On Thursday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new sanctions targeting Cuba’s nickel sector, following measures imposed on state oil company CUPET in June.
Russia, China, Mexico, and several other countries have provided humanitarian assistance to Cuba. Russia delivered around 700,000 barrels of oil in late March, one of the few major fuel shipments to reach the island since US restrictions were tightened.
The worsening shortages have disrupted electricity, transportation, water supplies, and healthcare. In June, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk warned that “children [in Cuba] are dying because doctors lack access to essential medical supplies and medicines.”
“Such severe sanctions packages that target entire sectors of an economy and produce broad, indiscriminate and harsh effects on populations are incompatible with basic principles of international human rights law,” he said.

Esketamine-induced dissociation is tied to better outcomes in treatment-resistant depression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
02:00:47 UTC
11:00:47 KST

Patients with treatment-resistant depression who improved after subcutaneous esketamine treatment reported higher levels of dissociation, particularly feelings that the world seemed unreal or distant, than patients who did not respond, according to a study published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.
Treatment-resistant depression refers to depression that has not improved after at least two adequate trials of standard antidepressants. Esketamine, a form of ketamine, has emerged as a treatment option for some people with this condition. Ketamine was originally developed as an anesthetic, but researchers later found that it could produce rapid changes in depressive symptoms.
The drug can also cause temporary changes in consciousness. Some patients describe feeling separated from their body or thoughts, while others say that their surroundings seem unreal, distant or dreamlike. These experiences are generally referred to as dissociation. Researchers have debated whether dissociation is simply a side effect of ketamine-based treatment or whether it is connected to the drug’s antidepressant action.
The current study examined data from an open-label clinical trial, meaning both researchers and participants knew what treatment was being administered, at Onofre Lopes University Hospital, affiliated with the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte in Brazil. Led by Kaike Thiê da C. Gonçalves at the University of São Paulo, the researchers followed adults receiving weekly subcutaneous esketamine.
Of the 30 people originally enrolled, 23 completed all eight treatment sessions and were included in the analysis. The group included 15 females and eight males (average age 34.3 years). Participants initially received 0.5 milligrams of esketamine per kilogram of body weight. The dose could be increased to 0.75 or 1 milligram per kilogram when depressive symptoms had not fallen by at least 50%.
The researchers measured depression before each treatment session and one week after the final session. They assessed dissociation 40 minutes after each dose using a clinician-administered questionnaire. The questionnaire measured overall dissociation as well as three experiences: derealization (feeling that the outside world is unreal); depersonalization (feeling detached from oneself); and amnesia (gaps in memory).
Twelve participants met the study’s definition of a treatment responder, meaning their depression scores fell by at least 50%. Responders had higher overall dissociation scores than the 11 nonresponders across the treatment period. They also reported significantly more derealization. Depersonalization and amnesia were higher among responders as well, but the differences were not statistically significant.
Notably, dissociation levels remained relatively stable across the eight sessions, and the researchers found no significant within-person relationship between dissociation and changes in depression scores. In other words, people who experienced more dissociation than others were more likely to respond, but a person’s dissociation level at a particular session did not reliably predict how much their own symptoms would improve.
The researchers concluded that dissociative experiences, particularly derealization, may represent clinically relevant correlates of antidepressant outcomes. They emphasized that these findings are exploratory and may help guide future research into whether different aspects of altered consciousness are relevant to treatment outcomes.
Several limitations are to be noted. For example, the study did not include a placebo group or blinding. In addition, the analysis also did not fully account for other medications, psychiatric conditions or outside psychotherapy. Importantly, because the researchers increased the dose for patients who were not adequately responding, higher dissociation scores might partly reflect greater cumulative drug exposure rather than a true biological marker of clinical improvement.
The study, “Dissociation and Antidepressant Response to Subcutaneous Esketamine: A Clinical Study,” was authored by Kaike Thiê da C. Gonçalves, Vagner Deuel de O. Tavares, Fernanda Palhano-Fontes, Patrícia Cavalcanti-Ribeiro, Victor Rocha Nóbrega de Almeida, David C. Barbosa, Tatiane Uetti Gomes Fernandes, Eduardo Igor Torquato Cardoso, Nicole Bezerra de Medeiros Lima, Aldielyson Jorge Cavalcante de Brito, Raynara Bolcont, Marcelo Falchi-Carvalho, Emerson Arcoverde, Dráulio Araújo and Nicole Leite Galvão-Coelho.

Tips for tackling jetlag when travelling with kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
01:44:29 UTC
10:44:29 KST

analysis
Travelling with kids: how can you minimise jet lag with your little ones?
Anyone who has flown with or near children can picture it: the crying kid, the frazzled parent and the cranky passengers.
Travelling with children can be tough, and the difficulties can escalate when you cross a time zone or two.
Things don't necessarily improve when you touch down, either. After long-haul travel, jet lag can impact our health for days afterwards.
Most adults have experienced jet lag, but what about when children are involved?
What exactly is jet lag?
Jet lag refers to the temporary misalignment of a person's internal body clock (or circadian rhythm) with the local time where they are. In other words, the body is still operating according to the time zone it has just come from, rather than the new time zone.
As the name suggests, jet lag is generally caused by air travel when you cross multiple time zones very quickly before the body can adapt.
It can make you feel fatigued and sluggish during the day and make it hard to sleep at night in your new location.
Is it worse flying in a certain direction?
Yes, jet lag is worse when you travel east.
When travelling east, you are essentially "losing" time. This means when you try to go to bed at your destination, your body clock still thinks it is much earlier in the day.
You might find yourself lying awake at night because your body isn't ready for sleep yet. Or you might wake up at a time that feels like the middle of the night.
When travelling west, your body clock is essentially "behind" the local time. This means you may start to feel sleepy earlier than usual because your body thinks it is later than it really is.
Fortunately for people travelling west, it's generally easier to stay awake later than it is to fall asleep earlier. This means you can often push through some afternoon or early evening sleepiness until a more reasonable bedtime.
How does jet lag affect kids?
Children tend to experience similar symptoms to adults, such as:
- finding it hard to get to sleep or stay asleep
- being cranky
- not wanting to eat at mealtime
- nausea
- generally feeling fatigued.
Surprisingly, not a lot of research has been done comparing the effects of jet lag in children with jet lag in adults.
What we do know suggests children might actually be affected a little less than adults. This might be because children produce more melatonin, which could help them adjust to new time zones a little quicker. Melatonin is the "sleepiness hormone" that our body naturally produces.
Evidence also suggests that as we age, we become less tolerant of jet lag. However, most of this evidence has looked at comparisons of young adults and older adults, so may not necessarily reflect the differences between adults and children.
Tips to reduce jet lag before you fly
The good news is, you can start adjusting your or your child's body clock before you leave home.
This generally requires precise control of light exposure and possibly adjusting sleep times in the days before departure.
Every hour you shift before boarding is one less hour to catch up at the other end, though this means you are starting the jet lag early, at home.
Shifting the body clock before travel is demanding for anyone, but with children you are also managing someone else's schedule, energy and patience. Someone who might not understand why they need to sleep an hour earlier than usual.
For many families, this isn't realistic. However, from the moment you disembark, there's plenty you can do.
Tips once you land
Your most powerful jet lag tool is free: daylight.
As a general rule of thumb, being exposed to morning light shifts your body clock earlier. Light in the late afternoon or evening shifts your body clock later.
Getting this timing right at your destination is the single most effective thing you can do to combat jet lag for you and your child.
Habitual time cues (everyday things that signal the time to your body, such as mealtimes or bedtime routines) can also help with the shift to a new time zone.
Try to move mealtimes to local schedules as quickly as possible.
Where you can, keep bedtime routines consistent. A familiar sequence of bath, story and lights out carries more weight than most parents realise. For young children, routine is one of the strongest signals that sleep is coming, regardless of what the clock says.
What about tech or medication?
Most jet lag apps rely on the same principles: that light, melatonin and exercise can shift the body clock, and that timing matters.
If you are using an app or related technology, the amount of personalisation it includes is likely to determine how useful it is. At a minimum, apps should include questions about your sleep history, usual sleep schedule, chronotype (whether you are a morning or evening person) and travel itinerary.
Some people also use melatonin supplements for themselves, or their children, while travelling.
But unless you are working with a healthcare provider like a paediatrician, it's generally not recommended to use these supplements. Taking the wrong dose, or taking melatonin at the wrong time, can actually make jet lag worse, for both adults and kids.
Madeline Sprajcer is a senior lecturer in psychology and Dean J Miller is a sleep and circadian scientist, both at CQUniversity Australia. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

Meet the gig workers helping train robots to do our dishes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
01:41:00 UTC
10:41:00 KST

Egocentric training's gig workers are helping robots learn how to do your dishes
Mohamad Dunggio recently strapped a mobile phone to his head and recorded himself doing his dishes over and over again for four hours.
It left him with wrinkly fingers, but he did not mind.
"I think it's OK because I exchange my time to earn money," said the 23-year-old from Gorontalo on Sulawesi in Indonesia.
Mr Dunggio is one of the thousands of gig workers around the world feeding the robotics industry's insatiable demand for training data.
Since April he has been earning extra cash making "egocentric training" videos, used to teach robots how to do things like household chores.
Egocentric training data is sensor or video recordings made from the perspective of the person doing the task, often captured with a head or chest-mounted camera with a focus on keeping the subject's hands in the frame.
Mr Dunggio said he was paid by three companies from Argentina, India and the US between $US3 ($4.22) and $US10 an hour to record himself performing tasks like dishwashing, cleaning, cooking, making the bed, ironing, folding clothes and sweeping.
"I think it's a good thing to do because you don't have to have any experience," he said.
How to teach robots
As the recent World Humanoid Robot Games in China demonstrated, robots have been advancing in literal leaps and bounds in recent years.
But the dream of a multi-function humanoid robot that can move around the home efficiently and reliably taking on a variety of domestic tasks has so far proven elusive.
Dana Kulić, a robotics professor at Monash University, said that for robots to navigate the huge variety and complexity of people's homes they needed to learn how to observe and react to their environments.
"Even if the task is just to fold the laundry, or wash the dishes, every person has a different set of dishes. Then the place where [the clothes] should be folded looks different," she said.
Professor Kulić said robotics researchers were using egocentric data in a way similar to how generative AI researchers taught large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT to predict the next word or letter in a sentence.
While egocentric data produced by actual robots, teleoperated by a human, tended to be more relevant, human egocentric data was cheaper, easier and could provide a much-needed variety of scenarios, she said.
The workers producing the data now include entire factories in South Asia, house cleaners in the US and home delivery drivers.
However, Professor Kulić said the ways human egocentric data was collected were not without issues.
They ranged from whether the contributors truly understood what the data was being used for to privacy concerns about filming in people's homes and data being sold on to third companies.
Strict requirements for videos
Mr Dunggio said overall he was happy with the side-hustle and did not feel exploited, even if others might feel differently.
"If people don't have work and are looking for income this is just an option," he said.
However, he said he felt a bit embarrassed going to the mall with a phone mounted on his head and was disappointed when some of his videos were rejected.
He also complained that some companies charged a transfer fee of about $US1 to withdraw accumulated earnings of under $US10.
On the plus side he got to learn some new skills.
"I never cooked for myself before, but now I know how to cook," he said.
Changes in demand for data
Sergio Bruccoleri is vice-president of delivery for Appen, an ASX-listed Australian company that collects and annotates datasets for the tech industry, including egocentric data for robotics.
Mr Bruccoleri, who is based in Barcelona, said the company could collect around 60,000 hours of video per month from as many as 5,000 contributors all over the world, including India, Canada, the US, Brazil, Mexico and the Philippines.
China was Appen's biggest market for robotics data with the US second, he said.
He said Appen's contributors produced videos in homes and increasingly in workplaces but also in controlled studios, sometimes with specialised cameras and equipment like sensor gloves.
However, he said Appen was moving away from the kind of data that was being collected at an industrial scale in "lower-cost countries" because it had become commoditised and de-valued.
The company was increasingly focused on wealthier countries like the US and Canada, where the robots were likely to be sold initially, while still gathering high value data elsewhere.
"The dishwashers in the US look very different from the dishwashers you would have elsewhere," he said.
In the past, Appen has faced criticism over pay and conditions. Contributors on forums still complain of issues from late payments to poor communication and unexplained account cancellations.
Mr Bruccoleri said some of Appen's systems were not perfect and the company tried to address contributor issues with open lines of communication.
He said Appen had a code of ethics and fair-pay standards and tried "as much as possible" to ensure pay was "always above the minimum wage set in that particular country".
Appen also had privacy guidelines for contributors and a tracing system which he said meant they should be able to request the data they produced be withdrawn, even after it had been sold.
Asked whether it was unfair that contributors were sometimes forced to pay fees to withdraw their earnings, Mr Bruccoleri said he believed it was but it was the payment platforms that took the fee.
"It's not limited to Appen. You see it in other platforms all the time," he said.
When can I have a robot to fold my clothes?
Robotics companies, particularly those in China, have this year been unveiling more and more competent humanoid models that appear close to the ideal of a Jetsons-style robot to do all our household chores.
But Professor Kulić believes that is still a way off.
She said there was a big difference between showing a robot folding clothes during a demonstration and having it working reliably for extended periods of time.
Then there was the cost, not only to produce the robots but also to maintain and repair them.
"I feel like there's many problems to be solved beyond just the ability to do a specific task," she said.
She compared robots to autonomous vehicles which worked "99 per cent of the time".
"But now that last 1 per cent is taking much more time than anyone initially thought it would," Professor Kulić said.
