'Still gets the heart going': What I learned from over 50,00 Australian Magpie swoopings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
01:28:00 UTC
10:28:00 KST

in brief
- Web developer Jon Clark built Magpie Alert after a terrifying bicycle swoop, creating Australia's main database for logging bird encounters.
- Researchers say simple defences such as staring back or changing routes remain the most effective ways to avoid swooping injuries.
Sydney web developer Jon Clark admits that being swooped by a magpie "still gets the heart going" despite having logged tens of thousands of public encounters with defensive birds.
After an "absolutely terrifying" encounter with a swooping magpie in 2013, Clark decided to put his technical skills to use by creating the community-driven database, Magpie Alert. The website has since become the nation's pre-eminent go-to for up-to-date information on aggressive magpies.
"I was just out on my bicycle one Sunday afternoon, minding my own business in the spring, and this great big magpie decided to start snapping at my ear," he told SBS News. "It was the first time I'd ever experienced it, and gosh, it scared me senseless."
Discovering that the information for logging and tracking the locations of dangerous magpies was "pretty limited", Clark built his site, which he says "took off" in 2016. He has since been contacted by local councils and Australia Post branches who are interested in helping communities stay alert about magpies in the area.
Users can file a report on any aggressive magpie they have encountered, tagging the location of the bird, the type of attack, and the time of the incident. Others can corroborate this information and share updates on whether the bird is still active in the area.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
As a British person who migrated to Australia some 15 years ago, Clark said the prevailing impression of Australia is that "everything's out to kill you". Having become accustomed to the relative lack of danger presented by the fauna populating the suburbs of north-west Sydney, assault by magpie came as a surprise.
"I was like, 'God, we've got sharks, we've got jellyfish, we've got snakes, spiders, and even the garden birds are out to get you'."
'Magpie heaven'
Magpie Alert data shows that September is the peak of swooping season. The website receives some 4,000 to 6,000 submissions each year, with around 45,000 users logging on to read the latest updates.
While magpies swoop right across the country, the ACT has the highest rate of incidents, something Clark attributes to having a high number of cyclists.
Behavioural ecologist Darryl Jones, who has been studying magpies for more than 30 years, told SBS News that the birds are drawn to human-created environments and have become concentrated in places where they can be supported by the local ecosystem.
"In the suburbs, there's everything they need in a small area," Jones said. "They're just pulling grubs and worms out of the ground and all they need is a lawn that gets watered and mown all the time."
"Without even trying, we have made magpie heaven".
Without even trying, we have made magpie heaven
Why magpies swoop
Only a small fraction of magpies swoop. Those that do are always male and will only do so when there are chicks in their nest.
Research conducted by Jones, professor emeritus at Griffith University, has shown that around 8 per cent of magpies will swoop — and only half of those will swoop pedestrians — while the vast majority only go for one or two people in their territory.
"When it's pedestrians, and they're only attacking a couple of people, they know those people individually," Jones said. "They know exactly who they are, and when they come out, they'll attack only those people."
In a suburban environment, magpie territories can be as small as a handful of backyards. In the bush, they are much larger as the birds need more space to find food.
"They stay in one area, one territory, and they live there permanently," Jones said. "They get to know the individual humans in their territory."
"We've done experiments where we were able to determine for sure that they can recognise up to about 30 people's faces by their facial features, just like we do."
While pedestrians may be unlucky to be swooped, aggressive magpies will swoop any cyclist that comes into their area, something Jones attributes to the speed at which they are moving.
Despite his challenging encounter, Clark said magpies are a "lovely bird" with a "beautiful call".
"I think everyone's got a character magpie in their neighbourhood," he said.
How to avoid being swooped
Each spring, videos of cyclists or children being swooped by magpies go viral online. However, Clark notes that attacks can be serious.
"We've had a couple of eye injuries ... a few people being blinded in one eye from the birds over the years," he said.
"Most of the worst accidents on the website are people falling off their bicycle after panicking while being swooped. There have been a few broken bones reported".
A 76-year-old man died in 2019 after crashing his bike while trying to escape a magpie. In 2021, a five-month-old was tragically killed after her mother stumbled and fell while trying to dodge a swooping magpie in Brisbane.
When entering unfamiliar territory and encountering a swooping magpie, Jones said the best advice is to walk backwards while watching the bird, as they do not attack if they are being stared at.
People living within the territory of a defensive magpie can befriend them by offering bird food, which Jones said can ensure they do not see that person as a threat.
Cyclists can either wear a realistic mask on the back of their helmets or attach cable ties to mimic sharp objects that the birds will avoid flying into.
"The simplest thing ... if you know there's an area where there are magpies, then you could just avoid that," Jones said.
Magpie Alert has recently been updated with an email function that can alert users in their inbox when a new, aggressive magpie is logged in their local area.
Clark says he would love to build a mobile app one day so people on the move can check for and document swooping birds, but funding constraints make that impossible right now.
He personally feels "more confident" in encountering swooping magpies than he once did, but confesses that the experience "always makes you jump".
"It's just a rite of passage."

Merz under pressure as two more German states hold elections
Germans began voting Sunday in two closely watched state elections that could deliver fresh gains for the far-right and far-left, piling pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz as he struggles with low approval ratings and tensions within his governing coalition.

Germans began voting Sunday in two state elections where far-right and far-left gains could send new shock waves to Berlin and rock the government of embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Merz, 70, has scheduled a crisis meeting of his centre-right CDU party leadership to discuss the first results as they come in from the regional polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The chancellor, in power for 16 months, has also cleared his calendar for the following days and skipped a trip to the UN General Assembly to deal with potential aftershocks from the votes.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The far-right, pro-Trump and Moscow-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) dealt a stunning defeat to his CDU two weeks ago in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, fuelling speculation that internal party support for Merz is wobbling.
"I'd be in favour of the AfD winning, because then they'll have to prove themselves: either something will happen, or it'll be the last time they get any votes," pensioner Peter Sommer told AFP outside a polling station in Schwerin, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's state capital.
The election debacle came as Merz's approval ratings have nose-dived and he has struggled to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his centre-left coalition partners the SPD.
Read moreHow far-right AfD breakthrough may ‘cause absolute chaos’ in Germany
The AfD will make fresh gains Sunday, polls suggest, although it is unlikely to come within reach of power in either state – unlike in Saxony-Anhalt where it fell just a few seats short of an absolute majority.
Polling stations opened at 8:00am (06:00 GMT) with voting set to last until 6:00pm.
Under-fire Merz received some badly needed support from CDU powerbrokers on Wednesday. Eight state premiers declared jointly that Germany needs "stability now more than ever" rather than "discussions about personnel".
They refrained from issuing a personal endorsement for Merz, however.
Two tight races
In Sunday's vote, the CDU faces different challenges unique to those regions.
In the northeastern coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Merz's party is an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD of popular state premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD.
While the AfD was polling at 36 percent against the SPD's 37, according to public broadcaster ZDF, Merz's CDU, at just six percent, was dangerously close to missing the five-per cent hurdle needed to stay in the state parliament.
A CDU crash below that line would be a historic first and heap enormous pressure on Merz.
In the city-state of Berlin, the ruling CDU is running a neck-and-neck race against the far-left Die Linke, which promises drastic steps to solve a dire housing crisis and is popular with young people.

A CDU defeat there would be another black eye for Merz – especially at the hands of Die Linke, which wants to curb corporate power and leans toward Moscow.
When Merz took office in May last year, he vowed to reboot a flagging economy, rebuild the military to deter Russia, and reduce irregular immigration to soothe voters' fears and lure them away from the AfD.
But the AfD now leads nationwide polls and Merz's personal approval ratings hover just above 10 percent, not helped by his occasionally blunt and abrasive comments.
Lowest support ever
"In personal terms, the situation is quite dramatic" for Merz, said pollster Roland Abold of the Infratest Dimap research institute.
"In our last survey in September, 13 percent were still satisfied with his political performance. These are the lowest figures we have ever recorded for an incumbent chancellor," Abold told AFP.
Some commentators point out that most of Merz's problems have originated abroad.
The Ukraine and Middle East wars have sent energy prices surging, fuelling a cost-of-living crisis.
Read moreGermany cuts energy tax to lower petrol prices as Merz faces state key elections
Worries about Russia have driven a massive German rearmament drive, sped up by US President Donald Trump's often hostile stance against European NATO allies.
And China's rapid rise is turning a long-time German export market into a fierce industrial competitor.
"Tough luck for Friedrich Merz," wrote Berenberg bank chief economist Holger Schmieding. Aside from the AfD challenge, the latest "surge in petrol prices and the public debate about his future are exacerbating his travails", he argued.
Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin "have triggered the crises that have sent oil and gas prices into the stratosphere", Schmieding pointed out.
"But although parts of the right-wing AfD are close to both of them... voters tend to lay the blame for their pain at the ruling coalition led by Merz rather than at the friends of AfD."
Nonetheless, Schmieding judged it more likely than not that Merz would weather the current political storm and serve out his term until 2029.

US issues security alerts across Middle East
The US has issued security alerts for its citizens across the Middle East, warning of further escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
The notices cover Israel, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, and Oman.
“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” the US State Department said on Saturday night.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly,” the notice read, urging Americans to refrain from traveling to the Middle East.
“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including U.S. businesses and other institutions.”
The alert came amid anticipation of potential new US strikes on Iran or Houthi targets in Yemen, as Saudi Arabia reportedly sought assistance in repelling the militant group’s offensive against forces of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
Axios reporter Barak Ravid said US President Donald Trump cut his weekend stay at Camp David short and will return to the White House on Saturday evening, one day earlier than planned.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have expanded the territory they control in western Yemen, capturing the port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi Arabia recently suspended operations on its East-West oil pipeline, also known as Petroline, after it was damaged in a drone attack that Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. The pipeline carries crude oil from the kingdom’s eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis previously declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to what the group described as an illegal siege of the parts of Yemen under its control.
A Saudi-led coalition first intervened in the Yemeni civil war in 2015 after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, the previous year. The current hostilities mark the biggest escalation in the conflict since the UN-brokered truce of 2022.

New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:16:08 UTC
09:16:08 KST

New US sanctions law undermines Ukraine peace efforts – Kremlin
The sanctions law signed by US President Donald Trump this week will undermine efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict through diplomacy, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
On Friday, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which authorizes tougher restrictions on Russia and tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
“Clearly, this cannot have a positive effect,” Peskov told RIA Novosti on Saturday when asked how the law would affect the prospects for a peaceful settlement in Ukraine and the possibility of a breakthrough in Russia-US relations.
Named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who co-authored the original bill with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal in 2025, the legislation remained stalled for months as Trump pursued diplomacy with Russia and resisted placing sole blame for the conflict on Moscow. Trump’s envoys also discussed normalizing economic ties with their Russian counterparts.
The Senate passed the measure 86-11 last month, followed by the House on Wednesday in a 262-159 vote.
The original proposal threatened tariffs of 500% on countries purchasing Russian energy, but the maximum rate was reduced to 100% after negotiations with the White House. Graham, who died unexpectedly in July, promoted the measure as “bone-crushing” sanctions.
The version adopted by Congress targets major buyers of Russian oil and gas, with China and India expected to be among those potentially affected. It also gives Trump broad discretion over the application of the tariffs, including the ability to waive or suspend restrictions in the national interest.
Peskov previously described the bill as an “unfriendly action” that would “complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine.”
The Russian Embassy in the US said the legislation does “a grand disservice” to Trump’s ‘Make America Great Again’ agenda, arguing that restricting Russia’s energy trade amid sharply reduced Middle Eastern supplies could send fuel prices soaring ahead of the midterm elections. It warned that confrontation with Russia and China is a lose-lose situation that only benefits the “Euro-Atlantic warmongers.”
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun condemned the law, saying China “carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit” and that its trade is not directed against any third country.

Chile’s Michelle Bachelet quits race to be next UN chief

Chile’s Michelle Bachelet quits race to be next UN chief
Santiago – Michelle Bachelet, the former president of Chile, withdrew her candidacy for the position of United Nations secretary-general on Sept 19, weeks after a straw poll showed her in second to last place among eight candidates.
“Today, I announced that I have decided not to continue with my candidacy for the position of secretary-general of the United Nations,” Bachelet, who served as Chile’s first female leader, said in a video posted on her social media accounts.
“Some may believe that the time was not right for a candidacy like the one I sought to represent. I do not regret having taken on this great challenge,” she said.
Bachelet stressed that by running for the top UN post, she had helped spark debate “that the next secretary-general should be a woman from Latin America”.
Chile’s government said in a statement that it had withdrawn its support for Bachelet’s candidacy in March.
Since then, it has not backed any of the candidates in the running.
The government also “reaffirmed its commitment to multilateralism and to reform of the United Nations”.
So far in three polls as part of the informal process to pick the next UN chief, the 15-member Security Council twice placed Costa Rica’s former vice-president Rebeca Grynspan in the lead.
Guyanese ex-foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett placed first in the third poll.
Bachelet was initially nominated last February by the administration of then president Gabriel Boric, and supported by the leftist leaders of Mexico and Brazil.
But the left-leaning 74-year-old’s candidacy lost momentum after Chile’s new leader, far-right President Jose Antonio Kast, withdrew his backing.
Earlier in September at a university event, Bachelet had appeared to recognise her underdog status, joking about her slim chances of leading the global body.
No woman has led the UN in its 80-year history, and only one Latin American has served as secretary-general: Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, from 1982 to 1991.
According to unwritten practice – one that is not always followed – the top position rotates among geographic regions. This time, it would be Latin America’s turn.
Bachelet’s withdrawal leaves four women and three men in the race to succeed the current UN chief, 77-year-old Antonio Guterres of Portugal, who completes his second five-year term on Dec 31. AFP

US news outlets express solidarity after Trump bars some reporters from White House

US news outlets express solidarity after Trump bars some reporters from White House
Mack Liederman
- President Trump banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, accusing them of publishing false, negative stories without providing evidence.
- Major media outlets and Democrats condemned the ban as unconstitutional and an attack on free press and democracy.
- Some Republicans supported the ban, citing "fake news," but others and conservative commentators warned it sets a dangerous precedent against press freedom.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Many major media outlets and some high-profile Democrats panned US President Donald Trump’s abrupt decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
The latest barrage of threats against the press came on the morning of Sept 19, when reporters for the outlets were denied access to the White House and had their badges confiscated.
On the evening of Sept 18, Trump had accused the three outlets of running “purposely negative stories” that were untrue, but did not give details. The administration has not said what led to the decision, which many First Amendment groups called unconstitutional and unlikely to survive a court challenge.
Condemnation from leading news outlets was nearly universal, including from many that compete directly with CNN, MS NOW and Politico.
“No news organisation – or person – should be retaliated against by the government over the words they use,” said Lauren Easton, a spokeswoman for The Associated Press, which filed suit over restrictions that Trump tried to impose on its White House access in 2025.
The New York Times, The Washington Post and press associations released statements calling the ban an attack on free speech and the free press.
Journalists at Fox News have also taken issue with the ban. One Fox contributor, Ari Fleischer, said conservatives should challenge liberal reporters. “Argue and defeat them,” he said. “Don’t ban them. Or one day they’ll ban us.”
Another contributor, Jonathan Turley, said that “barring disfavoured media from the White House is a terrible precedent and practice”.
Jacqui Heinrich, a Fox News anchor and president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, said on social media that the right to First Amendment protections “does not depend on whether the president likes a news organisation’s coverage”.
“This is about more than the rights of journalists,” Heinrich added. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”
Democrats pounced on Trump’s ban as an attempt to hide his administration’s shortcomings and to distract voters from other issues. They pointed out that Republicans were heading into a challenging election cycle with high inflation and an unpopular war with Iran started by Trump, whose support in the polls has sagged.
“Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said on social media. “This is a democracy. You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth.”
Congressman Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, called on the news media to boycott the White House if Trump “keeps violating press freedom”. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said Trump was censoring the press and trying to “hide his failures”. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont said that Trump wanted to “control the flow of information and silence media that might hold them accountable”.
Sanders said on social media: “We will not allow Trump to undermine the First Amendment, the Constitution and our democracy. We will not accept authoritarianism.”
High-ranking Republicans and members of the Trump administration mostly remained quiet on Sept 19. But Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has tried to restrict reporters’ access to the Pentagon, said he “fully supports” a ban on some outlets that he and Trump have labelled “fake news” for negative coverage.
“They endangered our troops with false stories, leaks, and trafficked in fiction and lies about the President,” Hegseth said, without providing examples or evidence.
Benny Johnson, a right-wing podcaster, celebrated the decision to block certain outlets from the White House and said Trump had been banned from social media platforms after the Jan 6 attack on the Capitol by his supporters.
“No one is infringing on their ability to do reporting,” Johnson said in a social media post.
The campaign of Mike Rogers, a Republican running with Trump’s backing for a Senate seat in Michigan, appeared to distance itself from the President’s decision.
Rogers “held a press conference just this morning with invites out to each of those outlets”, Alyssa Brouillet, a spokeswoman for his campaign, said in a statement. “That tells you where he stands.”
Meghan McCain, a conservative commentator, was more explicit.
“Unpopular opinion in my parts, but it’s insane and a very slippery slope to kick media outlets you don’t like out of the White House,” McCain said. NYTIMES
- Olivia Diaz and Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Memories of childhood scents associated with joy are encoded by neurons generated shortly after birth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:00:57 UTC
09:00:57 KST

A study published in PLOS Biology by Jules Dejou and colleagues shows that neurons developing around the time of birth in the olfactory bulb granule-cell layer (a region of the brain) are the ones encoding the memories of scents associated with joy in childhood. A separate primer by Chloé Guillaume and Elisa Galliano published in PLOS Biology discusses these results. In the study, juvenile mice exposed to attractive odors while in an enriched playful environment showed a preference for that odor in adulthood more than mice exposed to the same odor while in normal housing.
Memories evoked by odors are often unusually vivid and emotionally powerful. This is particularly the case when they originate in childhood. Compared with memories triggered by visual or auditory cues, autobiographical memories triggered by odors tend to come from earlier periods of life and are more often associated with positive emotions. Repeated exposure to the same odor in a consistent emotional context can gradually create strong associations that persist for many years. Such memories may be linked not to a specific reward, but to a broader sense of comfort, happiness, or well-being associated with familiar childhood experiences.
Olfaction is especially important early in life because it is functional from birth and can guide essential behaviors before other sensory systems are fully developed. The olfactory system also has unusually direct connections with brain regions involved in memory, reward, and emotion, including the amygdala, hippocampus, orbitofrontal cortex, and related limbic structures (a network of brain regions that control emotion and memory).
Odor information is initially processed in the olfactory bulb, where granule cells (a type of small neuron) and other interneurons (neurons that transmit signals between other neurons) help refine sensory signals before they are transmitted to higher brain regions. Many of these olfactory interneurons are generated early in life and can be shaped by early sensory experience, making them plausible substrates for long-lasting odor memories.
To identify the neurons responsible for encoding olfactory memories from childhood and to understand the neural mechanism that allows them to play an important role in forming a person’s identity, the study authors started with a survey involving 647 human participants. Participants were asked to recall an odorant that was significant in their childhood, going back as far as possible in time. They were then asked to rate the pleasantness and the presence of six basic emotions (happiness, surprise, fear, disgust, sadness, and anger) associated with that smell.
Results of this survey showed that the ratings were highest for positive emotions, namely happiness and pleasantness, followed by surprise. Ratings of negative emotions were lower. Participants were also asked how many times the event that led to their earlier odor memories occurred. Seventy-three percent of participants reported that the event occurred more than five times.
Finally, participants rated the hedonic value (the degree to which something is considered pleasant or unpleasant) of their childhood odorant, which they found to be predominantly pleasant. The authors used another dataset to see whether those smells are intrinsically pleasant or whether participants only perceived them that way. The results indicated that those smells do tend to be intrinsically pleasant, indicating that individuals prefer to make pleasant odors a part of their autobiographical memory.
Based on the human survey results, the researchers developed a mouse model. They divided 23-day-old (juvenile) mice into two groups. One group was exposed up to their 33rd day of life to an attractive odor such as limonene, citronellol, or camphor while the mice were in a positive, enriched, playful environment.
This pairing between the odor and the environment was repeated five times during the 10 days of the experiment. It was done every other day for 2 hours. The second, control group of mice was also exposed to the same odor, but in their ordinary housing. The study authors assessed the emotions of the mice by registering their ultrasonic vocalizations, with more numerous and higher frequency vocalizations indicating a more positive emotional state.
Later, when the mice were 2 months old (i.e., young adults), the study authors tested whether they showed a preference for that odor. The mice that learned to associate the odor with an enriched environment and positive emotions indeed showed a greater preference for it compared to mice that experienced it in their ordinary housing. The researchers observed that this memory recall relied on increased functional connectivity in the brain’s reward system.
Investigation of the neural basis of this smell memory found that neurons born around the first day of life in the olfactory bulb granule-cell layer tended to be particularly activated by the odor the mice learned to associate with positive emotions as juveniles. When these neurons were silenced using optogenetics (a biological technique that uses light to control neurons that have been genetically modified to express light-sensitive ion channels), the preference for the odor was reduced, suggesting that these neurons are a key part of the early memory recall mechanism.
However, by 6 months of age, that memory was gone, unless the mice were periodically re-exposed to the scent. In these older mice, memory persistence was no longer dependent on the neonatal-born granule cells. Instead, the persistence of the memory was associated with a large-scale reorganization of the brain’s functional networks, shifting away from the reward system to rely on strengthened connections within the olfactory-limbic system.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of childhood odor memories and their role in overall psychological functioning. However, it should be noted that while the initial survey was conducted on humans, the experimental manipulations were conducted on mice. While mice and humans share many physiological similarities, they are still very different species, and the exact neural network mechanisms in humans might differ.
The primer, “Neurons generated shortly after birth encode the scent of early-life happiness,” was authored by Chloé Guillaume and Elisa Galliano. The paper, “Positive early-life olfactory memory is rooted in the olfactory bulb and triggers large-scale changes beyond the olfactory system,” was authored by Jules Dejou, Anna Athanassi, Théo Brunel, Marc Thevenet, Anne Didier, and Nathalie Mandairon.

John Farnham's tribute concert will go ahead without him as the Australian music legend's family reveals his health has deteriorated.
The music-industry giant will be honoured by local and international performing greats at a blockbuster charity gig at Melbourne's Rod Laver Arena on Sunday, raising funds for the cancer support services that helped him through his own battle with the disease.
The 77-year-old, who has undergone several surgeries for oral cancer, now requires continuous oxygen support and 24-hour care.
A day before the sold-out event, Farnham's wife Jill and the couple's sons Robert and James, said they were "deeply moved by everything happening" at Rod Laver Arena.
"John's health has deteriorated in recent months," read a family statement posted to social media.

Zelenskyy established the annual President of Ukraine Cup in hand-to-hand combat
Kyiv • UNN
The tournament in Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast brought together 127 athletes from 11 institutions. Veterans and wounded soldiers competed for the first time.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree establishing the annual tournament "President of Ukraine Cup in Hand-to-Hand Combat." UNN reports this, citing a statement from the press service of the head of state.
Details
It is noted that in Ivano-Frankivsk region, Zelenskyy attended the final of the tournament, in which representatives of the Security Service of the President, the National Guard, the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence, the State Border Guard Service and the State Bureau of Investigation competed in seven weight categories in the "Full Contact" division.
This is an important tournament, an important sport that improves the qualities of all those who defend Ukraine, our state, and our people, and, of course, defend our freedom and our values. Regardless of this year's results, all of you are certainly winners — winners in spirit and through your deeds, because for many years and many days in a row, in your service and through your service to Ukraine, you have overcome fear and pain, and defeated war and death
It is reported that the event brought together a total of 127 athletes from eleven institutions, who competed in several divisions: "Full Contact," "Demonstration of Self-Defense Techniques," and "Adaptive Sport."
These are military formations, law enforcement agencies, and rescue services. This year, competitions in adaptive hand-to-hand combat were held for the first time among veterans and soldiers who were wounded while defending Ukraine against Russian aggression
Recall
The Ukrainian hand-to-hand combat team won first place in the team standings at the 2025 CSIT World Sports Games in Greece. The Ukrainians won 48 medals, including 13 gold.

Ukraine has signed the Council of Europe convention on the co-production of series
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has joined European rules on the co-production of series. The document opens access to funding, rights and new markets.
Ukraine has signed the Council of Europe Convention on the joint production of audiovisual works in the form of series. This was announced by Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture Tetiana Berezhna, reports UNN.
Details
According to her, this is an important step toward integrating Ukraine into the European cultural and audiovisual space.
For the first time, we are regulating the co-production of series. The document was signed during the Carpathian Integration Summit. For the Ukrainian industry, this creates new opportunities to produce series together with European partners, attract international funding, and enter new markets
She clarified that the convention makes it possible to obtain official co-production status and guarantees a share of the rights to the product created and the income from its use.
"The document also establishes flexible conditions for financial participation—the minimum contribution of a partner in multilateral co-productions may be small, opening up more opportunities for Ukrainian teams to participate in major international projects," the minister added.
Let us remind you
Ukraine is concerned about the inclusion of the film DAU in the competition of the Venice Film Festival.

The Verkhovna Rada refuted rumors about a "recess" and suspending its work
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada is not holding plenary sessions but continues to work in committees and working groups. The next session is scheduled for October 13.
Rumors about a "holiday" and a "break" in the work of the Verkhovna Rada do not correspond to reality — Parliament continues to function, just not in the format of plenary sessions. This was reported by the press service of the Verkhovna Rada Secretariat, according to UNN.
Details
They noted that Parliament continues to work during the break in plenary sessions — lawmakers work in committees, working groups, temporary investigative and special commissions.
The claim about a holiday and a break is being actively circulated. We remind you that Parliament works not only in the session hall. Parliament continues to work continuously
They added that, despite the absence of plenary sessions, the work of committees, subcommittees, working groups and factions does not stop for a single day.
We remind you

Nato welcomes Greenland deal as Trump says it will give US 'permanent security control'
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-20
00:00:27 BST
08:00:27 KST

Nato welcomes Greenland deal as Trump says it will give US 'permanent security control'
- Published
The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize it by force.
Nato said the deal would help stabilise the region, as Trump said Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic.
The leaders of Denmark and Greenland welcomed the deal to "strengthen security", saying it was expected to be signed next week - but did not outline its contents.
This comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.
No text of the agreement has been released. Trump said the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and would grant it the ability "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland", in a post on Truth Social.
He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".
A Nato spokesperson said the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.
The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.
Nielsen said it was "gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance".
"The agreement recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said the deal helped "to reaffirm Danish sovereignty" over the island.
"I simply note that Danish sovereignty is respected, that international law is respected, and that this is what we were asking for. So it's a good thing," Macron was quoted as saying by the AFP news agency.
Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.
His repeated demands to take Greenland earlier this year prompted an outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and other Nato members.
There is hope the crisis has now been brought to an end, with some Danish media interpreting the agreement as a quiet but significant triumph for the country's diplomacy.
"Don't tell Trump that it's the Kingdom of Denmark that has won," read one headline in the newspaper Berlingske on Saturday.
"Trump didn't get Greenland, but he was allowed to take a victory lap on social media," wrote a US correspondent for Politiken. Territorial integrity was a red line for Denmark and Greenland, and the US president has made no mention of any territory changing hands.
It is not yet clear what concessions or sweeteners, if any, have been agreed - and in Greenland, some are still nervous.
"[It's] news we have all been hoping for," MP Naaja Nathanielsen wrote on social media. But she added: "It is absolutely crucial that any agreement preserves our right to self-determination."
Former Greenlandic politician Aaja Chemnitz said she looked forward to the deal being finalised, but "until then, I'm sceptical".
"I don't have much confidence in Trump," she said.
The text of the agreement has not been published. The BBC has contacted the Danish Embassy in the US and the White House.
However, an unnamed US State Department official outlined the deal without providing specifics.
Among the agreed provisions is one stating the deal would not expire even if Greenland became an independent country in the future.
The official added that under the deal, the US has unilateral power to build additional military structures with no approval needed from Greenland or Denmark. It includes "permanent access, basing and overflights rights," the official said.
It also bans non-Nato countries from building bases in Greenland, and "bans adversaries from making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States".
The official added that under the current status quo, adversaries have been allowed to invest in Greenland's "sensitive sectors without investment screening".
The official specifically referenced Russia and China, saying it blocks them from deploying troops or making investments in "sensitive sectors".
Without the official text being released, it is unclear how exactly the deal differs from a 1951 agreement with Denmark, under which the US can send as many troops as it wants to Greenland.
The US already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base in the north-western tip of the territory.
Trump says Greenland is essential for his plan to build a Golden Dome defence system, designed to protect the US against missile attacks from Russia and China, and that European allies could co-operate in this endeavour.
The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles.

Syria says arrested Assad-era general who led attacks on rebels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19

Breadcrumb
Syria says arrested Assad-era general who led attacks on rebels
Syrian authorities on Saturday said they arrested a general who served under the rule of ousted president Bashar al-Assad, saying he led operations against formerly rebel-held areas during the country's 13-year civil war.
In a statement, security forces announced "the arrest of former Major General Ahmed Mohammad Ismail, a high-ranking commander in the Republican Guard of the former regime's army".
Military records indicate that "he began his service as a platoon commander, then served as a company commander in the 2nd Battalion of the 101st Airborne Regiment. He was subsequently promoted, at the beginning of 2016, to Chief of Operations of the same regiment, and directly participated in commanding military assaults on the cities of Aleppo and Daraa, as well as on Eastern Ghouta."
Located near Damascus, Eastern Ghouta was a rebel stronghold during the civil war until 2018, and the site of a major chemical attack five years prior.
US intelligence says more than 1,000 people were killed with sarin nerve gas in the suburb of the Syrian capital Damascus, in 2013 during Syria's civil war.
The attack was attributed to the Syrian government under the rule of Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in late 2024.
The government at the time denied involvement and blamed rebels.
Since Assad was overthrown in December 2024, Syria's new authorities have arrested dozens of former security officials, while trials began in April.
Earlier this month Syrian authorities said they had arrested nine former pilots including three generals accused of taking part in lethal bombings of towns and villages under Assad's rule.
Syria sentenced Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher al-Assad, and five other security officials to death in absentia in August for atrocities committed during the civil war.
The former president fled Syria as his government fell and is believed to be living in Russia.

John Farnham to miss tribute concert due to poor health

Unknown Publisher

Music icon John Farnham to miss tribute concert in his honour due to poor health
In short:
John Farnham will miss a tribute concert dedicated to his career due to poor health, the singer's family has confirmed.
The Australian music icon has been in poor health for several years and his family confirmed he required 24-hour medical care at home.
Some of the biggest names in Australian music, including Jimmy Barnes, Tina Arena, Human Nature, Jessica Mauboy, Kate Ceberano and Ross Wilson, are performing at the charity concert.
Australian music legend John Farnham will miss a tribute concert dedicated to his career due to poor health, the singer's family has confirmed ahead of the Melbourne event.
The concert, dubbed The Songs of John Farnham: A Living Legend, will be held at Rod Laver Arena this evening, with funds raised on the night going towards the cancer service that supported Farnham during his cancer battle.
In a statement posted on social media, Farnham's wife, Jill, and sons, Robert and James, wrote that the singer was "deeply moved" by the musical tribute but would be too unwell to attend the arena spectacular.
His family confirmed the 77-year-old You're the Voice singer required continuous oxygen support and was receiving 24-hour nursing care.
"Many people have been asking whether John will be involved in the concert or attending tomorrow night to watch it all happen," the Farnham family statement said.
"Unfortunately, he will not be able to attend and, as a family, we feel it is important to provide an update on John's health to help explain why.
"John's health has deteriorated in recent months. He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility.
"It has also become necessary for John to receive 24-hour nursing care at home, ensuring trained support is always available when he needs it."
Some of the biggest names in Australian entertainment are scheduled to take centre stage at the Farnham tribute tonight, including Jimmy Barnes, Tina Arena, Human Nature, Jessica Mauboy, Kate Ceberano and Ross Wilson.
International stars, including Canadian singer Celine Dion and American crooner Richard Marx, are also taking part in the event, which will raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia.
"We have kept these matters private while our family has adjusted to John's changing needs. However, we now feel it is important that John's fans and supporters understand his circumstances and why he cannot be there this weekend," the Farnham family said.
"If things were different, John would have loved nothing more than to attend the concert. He would undoubtedly have been a little overwhelmed by all the fuss, but he would also have wanted to thank everyone involved in person.
"As a family, we have decided that it is best for John to remain at home, where he can be safe and comfortable."
Australian pop band Human Nature, who featured in John Farnham's song Every Time You Cry, said they "can't wait" to celebrate the 77-year-old's career at tonight's concert.
"This weekend, we celebrate the extraordinary music and legacy of the one and only John Farnham — a true living legend and a hero to us all," the band said in a social media post.
"It's impossible not to feel emotional, and incredibly humbled, to have played even a small part in John's remarkable career.
"John, we love you. Thank you for welcoming us into your world."
The original yellow Wiggle, Greg Page, said in a social media post: "All our love and understanding is being sent to John and his family".
Farnham is one of Australia's most successful performers, with his 1986 album, Whispering Jack, selling more than 1.6 million copies.
The British-born singer was named 1987 Australian of the Year by then-prime minister Bob Hawke, and has won more than 20 ARIA awards.
In 2024 Farnham released an autobiography, The Voice Inside, which details the monumental triumphs of his career as well as the immense struggles he has faced.

The Kremlin presented a fake "report" on war crimes in Bucha
Kyiv • UNN
The Center for Countering Disinformation called the Russian propaganda "report" on Bucha a collection of manipulations and lies. The Russian Federation plans to use the pseudo-investigation at the UN.
Following another intensification of the information campaign denying russia's war crimes in the Kyiv region in 2022, the Kremlin presented a propaganda "report" filled with manipulations and fake claims about the events in Bucha. This was reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD), according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that the document was presented at the state-run propaganda news agency TASS with the active assistance of russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was authored by the so-called "International Public Tribunal on the Crimes of Ukrainian Neo-Nazis."
This structure is exclusively a propaganda entity created by the Kremlin and has no legal status or recognition whatsoever. The "report" itself is also a collection of manipulations and lies. In particular, deceased civilians are declared to have been "Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel" or to have "died of illnesses." The report's authors also cynically claim that Ukrainian soldiers deliberately killed elderly people in the Kyiv region in order to later blame russia for it
They emphasize that the occupiers are disguising the fake report as a "legal document" containing "irrefutable evidence" in order to give it weight in the information space. At the same time, russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson maria zakharova has already stated that they intend to use this pseudo-investigation at the UN General Assembly as an official position.
"Such measures are part of the Kremlin's systematic strategy. In an attempt to blur the evidentially confirmed mass killings of civilians, russia is creating a parallel information reality to justify its own war crimes before a foreign audience," the CCD concludes.
To recap
russia has launched another stage of an information campaign aimed at discrediting international investigations and denying the war crimes committed by the russian army in Bucha.

An American perspective: Why Yom Kippur still brings Jews together, even without belief - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
22:17:06 UTC
07:17:06 KST

In rabbinic usage, Yom Kippur is sometimes simply called Hayom – the Day. It’s a way of setting it apart from every other day – even Shabbat, which is itself set apart from every day except Yom Kippur.
But what is the purpose of ranking time this way? Isn’t all time, in fact, the same, and isn’t it only we humans, with our imagination, who invent these distinctions?
And yet, we make these distinctions all the time. And we make them because they are important. We believe in the distinctions. We know, for example, that time spent with our children and grandchildren has a higher value than time scrolling through social media with our minds seized by, say, images of famous people, expensive cars, or arguments that grow violent.
We know that some times are categorically superior to others: a brit milah, a baby naming, a loved one’s wedding, a birth, or the ceremony at the conclusion of life.
It’s in these instances that we see how time can contain life in its fullness, or conversely, in its shallowness. We are made viscerally aware of the value of time, of a moment, of a day. And so it is with Yom Kippur, the Day.
The power of Yom Kippur to create belonging
When I grew up in Minnesota in the 60s and 70s, many and perhaps most Jews I knew went to synagogue just two days a year, on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Some saw this as troubling. You might have heard that “Ed Shapiro, that nebuch, only goes to shul twice a year!” The thing about this imagined Shapiro wasn’t that he only went to synagogue twice a year; it was that he went at all.
Think about that with an open mind.
After some 3,300 years, almost 2,000 of them in exile, Shapiro, a Jew, a regular person, not a rabbinical scholar or a saint, living an otherwise completely secular life, feels compelled to leave the comfort of his armchair, the luxury of his big-screen TV with its televised golf game, to go to a place where they chanted in an ancient language, one that he did not understand.
It’s there he will go to pray to a God Shapiro doesn’t believe in. And yet there’s Ed, sitting when it’s time to sit, standing when it’s time to stand. Sweating and yawning.
Schuckling and looking at his watch.
This, all this, is the essence of The Day. A purely trans-intellectual takeover of the body and mind by an alien – and yet, somehow, totally familiar – feeling that he, our fictional Ed Shapiro, is a Jew and that Jews not only go to shul on Yom Kippur, but they also fast.
Ridiculous as it sounds to the outsider, Ed, a man of hearty appetite, will go without food or water for 25 hours. The truly fascinating thing, and I think the word “miraculous” is not out of place here, is that he does this based on a command from an unseen and un-believed-in Deity. That he doesn’t know why doesn’t make it any less impressive. In a very real sense, it makes it all the more impressive. After all, who really understands any of this?
In fact, if someone prevented Shapiro from attending shul – let’s say there was a gathering of people, perhaps not especially difficult to imagine these days, who stood in front of the prayer house and used their bodies to barricade the entrance – Shapiro, not what you’d call a heroic type, would very likely risk his physical well-being to force his way in.
A lesson in belonging, not belief
WHEN I WAS about 12 and didn’t want to go to synagogue on Yom Kippur, or really, at any time, my dad once told me a similar thing. “Pete, imagine they wouldn’t let you go inside.”
I have to admit, it was a hugely compelling thing to hear, especially given the regularity of swastikas, carved or drawn with permanent marker, found at my school. It wasn’t a lesson in belief. It was a lesson in belonging, and it worked on me exactly the way it must have worked on Shapiro, whoever he was.
This unknowable, unbelieved-in God has somehow made His presence and His will known and largely obeyed, after millennia of exilic existence, to Jews.
And they, sometimes without a deep knowledge of their traditions, continue to insist on being part of the Jewish people and that their children take part in the tradition. I am one of those Jews too, though my own road there has taken me to a different place than Shapiro’s.
No longer a teenager by any stretch of the imagination, I observe Shabbat, kashrut, and the Jews holidays. I put on tefillin every weekday morning. And I agree, hour to hour, to wrestle with the idea of God, with trying to “know” God.
In fact, even when I was young, I wrestled and wrestled hard – once going to a seafood restaurant with my cousin on the Day for all-you-can-eat fried shrimp. Why? Looking back, I rebelled because I cared. I wasn’t “parve” about any of it.
Just as no one can fully understand God, no one can fully explain Ed Shapiro, and millions liked him. Like me. Like us.
This is only one of the beauties, the honor of being part of our glorious, resilient, courageous, brilliant, and faithful peoplehood, a peoplehood some today insist doesn’t exist.
We hear from those who seem not to wish us well that we are only “a religion,” that Judaism (how I dislike the false “ism” inherent in that term) is not a nation, not a peoplehood. “I have no qualms with Jews, only Israel,” they say.
Ed Shapiro knows different. Ed feels the difference. And it’s in part that difference that makes Yom Kippur, Hayom, the Day.
It is the Day when God calls us together, calls His Am Segulah, His treasured nation, together to start another year afresh, to be sealed and inscribed for a good year.
To a year of health, joy, children, rejoicing, and true peace. To true shalem, when it will be effortless to see and to feel the wholeness of the world and our place within it.
May we be so inscribed.
The writer is a Grammy- and Emmy-nominated rock & roll performer, songwriter, film composer, visual artist, and award-winning author. He has been profiled in Time Magazine, Rolling Stone, The Wall Street Journal, Tablet, and NPR. His newest book is Suspended by No String: A Songwriter’s Reflections on Faith, Aliveness, and Wonder (Regalo Press/Simon and Schuster). Follow him at peterhimmelman.substack.com

The Ebenezer Scrooge model: Can Yom Kippur really bring repentance and change?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
22:17:00 UTC
07:17:00 KST

After nearly 25 hours without food or drink, in the culmination of prayers that emphasize the fragility of life, the supremacy of God, and the risk of divine punishment, synagogue-goers on Yom Kippur are exhausted, humble, and perhaps filled with remorse and trepidation. The shofar blasts hundreds of sounds and leaves a deep, echoing resonance in the soul.
But a week later, have those worshipers changed their behavior for the better? Do people really transform themselves? Repentance isn’t simply regret; it is regret that produces transformation.
Ironically, a fictional story written by 19th-century English writer and journalist Charles Dickens, one of the leading novelists of the Victorian era, did an outstanding job illustrating consequential moral change.
His 1843 novella A Christmas Carol can provide a vivid, instantly recognizable human story about Ebenezer (which means “stone of help” in Hebrew) Scrooge, whose surname is regarded as a catchword for avarice and bitterness toward society and who constantly shouted “Bah! Humbug!” to express his disgust with many traditions.
Wealthy from running a warehouse, he pays his clerk, Bob Cratchit, a paltry wage while living cheaply in the quarters of his dead business partner, Jacob Marley. When two men ask him for charity on Christmas Eve, he gives them the cold shoulder.
But at night, Marley’s ghost visits Scrooge and warns him that three spirits will appear before him and demand that he change his character. If not, Scrooge will be bound in heavy chains.
After being shown scenes of his loveless childhood, the ruthless way he treats others in the present, his future lonely death, and his neglected gravestone, Scrooge repents and performs good deeds as a way of life.
Yom Kippur has no ghosts, of course, but it does something rather similar. It asks us to confront who we were, who we have become, and who we might yet become.
His transformation isn’t merely feeling sorry. He undergoes something: a psychological process of recognition, confrontation with himself, an emotional awakening, a decision to change, and then changed behavior.
What does it really take to change?
Prof. Mario Mikulincer, a well-known Hebrew University of Jerusalem (HUJI) psychologist and researcher who serves as the academic director of the university’s Israel Center for Addiction and Mental Health, described this same process.
The Argentina-born psychologist explained that there is a natural human inclination not to feel sorry about misdeeds or admit mistakes. The brain’s executive function is to admit mistakes and improve.
Stress, fatigue, and routine wear down the prefrontal cortex that controls executive function, allowing the basal ganglia that control body movements and process emotions to take over.
“Habits,” he said, “operate automatically. When intention conflicts with habit under stress, habit almost always wins. People who succeed don’t have superior willpower; they build superior environments and friction-free routines.”
Having no food or drink on Yom Kippur provides the time to think about oneself and the future.
“Hunger reduces the amount of glucose in the body, so it reduces executive function. This can make people more impulsive,” he noted. “But it also gives you time to have thoughts that overcome the physical, to think of life and death, one’s existence, and anxiety.
“It can also help you to identify with the poor, who are often hungry. The religiously observant believe that God is surveying what we do and can help lead us to better behavior. That can lead to the expression of remorse and determination to be a better person.”
Mikulincer added that it was “a brilliant move” that Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, was accompanied by a long fast, as it promotes introspection. “When stress, exhaustion, or emotional triggers hit, executive function undergoes depletion, allowing habitual patterns to hijack behavior.”
Repentance is more than feeling sorry
RABBI MOSHE BEN MAIMON (Maimonides, or the Rambam) wrote in his book Hilchot Teshuvah (The Laws of Repentance) about the yetzer hara (the primal drive). He stated that genuine repentance is not just feeling remorse; with the same capability one has to sin, one must actively choose differently. The psychologist noted that “this is part of executive function.”
Psychologists also refer to the “False Hope Syndrome” in which people set unrealistically high expectations for self-transformation because deciding to change provides an immediate, cheap surge of dopamine and moral relief.
When the initial euphoria fades, the reality of effort sets in, leading to relapse, said Mikulincer. “A person can overcome physical temptations. I think everybody can change, but it’s hard to move immediately from black to white and meet all your goals. If the goals aren’t realistic, they’re better off working step by step.”
Guilt makes people think, “I did something bad,” and this motivates self-improvement. But shame makes them think, “I am bad,” which triggers defensiveness and behavioral paralysis.
“People should feel guilt so they can repair,” he commented. “Repentance is a powerful Jewish theme. A good measure of it improves behavior, but a pathological amount is harmful. If a person feels shame, he hides and has to lie, and then it’s very hard to improve. Self-loathing actually stops people from changing, and shame triggers denial, addiction, and anger.”
The repetitive, collective nature of the Yom Kippur confessional (viddui) uses plural language (“We have trespassed, we have betrayed, we have stolen, we have spoken slander ... We have turned away from Your commandments and from Your good laws, and it has yielded us no benefit,” recited aloud many times during the Yom Kippur service).
Psychologically, listing misdeeds out loud forces a person to bridge the gap between internal denial and objective reality – a necessary first step in any therapeutic recovery program.
“It’s brilliant, because it is said in the plural,” the psychologist continued. “One is part of a community, of something bigger, so you can shoulder the burden.”
Another well-known prayer is Unetanneh Tokef, which balances the terrifying fragility of human life with an impressive openness to change. It emphasizes that human nature is inherently flawed, but the door to transformation never closes.
Deeply ingrained behaviors are automated pathways in the brain. Asking someone to “just stop” a bad habit without replacing the underlying trigger and reward is neurobiologically unrealistic.
“The brain is plastic and can grow,” said Mikulincer. “With practice, prayer, medication, or deep breathing, you can produce brain change, but one must stick to it and have self-discipline.”
The final prayer, Ne’ilah (closing), said as the sun sets, gives those present in the synagogue the feeling that time is running out and directly confronts human self-deception and helplessness, causing worshippers to ask for divine assistance when willpower alone fails.
Some people emerge stronger after hardship while others don’t.
Mikulincer suggested that “suffering can destroy people, but if they overcome it, they can become stronger. Personality traits can really change; kindness and even optimism can be learned – at any age. Decades ago, it was thought that the brain is set like plaster by age 30. The brain has been proven to have neuroplasticity, the ability to change and create new synapses.”
Mikulincer spends all his professional time doing research, not treating patients. In 2021, he researched the phenomenon of people who abandoned a religious way of life and, this year, those who have become observant due to exposure to war and terror.
Asked if he has studied prisoners and whether they can be helped to change their behavior significantly, he said he hasn’t, “but maybe will do it. It’s an interesting subject to explore.”
Asked what would be the single most effective first step to take if one wants to become a better person in the new year, he concluded: “Forgive yourself more, be less critical, feel healthy guilt, admit mistakes, and give a chance for something to happen.”
Can a crisis really change us?
LIKE MIKULINCER (who is not religiously observant), Dr. Aaron Cherniak is also a licensed psychologist at the Israel Center for Addiction and Mental Health. He is the director of research at the Shaare Nefesh Resilience Center (affiliated with the Shaare Zedek Medical Center) and a modern Orthodox rabbi ordained at New York’s Yeshiva University.
He asserted that personality can change after adulthood, but it’s more gradual than dramatic. Traits like conscientiousness and emotional stability do shift over the lifespan, especially around major life transitions. But lasting change tends to come from sustained new behavior, not a single moment of insight.”
Making promises on Yom Kippur “gives us the instant gratification of feeling like ‘better’ people instantaneously, even though nothing about us has changed. The habits we have formed and our pattern of seeking immediate gratification do not change just because we have made a sincere commitment.
“Real growth happens with consistent choices to maintain that commitment over time, notwithstanding the challenge of doing so. None of this is to diminish the power of profound moments of insight that remind us that we desire change and can change.”
“Crises,” Cherniak continued, “are one of the more reliable catalysts for real personality and behavioral change, precisely because they disrupt routine and force a kind of reckoning that everyday life rarely demands.
“But permanence isn’t guaranteed by the crisis itself; it depends on whether the person has the support, meaning-making, and follow-through to consolidate that shift into something lasting, rather than reverting once the acute period passes.”
Prolonged stress keeps the nervous system oriented toward threat and survival, which narrows attention and depletes the cognitive resources – planning, impulse control, flexible thinking – that deliberate change relies on.
It also drains the kind of bandwidth needed to build new habits, since chronic stress tends to push people back toward familiar, well-worn coping behaviors rather than newer, less automatic ones, simply because the familiar option requires less effort under strain.
Timing matters. Attempting significant change during a period of acute, ongoing stress is much harder than during a period of relative stability, and it’s often more realistic to focus on stabilizing first before expecting deep behavioral change to take hold.”
Change doesn’t require motivation to come first; behavior, he said. “What we call motivation is driven largely by a sense of progress, not just by wanting something in the abstract – taking a step, even a small one, generates momentum that fuels the next step, so motivation is as much a byproduct of action as a precondition for it.”
Asked why intelligent people repeatedly make the same mistakes, Cherniak suggested that “intelligence and self-control run on different systems. Knowing better doesn’t mean acting better. Under stress or temptation, fast emotional and reward circuits tend to override slow, deliberate reasoning, no matter how sharp that reasoning is.”
He disagrees with the claim that some people cannot change for the better. “There are real obstacles to change – environmental instability, or a total lack of support and stability – not some fixed incapacity in the person. And often underneath those, the deeper barrier is a person’s own belief that they can’t change.
“There’s a teaching from Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik on this: he wrote that when Elisha ben Abuyah – the sage who became known as the ‘Other’ – believed a heavenly voice had permanently barred him from repentance, it wasn’t really God who closed that door. It was his own conviction that he was irredeemable.
“The moment he believed that, he stopped trying, and the belief became self-fulfilling. That’s the trap: ‘Can’t change’ is rarely the truth about a person. It’s usually the story they’ve come to believe about themselves – and that story does more damage than any real limitation ever could.”
The more you practice small acts of kindness, the more natural it becomes, because it starts to shape how you see yourself, and it usually feels good and makes people respond well to you, which makes you want to do it again. That’s what happened to Scrooge.
“It’s also something people pick up from example – kids who grow up watching kindness modeled, or communities that build regular opportunities to help others into everyday life, tend to produce more of it,” Cherniak concluded.

Saudi Arabia confirms Yemen's Houthi rebels tried to attack its capital with a ballistic missile
Saudi Arabia on Saturday confirmed that Yemen’s Houthi rebels tried to attack its capital with a ballistic missile, the first targeting of Riyadh since the escalation in fighting with the Houthis that has opened a new front in the Iran war.
The statement by the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis came long after the dawn attempt, which the coalition said was intercepted. Some residents in Riyadh heard an explosion. Later, some saw a plume of smoke near the airport. There were no reports of casualties or damage.
The statement also said the Houthis tried to attack civilian infrastructure in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu — where a key Saudi pipeline ends — and in Taif, Baysh and Farasan but they were thwarted, giving no further details.
The Houthis earlier claimed, without providing evidence, that they had targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh and facilities of Saudi oil giant Aramco in Yanbu, causing “massive fires.” Aramco, the world’s largest oil company, did not respond to a request for comment.
The growing conflict near another important global shipping corridor has brought new pressures for markets.
Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree claimed they attacked with cruise and ballistic missiles as well as drones. He said Saudi Arabia had attempted to target the rebel-held city of Sanaa in neighboring Yemen, without giving details. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify the claims.
Recent days have seen one escalation after another. On Thursday, the first civilian casualty was reported as the Saudi civil defense said debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed a Yemeni resident of Saudi Arabia.
And on Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said the Houthis had tried to attack Mecca, Islam’s holiest city, with a drone that it said was intercepted, calling the security of the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad a “red line.” The Houthis fiercely denied the accusation.
The United States, a close Saudi ally, has signaled it has no current fight with the Houthis. Regional officials have told The Associated Press that Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and instead has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt for air defense support.
Meanwhile, fighting has surged inside Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government. The rebels raced down the country's Red Sea coast over a week ago, seizing the key port city of Mokha and islands on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
That has improved their surveillance of passing ships, though the Houthis have said they are only targeting Saudi ones.
The fighting in Yemen also marks a return to a devastating civil war after four years of relative calm.
