Iran’s fishery products export capacities outlined
TEHRAN- The pavilion of Iran at the International Fisheries and Aquaculture Exhibition in St. Petersburg hosted senior Russian officials, and Iran’s aquatic products export capacities were outlined.
According to a Mehr News Agency report, during the ninth International Exhibition of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Related Technologies in St. Petersburg, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev and St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov visited the pavilion of Iran, where they were officially received by Vahid Salehi, Deputy Minister and Head of the country’s Veterinary Organization, and a number of representatives and members of the Iranian delegation.
During the visit, Salehi introduced the capacities of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the production, processing, and export of aquatic products and emphasized the country’s extensive capacities for developing specialized and commercial cooperation with Russia.
Referring to Iran’s position in aquaculture and the diversity of fishery products, the head of the country’s Veterinary Organization outlined production and export capacities and the capabilities of Iranian companies, saying: “With diverse capacities in the aquatic sector, production and processing infrastructure, and the active presence of the private sector, Iran is ready to expand its cooperation with Russia in this field.”
Emphasizing the importance of complying with health and quality requirements in the trade of aquatic products, Salehi stated: “Compliance with the health and quality principles and standards of destination countries, especially the member states of the Eurasian Economic and Customs Union, is a fundamental requirement for developing Iran’s aquatic products exports.”
He added: “Iran’s aquatic products exports are carried out based on specialized health requirements and controls, the quarantine regulations of the country’s Veterinary Organization, and the standards agreed upon with destination countries, and strict adherence to these requirements plays an important role in maintaining product health, increasing mutual trust, and sustainable trade development.”
The head of the country’s Veterinary Organization also emphasized the need to facilitate technical interactions, accelerate the exchange of documents, and strengthen communication between the specialized bodies of the two countries, saying: “Developing expert cooperation and creating regular channels for information exchange can strengthen the process of exporting Iran’s aquatic products to the Russian market and other member states of the Eurasian Economic Union.”
Iran’s fishery industry is a vital part of the country’s economy and food security, providing direct employment for approximately 285,000 to 300,000 people and indirect jobs for one million more.
Strategically leveraging access to the Caspian Sea in the north and the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman in the south, the sector is divided into two categories: capture fisheries and aquaculture, with the latter being the dominant force driving growth.
Production focuses on high-value species, including rainbow trout, common carp, and especially Pacific whiteleg shrimp.
As a major pillar of the non-oil economy, fishery exports reached over $700 million in 2025, with key markets including China, Iraq, and the UAE. Looking ahead, Iran aims to increase total fishery production to 1.8 million tons by 2030, with the goal of raising exports to $1.0 billion annually.
Iran's fish farming sector, a vital part of its non-oil economy, primarily produces rainbow trout, common carp, and whiteleg shrimp. Production is geographically distinct: cold-water trout farms are concentrated in provinces along the Alborz and Zagros Mountains, while shrimp farming is focused in the southern coastal provinces of Bushehr, Hormozgan, and Sistan-Baluchestan. In 2025, the sector saw significant growth, with shrimp production alone reaching 50,000 tons. This robust aquaculture sector is a key driver for exports, job creation, and regional economic development.

UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out

UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out
NEAR MANSOURI, Lebanon – The head of the United Nations peacekeepers in Lebanon said on Sept 19 it is critical to ensure that other UN agencies and Lebanese troops can assume the tasks carried out by the force before it begins withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Major-General Diodato Abagnara of Italy spoke to Reuters in southern Lebanon at a position operated by the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL, which has been monitoring hostilities in southern Lebanon for nearly 50 years.
Since a new war erupted between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah in March, the force has also provided security escorts for humanitarian aid convoys to residents in a small cluster of predominantly Christian southern Lebanese towns now encircled by Israeli troops. Residents in much of the rest of southern Lebanon have been forcibly displaced by Israeli strikes and evacuation orders.
The UN Security Council has ordered UNIFIL to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026, triggering concerns over whether aid deliveries can continue and how the force can transfer its positions to Lebanese troops.
“There are other United Nations entities here in the south, and so what is very important for us (is) to conduct a very smooth transition to different entities, or for the future of a new mission,” Abagnara told Reuters.
He said UNIFIL is already working with the UN’s country team to ensure humanitarian assistance in Israeli-occupied areas and information sharing with the Lebanese Army about “sensitive areas (and) how they can manage this situation”.
Abagnara acknowledged that it could be “very difficult” to hand over some of UNIFIL’s posts to Lebanese troops given that more than half lie within areas now controlled by Israeli troops.
Israel demolishes town near UN post
Diplomats worry UNIFIL’s departure will mean an end to the UN’s “eyes and ears” in southern Lebanon.
Abagnara spoke to Reuters at a position overlooking Mansouri, a town where Israeli forces have been carrying out demolitions since ordering residents to leave in June, despite a ceasefire. Reuters reporters could see excavators in the town knocking down trees and multi-storey homes.
Abagnara described demolitions as “another violation” of UN Security Council resolutions on Lebanon. Israel’s military has said it is destroying Hezbollah infrastructure across southern Lebanon.
As a US-backed plan for Lebanon’s army to disarm Hezbollah and take control of southern Lebanon has stalled, a diplomatic scramble is under way to address the vacuum that will be left by UNIFIL’s withdrawal.
Lebanon wants an extension. Other countries have discussed a new multinational mission, though it remains unclear what kind of mandate it would have.
Abagnara said an extension would be “a great honour” but that without a new Security Council decision, his force would need to stop operating at the end of 2026.
“It’s not a long time,” he said. “The presence of (the) United Nations in the south is very, very essential. And according to me, more now than ever.” REUTERS

New research links specific military branches and officer ranks to elevated ALS risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

New research provides evidence that the risk of developing amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, varies depending on a veteran’s military branch and rank. The findings suggest that those who served in the Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard, as well as military officers, tend to experience higher rates of the disease compared to Army veterans and enlisted personnel. The research was published in Neurology.
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative condition that slowly destroys motor neurons, the nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control voluntary muscle movement. As these cells break down, people gradually lose their ability to walk, speak, eat, and eventually breathe. While genetic factors play a role in who develops ALS, researchers estimate that environmental factors account for a substantial portion of the risk.
Military service is one of the most consistently identified risk factors for the disease. For instance, a 2026 study using the national ALS registry indicated that military veterans not only have a higher risk of developing the disease but also tend to experience a shorter survival time after diagnosis compared to civilians. Despite this established link, scientists still do not know exactly what aspects of military life increase this risk.
The United States military is composed of different branches, each with distinct environments, missions, and occupational hazards. By looking at how ALS rates differ across these branches and ranks, scientists can begin to pinpoint the specific exposures, such as chemical solvents, intense physical exertion, or psychological stress, that might be driving the increased risk. The research was conducted by Andrea L. Roberts, Marc Weisskopf, and their colleagues at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, who aimed to investigate these differences using an exceptionally large dataset of veteran health records.
“We have known for some 20 years that military veterans are at increased risk for ALS compared to non-veterans, but we still don’t understand why,” Weisskopf, a professor of environmental epidemiology and physiology, told PsyPost. “This work was a first step in trying to better understand that by seeing if there are differences in risk between different types of veterans. This kind of thing can help us start to narrow down to what specific things about military service might be increasing ALS risk.”
The researchers analyzed electronic health records from the Veterans Health Administration, focusing on veterans who received care between January 2000 and October 2024. To ensure they were looking at new cases of ALS, they only included veterans who had at least two years of medical history with the hospital system before any ALS diagnosis. The final sample was massive, including over 9.1 million men and nearly 785,000 women. Within this group, the researchers identified 13,935 men and 484 women who developed ALS.
The team categorized the veterans by their branch of service (Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, or multiple branches), their rank (enlisted or officer), and the length of their military careers. The researchers then used statistical models to compare the rates of new ALS cases across these groups, adjusting for factors like age, racial identity, and Hispanic ethnicity. Men and women were analyzed separately because military jobs and the resulting environmental exposures often differ by sex.
The results indicated distinct patterns depending on the branch of service. Among men, Army veterans were used as the baseline comparison group. Compared to the Army, men who served in the Air Force had a 29% higher rate of developing ALS. Navy veterans showed a 15% higher rate, and Coast Guard veterans had a 26% higher rate. On the other hand, men who served in the Marine Corps had a 22% lower rate of ALS compared to Army veterans.
“The lower rate among the Marines was not so much a surprise in that it had been seen in many studies before, but those all had few Marines,” Weisskopf explained. “So seeing it in this much larger population really confirmed that finding and left that as a bit of a puzzle as to why they seem to be at lower risk.”
When looking at rank, the researchers found that officers experienced higher rates of ALS than enlisted personnel. Male officers had a 64% higher rate of ALS than male enlisted personnel. For women, a similar pattern emerged, with female officers showing a 72% higher rate of ALS than their enlisted counterparts. Differences between branches were most pronounced among younger veterans, those ages 17 to 61, and tended to shrink in the oldest age groups.
“The higher rate among officers was a bit of a surprise,” Weisskopf noted. “Because there are differences in ALS by branch and rank, it suggests that there is likely something specific to military experience. Given the higher risk among those in the Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard, and officers we are considering how to probe those groups more specifically now.”
Despite these relative increases across certain branches and ranks, the researchers emphasized that the absolute risk to any individual remains low. “It’s important to realize that ALS is still relatively rare. So any single person’s overall risk is small, even if elevated because of military service,” Weisskopf said. “Nonetheless, it is hugely impactful for those who get it, so we want to figure out why some people get it and some don’t so we can both try and prevent occurrences and also better understanding how it develops can give us insight into possible therapeutic avenues.”
Surprisingly, the study found that a longer length of military service was associated with lower rates of ALS. This runs contrary to the idea that more time in the military means more exposure to risk factors. The authors suggest a few possible explanations for this pattern. Jobs with high exposure to risk factors might simply be associated with shorter service commitments.
Alternatively, veterans who serve longer might be more likely to seek treatment at private civilian clinics rather than veteran hospitals after retirement, meaning their ALS diagnoses would not appear in this dataset. The higher rates among Air Force, Navy, and Coast Guard veterans suggest that specific occupational hazards in those branches, such as exposure to jet fuel, aircraft exhaust, or radiation, might play a role in developing the disease. The higher risk for officers is also a point of interest, as enlisted personnel generally face more physical strain and chemical exposure.
Officers often experience different stressors and tend to have higher levels of education. Some previous studies have indicated that people with higher education are more likely to be diagnosed with ALS, which might partly explain the difference. If the risk is tied to unique features of an officer’s environment, identifying those factors could help protect future service members.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Veterans generally qualify for veteran healthcare based on service-related disabilities or specific environmental exposures. If the same exposures that increase the risk of ALS also make someone more likely to use this healthcare system, this could skew the results. To limit this issue, the researchers required all participants to have been in the health system for years before their diagnosis.
Weisskopf also highlighted a specific caveat regarding the findings for the Marine Corps. “Maybe that lower rate among Marines may not necessarily mean they are truly at lower risk,” he pointed out. “There are epidemiological reasons why we might see that if in fact they are at higher risk but that higher risk happens sooner after their military service. This is just speculation at the moment, but we are trying to see if we can address that question.”
The study also faced missing data, with rank information unavailable for over 900,000 male veterans. Because ALS is a rare disease and women make up a smaller percentage of the veteran population, the small number of cases among women made it difficult for the researchers to draw firm conclusions about branch differences for female veterans, as many comparisons did not reach statistical significance. The researchers also lacked genetic data, though they noted it is unlikely that genetic differences alone could explain the specific patterns seen across branches and ranks.
Moving forward, the research team hopes to identify the exact occupational hazards involved. “We are trying to get more granular on the military experience than just branch and rank,” Weisskopf said. “It has turned out, though, to be much harder than we thought to link military service data (DOD) with post service health data (VA).”
The study, “Association of Military Branch and Rank With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Incidence Among United States Veterans,” was authored by Andrea L. Roberts, Alexandre D. Vilela Braga, Ian W. Tang, Ran S. Rotem, Lauren R. Moo, Donald R. Miller, Steven D. Shirk, and Marc G. Weisskopf.

US, China trade teams set to huddle in New York on tariffs, AI and Iran
- The US and China will hold talks in New York on Sept 20 to discuss trade, AI, Iran, and maintain stability ahead of a leaders' summit on Sept 24 in Washington.
- Key issues include tariffs, rare earth exports, AI development, and energy disruptions from the Iran conflict, with both sides seeking to avoid escalating tensions.
- The US Treasury is pressing China on Iran sanctions, while China prioritises Taiwan concerns; AI and trade remain contentious but cooperation is sought to manage risks.
AI generated
NEW YORK – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng will lead talks on trade and other pressure points on Sept 20 in New York, ahead of next week’s summit between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.
The negotiators will lay the groundwork for a high-profile meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping later in Washington.
Bessent and He last met face-to-face near Seoul four months ago, just days before Trump visited Beijing in May.
Energy disruptions from the Iran war, the artificial intelligence boom, and trade and investment are likely to top the agenda, as both sides work to maintain stability in a tariff truce that expires in November.
Adding urgency for US officials to extend the deal are the Nov 3 midterm elections where inflation is a persistent voter concern.
The US is “at a stage with China where efforts to try and transform this relationship and strengthen it are no longer top of list”, said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
The objective is more about “trying to keep things stable, keep things from escalating and try to, in practical terms, keep the trade truce that was reached in Busan in place”, she said.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will also attend talks, according to a statement from his office.
“The Trump administration will continue to pursue balanced trade with China by monitoring the implementation of recent commitments, optimising trade in non-sensitive goods, and improving market access for American farmers, manufacturers and workers,” he said in the statement on Sept 18.
An announcement of new US tariffs over allegations of trading partners’ excess manufacturing capacity has been delayed until after the meeting, according to people familiar with the matter.
“Both sides want to avoid another flare-up, and relative stability in the relationship is likely to continue,” Nicole Gorton-Caratelli, Adam Farrar and Maeva Cousin of Bloomberg Economics wrote in a research note this week. “But as the US rebuilds its tariff wall, the risk of renewed escalation remains.”
The US and China have been working to reduce levies on American energy and agricultural products, Bloomberg reported earlier, part of a broader initiative to ease barriers on US$30 billion (S$38 billion) worth of products from each side under the Board of Trade mechanism launched earlier in 2026.
Export rebound
Chinese exports to the US have rebounded in 2026, showing the limits of Trump’s tariffs but also reflecting a surge in demand for AI-related electronics produced by China.
The New York talks are taking place ahead of the UN General Assembly meeting held in the city from Sept 22.
Bessent and He have held a series of discussions over the past 18 months, mostly in a third country to portray a sense of neutrality. Whether the meeting in New York signals greater trust or merely convenience given the UN meeting, it also suggests the next round will be in China for the sake of reciprocity.
Bloomberg has reported that Chinese officials were considering BYD for a possible business delegation joining Xi at the summit, a potentially provocative move given Trump’s tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles.
Trump has suggested he might be willing to allow a Chinese car company to build in the US, if it did so with American workers.
One Chinese official familiar with planning for the meeting said China’s top issue would be Taiwan, particularly a planned US weapons sale.
Easier discussions will be held around tariffs and agricultural products like soya beans, while AI, cars, technology and e-commerce will feature on the agenda, said the official, who asked for anonymity to discuss private conversations.
The official added that China would offer more permits for rare earths as a bargaining chip, without giving details on what Beijing would seek in return.
Maintaining flows of Chinese rare-earth magnets was a priority for Trump when he agreed to a truce in 2025. Since then, China’s monthly exports of the critical industrial components have been running substantially below the levels that prevailed before Beijing imposed export controls in April 2025.
In recent weeks, AI has rapidly emerged as a new fault line between the US and China.
‘Fearmongering’
Washington has restricted China’s access to advanced chips and accused Chinese firms of developing their own domestic models by “distilling” capabilities from American tech.
Beijing has pushed back on calls from US tech leaders to pace AI development in the interest of safety, with its Foreign Ministry dismissing such moves as “fearmongering” and state media denouncing them as “self-serving”.
“As the No. 1 and No. 2 superpowers in AI by a lot, it behoves all of us to put up guardrails, to have close communication,” Bessent told reporters earlier in September.
In a statement to Axios this week, he said “we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems”.
The US moves, Beijing says, are designed to contain its rise, and China refuses to let Washington take the lead on writing the rules for AI.
A more immediate threat to both economies is the energy shock, and the White House has stepped up pressure on Iran and its trading partners. China provides Tehran with an economic lifeline as the biggest buyer of Iranian oil.
Boosting sanctions
The US Treasury Department is ratcheting up pressure on financial institutions as part of its effort to choke off trade and financial flows between Iran and the rest of the world, fuelling speculation that Chinese banks could be targeted.
Bessent said during testimony to the House financial services committee earlier this week that he has had “private discussions” with Chinese officials on the issue and hopes to make further progress during the upcoming talks this weekend.
A US naval blockade has sharply curtailed crude oil flows to China, raising the prospect of refinery run cuts in the coming weeks across the teapot sector, which makes up one-third of national refining capacity.
“China has an interest in reopening Hormuz, but limited leverage to force either side to change course,” said Jesse Marks, founder of Rihla Research & Advisory and former Middle East policy adviser in the US government. “The longer the strait remains closed, the more US sanctions and the wider disruption to regional trade will begin to cut into China’s own economic interests in Iran.” BLOOMBERG

'I am pro-Abraham': Meet the unlikely allies risking everything for peace with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:33 UTC
22:49:33 KST

In much of the West, asking someone about the weather is about as inconsequential as small talk gets. In parts of the Middle East, however, even a conversation about the weather with someone across the border can cross a legal line. In countries where contact with Israelis is criminalized or restricted, a seemingly harmless exchange can carry the risk of imprisonment or execution.
The Abrahamic Movement was founded on the idea that these communication barriers can be challenged. Bringing together Israelis and people from across the Muslim world, the movement seeks to build relationships across religious and national divides, drawing on their shared Abrahamic heritage.
With artificial intelligence and international travel more accessible than ever, forms of diplomacy once largely reserved for governments and the wealthy are increasingly within reach of ordinary people, which is perhaps why the movement has grown so rapidly in recent years.
The Jerusalem Post spoke with Tom Wegner, CEO of the Abrahamic Movement initiative and author of The Abrahamic Revolution, as well as several members of the group, some of whom risked their freedom and potentially their lives by speaking with an Israeli journalist about their desire for peace.
Wegner originally started the group in 2019, though it did not gain momentum until after October 7, 2023, when 1,200 people were killed by Islamists.
Wegner realized that something had to change and reached out to the diverse contacts he had built over years of working in the IDF’s District Coordination and Liaison unit in Jericho, where he facilitated coordination between Israel and the Palestinian Authority’s police; as a spokesperson for former prime minister Ehud Barak; and as a spokesperson for the Peres Center for Peace.
Telling them that “the regional configuration is not working for us,” Wegner explained that the region’s destabilization had been apparent long before Hamas’s invasion. The massacre of the Yazidis, the civil wars in Yemen and Iraq, and the conflicts that followed were all evidence that something was not working compared to the seemingly functional Western world.
Shared Abrahamic identity
Though Europe seems peaceful compared with the often volatile Middle East, Wegner highlighted that the West has not always enjoyed such stability. Before the formation of the European Union, Europe experienced civil uprisings, invasions, and two world wars, resulting in hundreds of millions of deaths.
Wegner attributed much of that shift toward peaceful coexistence to the development of a European collective identity. That identity “wasn’t coerced on the people. It is not about oppressing someone to fit your narrative, but of creating an umbrella identity, which means that the French can continue to eat frogs and the Greeks can continue to break plates. The Protestants can remain Protestants, and the Catholics can remain Catholic, but everyone is part of a bigger story,” he explained.
The Abrahamic Movement seeks to create that same sense of collective identity in the Middle East, based on a shared Abrahamic heritage.
“The world has missed, to some extent, that 100% of the people involved in this conflict – whether a secular Jew, an Orthodox Jew, a very religious Muslim, a liberal Muslim, an ex-Muslim, a Christian Arab, a Druze, or an Alawite – agree on the Abrahamic narrative. Meaning, we all agree that we came from Abraham,” he said.
This shared heritage, he added, means it is important to view the conflicts as fighting among cousins and families rather than through the Western-centric lens of occupiers and colonists.
The idea that conflicts can be solved simply by drawing lines on maps, Wegner said, is too Western, too managerial, and too simplistic to address conflicts rooted in identity. Rather, he argued, the solution lies in creating a broader “in-group,” limiting the conflict that can arise from in-group and out-group social dynamics.
The Muslim Brotherhood’s opposition
Whether it is soccer hooligans in the UK, gangs in the United States, or ethnic groups in the Middle East, the same in-group versus out-group dynamic can contribute to conflict, with people defining themselves in opposition to those they see as belonging to another group, Wegner argued.
The concept is well established in social psychology, with research showing that in-group identification can contribute to out-group prejudice, stereotyping, and discrimination, creating conditions that can deepen hostility between groups.
Beyond creating a shared in-group identity, it is also imperative to create an identity that is oppositional to the Muslim Brotherhood and its Shia alternatives, like Hezbollah, Wegner insisted.
The Islamist identities are currently all-consuming, he said. The Muslim Brotherhood and Shia groups such as Hezbollah have no mainstream counter-ideology for the average individual living in a Muslim country and are therefore more effective in their recruitment.
The all-encompassing Islamist movements and their various branches provide thought leaders, media, education, healthcare, employment opportunities, social circles, community, and everything an individual could ever need. Wegner explained that all these factors can draw people toward an extreme ideology when no opposing ideology balances it out.
The idea of “Abrahamic Islam,” true to the Quran in its acknowledgment that the Children of Israel will return to the promised land (Surah Al-Isra, 17:104), “enables Muslims to remain loyal to their original religion,” he said, adding that this new ideological approach could be the driving force in finally ending Israel’s wars against extremist groups.
“Losing your honor in this part of the world is worse than losing your life. When it comes to Arab and Muslim society, you’re better off losing your life than losing your honor,” he said, highlighting that Hezbollah, Hamas, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and every other enemy of Israel face the choice to die in battle as a martyr or sacrifice their honor by surrendering to Israel.
“If we understand that killing all the radicals is not a very good or solid plan, then we should ask ourselves what the way out is. And over here, the Abrahamic Movement represents a way out for many reasons.... It implies that this is common ground, and when you come to common ground, that’s not surrendering,” he said. “That’s an identity that both of us can live with, without losing our honor.”
‘The Quran: A Zionist document’
Wegner believes that Jews “missed the Quran,” overlooking the wisdom it could offer and its potential to help Zionists communicate with people in the region in terms they can understand and accept.
Familiarity with the Islamic holy text, he said, has allowed him to win heated debates with Islamist scholars and bring large numbers of people closer to accepting the humanity of Zionists and their place in the region.
“The Quran is a Zionist document,” he claimed, recounting how heated debates often cool when he can cite Quranic verses in support of his position.
Though many seek to counter Islamists by relying on passages they believe undermine Islamic teachings, including frequently citing the Prophet Muhammad’s marriage to Aisha bint Abi Bakr, such arguments will never be fruitful and are no way to conduct diplomacy, he argued.
Instead, he pointed to the Quran’s numerous references to the Children of Israel, or the Jewish people, as a basis for engaging with Muslims on terms rooted in a text they recognize as authoritative.
In Surah Al-Ma’idah (5:21), Moses tells the Children of Israel to enter the holy land that God prescribed for them. In Surah Al-Isra (17:104), the Quran instructs the Children of Israel to live in the land until the end of days, while Surah Yunus (10:93) states that God settled the Children of Israel in a blessed place and provided them with good provisions.
“If we really want to speak with the Muslim world and create some sort of dialogue, the whole approach of saying ‘Muhammad was a pedophile,’ or all that jazz that basically tries to contradict Islam at face value, is not relevant. It’s not helping anyone,” he insisted. “It’s only creating more animosity and tension.
“We can probably get better results if we speak to our cousins the way cousins speak to each other, focusing on our shared heritage and the things that are common to us.”
Peace in the Middle East is often painted as a pipe dream, and many might call Wegner idealistic for his ambitions. But the Abrahamic Movement has gained tens of thousands of supporters and now has more than 20 branches across the Muslim world – including in countries that criminalize communication with Israelis – thanks solely to the efforts of volunteers and without funding.
Several members readily volunteered to speak with the Post about why they were so invested in peace despite the potential cost. One Pakistani member, in particular, insisted he did not want to speak anonymously, despite concerns about potential risks to his safety.
‘I am not pro-Israel; I am pro-Abraham’
Khurram Ali Raza, chairman of the movement’s Pakistan branch, insisted that the Post use his name despite repeated warnings that doing so could put him in danger.
While Pakistan does not have a specific law criminalizing contact with Israeli citizens, Islamabad does not recognize Israel, and Pakistani passports explicitly state that they are valid for travel everywhere except the Jewish state.
In a country where people are still lynched for accusations of blasphemy, Raza remained confident about his safety, despite acknowledging that his advocacy for normalization with Israel had already cost him a great deal.
Sharing several articles he had written for his website, Faith and Freedom News, about his desire for peace, Raza said he had already been investigated by Pakistani authorities, who initially appeared to suspect that he was working for Israel. He said the unfounded suspicions led to his imprisonment for four months in a jail where he said the conditions were “hell.”
“Somehow, I made them understand that I am doing this for peace, harmony and tolerance among these three religions, not for intelligence agencies or anything else,” he said. “I am not pro-Israel; I am pro-Abraham, and if you are pro-Abraham, the first religion is Judaism.... We are like brothers. We are from one family and one home.”
The conditions of Raza’s four-month detention, spent in a cramped room without a fan or light, have continued to affect him, but they have not deterred him from carrying out his work with the movement as openly as he can.
Despite being free, Raza said, it is impossible to access his website in Pakistan without a VPN, suggesting an unofficial block on his publications to prevent the masses from accessing them.
In his personal life, close relatives have also urged him to keep his distance, fearing that his work could have consequences for the wider family.
The lack of education in Pakistan, Raza argued, has led to many accepting without critical thought what they have been told about Jews and acting with hostility to those seen as part of an out-group.
According to Pakistan’s Education Ministry, the country’s current literacy rate stands at only 62.3%, meaning an estimated 60 million people remain illiterate.
Asked why, given all that he has suffered, he would continue to speak out in favor of a country he has never visited, Raza said that one day he will stand before God and answer for everything he has done in his life, and that he would be proud to answer for his efforts to promote peace and tolerance.
‘Iraq can benefit from establishing peace relations’
In May 2022, the Iraqi parliament passed the “Criminalizing Normalization and Establishment of Relations with the Zionist Entity” law, with 275 of 329 lawmakers voting in favor. The law imposes severe penalties, including life imprisonment or the death penalty, for a range of activities involving normalization or relations with Israel or Israelis.
Under Article 7, promoting Zionist or Masonic ideas, whether through public speeches, conferences, publications, or social media posts, is punishable by death or life imprisonment.
In July 2025, the Karkh Criminal Court in Baghdad sentenced a man to life imprisonment for promoting the “Zionist entity” on social media. According to Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, he had posted photos and videos supporting normalization with Israel, while Hebrew-language books and newspapers were seized from his home.
Despite the apparent risks of holding such views, speaking with the Post, and participating in the Abrahamic Movement, the Sunni scholar Abu Musa Al-Iraqi said he believes it is in Iraq’s interest to normalize ties with Israel.
“Iraq can benefit from establishing peace relations to prevent extremism and ideological and cultural terrorism from taking root among religious extremists, as well as to end this unjustified conflict,” Al-Iraqi, who used his alias, told the Post. “We can send messages of peace to future generations of Jews and Muslims. We do not want to pass this hostility on to them, but, rather, establish social and economic relations and communication to develop the land and reject the divisions created by extremists for narrow personal interests.”
Working closely with Iraq’s Sunni and Sufi communities, Al-Iraqi has had opportunities to study Islamic and Abrahamic texts. Through this research, he said, he came to understand that the conflict between Jews and Muslims “is not a genuine one.”
“Islam respects Judaism, but some Quranic texts and their meanings have been distorted and interpreted outside the context in which they were formulated, and misrepresented by those who are ideologically corrupted and do not want there to be a relationship or communication between Judaism and Islam, for purely political purposes,” he explained, adding that he understands Islam to be an extension of Judaism.
Though his research may have provided a clearer understanding of Islam, it was not well received in Iraq. Many newspaper articles Al-Iraqi sent to the Post showed individuals affiliated with the Popular Mobilization Forces, Hizb ut-Tahrir, and other Islamist groups complaining about an “Israeli influence network within Iraqi territory.”
Hizb ut-Tahrir even published a statement in June complaining of the “increasingly active” Abrahamic Movement’s presence in Iraq, saying it is largely viewed “as an extension of normalization with Israel.”
Except for Wegner himself, none of the Abrahamic Movement’s members or leaders interviewed by the Post have had the opportunity to visit Israel.
The movement faces no shortage of obstacles, from laws restricting contact with Israelis to Islamist groups that have openly opposed its activities.
There is no guarantee that personal relationships will translate into political change, or that large numbers of people will embrace the concept of Abrahamic Islam.
Still, movement members continue to risk their freedom, safety, and livelihoods in the hope of ending a conflict that predates the establishment of the Jewish state and, for many, living memory.

Mike Huckabee on Iran, Hezbollah, Saudi Arabia and Israel’s US relationship - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:25 UTC
22:49:25 KST

For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee is not a conventional diplomat. A Baptist pastor, former Arkansas governor, presidential candidate, and television host, he came to the post after decades in American public life and an even longer relationship with Israel.
He also came with a style of his own. Huckabee can move from geopolitics to Scripture to a homespun analogy without much warning. He is direct, sometimes blunt, and rarely sounds as though his words have made a preliminary stop at the State Department diplomatic-language desk.
When Huckabee joined me at The Media Line studios, I began with Iran. Despite the damage inflicted on Tehran and its military capabilities, Iran could still move toward nuclear capability, threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, and exert influence in the Red Sea through the Houthis. There are also concerns about what the Houthis might do next against Saudi Arabia.
Huckabee's thoughts on Iran
Where, I asked, does Huckabee think Iran and its regional proxies stand today?
“The good news is, thanks to President Trump, in concert with Israel, Iran is at their weakest point in 47 and a half years,” Huckabee said. “They’re weaker militarily, they’re weaker economically, and they’re growing weaker by the month.”
Whether that weakness eventually produces regime change is another question.
“Will it lead to regime change? We can only hope,” he said.
Huckabee rejected the idea that confronting Iran is chiefly Israel’s problem.
“A lot of people, particularly in America, may think, well, what does that have to do with us? It has everything to do with America, because the ultimate target has always been the United States.”
President Donald Trump said he had decided that Iran could not be allowed to possess nuclear weapons, enrich uranium, or control shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz.
“It’s a process, but it is a process that I believe is working.”
What about the Iranian people? I asked where they stood now and whether another popular uprising was possible.
Huckabee said Iranians seeking to challenge their government face a basic problem: They are largely unarmed.
“At some point, I do believe we’re going to see another uprising,” he said, adding that perhaps next time the people could be “better prepared, armed, and be able to truly resist” a government he expects to be weaker still.
Lebanon presents Washington with another problem. With UNIFIL preparing to leave, the question is whether the Lebanese Armed Forces can extend state authority into the south, prevent a security vacuum, and confront Hezbollah at the same time.
Huckabee believes it can, but not overnight.
“Incrementally, they can. I don’t think it’s going to be the flip of a switch,” he said. “They’re going to have to grow into the role of being the only army, the only security force.”
Hezbollah, he noted, remains active and is trying to rebuild after being badly weakened by Israel. As long as Iran can continue financing and arming it, Huckabee said, Hezbollah will remain a threat.
Huckabee says he has considerably less patience with UNIFIL
“UNIFIL is going to go out of business—way overdue for that to happen,” he said. “It’s been a totally ineffective entity.”
“I can’t say that I can point to one specific way in which UNIFIL has been instrumental in making Lebanon freer and better.”
When I pressed him on the timetable months or years? he answered, “It could be years.”
But Huckabee said his experience traveling between Jerusalem and Washington during talks over Lebanon had shown him “extraordinary progress.” One of the most important developments, in his view, was Lebanese recognition that Israel does not want Lebanese territory.
“They don’t want to annex one meter of Lebanese property. They don’t want to be there. They want to go home,” he said.
Israeli reservists, he said, are exhausted and want to return to their families, but Israel will not leave its northern communities exposed to renewed rocket, missile and drone attacks.
Huckabee said he longs for the day when the Lebanese army is strong enough to secure the area itself: “The Israelis can go home, the Lebanese will be at home, and there will be no Hezbollah.”
We also spoke about the new joint defense agreement involving Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, which pledges to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all. With three important US partners building their own collective security framework, I asked whether Washington sees that as a welcome development and what it means for the wider regional balance.
“It’s a wait and see,” Huckabee said.
These are sovereign countries entitled to make agreements they believe serve their interests, he said. All three have reasons to be concerned about Iran, while the arrangement could also be intended to protect them from the Houthis or other armed groups.
What he had not encountered was alarm in Washington.
“I never certainly saw or heard any anxiety in Washington that, ‘Oh my gosh, this is a terrible thing.’ I don’t think that anyone saw it that way.”
Would Israel help Saudi Arabia if the kingdom came under attack?
“I don’t know. I mean, that’s the honest answer. I don’t know.”
Huckabee said Israel would welcome a security agreement with Saudi Arabia and would like to see the kingdom join the Abraham Accords. He also pointed to existing military and intelligence contacts.
For what normalization can achieve, he looks to the United Arab Emirates.
“The UAE is the gold standard, the model of how this has all worked,” he said, pointing to gains in tourism, travel, trade and technological cooperation.
“I hope the Saudis will look next door and say, you know, this is working out pretty well for the Emirates. Maybe we ought to go the same path.”
Few issues are more closely associated with Huckabee than the territory Israelis generally call the West Bank and much of the international community calls the West Bank. He has strongly defended Israelis who live there, but he has also condemned recent attacks on Palestinians and described those responsible as terrorists.
Is Israel doing enough to stop terrorists
“Israel is increasingly aware that this has to be dealt with and dealt with in a very strong way,” Huckabee said.
He did not back away from his choice of the word terrorism.
“When you frighten people into changing the way they live because of things that you do to them, you don’t have to murder them, but you do terrorize them into being afraid to come out of their homes, being afraid to go shopping, being afraid to go to a place of worship,” he said. “So it’s unacceptable, whoever does it.”
At the same time, Huckabee stressed that those responsible represent a very small fraction of the Israeli population in the territory. He called them a “tiny, tiny sliver” and said many do not even live there.
“There are 500,000 Israelis living in Judean Samaria, living peacefully,” he said. “They don’t want to burn an olive tree. They don’t want to torch a mosque.”
I asked what more Israel should be doing.
Investigations and arrests need to be followed by real penalties, Huckabee said, particularly for offenses such as burning mosques, stealing livestock or taking over someone’s home.
“They need to be arrested,” he said of repeat offenders. “They need to spend a few nights, a few weeks, maybe a few months in jail.”
Huckabee confronts Tucker Carlson, antisemitism in American politics
Our conversation then moved to a different source of friction over Israel: the changing American political debate.
Huckabee recently encountered Tucker Carlson at Ben-Gurion Airport and challenged several of Carlson’s assertions about Israel. Carlson has since argued that Israel is driving the war with Iran for its own regional interests while US interests are being sacrificed.
I asked Huckabee whether similar arguments about Israel are now converging from opposite ends of the American political spectrum—and how worried he is about the long-term implications for the US-Israel relationship.
“I’m very concerned about it because it’s based on things that are fundamentally not true,” he said. “Tucker Carlson’s allegations about Israel are off the mark.”
Huckabee also rejected accusations of genocide and apartheid and claims that Israel is unsafe or unfair for Christians.
“As a Christian living in Israel, I find that utterly offensive and totally factless,” he said.
He has known Carlson for years and said he does not understand what has changed.
“This is not the same person I once knew and once worked with,” Huckabee said.
With the US midterm elections approaching, I asked whether events in the Middle East would have much effect on American voters.
Probably less than domestic issues, Huckabee said. He then turned to the Democratic Socialists of America and what he sees as the radicalization of part of the American left. He cited liberal commentator Bill Maher as an example of someone who has also criticized that movement.
“The Democrats historically, they’ve been different than the Republicans, but they haven’t been crazy,” Huckabee said.
He was equally unsparing about calls for socialism, saying replacing the American economic system with one that he believes has repeatedly failed is more than a conventional political disagreement.
Another subject has become impossible for anyone in the news business to avoid: artificial intelligence.
Huckabee warns about the dangers of AI
At The Media Line, we spend considerable time sourcing, vetting, and explaining information. That becomes more complicated as AI makes fabricated images, voices, and claims easier to produce and harder to detect. Technology leaders themselves have warned about the potential consequences.
What did Huckabee make of it?
“AI is like fire,” he said. “It can cook your food and warm your house. It can burn your house down and kill you.”
“How do you use it? That’s the question.”
For Huckabee, the danger is not theoretical. He pointed to his own long-running lawsuit against Meta, which he said stems from AI-generated material that damaged him professionally when he was hosting a television program in the United States.
“I saw firsthand what AI can do in creating perceptions, images, the misuse, the abuse of one’s name, image, and likeness,” he said. “And it has to be brought into some level of responsibility.”
Does that mean government regulation?
Huckabee is wary.
“I’m always hesitant to say I’d like to see the government get involved because the government usually messes up whatever they touch,” he said.
One possibility, he suggested, would be for the major AI companies themselves to establish ethical norms, much as other professions have developed standards without having every rule imposed by government.
“There was a sense of self-governing, self-regulation,” Huckabee said. “Maybe that’s the answer.”
Huckabee speaks on upcoming anniversary of Oct. 7
With the anniversary of Oct. 7 approaching, more than 1,000 pastors are expected to come to Israel for events organized by Christian and Jewish groups. Antisemitism, meanwhile, has risen rather than receded.
Can visits like these make a difference?
Huckabee hopes they can remind people of the scale of what happened on Oct. 7.
He translated the attack into American terms, asking his audience to imagine an assault from Tijuana into San Diego that, adjusted for population, left 40,000 Americans dead in one day and another 10,000 taken hostage.
“Ask ourselves as Americans, what would we do? How would we respond?”
He also invoked Sept. 11, 2001, and the lasting changes it brought to American life after the deaths of nearly 3,000 people.
“Twenty-five years later, our whole world changed in the United States because of that,” he said. “Scale that up 10 times plus, and it’s hard to even fathom what the response would be.”
I saved a different kind of question for last.
Huckabee is a Baptist pastor who spent more than a decade in the governor’s office and now serves as America’s ambassador to Israel. He has lived in the worlds of faith, politics, and diplomacy—three places where people can look at the same set of facts and come away insisting on very different versions of reality.
Is truth actually attainable? And how do you know when you have found it?
“Truth is objective. Perceptions are subjective,” Huckabee said.
Three people can stand on a street corner, witness an accident, and each see something different, he said. Their perceptions may differ, but that does not change what actually happened.
“The truth is not what I think. It’s not what I feel. It’s not what I believe. It’s what is.”
That, Huckabee said, is something younger people in particular need to learn in an age when opinion and fact are increasingly difficult to separate.
“What we have to do, especially among younger people, is to force people to move beyond what I think, what I feel, what I believe, and get to what is the absolute concrete fact upon which then I can feel, believe, and think.”
He left it there.
“Without objective truth that from any angle looks the same, we are in real trouble.”

US approves possible F-35 Saudi deal despite Israeli push to link normalization, sale - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:22 UTC
22:49:22 KST

The US State Department’s announcement on Thursday that it is advancing the sale of 48 F-35 aircraft to Saudi Arabia represents far more than a massive arms deal worth $24.3 billion. For Israel, it highlights a concerning diplomatic shift: one of Washington’s most valuable security leverage tools with Riyadh is now moving forward on its own track, without Saudi Arabia first being required to normalize relations with Israel.
The State Department approved the possible sale of 48 F-35A Lightning II aircraft, alongside 49 Pratt & Whitney F135 engines, communications and encryption systems, electronic warfare capabilities, simulators, training, spare parts and logistical support.
The move does not yet constitute a final contract. The announcement is a stage in the US arms sale process, and a legally required review period in Congress has now begun. In Saudi Arabia’s case, the official review period is 30 days.
The administration is presenting the deal as part of efforts to strengthen Saudi Arabia’s ability to confront current and future threats and deepen its joint operational capabilities with the United States and regional partners. The official announcement explicitly stated that the deal “will not alter the military balance in the region.”
In the United States, Israel’s qualitative military edge is enshrined in law. The statement touches on the core of Israel’s concern: Israel is currently the only country in the Middle East operating the F-35, in its Israeli configuration, the F-35I “Adir.”
US law requires the administration to ensure that arms sales to other countries in the region do not harm Israel’s “Qualitative Military Edge,” meaning its qualitative military advantage. The requirement was codified in legislation in 2008 and requires significant regional arms deals to be examined through the Israeli security lens as well.
The political price Israel sought for the F-35 deal
The Trump administration approved the sale of advanced F-35 aircraft to Saudi Arabia. Israel sought a diplomatic price.
However, Jerusalem’s concern is not only technical or related to air capabilities. In November 2025, Israeli officials said that Israel did not fundamentally oppose Saudi Arabia receiving F-35 aircraft, provided the deal was part of full normalization between Riyadh and Jerusalem.
“We told the Trump administration that supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia should be contingent on Saudi normalization with Israel,” an Israeli official said at the time.
Another Israeli official warned that providing the aircraft to Riyadh without receiving diplomatic concessions would be a “mistake” and a move that would work against US interests.
That link did not materialize. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said during his visit to the White House last year that he was interested in Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, but conditioned progress on the creation of a “clear path” toward a two-state solution.
The gap between Riyadh and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government on the Palestinian issue has remained. Despite that, the F-35 track continued to advance.
This is the central difference between the deal Israel hoped to see and the deal as it currently appears: Jerusalem wanted the stealth aircraft as part of a broader regional strategic package centered on normalization. Washington, at least at this stage, is not waiting for such an agreement before moving ahead.
China concerns surrounding the Saudi F-35 sale
Jonathan Ruhe, a specialist in US strategy at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA), told Walla that in his view, the F-35 deal should not move forward in its current form before two central issues are resolved.
The concern is not merely theoretical. The New York Times reported two days ago that US intelligence officials warned in internal assessments that China could obtain F-35-related technology through espionage in Saudi Arabia or through its security and technology ties with the kingdom.
One report by the Pentagon’s intelligence agency addressed, among other issues, Chinese access to Saudi bases and Saudi use of Chinese communications infrastructure. Reports on Thursday’s deal also noted that expanding security ties between Riyadh and Beijing are among the concerns surrounding the sale.
Ruhe’s second concern directly relates to Israel.
“The entire F-35 program is intended to support US-led collective defense,” he said. “America needs to demonstrate leadership in integrating Saudi Arabia into a new regional security architecture, and Riyadh also needs to show that it is a committed partner before it can receive F-35 aircraft.”
According to Ruhe, Israel’s qualitative military edge must remain part of the equation.
“Israel’s QME is a central factor in this regional integration, and it needs to be reflected in any possible F-35 deal with the kingdom,” he said.
Ruhe added that the United States has significant leverage in the matter.
“The United States has leverage here, because it can offer Saudi Arabia much more than China can,” he said.
Even if the deal is completed, a significant question remains over the exact capabilities that will be transferred to Riyadh.
The aircraft intended for Saudi Arabia are expected to be less advanced in several areas than Israel’s F-35I aircraft, partly as part of the US effort to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge. Israel also benefits from the ability to integrate unique Israeli systems into its aircraft.
The issue became more complicated after US President Donald Trump publicly said that Saudi Arabia would receive advanced aircraft similar to Israel’s. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reassured Netanyahu and told him that Saudi Arabia would receive a downgraded version and that the United States remained committed to preserving Israel’s qualitative military edge.
Therefore, even after the State Department announcement and assurances regarding reduced capabilities for Saudi Arabia, key details remain undisclosed: which capabilities will be included in the aircraft, what restrictions will be placed on their deployment and access, and what Israel will receive to ensure that its advantage is maintained.
But on the diplomatic level, a significant development has already taken place: the F-35, which Israel wanted to see as part of the price Saudi Arabia would pay for joining the Abraham Accords, is moving toward Riyadh even as normalization itself remains stalled.

Classified F-35 aircraft components disappear after diverted to Hong Kong from Australia - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:49:22 UTC
22:49:22 KST

A shipment of sensitive components for the F-35 stealth fighter jets, which was on its way from Australia to the United States for repairs, was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong and disappeared.
The incident raised concerns that China may gain access to the highly classified technology of sophisticated US weapons, Politico reported Friday.
According to three sources familiar with the details of the case, the shipment left Australia headed for the United States. However, the flight was diverted en route to Hong Kong. It is unclear who currently holds the classified components or whether they are being transferred to Chinese authorities
A broker handled the shipment for Lockheed Martin, the maker of the F-35. The Pentagon confirmed that some of the components were missing. The Defense Department’s F-35 Joint Chiefs of Staff said it was “aware of the issue with the shipment of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components” and that it was working with US authorities and industry partners “to recover the components, investigate the incident, and institute safeguards to prevent a similar incident from occurring again.”
According to two of the sources who spoke to Politico, the shipment included one of the aircraft’s cockpit canopies. The canopy is not just a transparent covering that protects the pilot, but a key component of the F-35’s stealth envelope.
China is trying to obtain more information about US aircraft
It is coated with a thin, transparent layer of radar-absorbing material that helps reduce the aircraft’s signature and hide it from enemy radar systems.
Access to the canopy could allow a rival country to examine its materials and production methods, compare them with information already collected through intelligence means, and even attempt to reverse-engineer the technology.
“It’s no secret that China is aggressively trying to obtain information about the F-35 through electronic espionage and other means. Even if they already had specifications or other information about the component, having a real item can provide them with additional information and verify or refine what they’ve already learned,” said JJ Gertler, former member of the House Armed Services Committee and a military aviation expert at the Congressional Research Service.
The previously undisclosed incident led to a series of briefings for staff members of key national security committees in Congress. Representatives from the State Department and the Pentagon held the first briefing in June, and additional briefings are expected in the coming weeks, according to Politico’s sources.
The transfer of components to Hong Kong is of particular concern in Washington due to China's tightening control over the city in recent years. Chinese national security laws give Beijing authorities extensive influence over what happens in Hong Kong and the ability to access equipment within its borders.
US State Department declined to comment
The Chinese Embassy in Washington said it was unaware of the incident. The US State Department declined to comment. Lockheed Martin said it could not discuss the status of shipments for security reasons, but stressed that it complies with all US regulations for the transfer of aircraft components. “Our teams handle each shipment with the utmost care and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the F-35 program and the security of our allies,” the company said.
The F-35 supply chain is a complex global system that relies on facilities in many countries to manufacture, transport, and repair parts. There are maintenance centers for the aircraft in Australia, but none of them are yet capable of repairing the cockpit canopies. That is why the canopy had to be shipped to the United States.
The countries participating in the program, including the United States, Britain, Australia, Denmark, Norway and Poland, use a shared global pool of spare parts. The components remain the property of the US Department of Defense until they are installed on the aircraft, but it is Lockheed Martin and not the Pentagon who manage information about the parts’ movements.
A 2023 report by the US Office of the Comptroller found that more than a million F-35 spare parts had gone missing in the five years prior to its release. The report said the Pentagon could not verify the loss of parts worth tens of millions of dollars because Lockheed Martin and prime contractors held the relevant information.

Istanbul prosecutors on Sept. 19 have ordered the detention of Pusula Portföy executive Serdar Turhan and Tera executive Alper Öztürk in an investigation into capital market transactions.
Four suspects had previously been remanded in custody in the investigation. Travel bans and asset freezes were also imposed on 51 people.
The latest orders follow regulatory intervention after Pusula and Tera disclosed defaults on payments to investors seeking to redeem their fund holdings.
Atlas Portföy also reported payment delays at a money market fund.
On Sept. 17, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) halted trading in funds run by seven asset managers on TEFAS, Türkiye’s electronic fund trading platform.
A total of 131 funds have been ordered into liquidation.
İşbank was assigned to oversee the liquidation of the affected Tera funds, while Ziraat Bank will handle those of the other six companies.
Cash from asset sales and maturing investments will be distributed in proportion to investors’ holdings, at intervals determined by the banks.
Outstanding payments from unfulfilled TEFAS redemption orders will be settled first.
The SPK set a three-month liquidation period, which it can extend. The affected funds are closed to purchases and redemptions through both TEFAS and other distribution channels.
The Central Bank pledged to increase funding through one-week repo auctions and reduce collateral haircuts. The banking regulator also temporarily eased capital rules for listed banks buying back their own shares.
The Financial Stability Committee described the fund problems as “temporary and manageable” on Sept. 17 and pledged measures to ease the liquidity squeeze and prevent contagion.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said on Sept. 18 that the difficulties were confined to a limited number of funds, with 90 percent of the market functioning normally.
“There is no widespread systemic risk,” he said. “We have quarantined the troubled segment.”

‘Translate this into Hebrew’: Pro-Israel Democrat warns US support for Israel is collapsing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
13:28:55 UTC
22:28:55 KST

One of Israel’s most consistent Democratic supporters in Congress is issuing an unusually stark warning: Israelis, he says, are failing to grasp how sharply American public opinion toward their country has changed.
Rep. Brad Sherman, a California Democrat who has served in the House since 1997, posted a series of messages on X on Friday urging Israeli officials and voters to watch a CNN segment from July detailing a steep decline in Israel’s standing among Americans. Sherman is a longtime member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and has repeatedly identified strengthening the U.S.-Israel relationship as a central part of his work in Congress.
“Every Israeli official and voter should watch this clip, and it needs to be translated into Hebrew,” Sherman wrote. He said he had spoken a day earlier with Israeli Ambassador to Washington Yechiel Leiter and added: “I don’t think he or the majority of Israelis realize what is at stake.”
Sherman argued that the danger goes far beyond the question of annual U.S. aid. If the trend continues, he warned, it could eventually affect Israel’s access to American weapons as well as the diplomatic backing it has received from Washington and other allies.
He also sharply criticized Israel’s handling of its international image, arguing that the country is unwilling to take even basic steps that could improve its standing abroad and has failed to devote sufficient resources to its Foreign Ministry.
Sherman singled out National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, saying his presence in the government represented an “existential risk” to Israel, and warned that Israel could not survive without friends around the world. Sherman has criticized Ben Gvir before, including ahead of Israel’s 2022 election, when he urged Israeli political leaders to ostracize politicians he described as extremists and warned that they could damage U.S.-Israel relations.
Sherman also addressed violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank. He argued that dismissing international criticism simply because Israelis believe it is unjustified reflects a misunderstanding of Jewish history, and said such incidents would continue damaging support for Israel unless the government bodies responsible for addressing them were led by officials committed to stopping the violence.
From +51 to -16 in eight years
The CNN segment Sherman highlighted aired July 24 and featured chief data analyst Harry Enten reviewing polls from Ipsos, Fox News, Marquette University Law School and the Pew Research Center. In every survey cited, Israel’s net favorability was negative: minus 10 points in Ipsos, minus 11 in Fox, about minus 20 in Marquette and minus 23 in Pew.
Enten said the shift was no longer confined to Democratic voters. “We’re not just talking about the Democratic base anymore,” he said. “We’re talking about the general electorate as well.”
The historical comparison was even more striking. According to the polling average presented by CNN, Israel had a net favorability rating of about plus 51 points at the comparable point in President Donald Trump’s first term in 2018. By July 2026, the figure stood at roughly minus 16, a 67-point swing over eight years.
“Israel used to be a consensus issue in American politics, and that was a pro-Israeli position,” Enten said. The shift, he added, was appearing “poll after poll after poll.”
The 67-point figure represents a change in net favorability, not a 67% decline. Net favorability measures the difference between the share of respondents expressing a favorable view and the share expressing an unfavorable one.
Pew’s March 23-29 survey found that 60% of U.S. adults held an unfavorable view of Israel, compared with 37% who viewed it favorably. In spring 2022, the balance had been reversed, with 55% favorable and 42% unfavorable.
Marquette University Law School recorded a similar trend. Its April survey found 54% of U.S. adults viewed Israel unfavorably and 33% favorably. By late July, favorable views had slipped to 31%, while 55% held an unfavorable opinion.
Growing pressure over US military aid
The CNN segment also pointed to mounting opposition to U.S. military assistance for Israel. Enten cited Washington Post-Ipsos polling in which 55% of Americans said Washington should reduce or end military aid, including 51% of respondents without college degrees and 62% of college graduates.
For Sherman, the numbers carry particular significance because of his political record. He has served in Congress for nearly three decades, is a senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and has long been associated with congressional efforts to strengthen ties with Israel. His official House biography describes him as the committee’s second-ranked Democrat and lists the Israel Allies Caucus among his caucus memberships.
Sherman has repeatedly backed the U.S.-Israel alliance and argued that support for Israel must remain bipartisan. His decision to publicly warn Israelis about the erosion of American support therefore represents a notable intervention from a lawmaker who has spent much of his career defending the relationship.
